The command to return to 'these thy cities' is not metaphorical but refers to specific urban centers where covenant life could be renewed.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 39:11-12 teaches that those who have wandered from the path can return, but the return requires effort and commitment — 'the Lord cannot walk in crooked paths.' The Book of Mormon repeatedly emphasizes that divine help enables but does not replace human striving in the path of return. Helaman 15:7-9 describes the repentance and return of the Nephites, emphasizing the preparation and rebuilding necessary for restoration.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 25:7-10 contains the command to Emma Smith to 'receive the counsel of him who has called thee.' The principle of clear waymarks — established through prophetic voice and revealed instruction — runs through LDS restoration theology. The restoration movement itself can be understood as establishing waymarks for the return of God's people to full covenant relationship.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple represents the ultimate destination toward which all waymarks point. The temple endowment itself is structured as a journey homeward — passing through ordinances that mark the way from fallen mortality to celestial presence. The ritual progression through the temple enacts Jeremiah's command: the heart is fixed on the pathway, waymarks are passed, and the journey culminates in the house of the Lord.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ is the ultimate waymark — 'I am the way, the truth, and the life' (John 14:6). In the Incarnation, God marks out the path of return by becoming the path Himself. The road that Israel is commanded to travel in Jeremiah 31:21 finds its fulfillment in the path to the Cross and through the Resurrection — the way home passes through Christ. Additionally, the marker stones of verse 21 prefigure the 'living stones' (1 Peter 2:5) that form the Church, the household of faith that guides believers toward their restoration home.
commentary.application: This verse moves the reader from the comfort of divine love (verse 20) into active participation in restoration. The question it poses is: What waymarks are you setting? What concrete steps mark your path toward covenant return and renewal? In modern covenantal life, this might mean: establishing regular family prayer and scripture study as waymarks in spiritual discipline; creating consistent patterns of sacrament participation and temple attendance as markers along the path; speaking clearly about faith commitments to guide others and oneself. The verse also invites examination of the 'road by which you went' into compromise or distance — and to use that same road, retraced, as the path home. This is deeply practical: restoration is not instantaneous teleportation but a deliberate journey in which you participate by your choices. The command to 'set thine heart toward the highway' is a command to psychological and spiritual alignment: to stop being divided in intention and to direct the whole self toward covenant return. For those in estrangement from faith, this verse offers the possibility that the very experience of distance has etched the path of return into memory and heart.

text_kjv: How long wilt thou go about, O thou backsliding daughter? for the LORD hath created a new thing in the earth, A woman shall compass a man.

commentary.narrative: Verse 22 is among the most enigmatic in Jeremiah and has generated centuries of interpretive debate. The opening question — 'How long wilt thou go about, O thou backsliding daughter?' — expresses exasperation with Israel's hesitation and vacillation. The 'backsliding daughter' (bat shobevah) is not a new appellation; it echoes Jeremiah's frequent designation of Israel as faithless and wayward. But now, in the midst of the oracle of restoration, God expresses impatience: How long will you waver? The expectation is that Ephraim/Israel should respond to the call of verses 20-21 with immediacy. The hesitation suggests the depth of psychological and spiritual damage exile has inflicted — even when invited home by God's own voice, the wounded soul holds back. Yet God's response is not further judgment but a declaration of unprecedented action: 'the LORD hath created a new thing in the earth.'
commentary.narrative_continued: The phrase 'created a new thing' (bara chadashah) employs the verb bara, which in Hebrew designates creation that is entirely new, without precedent — divine action that brings into being what did not exist before. This is the language of Genesis 1:1, where God bara the heavens and the earth. God is not promising to repair, restore, or rebuild but to create something genuinely new. What this new thing is remains the central interpretive challenge. The statement 'A woman shall compass a man' (neqevah tesovev gaver) is the verse's most disputed phrase. The verb sovev can mean 'to surround, encircle, compass, go around' — it is the verb used when armies besiege a city. It can also mean 'to turn around, revolve, court, woo.' The substantives neqevah (woman, female) and gaver (man, warrior, strength) are clear in denotation but wide open in their application.
commentary.narrative_continued_2: The TCR rendering notes three major interpretive trajectories: (1) Israel (the faithless woman) will return to court/embrace God (the man/warrior) — a reversal of the normal pattern where the man is the active suitor; (2) a woman will protect a warrior — signaling a complete reversal of gender roles as a marker of a new eschatological era; (3) a reference to restored fertility and the normal cycles of male and female in a population returned from exile. Each interpretation attempts to make sense of what 'new thing' God has created. What is certain is that the verse announces something without parallel — some reversal or renewal that was not previously possible. The uncertainty is not a weakness of the text but a feature: it invites readers to hold multiple layers of meaning simultaneously and to understand that God's restoration transcends single categories or interpretations.

word_study.meaning: Chamaq in the Hithpael form (reflexive) suggests 'to turn oneself about, to waver, to hesitate, to go this way and that.' The root conveys indecision and lack of commitment — the kind of aimless wandering that characterizes those who have not yet made the turn back to covenant.
word_study.significance: The feminine singular form addresses Israel directly and personally. The hesitation is not primarily about external obstacles but about internal will — Israel is vacillating, going back and forth instead of fixing her heart on the highway as commanded in verse 21.

word_study.meaning: Bat means 'daughter'; shobevah (from shuv) is 'turning, turning away, backsliding' — literally, 'the daughter who turns.' The designation carries both accusation and endearment: she is still addressed as 'daughter,' even while being named for her infidelity.
word_study.significance: The maintenance of the filial relationship despite the accusation mirrors the paradox of verses 20-21: judgment and love coexist. God can call Israel backsliding and still call her daughter, because the relationship is not based on Israel's faithfulness but on God's covenantal commitment.

word_study.meaning: Bara is the verb of creation ex nihilo — bringing into being what did not previously exist. Chadashah means 'new, renewed, unprecedented.' The phrase indicates divine action that transcends ordinary restoration; it is creation in the fullest sense.
word_study.significance: This word choice elevates the promise beyond human repair or restoration. God is not simply undoing the exile but creating conditions and realities that have no precedent. In LDS theology, this language parallels the 'new and everlasting covenant' — the restoration of eternal truths in new form.

word_study.meaning: Neqevah ('woman, female') is the feminine form relating to biological sex; tesovev (from svv, 'to turn around, surround, encompass, court') is the feminine form of a verb that can mean 'to encircle' (as in siege), 'to rotate,' or in romantic contexts, 'to court, woo'; gaver ('man, warrior, strength') refers to an adult male, often in his capacity as warrior or leader. The phrase structure suggests the woman acts and the man is the object of the action, reversing typical patterns.
word_study.significance: The ambiguity is not a flaw but a theological richness. The verse may be saying that Israel (personified as a woman) will embrace God (the warrior, the man of strength). Or it may be saying that in the new creation, roles will be fundamentally reconfigured. Or it may simply mean that new fertility and normal male-female relationships will flourish. Each reading opens different theological possibilities.

cross_references.connection: God declares 'Behold, I will do a new thing; now it shall spring forth; shall ye not know it?' — parallel language of unprecedented divine action that transcends past categories.
The vision of the new heaven and new earth where God 'shall wipe away all tears' and makes 'all things new' — the eschatalogical fulfillment of Jeremiah's promise of God creating a new thing.
God's courtship of Israel in the wilderness, speaking tenderly to her and restoring her as a bride — parallel imagery of the reversal of exile into intimate covenant renewal.
Describes the vision given to Joseph Smith and Sidney Rigdon of the kingdom of God in the heavens — a 'new thing' revealed in the Restoration that was not seen 'from the foundation of the world.'

commentary.historical_context: The verse's historical setting is the late 7th or early 6th century BCE, when the reality of northern Israel's exile (over a century past) seemed permanent, and Judah faced its own imminent doom. Jeremiah's promise of creating something 'new' would have seemed impossible to those shaped by centuries of loss. In ancient Near Eastern political thought, restoration of an exiled population was understood as extraordinary, often requiring divine intervention. The language of a 'new thing' reflects the astonishment that God could create anything genuinely novel — the restoration was not simply returning to the status quo ante but the creation of something previously unimaginable. The gender-reversal language in 'a woman shall compass a man' may also reflect ancient Near Eastern marriage customs, where the male was typically the active suitor and the woman was courted. If Jeremiah is using this reversal as a figure for Israel's new posture toward God, he is suggesting that in the renewed relationship, Israel will actively seek and embrace God with the intensity a bride brings to courtship.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon opens with Nephi's vision of things 'not yet come to pass' (1 Nephi 1:4-5) — an echo of Jeremiah's 'new thing' language. The entire Restoration movement is presented as the 'new thing' God creates in the latter days — not merely restoration of old truths but the restoration of full covenantal relationship in new form. Alma 41:8-9 teaches that restoration is not simply returning to previous state but implies 'advancement in virtue and wisdom' — the new thing transcends the old.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 76 is Joseph Smith's vision of the new heaven and new earth — the 'new thing' God has created. Doctrine and Covenants 27:13-14 references the 'new and everlasting covenant' — a phrase that echoes this Jeremianic language of newness. The Restoration itself is presented as God's 'new thing' in the latter days.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple ordinances represent the 'new thing' God has created for covenant renewal and progression. The endowment teaches the creation of new covenantal relationships and the transformation of human nature through ordinance — the making of something genuinely new within the individual soul.

commentary.christological_typology: The 'new thing' God creates in Jeremiah 31:22 finds its ultimate fulfillment in Christ and the new covenant. The Incarnation is the ultimate 'new thing' — God creates in human history something unprecedented, the union of divine and human nature. The reversal of the typical pattern (where the warrior/man courts the woman) finds a parallel in Christ's role as both the Bridegroom (active, initiating) and as the one who becomes vulnerable, dependent, 'compassable' by His people. The language of 'woman shall compass a man' ultimately describes the Church (the Bride) embracing Christ (the Groom) and Christ embracing the Church — a mutuality that is new in creation.
commentary.application: For modern readers, verse 22 offers both invitation and challenge. The invitation: God is not bound by what has always been. The patterns that hold you captive — whether inherited trauma, generational sin, or circumstances that seem immutable — are not the final word. God 'creates new things' and can create something genuinely novel in your life. The challenge: the verse addresses hesitation — 'How long wilt thou go about?' — calling out the wavering of those who have been invited home but who linger, doubting whether return is truly possible or whether they can truly be restored. The verse demands a decision: Will you move toward the new thing God is creating, or will you continue to waver? Practically, this might mean: accepting that your past does not determine your future, that God can create new possibilities in relationships, in personal growth, in spiritual capacity. It means moving from the comfort of what is known (even if broken) into the territory of God's new creation — which requires faith and risk. For those in estrangement, verse 22 suggests that the return will not be simply replication of the previous relationship but something genuinely transformed — a new creation that honors the past but transcends it.

text_kjv: Thus saith the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel; As yet they shall use this speech in the land of Judah and in the cities thereof, when I shall bring again their captivity; The LORD bless thee, O habitation of justice, and mountain of holiness.

commentary.narrative: The oracle now shifts from northern Israel (Ephraim) to southern Israel (Judah). Verses 23-24 promise restoration for Judah specifically, while maintaining the overarching restoration theme that encompasses both divisions of what was once a single people. The introduction 'Thus saith the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel' frames this as direct prophetic utterance, carrying the full authority of God's covenantal commitment. The verb phrase 'As yet they shall use this speech' (od yomru et hadavar hazeh) employs a temporal indicator — 'yet,' 'still' — that emphasizes continuity: though exile and separation seem absolute, a time will come when this speech is heard again in Judah's cities. The phrase 'when I shall bring again their captivity' (beshubi et shevutam) uses the same root shuv that has appeared throughout the chapter (return, repentance, restoration). The causative form 'I shall bring again' emphasizes divine agency: this is not spontaneous return but God-directed reversal.
commentary.narrative_continued: The speech that will be 'used' again is the blessing: 'The LORD bless thee, O habitation of justice, and mountain of holiness.' This appears to be a blessing formula — the kind of blessing pronounced over the land and people by priests or leaders in the pre-exile period. The TCR rendering translates neveh tsedeq as 'pasture of righteousness' rather than 'habitation of justice,' which enriches the image: Jerusalem is not merely a place where justice is administered but a place where righteousness 'pastures' — where it lives, grazes, flourishes naturally as if in a fertile meadow. Coupled with 'mountain of holiness' (har haqqodesh), this double image portrays Jerusalem as a place where both moral rectitude and sacred presence are indigenous to the landscape itself. The promise is that this blessing formula — heard perhaps in the temple during feast days and special occasions — will be spoken again after the exile.
commentary.narrative_continued_2: The verse promises not only physical return but the recovery of covenant language and ritual practice. Blessing formulas are not mere words; they are the speech-act by which community affirms its relationship to God and to place. The promise that 'they shall use this speech' means that Judah will reclaim not just geography but the language of covenant, the spoken affirmation of belonging to God and to the land given by God. This signals the restoration of religious life — not in isolation but integrated with settlement, agriculture, and civic life ('in the land of Judah and in the cities thereof'). The blessing will be used 'in the land and in the cities' — indicating that restoration is comprehensive, covering both rural areas and urban centers.

word_study.term_original: יֹאמְרוּ אֶת־הַדָּבָר הַזֶּה (yomru et hadavar hazeh)
word_study.meaning: Amar means 'to speak, say, use words'; davar is 'word, speech, matter, thing'; hazeh is 'this.' The phrase specifically indicates the speaking/use of particular words — not just speaking in general but using the specific blessing formula that follows.
word_study.significance: This emphasizes that restoration includes the recovery of covenant language. The language we speak shapes our reality and our identity. The promise that Judah will 'use this speech' again means Judah will reclaim the vocabulary of faith and blessing.

word_study.meaning: Shubi is the causative form of shuv ('I will cause to return'); shevut is 'captivity, exile, the state of being carried away.' The phrase literally means 'cause the captivity to return' — a wordplay where the reversal of exile is expressed through the verb for return.
word_study.significance: This is the verb form used in prayers and liturgy throughout the exile period ('Restore our fortunes, O Lord'). The promise is that God will actively reverse the exile, not gradually but decisively.

word_study.meaning: Neveh can mean 'dwelling, habitation, pasture, encampment' — a place where things naturally reside or where creatures find sustenance. Tsedeq is 'righteousness, justice, moral rectitude.' The phrase suggests that righteousness is not imposed on Jerusalem from outside but is the natural 'pasture' — the native condition — of the place.
word_study.significance: The image transforms Jerusalem from a political center into an ethical and spiritual reality. The city is not merely just in policy but just in nature — justice 'grazes' there as naturally as sheep in a meadow. This reflects the ideal vision of Jerusalem as the place where God's kingdom is most fully expressed.

word_study.meaning: Har is 'mountain'; qodesh is 'holiness, sacred, set apart for God.' The phrase designates Mount Zion, where the temple stood, as the sacred mountain — the place where heaven and earth intersect, where God's presence is most concentrated.
word_study.significance: In ancient Near Eastern cosmology, sacred mountains were understood as cosmic centers — points where the divine realm overlapped with the human. Mount Zion, as the 'mountain of holiness,' is not merely a geographic location but a theological reality: it is the axis mundi around which restored Jerusalem orients itself.

cross_references.connection: A prayer for Jerusalem's peace and prosperity, ending with 'May the LORD bless thee' — the same blessing formula invoked in Jeremiah 31:23 as the speech that will be heard again.
God promises to make Zion's wilderness like Eden, her desert like the garden of the Lord — parallel imagery of Jerusalem transformed into a place of natural righteousness and flourishing.

The mountain of the Lord's house is established and to it all nations shall flow, 'and he will teach us of his ways' — the same vision of Jerusalem as the center from which righteousness and justice emanate.
Christ speaks of the New Jerusalem and its blessings — echoing the language of Jeremiah's promise of a Jerusalem where righteousness and holiness are foundational rather than aspirational.
The vision of the holy city, New Jerusalem, coming down from God out of heaven — the ultimate fulfillment of Jeremiah's promise of a restored Jerusalem as the 'mountain of holiness.'

commentary.historical_context: Judah was not exiled as suddenly or completely as northern Israel had been. The Babylonian exile (586-538 BCE) was severe but not total: some population remained, the temple was eventually rebuilt, and the exile lasted 'only' about fifty years in its most acute phase. By the late exilic or early post-exilic period, when Jeremiah 31:23-24 was likely written or compiled, the question was not whether return would occur but how quickly and how completely. The blessing formula 'The LORD bless thee, O habitation of justice, and mountain of holiness' would have been familiar to the exilic audience from pre-exile temple liturgy. The promise that this blessing would be used again in Judah's cities was a promise of the recovery not just of territory but of religious practice and communal identity. Ancient Near Eastern sources indicate that the return from Babylonian exile was a gradual, partial process — some returned, others remained; the temple was rebuilt but on a smaller scale than before. Jeremiah's oracle, however, promises a restoration that is complete and comprehensive, marked by the recovery of the full liturgical and covenantal language.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The promise that covenant language will be restored parallels 2 Nephi 29:3-14, where God promises that His word will go forth in many forms — the Book of Mormon, the Bible, the words of Joseph Smith. The Restoration includes not just physical gathering but the recovery of the full language of God's covenant.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 29:11 speaks of God restoring all things in the latter days — including the restoration of language, knowledge, and the full understanding of God's ways. Doctrine and Covenants 45:59-60 speaks of the Lord coming to His holy temple (the celestial room) and there blessing His people — the promise of Jeremiah 31:23 finding fulfillment in LDS temple theology.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The blessing formula is the language of the temple — the place where righteousness and holiness are most concentrated. The promise that covenant language will be restored is the promise that the temple and its ordinances will be restored. In LDS temple theology, the blessing given at the end of the endowment embodies this same pattern: God blesses the people, affirming their identity as covenant bearers and their connection to the sacred mountain (Zion).

commentary.christological_typology: Christ is the fulfillment of both the 'habitation of justice' and the 'mountain of holiness.' In the Incarnation, Christ becomes the place where God's justice and holiness dwell in perfect unity. The Church, as the body of Christ, becomes that 'habitation of justice' — the place where righteousness is meant to flourish. In Revelation's vision of the New Jerusalem descending from God, the fullest realization of Jeremiah's prophecy is achieved: a city where justice and holiness are not temporary achievements but eternal conditions, where the blessing formula 'the LORD bless thee' is eternally operative.
commentary.application: Verse 23 invites modern readers to consider what covenant language marks their community and their lives. Are the blessings of God actively spoken and affirmed in your family, your congregation, your relationships? The promise that Judah will 'use this speech' suggests that restoration is not a private experience but a communal one, marked by the public, spoken affirmation of blessing and covenant. The verse also poses the question: What does righteousness look like as the natural condition of a place — not imposed from outside but embedded in the very nature of the community? How might your family, your ward, your community become a 'habitation of justice'? Practically, this might mean: regularly blessing your family and your home; creating spaces where righteousness is the expected and natural mode of interaction; speaking the language of God's covenant with clarity and conviction; understanding that restoration includes the recovery of the speech-acts by which we affirm identity and belonging. For those seeking to build Zion — whether locally in stakes and wards or in the ultimate sense of the New Jerusalem — this verse reminds us that Zion is built not just through correct policies or structures but through the recovery and constant use of covenant language that binds people to God and to each other.

text_kjv: And there shall dwell in Judah itself, and in all the cities thereof together, husbandmen, and they that go forth with flocks.

commentary.narrative: The final verse of this section of the restoration oracle shifts from liturgical language to concrete, economic detail. Where verse 23 promised the recovery of blessing formulas and covenant speech, verse 24 promises the return of the material conditions of normal life: agriculture and pastoralism. The phrase 'there shall dwell in Judah itself, and in all the cities thereof together' (veyashevu bah Yehudah ve'kol 'arav yachdav) emphasizes that restoration is comprehensive and simultaneous — not a slow trickle of return but a collective re-population. 'Together' (yachdav) suggests unity and synchronicity; the land will be filled, cities will be inhabited, the wilderness will be claimed once again. The vision includes two primary modes of economic activity: 'husbandmen' (ikkarim, farmers, plowmen) and 'they that go forth with flocks' (noseu ba'ever, those who move about with flocks, pastoral peoples).
commentary.narrative_continued: The inclusion of both settled agriculture and pastoral nomadism is theologically significant. These were often portrayed as incompatible, even conflicting ways of life in ancient Near Eastern contexts — the tensions between farming societies and pastoral peoples run throughout the Bible (consider Cain and Abel, Esau and Jacob). The promise that both can dwell 'together' in restored Judah signals the transcendence of old divisions. The vision is not of one mode of life displacing another but of coexistence and complementarity. This reflects the ideal vision of Israel: diverse in livelihood but unified in covenant. The verse is spare in language, offering no elaborate promise, no ecstatic visionary language. Instead, it grounds restoration in the mundane reality of daily work — farmers in the fields, shepherds moving with their flocks. Restoration is not a transcendent escape from material reality but the sanctification of ordinary, necessary work.
commentary.narrative_continued_2: The progression from verse 23 to 24 mirrors the progression throughout Jeremiah 31: from the inner emotional and spiritual transformation (verses 19-20) to the external, material conditions of return (verses 21-24). God's restoration is holistic — it encompasses the whole person in the whole society. The blessings spoken in verse 23 are not merely spiritual affirmations but have material consequence: they result in the dwell of husbandmen and shepherds, the economic vitality of the land, the restoration of the productive cycles that were interrupted by exile. This is counter to much modern religious thought that separates spiritual blessing from material flourishing. In Jeremiah's vision, they are inseparable: a restored people is a people who work, produce, settle, and flourish in the land.

word_study.meaning: Yashav means 'to sit, dwell, abide, settle' — it is the verb of permanent, stable habitation, not temporary presence. The perfect form indicates the action as completed or assured, moving from future promise to present reality.
word_study.significance: For a people in exile, the promise of yeshivah (dwelling) is the promise of home — not visiting the land but being rooted in it. In Latter-day Saint covenant language, this echoes the promised 'inheritance' in Zion — a place of permanent belonging.

word_study.meaning: From iker, meaning 'to work, to till'; ikkarim are farmers, plowmen, those who work the soil. The term emphasizes labor and the cultivation of the earth as a fundamental human activity.
word_study.significance: The inclusion of farmers in the restoration vision affirms that physical labor and agricultural work are essential to human flourishing. This reflects the biblical principle established in Genesis 2:15 that humans are created to 'dress and keep the garden' — work is not a curse but a calling.

word_study.meaning: Nasa means 'to journey, to move, to travel'; eder is 'flock, herd.' The phrase describes the pastoral life of shepherds who move with their herds in search of pasture — not itinerant in the sense of being without purpose, but mobile in service of sustaining flocks.
word_study.significance: The inclusion of pastoral peoples alongside settled farmers acknowledges that there are multiple valid forms of livelihood within the covenantal community. This reflects the reality that ancient Israel included both farmers and shepherds, and the promise is that both will have a place in restored Israel.

word_study.meaning: From yahad, 'to be one, to unite'; yachdav means 'together, as one, in union.' The adverb emphasizes simultaneity and unity of action.
word_study.significance: The promise is not merely that farmers and shepherds will return but that they will return together, dwelling in the same land and cities in harmony. This resonates with the covenantal ideal of klal Yisrael — the whole of Israel as a unified people despite internal diversity.

cross_references.connection: Humans are created to 'dress and keep the garden' — the foundational affirmation that work and agricultural cultivation are part of the divine order, not a curse.
'The meek shall inherit the earth; and shall delight themselves in the abundance of peace' — the promise of restored Israel dwelling in peace and productive security.

Vision of the new heavens and new earth where 'they shall build houses, and inhabit them; and they shall plant vineyards, and eat the fruit of them' — parallel imagery of restoration that includes productive labor and material flourishing.

The law of consecration in the Kirtland era specifies that land should be given to the poor 'that every man may improve' and 'beautify' his inheritance — echoing the principle that restored Israel includes the opportunity to work and develop the land.
The Lamanites who repent 'buried their weapons of war, for peace' and returned to farming — showing that restoration includes the transition from warfare to productive, peaceful labor.

commentary.historical_context: The post-exilic restoration of Judah (after 538 BCE, following the Persian edict of Cyrus) involved the actual return of exiled peoples to their land and the rebuilding of infrastructure. Archaeological and textual evidence indicates that the early post-exilic period was a time of gradual repopulation and reconstruction — not an immediate explosion of settlement but a slow rebuilding process. The farming economy was dependent on established systems: field terraces, storage facilities, predictable water sources. The pastoral economy required access to grazing lands and established migration routes. The promise in Jeremiah 31:24 that both modes of life would flourish together reflected the ideological vision of what restored Judah could be — a people economically diverse but spiritually unified. The historical reality was more complex: there were tensions between those who had remained in the land and those returning from exile; landholdings and property rights had to be renegotiated; the balance between agricultural and pastoral economies had to be reestablished. Yet the prophetic vision offered hope that these practical challenges could be overcome and that genuine restoration — not merely return but flourishing — was possible.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon repeatedly portrays restored peoples engaged in productive labor — Alma's people in Alma 37:7-9 return to the land and 'till the ground' and 'tend their flocks.' The principle that restoration includes the opportunity to work the land and sustain oneself through productive labor runs through the Nephite historical narrative.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 42:42-44 emphasizes that 'he who keeps the commandments, the Lord is bound; but he who keepeth not his commandments is not bound' — and among the commandments is the responsibility to improve and beautify one's inheritance. Doctrine and Covenants 136:28-29, given during the westward exodus, promises that the Saints will have 'plenty' as they move forward — the same promise of material sustenance accompanying spiritual covenant.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple endowment teaches that humans are created to 'multiply and replenish the earth' and to have 'dominion' over the land (Genesis 1:28-29). The promise of restoration in verse 24 — of farmers and shepherds dwelling in the land — is the fulfillment of this primordial covenant to be caretakers of creation.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ is portrayed in the Gospels as the good shepherd (John 10:11-14), identifying Himself with the pastoral tradition. His ministry includes attention to both material and spiritual needs — He feeds the five thousand, He heals the sick, He affirms that 'man shall not live by bread alone.' In Revelation, Christ is the shepherd of the redeemed multitude (Revelation 7:17), and the ultimate restoration vision includes a people who 'dwell' in the presence of God in a land renewed and restored. The promise of verse 24 finds fulfillment in the vision of Christ's kingdom where both the spiritual and the material are redeemed.
commentary.application: Verse 24 grounds the restoration promise in the concrete reality of work, livelihood, and material well-being. For modern readers, this offers a corrective to purely spiritual conceptions of restoration: true redemption includes the restoration of the capacity to work, to produce, to sustain oneself and one's family. In the context of Latter-day Saint covenant practice, this connects directly to the principle of self-reliance — the capacity to support oneself and one's household is not merely economic necessity but a spiritual principle connected to dignity and participation in God's creative work. The verse also suggests that different forms of contribution — farming and shepherding, settled and mobile, various professions and vocations — all have a place in the restored community. The promise 'together' suggests that diversity of livelihood need not mean conflict; rather, the covenantal community can hold multiple vocations and ways of life in unity. Practically, this might mean: taking seriously the restoration of your capacity to work and contribute; viewing your labor not merely as survival but as participation in God's creative purposes; honoring the various forms of work and livelihood within your community; seeking to create economic conditions where all can engage in productive, dignified labor. For those in economic hardship or displacement, verse 24 offers the promise that restoration is possible — not immediately, not without effort, but surely. The husbandmen will dwell again in Judah; the shepherds will go forth with their flocks.

text_kjv: For I have satiated the weary soul, and I have replenished every sorrowful soul.

commentary.narrative: After the vision of Rachel's weeping and the promise of her children's return (verses 15-17), God now speaks directly to the condition of the exiles themselves. This verse addresses not just restoration of territory, but restoration of the human person—the inner exhaustion that exile produces. The exiled people are not merely geographically displaced; they are emotionally, spiritually, and psychologically depleted. Jeremiah uses the word nephesh ('soul,' 'life,' 'being') twice to emphasize the wholeness of the person affected. The promise is not abstract but visceral: God will satisfy the weary and fill those who languish. The Hebrew verb hir'veti (from ravah, 'to drink deeply, to water abundantly') carries the image of irrigation—water poured into parched ground. This is how restoration begins: not with new political arrangements, but with the renewal of life itself within the people.

word_study.meaning: exhausted, faint, weary; describes a state of depletion from hard labor or suffering
word_study.significance: The exile was not merely a loss of land but a wearing away of the soul. The term suggests the long, grinding fatigue of captivity—not a dramatic moment of crisis but the slow erosion of hope and strength. God promises to address this specific condition.

word_study.meaning: to grieve, to sorrow, to languish; describes emotional pain and the weakening that comes with grief
word_study.significance: The parallel to 'weary' shows that spiritual and emotional depletion are central to the exile experience. Da'av describes not just sadness but the way sorrow physically weakens a person. The restoration promise addresses this inner breaking.

word_study.meaning: to fill, to be full, to complete; in this context, to fill emptiness with fullness
word_study.significance: This verb is key to understanding God's restorative work. Where exile created emptiness—empty homes, empty fields, empty hearts—God now acts to fill that void. The Covenant Rendering notes that milleti ('I will fill') depicts God 'pouring fullness into emptiness—the opposite of the famine and deprivation of exile.'

cross_references.connection: God's commission includes not only 'to pluck up, to break down' but also 'to build and to plant'—what He tears down in judgment, He rebuilds in restoration. This verse marks the beginning of that building phase.

Isaiah similarly promises that God 'fainteth not, neither is weary' and gives 'power to the faint' and 'strength to them that have no might'—the same theme of divine power addressing human exhaustion.
The image of God filling and satisfying ('my cup runneth over') echoes this promise of complete satisfaction beyond the exile's deprivation.

In the vision of the redemption of the dead, Joseph Smith records how Christ visited those in captivity and brought them the gospel of light and truth—a spiritual parallel to Jeremiah's promise of material and spiritual restoration.

commentary.historical_context: The Babylonian exile (586 BCE onward) created conditions of profound demoralization. Archaeological evidence and cuneiform records show that exiled populations suffered not only displacement but loss of social status, disruption of family systems, and economic marginalization. The psychological toll of exile—the loss of homeland, temple access, and cultural continuity—was as debilitating as any physical hardship. When Jeremiah speaks of satisfying the weary and filling the languishing, he addresses the specific crisis of morale that threatened to make the exile permanent in the hearts of the people. This verse meets them where they actually are: not asking for political solutions, but for inner renewal.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 32 uses the metaphor of planting a seed in the heart and allowing it to grow and become fruit-bearing—a spiritual parallel to the restoration described here. Just as the exiles need their spiritual and emotional 'soil' renewed, Alma teaches that faith begins as something small and needs to be carefully tended and nourished.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 29:8 promises that after judgment, the earth and its inhabitants will be 'renewed and made whole.' This is the principle Jeremiah articulates: restoration is not merely returning to the status quo ante, but making the people whole again—soul, spirit, and body.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: In temple worship, the principle of renewal and sanctification parallels this verse. As the temple offers restoration of broken covenants and renewal of spirit to individual members, so God offers collective restoration to His people in exile.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ in His ministry described Himself as one who came to heal the broken-hearted and bind up their wounds (Luke 4:18, citing Isaiah 61:1). The promise of satisfying the weary and filling the languishing prefigures Christ's restorative work, particularly His offer of living water (John 4:14) that permanently quenches spiritual thirst and His promise of rest to the heavy-laden (Matthew 11:28).
commentary.application: Modern covenant members facing exhaustion—whether from spiritual trials, loss, or the accumulated weight of mortality—can recognize in this verse that God's first response to depletion is not to demand more effort, but to satisfy and fill. The promise teaches that restoration begins with the renewal of the inner person. When approaching scripture study, temple worship, or prayer during seasons of weariness, members can claim this promise: God sees the specific condition of exhaustion and commits Himself to filling what exile (whether literal or spiritual) has emptied.

text_kjv: Upon this I awaked, and beheld; and my sleep was sweet unto me.

commentary.narrative: This verse breaks the narrative to reveal something crucial about how Jeremiah received these restoration oracles: they came to him as a dream or night vision. The prophet awakens refreshed, his sleep having been pleasant—a striking contrast to the recurring nightmares and visions of judgment that dominate so much of Jeremiah's prophetic experience. The word translated 'awoke' (hiqitzoti) suggests not merely waking, but becoming alert or watching—the prophet transitions from the dream-state into consciousness still holding the vision clearly. What makes this moment remarkable is the emotional tenor: Jeremiah slept well. Throughout the book, his calling has brought him insomnia, inner torment, and the psychological burden of announcing judgment. But the restoration oracles are so welcome, so different from his usual burden, that they transform even his sleep into something pleasant. This is a rare moment where the prophet's inner state reflects peace rather than anguish. The Covenant Rendering notes that this verse presents 'an enigmatic' quality—it may be Jeremiah's way of authenticating these restoration promises as genuinely divine, coming through the sacred medium of dream-vision, or it may reflect the prophet's own psychological transformation: at last, he has something joyful to proclaim.

word_study.meaning: to awake, to rouse oneself, to be alert; carries overtones of watchfulness and heightened awareness
word_study.significance: This is not mere waking from sleep, but awakening to something. In the prophetic context, it suggests the transition from receiving revelation (in dream) to conscious awareness of what was received. Jeremiah doesn't groggily emerge; he awakes and is alert to what the vision has shown him.

word_study.meaning: to see, to look, to perceive; in prophetic contexts often means to perceive divine truth
word_study.significance: The prophet not only awakes but actively looks around—perhaps at the changed reality the vision has shown him, or simply absorbing the fullness of what he has witnessed. The verb emphasizes conscious perception and testimony.

word_study.meaning: pleasant, sweet, delightful; describes something that is agreeable and satisfying to the senses or spirit
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering notes that this word appears elsewhere to describe pleasant things—and its use here to modify the prophet's sleep is deeply significant. For Jeremiah, whose entire calling has been to announce devastation, a pleasant sleep is itself a sign of divine grace. The restoration oracles have brought him peace even at night.

cross_references.connection: The vision of the almond branch (shaqed) establishes the pattern of God communicating His purposes through night visions—'I will watch (shoqed) over my word to perform it.' This verse continues that pattern.
Daniel receives a troubling dream; Jeremiah receives a comforting one. Both prophets experience revelation through sleep-visions, but with different emotional content reflecting different messages.
Lehi receives his great vision while sleeping and awakens to recount it to his family—the same pattern of night-vision followed by awakening and testimony.

Joseph Smith and Sidney Rigdon were 'caught up' in vision and later recalled and recorded it—describing visions received while in an altered state that are vividly remembered upon return to normal consciousness.

commentary.historical_context: In ancient Near Eastern dream interpretation, dreams were understood as one of the primary channels of divine communication. The Bible distinguishes between false dreams (often from other spiritual sources) and true dreams from God. For a prophet like Jeremiah, who has spent his ministry announcing destruction and suffering rejection, the experience of receiving restoration oracles in a dream—and then experiencing peaceful sleep—would have been both authenticating and transformative. The dream-vision tradition in the ancient Near East was well-established; Egyptian, Hittite, and Mesopotamian literature all record royal and priestly dreams as vehicles for divine instruction. The fact that Jeremiah awakens with clear memory and finds his sleep pleasant suggests a dream of divine origin (not a tormented nightmare from his own anxieties).

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Lehi, Nephi, and others in the Book of Mormon receive crucial guidance through dreams and visions (1 Nephi 8; 2 Nephi 4:25). Like Jeremiah, these prophets receive vision content that redirects their understanding and gives them hope. The pattern suggests that divine mercy often comes to us when our conscious minds are at rest—in dream, vision, and meditation—when the anxieties of the day do not crowd out the still, small voice.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 45:58-59 speaks of the elect hearing Christ's voice in dreams and visions. Joseph Smith's First Vision itself came while he was in a state of spiritual seeking, and many of his revelations came through visions and revelatory experiences that involved a heightened spiritual state distinct from ordinary consciousness.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The dream-vision experience parallels the temple setting, where members engage in a mode of perception and revelation distinct from the ordinary world. Both create a 'thin place' where heaven and earth draw near, and ordinary consciousness is suspended to permit revelation.

commentary.christological_typology: The Gospels record that divine revelation came to figures around Jesus in dreams—Joseph was warned to flee to Egypt (Matthew 2:13), the Magi were directed in their journey (Matthew 2:12). The pattern of divine truth coming through dream-vision is part of the scriptural testimony that God communicates through multiple modes. Christ's resurrection appearances (which have a visionary quality) also represent a mode of revelation beyond ordinary sight. Jeremiah's pleasant dream prefigures the comfort and peace that knowing Christ brings.
commentary.application: For modern members, this verse invites reflection on the role of dreams, meditation, and spiritual seeking in receiving divine guidance. While not all dreams are prophetic, the verse suggests that God can reach us in states of consciousness beyond our waking, analytical minds. The specific detail that Jeremiah's sleep was pleasant—that restoration oracles brought him peace even at night—teaches that divine promises can penetrate and transform our deepest inner state. Members facing anxiety or spiritual turbulence might recognize in this verse that God's restorative work sometimes begins not with external change, but with inner peace—a 'sweet sleep' that comes from knowing that restoration is coming.

text_kjv: Behold, the days come, saith the LORD, that I will sow the house of Israel and the house of Judah with the seed of man, and with the seed of beast.

commentary.narrative: God moves from satisfying the weary to replanting the land itself. This verse announces a comprehensive restoration: both kingdoms (Israel and Judah, which have been separated and scattered) will be reunified and repopulated. The metaphor shifts from irrigation (verse 25) to agriculture: God is the farmer sowing seed in the soil of the promised land. Both 'the seed of man' and 'the seed of beast' are mentioned—a completeness that suggests not just human repopulation but the full restoration of the land's fertility and natural order. This reverses the judgment announced in 4:23-26, where Jeremiah envisioned the land returned to formless chaos, void of human and animal life. Now God promises to deliberately plant what He permitted to be uprooted. The verb zarati ('I will sow') is future-oriented; this is not yet complete, but is God's declared purpose. The naming of both 'the house of Israel' (the northern kingdom, largely lost to Assyrian exile) and 'the house of Judah' (the southern kingdom, soon to face Babylonian exile) together suggests that God's restoration plan encompasses not just the return of Judah from Babylon, but an ultimate reunification of all Israel. This echoes the earlier promise in verses 1-14 of both kingdoms finding their way home.

word_study.meaning: to sow, to scatter seed; when used of God's action toward people, can mean to plant, establish, or multiply
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering notes that this verb 'reverses the metaphor of judgment: where exile scattered and depleted the population, God will now plant new life.' The same seed-language is used in Jeremiah 1:10 where God sets the prophet 'to build and to plant.' Here, God Himself acts as the planter, directly reversing the work of uprooting and tearing down that characterized judgment.

word_study.meaning: seed of humanity, human offspring; describes the population repopulation of the land
word_study.significance: The term zera (seed) when applied to human beings emphasizes both continuity and multiplying growth. This is not merely individual return, but the establishment of generations—the promise that the exiled line will continue and flourish.

word_study.meaning: seed of livestock/animals; describes the animal populations of the land
word_study.significance: This phrase ensures that restoration is comprehensive—not just human, but ecological. The land's fertility and animal life will be restored. In covenant theology, the health of the land is tied to the people's covenant faithfulness. The promise of beast-restoration suggests a return to covenant blessing on the land itself.

cross_references.connection: God's commissioning of Jeremiah uses identical language: 'to build and to plant.' This verse shows God Himself now doing directly what He called His prophet to proclaim.

In the judgment vision, Jeremiah sees the land returned to tohu va-vohu (formlessness and void), bereft of all human and animal life. Verse 27 reverses that vision entirely—the void will be filled again.

Isaiah similarly promises that God will gather His people from the east and west: 'I will say to the north, Give up; and to the south, Keep not back: bring my sons from far, and my daughters from the ends of the earth.'

Ezekiel uses the same agricultural metaphor for restoration: 'But ye, O mountains of Israel, ye shall shoot forth your branches, and yield your fruit to my people of Israel; for they are at hand to come.'
Nephi cites this restoration passage as evidence that God remembers His covenant with Israel despite their dispersion, connecting Jeremiah's promise to the latter-day gathering.

commentary.historical_context: In ancient agrarian societies, the land's productivity was directly linked to population prosperity. A depopulated land meant famine and loss; a populated, cultivated land meant security and increase. The Babylonian exile left Judah's land depleted and largely empty of the native population (though not entirely evacuated, as archaeological evidence shows some continuity). God's promise to 'sow' the land with both human and animal 'seed' would have been understood as a complete reversal of exile: not just permission to return, but God's active work to restore fertility, population, and abundance. The farming metaphor was also common in ancient Near Eastern royal inscriptions, where kings described themselves as tending the land and its people. Here, Jeremiah presents God as the true King and cultivator.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Jacob teaches that the Lord will again 'stretch forth his hand another time' to recover a remnant of Israel (2 Nephi 29:1-2). The Book of Mormon presents restoration as an active divine work spanning generations—God plants His people in the Americas as part of the same comprehensive restoration Jeremiah announces.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 29:8 promises renewal of the earth and its inhabitants: 'The end shall come, and the heaven and the earth shall be consumed and pass away, and they shall be no more an they that dwell upon the earth shall pass away.' But this precedes a new creation—the same movement from judgment to restoration Jeremiah describes.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The sowing metaphor connects to temple theology: the temple is where heaven and earth meet, and the promises of the covenant are sealed upon families 'for time and all eternity.' Sowing with 'seed of man' invokes the covenant promise of posterity—a central temple teaching. The sealing of families ensures that restored people remain unified in covenant.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ is the seed who brings forth much fruit (John 12:24)—'except a corn of wheat fall into the ground and die, it abideth alone: but if it die, it bringeth forth much fruit.' The language of sowing and increase points to Christ's redemptive work, which produces a harvest of believers gathered into God's kingdom. The restoration of Israel through sowing is a type of the gathering of Christ's elect.
commentary.application: This verse invites modern members to see divine restoration as active and comprehensive. God does not merely permit return or passively accept repentance; He actively plants and cultivates new growth. In personal life, this means that restoration from sin, loss, or spiritual exile is not something we achieve through our own efforts alone, but something God accomplishes through His power. The metaphor of sowing also suggests time and patience—seeds planted do not yield fruit immediately. Members undergoing spiritual restoration or family healing should recognize that God is at work even when outward results are not yet visible, just as seeds work beneath the soil before the harvest appears.

text_kjv: And it shall come to pass, that like as I have watched over them, to pluck up, and to break down, and to throw down, and to destroy, and to afflict; so will I watch over them, to build, and to plant, saith the LORD.

commentary.narrative: This verse is the theological center of Jeremiah 31 and perhaps of the entire book. It directly echoes God's commissioning of Jeremiah in 1:10, but inverts its application: the verbs of judgment that defined Jeremiah's calling are now declared to be complete and exhausted; the verbs of restoration will now characterize God's future work. The structure is perfectly parallel: 'as I have watched over them...to [destroy, destroy, destroy, destroy, destroy]; so will I watch over them to [build, plant].' Five destructive actions are answered by two restorative ones—suggesting that restoration, though different in nature, is not less powerful or thorough. The verb shaqadti ('I watched over') is crucial: the same vigilance, the same divine attentiveness that executed judgment will now execute rebuilding. The Covenant Rendering notes the wordplay with the almond branch (shaqed) from 1:11-12: God 'watches' (shoqed) over His word—first for judgment, now for restoration. God does not work capriciously; He invests the same careful attention and consistency in building up that He invested in tearing down. This is a remarkable comfort: the God who showed such terrible consistency in judgment will show equal consistency in restoration.

word_study.meaning: to watch, to be wakeful, to be vigilant; carries the sense of persistent, attentive watching
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering highlights the wordplay with the almond branch (shaqed) vision: 'I am watching over my word to perform it.' The same vigilance that executed judgment will now supervise restoration. God's attentiveness is not sporadic but constant.

word_study.meaning: to pluck up, to uproot, to pull out by the roots; suggests total removal
word_study.significance: This is the first of five verbs describing judgment—all now declared complete. The progression from uprooting suggests the totality of exile: not just displacement, but removal from the very soil of identity and covenant.

word_study.meaning: to tear down, to break down, to demolish; used of destroying walls, cities, structures
word_study.significance: This appears second in the sequence and adds to the image of total destruction—not just uprooting individuals, but dismantling institutions and structures.

word_study.meaning: to throw down, to overthrow, to ruin; suggests violent destruction
word_study.significance: The third verb intensifies the image—the destruction is not passive abandonment but active, violent overthrow of what stood before.

word_study.meaning: to perish, to be lost, to be destroyed; suggests total annihilation
word_study.significance: The fourth verb reaches toward absolute destruction—not merely damage but extinction. Used with 'destroy' (avayd) suggests the judgment reaches its ultimate extreme.

word_study.meaning: to bring harm, to do evil, to afflict; describes causing suffering and hardship
word_study.significance: The fifth and final verb suggests that God did not destroy blindly, but with purpose—bringing affliction to bring repentance and return. The shift now moves toward restoration.

word_study.meaning: to build, to construct, to establish; suggests making new structures and institutions
word_study.significance: This verb now replaces the first cluster. Building will follow uprooting—the exiles will not merely return to a rebuilt land, but to new institutions and a new relationship with God (the new covenant of verses 31-34).

word_study.meaning: to plant, to establish, to set down; suggests cultivation and growth
word_study.significance: This echoes verse 27 and 1:10. God will not merely rebuild rubble but plant new life—both literal (the people in the land) and spiritual (the new covenant). The language suggests not restoration to the previous state, but a new order.

cross_references.connection: God's original commission to Jeremiah lists both verbs of judgment and verbs of building and planting. This verse declares that the judgment phase is complete; now begins the building phase. The structure is identical: 'to pull up and to break down, to destroy and to overthrow, to build and to plant.'

The vision of the almond branch (shaqed) with the wordplay 'I watch (shoqed) over my word to perform it' establishes the pattern continued in verse 28: God's watchfulness ensures His purposes come to pass—both judgment and restoration.

Though the Lord brings grief, He will have compassion according to the multitude of His mercies. 'The Lord will not cast off forever.' This expresses the same theological claim: judgment is real but not permanent; compassion follows.

Isaiah similarly promises: 'For a small moment have I forsaken thee; but with great mercies will I gather thee.' The pattern of judgment followed by comprehensive restoration is common in the prophetic literature.

Alma teaches the principle of restoration: 'And it is requisite with the justice of God that men should be judged according to their works; and if their works were good in this life, and the desires of their hearts were good, that they should also, at the last day, be restored unto that which is good.' Restoration follows judgment according to justice.

commentary.historical_context: Jeremiah's five-verb sequence of judgment (uprooting, tearing down, overthrowing, destroying, afflicting) describes precisely what happened during the Babylonian exile (586 BCE): cities were demolished, the population was deported, the Temple was destroyed, and the land lay largely empty. By the time Jeremiah spoke verses 27-28, this destruction was either imminent or already beginning. His promise that God would 'watch over' this destruction just as carefully as He would watch over restoration was audacious: it claimed that even the catastrophe was under divine control, not random military conquest. God was not being defeated by Babylon; He was actively using Babylon to accomplish His judicial purposes. This theology—that judgment is not the end of God's sovereignty but an expression of it—would have been difficult for exiles to accept but was crucial for maintaining faith during captivity.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Nephi records that after the Nephites fell into apostasy and were destroyed, the Lord would again establish His covenant people (2 Nephi 30:7-8). The same pattern appears: destruction for judgment, followed by building and planting of a restored remnant. The Book of Mormon itself is a record of this restoration cycle played out on another continent.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 101:23-25 declares that the righteous shall inherit the earth and all things shall be renewed. D&C 29:22-24 similarly describes destruction and renewal: 'For I will show unto you the palms of your hands, and upon the soles of your feet I will show them.' The pattern of judgment and restoration is central to Joseph Smith's revealed theology.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: In temple endowment narrative, the journey of humanity involves both testing (judgment-like phases) and exaltation (restoration-building-planting). The same God oversees both; the temple covenants acknowledge both the reality of opposition and the ultimate triumph of the restored order.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ's work involves both judgment and mercy, both destruction of sin and restoration of righteousness. He comes first as the Lamb, then as the Lion. His crucifixion appears to be destruction (the tearing down phase), but accomplishes resurrection and restoration (the building and planting phase). The same Christ who judged sin in His crucifixion restores righteousness in His resurrection. Jeremiah's verse prefigures Christ's total work—both its judgmental and restorative dimensions executed with equal divine attention.
commentary.application: This verse is profoundly comforting for members who have experienced divine discipline or the consequences of sin. It teaches that God's discipline (the 'plucking up' and 'breaking down' phases) is not an indication of withdrawal from covenant relationship, but of active divine attention and purpose. The same God who disciplines will restore. Moreover, for communities or individuals in phases of rebuilding, this verse promises that God will 'watch over' the restoration process with the same vigilance He exercised over judgment. Restoration is not accidental or half-hearted, but divinely supervised and consistent. Members in seasons of renewal—after repentance, after trial, after loss—can claim this promise: God is watching to build and plant with the same care and certainty He showed in previous discipline.

text_kjv: In those days they shall say no more, The fathers have eaten a sour grape, and the children's teeth are set on edge.

commentary.narrative: This verse directly addresses one of the most persistent complaints of the exiled people: the sense of suffering for the sins of previous generations. The proverb—'the fathers ate sour grapes, and the children's teeth are set on edge'—expressed a theology of collective punishment that felt fundamentally unjust. It is quoted also in Ezekiel 18:2, where God explicitly rejects it. The proverb suggests that consequences fall inappropriately on the wrong generation; the parents engage in sin (eating the sour, unripe fruit), but the children experience the bitter result (teeth set on edge). In the context of exile, the complaint took a specific form: 'We are suffering for Judah's centuries of idolatry and injustice; why must we, who were born in exile or are ourselves repentant, bear the full weight of that corporate sin?' God's promise is revolutionary: the restoration will bring a new principle into operation. No longer will children suffer collective punishment for their parents' sins. God declares this false proverb will become obsolete—not merely corrected, but rendered unnecessary by a new era of justice and individual accountability. The phrasing 'in those days they shall say no more' indicates that the proverb will literally fall silent; it will no longer be spoken because it will no longer reflect reality. This is not a softening of God's demands, but an elevation of individual responsibility and accountability.

word_study.meaning: unripe grape, sour grape; fruit that is not yet ready for consumption, still hard and bitter
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering notes that 'boser describes fruit that is not yet ready—the metaphor suggests premature, inappropriate consequences falling on the wrong generation.' The term emphasizes not just bitterness but wrongness—the children receive consequences not yet meant for them, consequences that belong to a prior generation.

word_study.meaning: to be dulled, to be blunted, to be set on edge; describes teeth being made sensitive or numb by extreme sourness
word_study.significance: The physical sensation of teeth dulled or set on edge by sourness is the consequence of eating unripe fruit. The metaphor works because it is viscerally real: everyone would have experienced this. The term suggests a painful consequence that seems disproportionate to what the current generation did.

cross_references.connection: Ezekiel quotes the same proverb and explicitly rejects it, declaring that 'the soul that sinneth, it shall die'—establishing the principle of individual accountability that Jeremiah 31:29-30 will now implement.

God's declaration that He visits 'the iniquity of the fathers upon the children unto the third and fourth generation' establishes the principle of corporate/familial accountability. Jeremiah 31:29-30 modifies this principle to emphasize individual responsibility in the restoration era.

The law explicitly forbids punishing children for their fathers' sins: 'The fathers shall not be put to death for the children, neither shall the children be put to death for the fathers: every man shall be put to death for his own sin.' Jeremiah's promise brings the restoration into alignment with this legal principle.

Lehi teaches that men are free to choose liberty and eternal life or captivity and death—establishing individual accountability as fundamental to God's plan. Jeremiah's promise aligns with this Book of Mormon principle.

Modern revelation declares 'I, the Lord, forgive sins unto those who confess their sins before me and ask forgiveness.' Individual accountability is tied to individual repentance and forgiveness, not collective punishment.

commentary.historical_context: The complaint about intergenerational injustice was not unique to Judah, but would have been particularly acute in the Babylonian exile. The generation born in exile or deported as young people would have little personal responsibility for Judah's pre-exilic idolatry, yet experienced the full consequences. Archaeological evidence shows that exiled populations maintained strong family and clan identity, and questions about justice would have been central to their survival and morale. The proverb 'the fathers ate sour grapes' appears to be an actual saying among the exiles, expressing their sense of victimization. God's response—that this principle will become obsolete in the restoration—implies a fundamental theological shift in how justice operates: no longer mediated through the clan and collective punishment, but through individual accountability and covenant.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 41-42 extensively develops the principle that God's justice operates on the basis of individual works and desires. 'The mystery of godliness' requires that individuals be accountable for themselves, not vicariously bearing the consequences of others' sins. This principle reaches its ultimate expression in Christ, who takes upon Himself the sins of the world so that individuals can repent and be forgiven.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 29:44-45 teaches that each person will be judged according to their own works and beliefs. D&C 88:41 declares 'The end of the commandment is love,' suggesting that the new covenant (and thus the restoration era) emphasizes individual relationship to God rather than corporate institutional mediation.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: In temple covenants, the emphasis is on individual commitment and individual sealing. While sealings bind families, they do so on the basis of individual faithfulness. Each person must personally make and keep covenants; parental faithfulness does not automatically transfer to children (though it creates powerful spiritual conditions for their individual choices).

commentary.christological_typology: Christ's redemptive work establishes a new principle: individuals are no longer bound by collective guilt or corporate punishment. Each person is 'born again,' given a new start, offered forgiveness and restoration on the basis of their own relationship to Christ (John 3:3-7). Christ breaks the chain of intergenerational consequence by taking upon Himself the sins of all—not so that individuals escape accountability, but so that individuals are freed to respond to God on the basis of faith, repentance, and covenant, not historical guilt.
commentary.application: This verse speaks directly to members who struggle with the effects of family dysfunction, intergenerational trauma, or inherited consequences of others' choices. The promise is not that family history has no effect—seeds of character, both good and harmful, are indeed passed down. But it is that ultimate accountability and ultimate restoration are individual, not collective. An individual member is not bound by a parent's sin or unbelief; each person must work out their own salvation. This is both humbling and liberating: humbling because it means personal responsibility cannot be escaped by blaming family history; liberating because it means no one is trapped by what previous generations did. The restoration principle promises that in the Lord's eyes, each person stands on their own covenantal footing.

text_kjv: But every one shall die for his own iniquity: every man that eateth the sour grape, his teeth shall be set on edge.

commentary.narrative: This verse completes the teaching of verses 29-30: if verse 29 promises that the false proverb will become obsolete, verse 30 establishes the new principle that will replace it. God is not softening justice or abandoning accountability; rather, He is clarifying and individualizing it. Every person will bear the consequences of their own sin, not vicariously suffer for others' transgressions. The shift in terminology is significant: from 'they shall say no more' (the proverb becomes silent) to 'every one shall die for his own iniquity' (the principle becomes active). The parallelism is maintained: just as verse 29 used the metaphor of eating sour grapes and teeth being set on edge, verse 30 uses the identical metaphor but applies it to individual rather than collective consequences. This is not a promise that sin will go unpunished or that consequences disappear. Rather, it establishes that the equation is now direct: the person who eats the sour grape experiences the consequence. No proxy suffering, no collective punishment, no escape through anonymity in the masses. This principle is fundamental to the new covenant promised in verses 31-34, where 'every one' will know the Lord individually and be able to repent individually. Accountability and covenant relationship are henceforward personal, not merely institutional or collective.

word_study.meaning: to die, to perish; in covenant contexts, often means to suffer the penalty of broken covenant, not necessarily literal death
word_study.significance: The term suggests the ultimate consequence—bearing fully and finally what one has deserved. The shift from collective death to individual death is the key: each person faces their own ultimate accountability.

word_study.meaning: iniquity, guilt, transgression; describes both the sin and the inherent guilt or consequence bound up in it
word_study.significance: Avon is not merely an external penalty imposed by God, but something intrinsic to the sin itself. Eating the sour grape naturally results in dulled teeth—the consequence flows from the action itself. God does not arbitrarily punish from the outside; He lets the natural consequences of sin work themselves out.

cross_references.connection: Ezekiel explicitly develops this principle: 'What mean ye, that ye use this proverb concerning the land of Israel, saying, The fathers have eaten sour grapes, and the children's teeth are set on edge? As I live, saith the Lord God, ye shall not have occasion any more to use this proverb in Israel. Behold, all souls are mine...the soul that sinneth, it shall die.'
Paul writes: 'The wages of sin is death.' This New Testament formulation of the same principle—that sin produces its own inevitable consequence—echoes Jeremiah's teaching.

Alma teaches restoration and recompense: 'That same spirit which doth possess your bodies at the time that ye go out of this life, that same spirit will have power to possess your body in that eternal world.' Each soul reaps what it sowed.

Modern revelation clarifies: 'There is a law, irrevocably decreed in heaven before the foundations of this world, upon which all blessings are predicated—And when we obtain any blessing from God, it is by obedience to that law upon which it is predicated.' Cause and effect; individual action produces individual consequence.

commentary.historical_context: The Babylonian exile lasted roughly seventy years (586-516 BCE). The generation born in captivity or deported as children would have reached adulthood or old age in exile. For them, the ancient proverb about parents' sins falling on children would have felt deeply unfair: they had no choice in the sins of their forefathers, yet experienced the full consequences. God's promise to change this principle addresses a real crisis of justice perception among the exiles. Moreover, the principle of individual accountability was connected to the possibility of individual return: not only would individuals be judged for their own deeds, but individuals could repent and return. The promise made sense theologically and practically: if accountability is individual, then opportunity for restoration is also individual.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon repeatedly emphasizes individual accountability: Alma's teaching of restoration in Alma 41-42, Lehi's teaching of free agency in 2 Nephi 2, Mormon's commentary on individual responsibility in Mormon 2:26. The principle that each person is responsible for their own choices and will face their own consequences (or enjoy their own blessings) is foundational to Book of Mormon theology.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 75:5 declares 'He that is slothful shall not be worthy to take up his cross and follow me.' D&C 64:34 promises 'I, the Lord, forgive sins unto those who confess their sins before me.' Both verses operate on the principle of individual accountability and individual redemption. Joseph Smith's theology consistently moved away from inherited guilt or proxy responsibility toward individual covenant relationship.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: In the temple, each individual takes covenants for themselves—not vicariously or through proxy standing (except for the deceased in proxy ordinance, which is a special principle). Baptism for the dead allows the deceased to respond individually to the gospel; living members must individually accept and keep covenants. The temple embodies the principle of verse 30: each soul stands individually before God.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ's atonement establishes a new principle whereby sin produces its consequence, but that consequence can be borne by a substitute (Christ) if the individual accepts the covenant. However, this acceptance is itself individual—each person must 'come unto Christ.' The principle of individual accountability does not disappear; rather, it is fulfilled through Christ's individual sacrifice. Those who reject Christ still 'die for his own iniquity'; those who accept Him have their iniquity borne by the Lamb. Verse 30 thus prefigures the mechanism by which Christ's atonement operates: it respects individual accountability while offering individual redemption.
commentary.application: This verse removes the excuse of inherited guilt while affirming the reality of personal consequences. Modern members cannot blame their choices on their family history or social circumstances; each person is accountable for their own actions. Conversely, each person has the power to change their trajectory through repentance: 'Every man that eateth the sour grape' (makes that choice) will experience the consequence—but if they stop eating sour grapes, they stop experiencing that consequence. This principle is both challenging and liberating. It challenges members to take full responsibility for their choices, without relying on excuses. It liberates members from bondage to family history or inherited dysfunction: you are not permanently bound by what previous generations chose. The restoration principle promises that each individual has the power to change their covenant standing through their own choices and repentance. This is the foundation of the new covenant about to be announced in verses 31-34, where individual relationship with God and individual knowledge of the Lord become central.

text_kjv: The word that came to Jeremiah from the LORD in the tenth year of Zedekiah king of Judah, which was the eighteenth year of Nebuchadrezzar.

commentary.narrative:
Jeremiah 32 opens with precise chronological anchoring that tells us far more than a date. We are in 588/587 BCE, during the final siege of Jerusalem—the moment when Jeremiah's decades of warnings have culminated in catastrophe. The dual dating system (tenth year of Zedekiah / eighteenth year of Nebuchadnezzar) is not incidental administrative detail; it is theological statement. Judah's calendar is now synchronized with Babylon's because Judah is a vassal state. The king who rules Jerusalem does so only by permission of the foreign power besieging it. This synchronization of regnal years mirrors the political reality: Judah has lost sovereignty, and the clock of history is running by Babylon's rhythm, not Jerusalem's.

The 'word that came to Jeremiah' (devar-YHWH) is Jeremiah's authoritative formula.
