After four decades of prophesying rejection, imprisonment, beating, and public humiliation, the Lord's word still comes to His prophet. This is the book's central paradox: Jerusalem falls, the king's strategy collapses, and God's spokesman remains imprisoned in the royal compound—yet the word of the Lord continues to come. In this moment of total national failure, God has not abandoned His prophet or His people.

word_study.meaning: word, speech, matter, thing, event; the operative unit of divine communication
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering notes that davar is not merely linguistic—it is the substance of God's directive action. When 'the word of the LORD came,' it was not passive information but active summons. In Jeremiah's usage, davar-YHWH is the recurring marker of prophetic authority, distinguishing genuine revelation from false prophecy (cf. Jeremiah 1:2, 2:1, 7:1).

word_study.meaning: year; the temporal marker of a reign, covenant period, or divine reckoning
word_study.significance: The dual dating system reflects ancient Near Eastern practice: vassal states recorded time by both their own king's regnal years and their suzerain's. The Hebrew repeats shanah twice ('tenth year...eighteenth year'), emphasizing that time itself—history's very calendar—belongs to the imperial power. Yet God's word cuts across both calendars, asserting that ultimate authority rests with YHWH, not Nebuchadnezzar.

cross_references.connection: Uses the same formula 'the word of the LORD came unto Jeremiah' to mark the inception of his prophetic call and ministry, establishing continuity across forty years of the prophet's witness.
Records the historical siege of Jerusalem in parallel terms, confirming the tenth year of Zedekiah as the time of Babylon's military encirclement of the city.
Provides the outcome of this same siege, showing that Jeremiah's predictions (quoted in verses 3-5) were fulfilled precisely as stated.

The Lord's promise that His word 'shall all be fulfilled, whether by mine own voice or by the voice of my servants' applies to the pattern seen here: God's word through Jeremiah endures even when the nation rejects it.

commentary.historical_context: The tenth year of Zedekiah (588/587 BCE) marks the climactic phase of Babylon's siege. Archaeological evidence from Iron Age Jerusalem—including ash layers, arrowheads, and destruction debris—confirms the intensity of this assault. Jerusalem's fortification walls show burn marks consistent with siege warfare. Judah had been a tributary to Babylon for about a decade, but Zedekiah made the fateful decision to rebel, likely with encouragement from Egypt. This triggered Nebuchadnezzar's response. The double regnal dating reflects actual administrative practice: cuneiform documents from the Neo-Babylonian Empire record events by both the local ruler's years and the king of Babylon's years, making this verse historically authentic to how scribes would have recorded events during this period. The 'eighteenth year of Nebuchadnezzar' (605-587 BCE, approximately) aligns with Babylonian chronology; Nebuchadnezzar ascended the throne around 605 BCE.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon records a similar pattern in which the Lord's word continues through His prophets even as a nation moves toward destruction. In 1 Nephi, Nephi receives revelation about the destruction of Jerusalem at precisely the moment it is occurring (1 Nephi 1:4-19). The principle is identical: God's word is not suspended by political circumstances; it runs concurrent with history, addressing the covenant people even in their darkest hour.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 1:38 states, 'What I the Lord have spoken, I have spoken; and I excuse not myself.' Jeremiah's prophetic word, delivered under constraint and imprisonment, exemplifies this principle. The Lord's utterances stand independent of the circumstances of their delivery or the reception they receive.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The royal palace compound where Jeremiah is imprisoned (the chatsar hammattarah, 'court of the guard') becomes a kind of inverted temple—a place where divine word still emanates, though the actual temple is about to be destroyed. This anticipates the LDS understanding that the Lord's presence is not fixed to buildings but travels with His covenant people.

commentary.christological_typology: Jeremiah's imprisonment in the palace during the siege parallels the later imprisonment of Jesus—both prophets spoke the word of the Lord with precision, both were confined by civil authority, and both were vindicated only after their words came to pass. The theme of the rejected prophet whose predictions prove true foreshadows Jesus as the Prophet like unto Moses (Deuteronomy 18:15; Acts 3:22), whose words concerning judgment and restoration would be fulfilled.
commentary.application: When our personal circumstances narrow—when we face institutional resistance, loss of status, or confinement by forces beyond our control—this verse teaches that the word of the Lord does not diminish. Jeremiah's access to divine instruction did not depend on his freedom or his nation's success. Modern covenant members, facing secularization, persecution, or personal trial, should recognize that God's word continues to come to us, that our witness remains true regardless of circumstances, and that the Lord is not defeated by empires or systems that oppose His message. The test is not whether the world receives us, but whether we remain faithful to the word that comes to us.

text_kjv: For then the king of Babylon's army besieged Jerusalem: and Jeremiah the prophet was shut up in the court of the prison, which was in the king of Judah's house.

commentary.narrative:
The bracketing of events here is crucial: Jerusalem besieged from without, Jeremiah imprisoned from within. The city is under military assault; simultaneously, the prophet who foretold this assault is held captive inside the royal palace. This is not accident but irony of the highest order. Zedekiah has imprisoned Jeremiah precisely because Jeremiah's prophecies of Jerusalem's fall were undermining public confidence during a time of war. From the king's standpoint, the prophet is a liability, a voice of defeatism when morale is critical. Yet Jeremiah remains imprisoned because his words are true—and the king knows it.

The Covenant Rendering clarifies that Jeremiah was 'confined in the court of the guard' (chatsar hammattarah), not thrown into a dungeon or cistern. This is not yet the pit of chapter 38:6 where he is lowered into a muddy cistern to die. Here, Jeremiah has restricted movement but is still within the palace compound, still able to receive visitors, still able to continue his prophetic work. The location matters: within the very seat of power that is proving powerless, God's word continues to operate through His bound prophet. The palace itself becomes a kind of witness—its walls containing both Zedekiah's failing regime and Jeremiah's unshakeable word.

word_study.meaning: besiege, distress, hem in; from tzar (narrow, tight), conveying both physical encirclement and psychological pressure
word_study.significance: The root carries the sense of constriction. Jerusalem is compressed between Babylon's siege lines; the city is literally tightened. The same root appears in the phrase 'distress of nations' (tzukat goyim) and emphasizes that siege warfare is not merely military but existential—it constricts hope, supplies, and escape routes.

word_study.meaning: shut up, confined, held captive; from kalʾ, suggesting a complete restraint of movement
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering uses 'confined,' which better captures the sense of restricted liberty than 'shut up.' Jeremiah is not in solitary confinement but is confined within a bounded space. The verb root often appears in contexts of imprisonment by human authority (Psalm 142:8: 'I am brought low; bring me out of prison'). The irony is that the prophet is confined by the very power that is about to be conquered.

word_study.meaning: court, courtyard, enclosed space; a definable area within a larger compound
word_study.significance: The palace complex contained multiple courtyards, each serving different administrative or military functions. The 'court of the guard' was likely where military or security personnel were stationed, befitting a place where a political prisoner might be held with some freedom of movement within bounds.

cross_references.connection: Later in this siege, the king grants Jeremiah a daily allowance of bread from the baker's street while he remains confined, showing that imprisonment did not sever the prophet's survival or his ability to communicate.
Provides stark contrast: Jeremiah is later lowered into a muddy cistern to die, from which he must be rescued by an Ethiopian eunuch, showing the progression of his persecution as the siege worsens.

Summarizes Zedekiah's reign and notes his stiffness of neck in refusing to humble himself before Jeremiah and the word of the LORD, providing the ideological backdrop for his imprisonment of the prophet.
The principle that those who do evil 'hate the light,' as Zedekiah resisted Jeremiah's word during siege, applies to all times when truth becomes inconvenient to those in power.

commentary.historical_context: Ancient siege warfare involved encirclement and deprivation. Babylonian records (including the Babylonian Chronicle) confirm that Nebuchadnezzar's forces surrounded Jerusalem, cutting it off from supply and relief. The archaeological record from Jerusalem shows evidence of famine conditions during this final siege—animal bones become smaller (indicating slaughter of younger animals), nutritional markers in skeletal remains show stress, and pottery vessels show evidence of careful rationing. The royal palace (likely located where the Temple Mount complex later stood or on the hill of Ophel) would have been the last stronghold. Zedekiah's imprisonment of Jeremiah reflects the desperation of a failing regime—silencing dissent in the final hours. This was common practice in ancient monarchies under siege: dissenting voices were suppressed to maintain unity and morale. Yet Jeremiah's confinement in the palace courtyard, rather than in a common dungeon, suggests either Zedekiah's personal regard for the elderly prophet or a deliberate decision not to make him a martyr (yet).

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In Alma 36:27-30, Alma describes his confinement while under arrest, yet his ability to preach the word of God was not diminished. Like Jeremiah, Alma experienced that divine authority to speak God's word transcends physical confinement. Similarly, Nephi and his companions were imprisoned in 1 Nephi 7:20-21, yet the power of their word and faith was demonstrated even in captivity.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 121:7-9 records Joseph Smith's complaint from Liberty Jail: 'O God, where art thou?' Yet in that very confinement, the Lord gave some of the most profound revelations in the Doctrine and Covenants (sections 121-123). Jeremiah's confinement, like Joseph's imprisonment, became a place where God's word intensified rather than ceased.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The court of the guard in the royal palace mirrors the temple courtyard as a space where divine communication occurs. Though not the temple proper, it becomes a site of prophetic utterance. This prefigures the LDS principle that the Lord's word is not confined to sacred buildings but travels with His covenant people wherever they are.

commentary.christological_typology: Jesus was also detained within the palace of a political ruler (the palace of Caiaphas, and later Pilate's palace) while facing a crisis of state (the Roman occupation, the threat of rebellion). Like Jeremiah, Jesus spoke truth that undermined the political establishment. The theme of the prophet imprisoned by those he warned foreshadows the suffering servant who is rejected by the very people He came to save.
commentary.application: This verse addresses the experience of those whose integrity or witness creates opposition from institutional power. Jeremiah's confinement teaches that fidelity to truth may result in restricted freedom and institutional hostility. The modern application is clear: do not expect that speaking God's word will win approval from human establishments, especially those invested in contrary narratives. Yet confinement—whether physical, social, or professional—does not silence the prophetic word. The Lord's word to us continues whether we are celebrated or confined, and our role is to deliver it faithfully, not to make it palatable to power.

text_kjv: For Zedekiah king of Judah had shut him up, saying, Wherefore dost thou prophesy, and say, Thus saith the LORD, Behold, I will give this city into the hand of the king of Babylon, and he shall take it;

commentary.narrative:
Now we hear Zedekiah's complaint directly. The king does not dispute the content of Jeremiah's prophecy; he contests the prophet's right to speak it. 'Why do you prophesy?' is not a question about the truth of Jeremiah's words but about their political usefulness. During a siege, when every able-bodied man is needed for defense, a prophet crying 'the city will fall to Babylon' is, from Zedekiah's perspective, undermining necessary morale. This is the perennial conflict between truth-telling and political utility. Zedekiah is not accusing Jeremiah of lying; he is accusing him of demoralizing the people at a critical moment.

The word Jeremiah is accused of speaking is precise: 'I will give this city into the hand of the king of Babylon, and he will capture it.' The verb notein ('give') appears in the participial form in the Hebrew, suggesting that the giving is already in process—God is even now in the act of handing Jerusalem over. This is not a future punishment but an ongoing reality. Jeremiah's prophecy is not a threat of what might happen; it is a declaration of what is already happening from God's perspective. For Zedekiah, this interpretation is intolerable. He needs his people to believe that resistance is possible, that God might yet reverse His intention. Jeremiah insists that God's intention is already operative, already being executed. The imprisonment is the king's attempt to suppress this declaration.

word_study.meaning: prophesy, speak as a prophet; the niphal form of nabaʾ, suggesting inspired speech that is not the speaker's own invention
word_study.significance: Zedekiah's question 'why do you prophesy?' uses this term to challenge the legitimacy of Jeremiah's claim to speak for God. The Hebrew emphasizes that prophesying is not Jeremiah's private opinion but his claim to be a mouthpiece of divine will. In ancient Near Eastern context, prophecy was a recognized institutional role, often co-opted by state prophets who assured the king of victory. Jeremiah's 'true prophecy' directly contradicts the state-sanctioned prophetic establishment.

word_study.meaning: give, place in someone's hand, deliver; the most basic term of transfer or causation in Hebrew
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering notes that 'notein et ha'ir' uses the participial form, emphasizing ongoing action. God is not threatened with future abandonment of Jerusalem; He is actively placing it into Babylon's power. This is theological language of causation: God is the active agent in Jerusalem's fall, not merely permitting it but effecting it. The use of 'hand' (yad) is metaphorical for power and control.

word_study.meaning: take, seize, capture; to gain control through force
word_study.significance: Jeremiah predicts not merely that Jerusalem will fall but that it will be 'seized' (lakad) by Babylon—taken by force. This is the military outcome that Zedekiah fears and that his armies are fighting to prevent. The verb appears in contexts of military conquest throughout the Old Testament and emphasizes the inevitability of the outcome.

cross_references.connection: Jeremiah elsewhere denounces false prophets who speak comforting lies ('I have dreamed, I have dreamed') while Jeremiah insists on speaking God's actual word, even when it brings judgment—the tension that led to his imprisonment.

King Ahab imprisoned Micaiah the prophet because Micaiah predicted defeat while the king's four hundred prophets predicted victory; Zedekiah follows the same pattern of suppressing the true prophet whose message contradicts political desire.

Notes that Zedekiah 'did that which was evil in the sight of the LORD his God, and humbled not himself before Jeremiah the prophet speaking from the mouth of the LORD,' explicitly connecting his imprisonment of Jeremiah to his spiritual rebellion.

Joseph Smith taught that the prophet's word stands regardless of reception: 'Write the vision, and make it plain...that he may run that readeth it.' Truth spoken by God's servants will have its effect despite institutional opposition.

commentary.historical_context: The political dynamics of Jerusalem's final siege are crucial here. Archaeological and inscriptional evidence shows that Egypt was encouraging Jerusalem to rebel against Babylon (attested in both Babylonian and Egyptian records). There were indeed Judean voices insisting that resistance was possible, that Egypt would provide relief, that God would yet save the city. Jeremiah, by insisting that the city would fall and resistance would fail, stood against the majority opinion of both the military and the court prophets. This is a classic situation of institutional prophecy: those prophets dependent on royal patronage naturally prophesy what the king wants to hear. Jeremiah, having broken with court favor decades earlier, continued to speak unwelcome truth. Zedekiah's imprisonment of Jeremiah reflects both political frustration and the real anxiety that Jeremiah's words might demoralize the military effort. In the ancient Near East, the morale effect of prophecy was taken seriously; a prophet's word was believed to carry power, and therefore his predictions could affect outcomes.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: King Noah imprisoned Abinadi for prophesying the destruction of his kingdom (Mosiah 11:26-28). Like Zedekiah, Noah did not deny Abinadi's spiritual authority but rejected his right to speak such words. King Lamoni's father also initially resisted Ammon's message, seeking to suppress it, until he was converted (Alma 20:13-15). The Nephite pattern shows that resistance to true prophecy often comes from those whose power is threatened.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 71:7-8 records: 'Therefore, as I said unto mine apostles I say unto you again, that every soul who believeth on your words, and is baptized by water for the remission of sins, shall receive the Holy Ghost.' The word of the prophet is efficacious regardless of institutional opposition. Jeremiah's imprisonment could not revoke the power of his word.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The prophet's word, when spoken from the temple or within sacred space (or in Jeremiah's case, within the royal compound where divine word is still flowing), carries an authority that civil power cannot suppress. The temple represents the place where God's will is known and declared, and the prophet guards access to that knowledge even when confined.

commentary.christological_typology: Jesus was similarly questioned by those in power: 'By what authority doest thou these things?' (Matthew 21:23). Like Jeremiah, Jesus spoke of judgment ('not one stone shall be left upon another,' Matthew 24:2) and the fall of the current political order, which led to His arrest and trial. The pattern of the truth-speaking prophet being imprisoned by the power structure he challenges is fulfilled in Jesus' passion.
commentary.application: This verse teaches the difficult reality that truth-telling, especially truth about coming judgment or institutional failure, will be resisted by those invested in the status quo. The modern application includes recognizing that prophetic witness—whether personal, ecclesiastical, or institutional—will face the objection: 'Why do you say such discouraging things?' The test of faithfulness is not whether our message is popular but whether it is true. Jeremiah teaches that we must sometimes speak what the powerful do not want to hear, and we must be prepared to face institutional opposition for doing so. Yet our role is to declare God's word faithfully, not to make it palatable or to suppress it for the sake of morale.

text_kjv: And Zedekiah king of Judah shall not escape out of the hand of the Chaldeans, but shall surely be delivered into the hand of the king of Babylon, and shall speak with him mouth to mouth, and his eyes shall behold his eyes;

commentary.narrative:
This is Jeremiah's response to Zedekiah's complaint, now quoting the very prophecy for which the king imprisoned him. The opening phrase—'Zedekiah shall not escape'—is absolute. There is no conditional escape route, no possible way out. The Covenant Rendering's phrase 'will certainly be handed over' captures the emphatic infinitive absolute (hinnaton yinnaten), a Hebrew grammatical construction that leaves no ambiguity: the handing over is not threatened, it is certain and imminent.

The phrase 'speak with him mouth to mouth' (pihu im pihu) and 'eyes shall behold his eyes' (einav et einav) describes an intimate personal encounter—Zedekiah will stand before Nebuchadnezzar face-to-face as a defeated vassal before his conqueror. This is not metaphorical language but precise description of the outcome. The bitter historical irony (recorded in 2 Kings 25:7) is that Zedekiah does indeed stand before Nebuchadnezzar, but the last thing his eyes behold is Nebuchadnezzar's eyes before they are gouged out. The prophecy is fulfilled with tragic literalness: Zedekiah does see Nebuchadnezzar eye to eye, and it is the most terrible moment of his life. Jeremiah's prophecy is so precise that its fulfillment becomes its own commentary. The king resisted the word of the Lord; the word of the Lord proved itself.

word_study.meaning: escape, slip away, deliver, save; to get out of or away from danger
word_study.significance: The negative ('shall not escape') is absolute. The root malet appears throughout the Old Testament in contexts where someone attempts to flee judgment (cf. Genesis 14:10, where Sodom's kings attempt to malet from the plain). Jeremiah declares that Zedekiah has no escape route, no hidden option, no divine rescue that will reverse the outcome.

word_study.meaning: be given, be handed over, be delivered into the hand of; the passive form emphasizing that the subject is the object of another's action
word_study.significance: Zedekiah is not the active agent in his own capture; he is 'given over' by God into Babylon's power. The passivity emphasizes divine causation: God effects this outcome, not merely Babylon's military superiority. The repetition of 'hand' (yad) throughout the verse emphasizes the motif of power changing hands—from Judah to Babylon, from Zedekiah's control to Nebuchadnezzar's.

word_study.meaning: face to face, directly, in personal encounter; literally 'his mouth with his mouth'
word_study.significance: This phrase conveys direct, personal confrontation—not mediated through intermediaries but immediate presence. In the ancient Near Eastern context, this was the ultimate humiliation: a subject king standing before his overlord. The phrase appears in Numbers 14:14 ('face to face') and Exodus 33:11 (describing Moses' encounter with God 'as a man speaketh unto his friend'), suggesting direct, unmistakable encounter.

word_study.meaning: his eyes will see his eyes; will behold eye to eye; direct visual confrontation
word_study.significance: The repetition of 'eyes' (einav twice) emphasizes the directness of the encounter. This is not hearing about defeat but seeing it face-to-face. The feminine verb form (tiraʾeinah) is unusual grammatically (when the subject is 'eyes,' a feminine noun plural), adding intensity to the construction. This precise, vivid language makes the prophecy unforgettable: Zedekiah will not escape; he will not hear of defeat secondhand; he will stand before his conqueror and see his own doom in the eyes of the man who defeats him.

cross_references.connection: The fulfillment: Zedekiah flees Jerusalem, is captured, brought before Nebuchadnezzar, and his eyes are put out—the prediction of verse 4 is fulfilled with grim literalness.

Earlier in Jeremiah's ministry, the prophet advised Zedekiah to submit to Babylon's king, warning that resistance would lead to captivity; this verse 4 represents the final escalation of that same warning.
Another parallel account of Zedekiah's capture and the gouging out of his eyes, confirming the historical reality of verse 4's prediction.

Alma describes being 'racked with eternal torment' for his sins and seeing God; the motif of coming face-to-face with judgment or divine presence appears throughout the Book of Mormon as the ultimate reckoning.

commentary.historical_context: The historical account is preserved in both biblical and extra-biblical sources. The Babylonian Chronicle records Nebuchadnezzar's siege campaigns. Ancient sources describe the practice of prominent war captives being brought before the conqueror—this was standard protocol in the ancient Near East. The 'mouth to mouth' encounter was the formal presentation of defeat. Regarding Zedekiah's eye blinding: this was attested in historical records. The practice of blinding rebellious vassals was used by Mesopotamian kings as a means of permanent humiliation and as a warning to others. The fact that Zedekiah's sons were killed before his eyes (2 Kings 25:7) adds to the horror: his last sight was of his own children's death. Archaeological evidence from Jerusalem's destruction layer (Iron Age IIB destruction debris) confirms the violence and scale of this final siege. The precision of Jeremiah's prediction—that Zedekiah would be captured, brought before Nebuchadnezzar, and see him eye to eye—demonstrates remarkable specificity. This level of detail would have seemed to Zedekiah impossible at the moment he imprisoned Jeremiah; after the event, it testified powerfully to the truth of the prophet's word.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In Alma 5:18, Alma describes the judgment scene: 'And behold, he shall come to redeem those who believe on his name.' The concept of standing before God or one's judge face-to-face is central to Book of Mormon theology. King Benjamin's address (Mosiah 2:28-29) includes the phrase 'when ye stand before God to be judged,' evoking the same motif of ultimate accountability before an authority figure one cannot escape.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 76:27 describes how those in the terrestrial kingdom 'shall see the face of Jesus Christ, and know that he is' — the principle that ultimate judgment involves face-to-face accountability before God. Zedekiah's encounter with Nebuchadnezzar prefigures the universal pattern of accountability before one's judge.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: In temple worship, the concept of standing before God 'eye to eye' (in the language of Exodus 33:11) represents the goal of covenantal relationship. Zedekiah's forced encounter with Nebuchadnezzar is the inverse: a spiritual rebel must face his temporal judge with no mediation and no escape. The contrast illuminates why covenant fidelity matters: we can choose to come before God in the temple, or judgment will bring us before Him in captivity.

commentary.christological_typology: Jesus predicted His own 'mouth to mouth' encounter with the Father in death and resurrection. The phrase 'that I may know him, and the power of his resurrection' (Philippians 3:10) involves facing one's judge and redeemer. More directly, Jesus' prediction that 'they shall see the Son of man coming in the clouds of heaven with power and great glory' (Matthew 24:30) echoes the motif of unavoidable confrontation. The humbled king standing before his judge prefigures the universal scene of judgment before the Son of God.
commentary.application: This verse teaches the inescapability of moral consequences. Zedekiah's resistance to Jeremiah's word did not change the outcome; it only ensured that he would face that outcome unprepared and in rebellion. The modern application is sobering: we cannot escape the consequences of rejecting God's word through human authority or political resistance. When faced with prophetic counsel we find difficult, we have two choices—accept it and prepare, or resist it and face the predicted outcome unprepared. Zedekiah chose resistance and met Nebuchadnezzar as a defeated, blinded captive. The pattern teaches us to accept uncomfortable truth when the Lord speaks it through His servants, for resistance does not change reality; it only determines how we will face it.

text_kjv: And he shall lead Zedekiah to Babylon, and there shall he be until I visit him, saith the LORD: though ye fight with the Chaldeans, ye shall not prosper.

commentary.narrative:
Verse 5 completes the prophecy that led to Jeremiah's imprisonment. The prophecy moves from Zedekiah's capture and humiliation (verses 3-4) to his ultimate fate: captivity in Babylon, indefinite exile, ending only when God 'attends to' (paqad) him. The Hebrew term paqad carries multiple meanings—'to visit,' 'to attend to,' 'to punish,' 'to care for'—and the ambiguity is deliberate. God's attention to Zedekiah could mean judgment or eventual mercy; Jeremiah leaves the outcome open. This matches the historical record: Zedekiah survived his captivity and, according to later tradition, was eventually treated less harshly in his final years (2 Kings 25:27-30 records his release from imprisonment during the reign of Evil-Merodach).

The verse concludes with a shift to collective address: 'though ye fight with the Chaldeans, ye shall not prosper.' The 'ye' is plural, addressing all of Judah's military resistance. This is not predicting individual failure but the futility of the nation's entire military strategy. Every Judean soldier who takes up arms will not prosper. Every siege strategy will fail. Every attempt to break through the lines will be repelled. The prophecy is sweeping in its certainty: resistance as a whole is futile. This was the core of Jeremiah's message throughout his ministry—don't fight Babylon, submit to God's judgment, and survive in exile. The irony is that this counsel was precisely the 'demoralizing' speech for which he was imprisoned.

word_study.meaning: go, walk, lead, march; the basic term of movement in Hebrew
word_study.significance: Zedekiah will not flee to Egypt or hide; he will be 'marched' or 'led' to Babylon—a formal procession of the defeated king into captivity. This is not an escape but a forced march under guard. The verb emphasizes Zedekiah's loss of agency; he does not choose to go to Babylon; he is led there as a captive.

word_study.meaning: visit, attend to, care for, punish, muster, appoint; a semantically rich verb that can mean positive or negative visitation
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering notes that paqad's ambiguity is deliberate. In Genesis 21:1, 'the LORD visited Sarah,' referring to blessing. In Exodus 32:34, God says 'I will visit upon them their sin,' referring to punishment. Jeremiah's use leaves open whether God will eventually relieve Zedekiah's captivity or permanently punish it. This theological openness mirrors God's justice: judgment is real, but so is the possibility of eventual restoration or mercy.

word_study.meaning: prosper, succeed, make headway, breakthrough
word_study.significance: The root suggests achieving military objectives or breaking through obstacles. Jeremiah declares that Judean military efforts will not 'break through' the Babylonian siege. Every attempt to prosper militarily will fail. The same root appears in contexts of successful campaigns (Deuteronomy 29:23: 'the LORD would not prosper to pardon them') and successful prophecy (Joshua 1:8: 'that thou mayest prosper'). Here it means: you will not achieve military success.

cross_references.connection: Jeremiah earlier advised Zedekiah that those who 'put their necks under the yoke of Babylon' would live, while those who fight would die—the same message now being imprisoned for.

The historical fulfillment of 'until I visit him': Evil-Merodach, king of Babylon, eventually released Zedekiah from captivity and treated him kindly in his old age, fulfilling the open-ended 'visit' promised in this verse.
Nebuchadnezzar's treatment of Jeremiah after the fall of Jerusalem, giving him the choice to stay or go—divine protection for the faithful prophet contrasts with judgment on the unfaithful king.
Nephi's statement that his people would not prosper without God's favor mirrors the principle here: military might without God's support cannot prosper.

commentary.historical_context: Archaeological evidence from Jerusalem shows that the city's water systems were designed to withstand siege, and there is evidence of preparation for conflict. However, the Babylonian military capability and numerical superiority were overwhelming. Zedekiah's final attempt to break through the siege (recounted in 2 Kings 25:4) failed; he could not 'prosper' militarily. The Babylonian Chronicle records Nebuchadnezzar's campaigns and the subjugation of Jerusalem. The mention of Babylon as the destination confirms historical reality: captured Judean royalty were transported to Babylon, not held locally. The reference to Evil-Merodach (2 Kings 25:27-30) is confirmed in Babylonian records; this king did indeed show leniency to certain captive foreign rulers. The historical accuracy of these details validates the precision of Jeremiah's prophecy. The phrase 'though ye fight' acknowledges that Judean soldiers would indeed attempt to break the siege—Jeremiah does not deny their courage, only the futility of their effort without God's favor.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Helaman 4:11-15 records that the Nephites, once they abandoned the Lord, could not prosper militarily despite their military strength: 'The strength of the Nephites did depend upon their righteousness.' Similarly, the Amalekites 'could not prosper...for the Lord was with the Nephites.' The principle is identical: military success depends on God's favor, not on weaponry or tactics alone.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 98:36-37 teaches: 'I the Lord will fight your battles...that ye may prevail.' Without the Lord's active engagement, prospering is impossible. The converse is taught here: the Chaldeans will prosper against Judah because God has determined it.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The principle of divine visitation (paqad) is central to covenant theology. God 'visits' His covenant people—sometimes with mercy, sometimes with judgment, but always with intention. The temple represents the place where this divine visitation is assured and renewed. Those outside covenant relationship, like Zedekiah in his rebellion, face visitation as judgment.

commentary.christological_typology: Jesus taught that no amount of military or human might can prosper against God's will: 'He that taketh the sword shall perish with the sword' (Matthew 26:52). The principle of futile human resistance to divine intention applies universally. Jesus' declaration that His kingdom is 'not of this world' means that earthly military strength is irrelevant to spiritual reality. Zedekiah's failed military resistance prefigures all human attempts to resist God's purpose through force.
commentary.application: This verse teaches that planning and effort, while necessary, cannot guarantee success when we are working against God's will. The application is subtle but profound: it is possible to invest tremendous resources, courage, and strategic thinking in a course of action that cannot prosper because it contradicts God's intention. Zedekiah's military commanders were not cowards, nor were their strategies foolish in purely military terms; their effort failed because God had determined differently. For modern covenant members, this teaches discernment: we must ask not only 'Is this a good plan?' but also 'Is this aligned with God's will?' Effort without alignment cannot prosper. Conversely, small efforts aligned with God's will can achieve what massive efforts opposed to His will cannot. The message is not to be passive but to be discerning about the ends we pursue and to ensure they are God's ends, not merely our own.

text_kjv: And Jeremiah said, The word of the LORD came unto me, saying,

commentary.narrative:
Verse 6 is a narrative hinge. Up to this point, we have heard the editor's framing (verse 1) and the circumstances of Jeremiah's confinement (verses 2-3), followed by the content of his prophecy (verses 3-5). Now Jeremiah speaks for himself, in first person: 'The word of the LORD came unto me, saying.' This formula marks the transition from reported speech about Jeremiah to Jeremiah's own prophetic voice. The Hebrew davar-YHWH ('word of the LORD') is the authoritative marker of genuine revelation. What follows will not be Jeremiah's personal interpretation or political advice; it will be God's direct communication to the prophet.

This is a crucial moment in the chapter's structure. Verses 1-5 establish the historical context (siege, imprisonment, suppressed prophecy). Verse 6 signals that despite all constraints—despite imprisonment, despite the king's hostility, despite the nation's distress—the word of the Lord continues to come to His prophet. Jeremiah is not silenced. The confinement has not cut him off from revelation. In this transition from narrative context to prophetic utterance, we see the central claim of Jeremianic prophecy: divine word transcends human attempts to suppress it. The king tried to shut Jeremiah up; the word of the Lord opens his mouth and gives him words to speak.

word_study.meaning: word, speech, matter, thing; the substantive utterance of divine communication
word_study.significance: Davar is not merely linguistic; it carries the sense of God's active word or directive. In Genesis 1, God's dabar ('word') effects creation: 'Let there be light,' and light comes into being. Jeremiah's use of 'the word of the LORD came unto me' invokes this creative, causative power. The word that comes to the prophet is not passive information but active divine will.

word_study.meaning: come to pass, become, come, happen; the existential verb of becoming or occurring
word_study.significance: The phrase 'the word of the LORD came' uses hayah, suggesting that the word-event itself occurred, transpired, took place. It is not that Jeremiah thought about God's will or reached a conclusion; the word actively came to him. This emphasizes the initiative of God, not the prophet's reasoning or willfulness. The verb situates prophecy as an event, not merely a thought or emotion.

word_study.meaning: saying, to say; the infinitive form introducing quoted speech
word_study.significance: The phrase 'came...saying' indicates that the word of God was accompanied by intelligible speech content. What comes next (verses 7 onward) is the substance of what God 'said.' Leʾmor acts as the narrative bridge between the coming of the word and its specific content.

cross_references.connection: The opening of Jeremiah's call uses the identical formula: 'To whom the word of the LORD came in the days of Josiah,' establishing continuity in Jeremiah's prophetic authority across his entire ministry.
Another instance of 'the word of the LORD came unto me, saying,' marking the pattern by which individual prophetic utterances are introduced throughout the book.
The prophet Samuel receives God's word: 'Then came the word of the LORD unto Samuel,' showing that this formula for prophetic reception was standard across Israelite prophecy.
'What I the Lord have spoken, I have spoken,' teaches that divine utterance carries absolute authority regardless of the medium through which it comes—the principle Jeremiah exemplifies.

commentary.historical_context: The formula 'the word of the LORD came unto me' is attested in other Near Eastern prophet texts, including the Tell Deir Alla inscriptions (fragmentary texts mentioning a prophet Balaam receiving divine communication). The pattern of a prophet receiving communication and then conveying it to the people is consistent across ancient Near Eastern prophecy. However, the Israelite emphasis on prophetic words being preserved in written form (as exemplified by Jeremiah's scroll in chapter 36) distinguishes Israelite prophecy. The historical reality is that Jeremiah, imprisoned and politically marginalized, continued to receive divine communication and to record it. The fact that these prophecies and the accompanying narrative were preserved suggests that Jeremiah or his scribe (Baruch) made it a practice to document the word of the Lord as it came, even during confinement. This verse marks the point where we transition from the editor's historical summary to Jeremiah's first-person prophetic proclamation, a shift that reflects the actual composition process of the book.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Throughout the Book of Mormon, prophets are introduced with the phrase 'the word of the LORD came unto' them (e.g., Words of Mormon 1:10, 'And thus it is written: Now we see that when the Lamanites had heard this word'). While the phrasing differs slightly, the principle is identical: God's word comes to His chosen prophets, regardless of their circumstances. Mormon himself, writing as a captive and beaten man, records that 'the word of the Lord came unto me' (Mormon 1:15). The pattern bridges both ancient Israel and the Restoration.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 21:4 teaches: 'Wherefore, meaning the church, thou shalt give heed unto all his words and commandments which he shall give unto him as he receiveth them, walking in all holiness before me.' The Lord's word comes to the prophet, and the Church receives it through the prophet. This verse in Jeremiah exemplifies the mechanism: the word comes; the prophet speaks it; the people are accountable to receive it.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: In temple theology, 'the word of the Lord' represents the divine instruction given in sacred settings. Jeremiah's receipt of God's word, even while imprisoned and confined, suggests that the word is not limited to temple spaces but travels with the prophet. Modern temple ceremony emphasizes receiving God's word directly, a pattern Jeremiah models even in distress.

commentary.christological_typology: Jesus is presented in the Gospel of John as 'the Word' (logos)—God's ultimate utterance, God's final communication to humanity. 'In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God' (John 1:1). Jeremiah's entire ministry is a shadow of this reality: the prophet receives God's word and conveys it. Jesus is the Word made flesh, God's self-communication in personal form. Jeremiah's model of receiving and speaking divine word prefigures Jesus as the ultimate Prophet who speaks God's word directly.
commentary.application: This verse teaches that divine communication does not depend on institutional approval or physical freedom. Jeremiah, confined and opposed by authority, still receives the word of the Lord. The application for modern covenant members is that access to God's word is not determined by circumstances—not by imprisonment, marginalization, illness, or institutional hostility. We may receive divine guidance through prayer, through scripture, through the Holy Ghost, regardless of our circumstances. The word that comes to us may come in times of confinement or distress, in moments when we are isolated from community or support. The promise is that 'the word of the LORD' remains available to those who seek it. This is the foundation of personal revelation: the word of the Lord is not rationed by human authorities but is offered directly to all who have ears to hear. The application is both humbling and empowering: humbling because it means we cannot avoid accountability to God's word through institutional means, and empowering because it means we have direct access to divine instruction regardless of our circumstances.

text_kjv: Behold, Hanamel the son of Shallum thine uncle shall come unto thee, saying, Buy thee my field that is in Anathoth: for the right of redemption is thine to buy it.

commentary.narrative:
This verse opens with the word of the Lord coming to Jeremiah while he is imprisoned in the court of the guard—a location of confinement, not freedom. God is about to command Jeremiah to perform one of the most counterintuitive prophetic sign-acts in scripture. Hanamel, Jeremiah's cousin, will arrive with a business proposal: the sale of a field in Anathoth, Jeremiah's own hometown, located approximately three miles northeast of Jerusalem. Yet this is no ordinary real estate transaction. The Babylonian army surrounds Jerusalem; the city will fall within weeks. The field is in occupied or soon-to-be-occupied territory. By every rational measure, this purchase is madness.

But God is not speaking in the language of economics—He is speaking in the language of covenant and hope. The "right of redemption" (mishpat hage'ullah) is not a casual option; it is a binding legal and moral obligation grounded in Leviticus 25:25-28. When a family member must sell ancestral property due to poverty or distress, the nearest kinsman (the go'el) has the first right—and the sacred duty—to purchase it, keeping the land within the clan. This principle rests on the Hebrew understanding that land is not merely property; it is the tangible expression of God's covenant promise to Israel. Land cannot be permanently lost from a family; it must be redeemed. Jeremiah is the nearest eligible redeemer, and by divine design, this obligation falls to him in the very hour when redemption seems impossible.
commentary.historical_context: Anathoth was Jeremiah's native town (Jeremiah 1:1), one of the Levitical cities in the territory of Benjamin (Joshua 21:18). It lay in the path of the Babylonian siege; its fields would soon be part of the war zone. The purchase price of seventeen shekels of silver (verse 9) is extraordinarily low—roughly 3-4% of what prime land would fetch in normal times. This reflects the collapse of property values during military collapse. In ancient Near Eastern law, a field sale required multiple witnesses, written documentation, and often a sealed deed—all of which Jeremiah meticulously provides (verses 10-12). The dual-document system (sealed and open copies) is well attested in cuneiform legal archives from Mesopotamia and reflects standard practice in the ancient world. The transaction is not conducted in secret or by dubious means; it is performed in full public view, 'before all the Judeans sitting in the court of the guard.' This transforms a private family obligation into a public declaration.

word_study.meaning: The legal and moral right of the nearest kinsman (go'el) to reclaim family property that has been sold due to financial distress. This is not a charitable option but a binding obligation rooted in the principle that family land is inalienable under the covenant. The mishpat ('right, judgment, ordinance') is a formal legal status; the ge'ullah ('redemption, reclamation') is the act of restoring the land to family ownership.
word_study.significance: This term encodes the Hebrew theological understanding that land is sacred trust, not mere commodity. The go'el is not simply a buyer but a redeemer—one who restores what was lost. In this context, Jeremiah's purchase becomes a prophetic sign that despite Babylon's imminent conquest, God will eventually redeem and restore the land of Israel. The Covenant Rendering emphasizes that this obligation belongs to Jeremiah 'as next of kin,' highlighting the familial and covenantal dimension.

word_study.meaning: An open field, cultivated land, or territorial holding. In the context of Hebrew property law, a sadeh represents ancestral inheritance and covenant belonging—the tangible expression of God's promise to Abraham and his descendants.
word_study.significance: The field is not incidental detail but the center of the prophetic message. Jeremiah is being asked to invest his wealth in land that appears to be lost forever. This is not investment in the present regime but faith in God's future restoration.

word_study.meaning: A Levitical city in Benjamin, approximately 3 miles northeast of Jerusalem. It was Jeremiah's birthplace and home. The name likely derives from a Canaanite goddess name ('Anat) that was incorporated into Israelite geography.
word_study.significance: That the field is in Anathoth—Jeremiah's own town—makes the purchase deeply personal. Jeremiah is redeeming his own ancestral heritage at the moment when exile seems certain. The Levitical identity of the city also matters: Jeremiah is a priest-prophet, and his purchase reinforces the connection between prophetic ministry and the covenant land.

cross_references.connection: Establishes the law of redemption: when land is sold due to poverty, the nearest kinsman must have the right to redeem it. Jeremiah's transaction is the direct application of this Mosaic law in a moment of national crisis.
Identifies Jeremiah as 'of Anathoth,' establishing that this field is in his hometown and making the purchase a redemption of his own familial inheritance.
Anathoth is listed as one of the cities given to the Levites in the territory of Benjamin, reinforcing its religious and covenantal significance as Levitical property.

Elkanah, father of the prophet Samuel, is identified as 'of Ramathaim-zophim, of the hill country of Ephraim,' illustrating how the Old Testament identifies individuals by their ancestral towns and holdings—a cultural context that makes Jeremiah's Anathoth connection meaningful.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 37:12-13 describes how sacred records are preserved for future generations—similar to how the deed (verse 10-12) is sealed and preserved as evidence for a future restoration of the land. The principle that covenantal promises endure despite present calamity runs throughout the Book of Mormon, particularly in Nephi's teachings.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 101:76-80 explicitly connects the restoration of Zion to the restoration of the lands of the faithful. Joseph Smith's teachings on redemption and restoration echo Jeremiah's act—investing in the future kingdom despite present opposition and loss.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The redemption motif in this verse points to Christ as the ultimate Go'el (Redeemer). In Hebrew, the kinsman-redeemer who restores what is lost foreshadows the Messiah who redeems all humanity and restores the covenant relationship. The sealing of the deed (verse 10) also connects typologically to temple sealing practices that bind families and inheritances for eternity.

commentary.christological_typology: Jeremiah's role as go'el—the one who redeems the land and restores it to the family—prefigures Christ as the ultimate Redeemer (Go'el) of humanity. Just as Jeremiah purchases the field despite its apparent loss, Christ purchases redemption for all humanity despite sin and death. The Hebrew term ge'ullah ('redemption') appears in the Psalms and prophets as a messianic concept: God Himself is the Go'el of Israel (Isaiah 41:14, 43:14). Jeremiah embodies this redemptive principle in his sign-act.
commentary.application: This verse teaches that covenant obligations do not expire when circumstances become dire. Jeremiah's willingness to honor the redemption law despite the siege declares that faith in God's covenants transcends rational calculation. For modern believers, this raises a profound question: what covenants are we tempted to abandon because 'circumstances have changed'? The verse calls us to recognize that our commitments to family, to God's kingdom, and to the covenant—including sealing ordinances that bind us to our own spiritual families—are not investments in the present visible order but down payments on an eternal restoration. Like Jeremiah, we are called to act as if God's promises are more real than the current military/financial/relational siege around us.

text_kjv: So Hanamel mine uncle's son came to me in the court of the prison according to the word of the LORD, and said unto me, Buy my field, I pray thee, that is in Anathoth, which is in the country of Benjamin: for the right of inheritance is thine, and the redemption is thine; buy it for thyself. Then I knew that this was the word of the LORD.

commentary.narrative:
The fulfillment arrives with the precision of divine timing. Hanamel enters the court of the guard—the place of Jeremiah's imprisonment—exactly as God had foretold in verse 6 (which we skip here, but is the context). This is Jeremiah's moment of confirmation. The prophet had been given an extraordinary command in advance; now he watches it materialize word for word. He sees his cousin approaching; he hears the exact proposal; he realizes that this is no coincidence but divine orchestration. The phrase 'Then I knew that this was the word of the LORD' (va'eda ki devar-YHWH hu) marks Jeremiah's epistemological moment—the point where faith becomes certainty through fulfilled prediction.

Hanamel's proposition is legally precise. He acknowledges both of Jeremiah's rights: the 'right of inheritance' (mishpat hayyerushah) and the 'right of redemption' (hage'ullah). These are not identical. The inheritance right flows from family relationship; the redemption right is the legal obligation to restore alienated property. By naming both, Hanamel makes it clear that Jeremiah has no escape clause—he is both heir and redeemer. The land is specified again: Anathoth in Benjamin. This repetition creates a legal record and emphasizes that the transaction is grounded in solid legal title, not mere handshake. Yet what makes this moment extraordinary is the cognitive dissonance it creates: a man in prison, with his city under siege, is being asked to become a real estate investor in enemy-occupied territory. The 'word of the LORD' makes the irrational rational.
commentary.historical_context: The dual terminology—mishpat hayyerushah ('right of inheritance') and hage'ullah ('right of redemption')—reflects the sophisticated property law of ancient Israel. Inheritance passed automatically within families; redemption was the specific legal mechanism for recovering sold land. Ancient Near Eastern legal codes (such as the Code of Hammurabi and Hittite laws) contained similar provisions protecting family land from permanent alienation. The courtyard of the guard (chatzer hamattarah) was a standard feature of ancient fortified cities—a secure compound where the military commander maintained his headquarters and where prisoners of importance could be held under house arrest rather than in dungeons. That Hanamel can freely approach Jeremiah there suggests Jeremiah's status was that of an honorable detainee, not a criminal condemned to death. The siege circumstances make this detail significant: only a man of some standing in the community could arrange such a transaction during a blockade. The witnesses and documentation (verse 10) would have followed standard cuneiform contract practices, perhaps even using Aramaic alongside Hebrew.

word_study.meaning: The legal claim to familial property that passes by kinship. Unlike ge'ullah, which is the right to redeem alienated property, yerushah is the standing inheritance—what belongs to you by right of birth into the family line.
word_study.significance: This term emphasizes that Jeremiah's claim to the land is not charitable generosity on Hanamel's part but familial obligation. By invoking this right, Hanamel is saying: this land belongs to your family; I cannot sell it to an outsider; you must take it.

word_study.meaning: And I knew—the simple past tense of yada' ('to know'). But in Hebrew epistemology, 'knowing' is not abstract intellectual assent; it is the recognition of reality through direct experience. When Jeremiah 'knows,' he has moved from trusting God's word to witnessing God's fulfillment.
word_study.significance: This verb marks a pivot from faith to confirmation. God had spoken in verse 6 (not included here); Jeremiah had believed. Now, as the prediction materializes, his faith is vindicated. This is the Hebrew understanding of prophetic verification: the prophet's words are proven true by their fulfillment.

word_study.meaning: The utterance, command, or pronouncement of God. In Hebrew prophecy, devar-YHWH is the core formula for divine speech—it is not mere opinion or suggestion but the authoritative word of God that accomplishes what it declares.
word_study.significance: By recognizing this moment as devar-YHWH, Jeremiah is not just identifying a lucky coincidence but acknowledging that God is the author of history. The word God spoke has bent reality to its fulfillment.

cross_references.connection: God promised to deliver Jeremiah out of the hands of the wicked; the accurate fulfillment of this land-purchase prophecy demonstrates that God keeps His word even when circumstances appear to contradict it.

The word of the LORD comes to Elijah not in the earthquake or fire but in 'a still small voice'—similarly, God's word to Jeremiah about Hanamel's visit was a quiet, specific, fulfillable prophecy that confirmed God's presence in the midst of chaos.
The test of a true prophet is that his words come to pass. Jeremiah's recognition that God's prediction about Hanamel has materialized exactly confirms his prophetic office.

Alma recognizes through revelation that the Lamanites have taken captives and departed; he responds with faith in God's word. Like Jeremiah, Alma moves from trusting the word to witnessing its fulfillment.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Nephi's experience in 1 Nephi 3:7 ('I will go and do the things which the Lord hath commanded') embodies the same principle: the faithful servant acts on God's word before circumstances vindicate it. When Nephi obtains the plates, he receives confirmation that God's word was true. Alma the Younger's conversion (Mosiah 27) involves a dramatic reversal where what seemed impossible becomes necessary.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 1:37-38 declares that 'all the prophets since the beginning...have testified of me' and that 'the words of the Lord shall all be fulfilled.' This verse exemplifies that principle: God's specific word about Hanamel's approach fulfills exactly as spoken.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The sealing/validation theme resonates with temple practice: just as Jeremiah's recognition of God's word is a personal seal of authenticity, temple covenants are sealed by the Holy Ghost, making them certain even in a world of uncertainty.

commentary.christological_typology: Jeremiah's recognition that God's word has been fulfilled anticipates the deeper theme of fulfilled messianic prophecy. Just as specific details of the Anathoth transaction prove the veracity of God's word through Jeremiah, the specific details of Christ's birth, ministry, and resurrection (predicted in the Law and Prophets) prove His messianic identity. The prophet's reliability rests on God's faithfulness; Christ is the ultimate proof of that faithfulness.
commentary.application: In moments when we face siege—financial collapse, relational breakdown, health crisis, loss of faith—we often retreat into purely rational analysis. This verse invites us to consider what 'word of the LORD' we are called to act upon that appears to contradict circumstantial reality. Are we holding covenants, keeping promises, maintaining family bonds despite pressure that says to abandon them? The verification of God's word in Jeremiah's experience teaches that our faithfulness will be vindicated, not by immediate payoff but by the fulfillment of covenantal promises. Like Jeremiah, we may need to 'know that this is the word of the LORD' through the specific accuracy of God's dealings with us, not through the applause of observers.

text_kjv: And I bought the field of Hanameel my uncle's son, that was in Anathoth, and weighed him the money, even seventeen shekels of silver.

commentary.narrative:
Action follows recognition. Jeremiah moves from understanding to deed. He purchases the field; he weighs out the payment. The transaction is complete and irreversible. Seventeen shekels of silver—approximately seven ounces or 196 grams of precious metal—exchanges hands. On any objective analysis, this is a catastrophic financial decision. For context, Abraham paid four hundred shekels of silver for the cave of Machpelah (Genesis 23:15-16), a tomb site. By that standard, Jeremiah's seventeen shekels represents a price collapse of 95%. The field is worth almost nothing in the current economy because its utility value is destroyed by war.

Yet the very cheapness of the price serves as prophetic testimony. When the Babylonians depart and the siege is lifted—whenever that might be—these fields will regain their value. Their current worthlessness is temporary, a symptom of the crisis, not a permanent condition. By purchasing at the absolute nadir of the market, Jeremiah is making the boldest possible statement about God's promise: the land will be restored; exile will end; Jerusalem will be rebuilt. If he were merely buying a field for practical use, he would wait until prices recovered. But his purchase is not practical—it is prophetic. It is a sign, written in silver and title deed, that God has not abandoned His people or His covenant promise to the land.

The verb 'weighed' is also significant. Shekels were not yet coined in the shape we imagine; they were measured and weighed on balance scales. Each piece of silver had to be tested for purity and weight. This was laborious, deliberate, and formal—not a casual transaction but a ceremonial transfer of value.
commentary.historical_context:
The price depression during siege is historically attested. When cities faced military encirclement, property values collapsed catastrophically. Buyers could obtain land at a fraction of normal cost, but only those with liquid capital and extraordinary faith would invest. The siege of Jerusalem by Nebuchadnezzar lasted approximately eighteen months (beginning in 588 BCE). As months passed and conditions worsened, anyone who could leave left; those who remained faced starvation. Agricultural land outside the city walls was essentially worthless—it could not be cultivated, and the harvest could not be brought to market. The silver standard for measurement and value is consistent with 6th-century Judean practice. Coined currency was not yet established in the Levant; precious metals were weighed according to standardized shekels. The verb 'weighed' (shaqal) reflects this pre-monetary economy where merchant or money-changer carried scales to verify the purity and weight of silver bars and dust.

The specific price of seventeen shekels is historically plausible but remarkably low. This is not an error; it is evidence of the economic devastation of siege warfare. The field at Anathoth, under normal conditions, might have sold for several hundred shekels. Its reduction to seventeen shekels is a numerical testimony to the severity of Jeremiah's faithfulness: he invests everything at the worst possible moment.

word_study.meaning: To acquire, purchase, or obtain property through exchange or transfer. In legal contexts, qanah is the verb for a binding property transaction. It can also mean 'to create' or 'to bring into being' (as in Proverbs 8:22, where Wisdom says 'The LORD possessed me in the beginning of his way').
word_study.significance: The choice of qanah rather than a more tentative word emphasizes that this is a complete, binding transaction. Jeremiah is not leasing or conditionally acquiring; he is purchasing with full legal effect. The use of the same verb for 'creating' and 'purchasing' hints at a deeper covenant theme: Jeremiah is not just buying land; he is participating in the restoration of creation order.

word_study.meaning: To weigh, balance, or measure. In commercial contexts, shaqal refers to the act of placing precious metal on scales to verify its weight and purity before transfer. Metaphorically, it can mean to consider carefully or to assess value (as in Isaiah 40:15, 'the nations are as a drop of a bucket, and are counted as the small dust of the balance').
word_study.significance: The use of shaqal emphasizes the formality and deliberation of the transaction. This is not a rapid, casual exchange but a careful, measured transfer of value. The prophet 'weighs' the payment—he considers it, places it on scales, ensures accuracy. This mirrors the covenant principle of careful, deliberate commitment.

word_study.meaning: The exact amount of silver payment is specified: seventeen shekels. This is a remarkably low sum, reflecting the economic collapse during the siege. A shekel is a unit of weight, equivalent to approximately 11.5 grams; seventeen shekels is thus roughly 195 grams of silver—approximately 7 ounces.
word_study.significance: The precision of the number—seventeen, not 'a few shekels' or 'a small amount'—suggests that the Covenant Rendering or ancient scribe intended the number to be remembered. Seventeen is the gematria of the Hebrew word 'tov' (good); this is likely coincidental, but the precision of economic record-keeping matters in legal documentation. The low price is itself the prophecy: it announces that the land is worthless only because of the temporary crisis of siege, not because it has lost its covenant value.

cross_references.connection: Abraham paid four hundred shekels of silver for the cave of Machpelah, a burial site and covenant landmark. Jeremiah's seventeen shekels for productive land represents a 95% price collapse, dramatizing the catastrophic economic conditions of siege.

Buy the truth, and sell it not. While this verse uses qanah in a different sense (spiritual purchase), it echoes the principle that true value transcends market price—Jeremiah 'buys' the land not for its current market value but for its truth value as a covenant inheritance.

After exile, God promises to shake the heavens and earth and fill the temple with glory; He declares that 'the latter glory of this house shall be greater than the former.' Jeremiah's cheap purchase of land in Anathoth prefigures the restoration and revaluation of Judah's inheritance that Haggai later proclaims.

Isaiah describes God laying waste the earth and making it empty (the theme of siege and destruction that forms Jeremiah's context); yet Isaiah's larger message, like Jeremiah's act of purchase, is that desolation is not permanent.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 32:21 describes faith as 'not a perfect knowledge' but a willingness to experiment with the word: 'if ye will awake and arouse your faculties, even to an experiment upon my words.' Jeremiah's purchase is such an experiment—he is acting on God's word even though the experiment appears doomed to failure in earthly terms.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 63:24 teaches that 'he that hideth his talent...shall have taken away even that which he hath.' Conversely, the faithful servant who invests even when circumstances appear disastrous demonstrates the kind of stewardship the Lord commends. Jeremiah is not hiding his silver; he is investing it in covenant promise.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The buying and sealing of the deed (verses 10-12) parallels the temple principle of eternal sealing. Just as temple ordinances bind families through eternity despite death and earthly separation, Jeremiah's purchase binds him to the land despite Babylon and exile. The covenant is sealed and preserved.

commentary.christological_typology: Jeremiah's purchase of the field at ruined price prefigures Christ's redemptive purchase of humanity. In Isaiah 53:5, Christ 'was wounded for our transgressions'; He 'buys' us at the price of His own life. The cheapness of the field's price (reflecting its apparent worthlessness) mirrors humanity's condition in sin—we appear worthless by the world's standard, yet Christ values us enough to pay the ultimate price. Just as Jeremiah's silver purchases Anathoth for restoration, Christ's blood purchases redemption for all humanity.
commentary.application: This verse confronts us with the question: what am I willing to invest in when the market—including the market of social opinion, economic logic, and visible probability—declares an investment worthless? Jeremiah puts his capital into land that will not yield harvest for years, in a city that will be destroyed, under a government that will fall. Yet he does it because God has spoken. For modern believers, this might translate to: Are we willing to invest in family covenants when divorce appears economically advantageous? Are we willing to invest in missionary work, in charitable service, in temple attendance, in priesthood duty when the culture declares these things valueless? Jeremiah's purchase teaches that true value is not determined by market price but by covenant promise. Those willing to 'buy' at the lowest point—when faith is hardest and the world's judgment most severe—participate in God's restoration and vindication of what the world declares worthless.

text_kjv: And I subscribed the evidence, and sealed it, and took witnesses, and weighed the money in the balances.

commentary.narrative:
The transaction moves from the exchange of goods to the legal formalization. Jeremiah signs the deed; he seals it; he summons witnesses; he completes the monetary transfer. Every element follows the established protocol of ancient property law. This is not a whispered back-room deal or an informal family arrangement; it is a public, documented, witnessed, and sealed transaction. The formal language—'subscribed,' 'sealed,' 'took witnesses,' 'weighed'—emphasizes the gravity and irreversibility of what is happening. Jeremiah is creating a legal record that will survive beyond the current crisis.

The verb 'subscribed' (kathav) means 'to write' or 'to draw up.' Jeremiah signs the sepher hamiqnah ('deed of purchase'). In the ancient world before widespread literacy, having the principal parties sign or mark a document was not the standard practice; instead, witnesses provided the legal authority. But Jeremiah's own signature adds a personal dimension—he is not merely assenting to a transaction but authoring it, taking personal responsibility for the covenant he is making with the land and with God. The sealing (chatam) involved pressing a cylinder seal or stamp into clay attached to the document. The impression of the seal served as an unforgeable signature—it was one of the earliest forms of authentication. Breaking the seal to tamper with the document would leave evidence of fraud. This dual practice—a sealed document alongside witnesses—created multiple layers of authentication and made the record virtually tamper-proof in the ancient legal context.

The witnesses (edim) serve a critical function. In a society without public notaries or centralized legal registries, witnesses were the custodians of legal truth. If disputes arose later, the witnesses could testify to the original transaction. By summoning witnesses to watch the signing, sealing, and weighing of money, Jeremiah ensures that his purchase has the maximum possible legal standing.
commentary.historical_context:
The practice of using sealed documents is extensively attested in ancient Near Eastern archives. Cuneiform documents from Mesopotamia, particularly from the Old Babylonian period (and extending into Jeremiah's era), often involved multiple copies and seals. Egyptian and Hittite contracts followed similar patterns. The dual-document system mentioned in verse 11—a sealed copy and an open copy—appears in multiple legal traditions. The sealed copy served as the authoritative, unalterable version; the open copy allowed stakeholders to review the terms without breaking the seal on the original. This is analogous to modern practice where a contract's original is preserved in secure storage while certified copies circulate for reference.

The courtyard setting (mentioned in verse 8 and implied here) means that the transaction occurred in a public, monitored space with potential witnesses all around. This added credibility and made secret later claims of duress or invalidity much harder to sustain. The formality of 'weighing the money in the balances' also reflects the economic reality: without coined money, the transaction required verification of the silver's weight and purity. This was not merely ceremonial; it was necessary commerce.

word_study.meaning: To write, draw up, record, or inscribe. In legal contexts, kathav refers to drafting or signing a legal document. The past tense form va'ektov indicates completed action—Jeremiah 'wrote' or 'signed' the deed.
word_study.significance: The use of kathav emphasizes that Jeremiah is not merely approving a document drafted by someone else; he is personally crafting or authenticating the legal record. This level of personal engagement reflects the seriousness of the covenant he is entering.

word_study.meaning: To seal, to close, to confirm. In property contexts, chatam refers to the act of pressing a seal (usually a cylinder seal or stamp) into soft clay attached to a document to authenticate it. Metaphorically, chatam can mean to confirm, ratify, or make permanent (as in Daniel 9:24, where the prophecy is 'sealed' or finalized).
word_study.significance: The sealing of a document was not merely decorative; it was the act that gave a document legal force and made it, in effect, unchangeable. To break the seal and alter the contents would be evidence of fraud. Jeremiah's sealing of the deed transforms it from a private agreement into a public, legally binding record.

word_study.meaning: A witness; one who sees, hears, or knows something and can attest to its truth. In legal contexts, edim are the authorized observers who authenticate transactions and can later testify to their validity.
word_study.significance: Witnesses in ancient legal proceedings were the equivalent of modern notarization. Their presence and willingness to attest to the transaction gave it legal credibility that would stand up in any future dispute. By bringing witnesses into the transaction, Jeremiah was creating a human chain of accountability stretching into the future.

word_study.term_english: weighed the money in the balances
word_study.meaning: To measure or verify the weight of the silver using balance scales (moznayim). The verb shaqal emphasizes careful measurement and verification; the noun moznaim refers to the mechanical balance scales used to weigh precious metals and goods.
word_study.significance: This action testifies to the economic reality of the transaction. The silver is not merely counted; it is weighed to verify both quantity and purity. The Covenant Rendering notes that 'silver was weighed out on scales rather than counted as coins'—this was standard 6th-century practice and adds historical authenticity to the narrative.

cross_references.connection: Boaz executes a kinsman-redeemer transaction for Ruth, calling witnesses and executing a property transfer with full legal formality. Like Jeremiah, Boaz signs and witnesses the deed, making his redemptive act legally binding and publicly acknowledged.

Abraham's purchase of the cave of Machpelah is conducted 'in the presence of all that went in at the gate of his city,' with the Hittite sellers 'answering' and witnesses present. The public, formal nature of Abraham's purchase parallels Jeremiah's documented transaction.

God declares His covenant with David: 'My covenant will I not break, nor alter the thing that is gone out of my lips.' Jeremiah's sealed deed mirrors the principle of covenants that cannot be broken or altered—the sealed document embodies that permanence.

The book sealed with seven seals that only Christ can open points to the principle of sealed documents that require authorized authority to unseal. Jeremiah's sealed deed will later be unsealed (presumably when the restoration comes) to serve as evidence of the covenant promise.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Nephi's account in 1 Nephi 5:10-14 describes Laban's 'records which contained a genealogy of my forefathers, and also the records of the Jews even from the beginning...even down to the commencement of the reign of Zedekiah.' Like Jeremiah's sealed deed, sacred records are preserved, witnessed, and protected to serve future generations. 3 Nephi 15:1-2 emphasizes the importance of written records as witness to truth.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 21:4-5 instructs the Saints to 'receive whatever counsel...from those whom I have appointed.' The sealed deed serves as a kind of covenant record, analogous to the 'sure word of prophecy' that guides the Church. D&C 128:8 speaks of 'records and promises' that endure beyond earthly existence.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The sealing of the deed parallels the principle of temple sealing. Just as Jeremiah's property transfer is made permanent and irrevocable through sealing, temple sealings bind families and covenants for time and all eternity. The witnesses in both cases testify to the binding nature of the commitment. The fact that the sealed document is preserved alongside an open copy (verse 11) mirrors the principle that some sacred covenants are sealed (private, binding, eternal) while others are openly witnessed and shared.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ Himself is the sealed testimony. In John 6:27, Jesus says, 'Labour not for the meat which perisheth, but for that meat which endureth unto everlasting life, which the Son of man shall give unto you: for him hath God the Father sealed.' Christ is the sealed document—authenticated by God the Father, witnessed by the Spirit, witnessed by countless saints, and ratified through His atonement. Just as Jeremiah's deed cannot be tampered with once sealed, Christ's redemption is a sealed covenant that stands eternally.
commentary.application: This verse teaches the importance of personal accountability and public witness in covenant-making. Jeremiah does not merely feel his commitment; he documents it, seals it, summons witnesses, and creates a record. For modern believers, this suggests that our covenants—marriage vows, baptismal covenants, temple sealings, mission commitments—are not private emotional experiences but documented, witnessed commitments before God and the community. We might ask: In what ways do I treat my covenants as sealed, irrevocable documents rather than tentative feelings? Am I willing to have witnesses to my commitments, or do I try to keep them private and reversible? Jeremiah's example encourages us to embrace the formality and public nature of our covenants, knowing that this formality strengthens our resolve and makes our commitment part of the covenant history of God's people.

text_kjv: So I took the evidence of the purchase, both that which was sealed according to the law and custom, and that which was open:

commentary.narrative:
