For Jeremiah to promise that Jerusalem would become renowned among 'all the nations of the earth' for its restoration was audacious: it claimed that God's power to restore exceeded His power to destroy, and that the testimony of that restoration would reverberate globally. The historical fulfillment, while partial (the restored Jerusalem of the Second Temple period was never a dominant geopolitical power), vindicated Jeremiah's vision: the Return became a powerful testimony to God's faithfulness. In the modern LDS context, the parallel holds: the restored Church's growth and witness among nations testifies to its truth in ways that internal debate cannot.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: 1 Nephi 14:13-14 describes the future state where the Church of the Lamb of God will grow and overcome all other nations and kingdoms — a latter-day echo of Jeremiah's vision that God's restored people will become a sign to all nations.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 65:2-6 describes Zion's role as a sign and witness to the nations, and as a place of gathering and power. The vision parallels Jeremiah's promise that Jerusalem's restoration will be renowned worldwide.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple is the 'name' or signature of God's covenant with a people. Jeremiah's promise that Jerusalem's name will become great is rooted in the promise of temple restoration (see Jeremiah 31:40). The Kirtland Temple dedication prayer (D&C 109) echoes this language of making the Lord's 'name' known among all people through the temple.

commentary.christological_typology: Jerusalem's transformation from ruined city to witness among nations prefigures the Exaltation of Christ. Just as Jerusalem, once humiliated and destroyed, becomes the center of a global witness, Christ, once crucified and seemingly defeated, becomes the foundation of all creation's redemption. The 'fear and trembling' of the nations echoes Philippians 2:10-11, where every nation and language acknowledges Christ's lordship. The restoration of Jerusalem is a type of the cosmic restoration that Christ will accomplish.
commentary.application: For modern covenant members, this verse teaches that personal and communal spiritual growth has a witness value beyond the individual. Your repentance, your family's faithfulness, your community's integrity — these become testimonies to others of God's power. The promise that Jerusalem's 'name' (reputation, essence) will be glorified applies to individuals and communities who genuinely submit to God's restoration. This counters shame and despair: what has been broken can become a beacon; what has failed can become a sign of God's power. In missionary work, in family reconciliation, in Church growth in various nations, Latter-day Saints see the fulfillment of this principle: the restored gospel's expansion among nations testifies to its truth.

text_kjv: Thus saith the LORD; Again there shall be heard in this place, which ye say shall be desolate without man and without beast, even in the cities of Judah, and in the streets of Jerusalem, that are desolate, without man, and without inhabitant, and without beast,

commentary.narrative:
This verse quotes the people's own despairing words back to them — a rhetorical technique Jeremiah uses throughout the book. The people have declared that the land will remain charev ('desolate, waste') forever, emptied of human life and animal life alike. The threefold repetition of me'ein ('without, void of') — 'without person, without inhabitant, without animal' — hammers the totality of perceived desolation. This exact formula had appeared in Jeremiah 32:43 as a divine judgment, a threat of complete abandonment. Now, that very formula is quoted only to be inverted.

The rhetorical structure is profound: God does not simply reassure the people; He enters into their despair, quotes their diagnosis of hopelessness back to them, and then pronounces its reversal. This is a stylistic technique of prophetic authority — the prophet does not minimize the people's fear but acknowledges its foundation in real devastation, then shatters it with a counterword. The promise is not that the devastation did not happen (it did) but that it will not be final. The land will again be alive — not merely inhabited but filled with the sounds and activity of human and animal life.

word_study.meaning: From charav (חרב), meaning 'to lie waste, be ruined, become desolate.' The root carries the sense of devastation and emptiness — a place devoid of its former vitality. This is the same root used for the destruction of the temple and the ruin of Jerusalem.
word_study.significance: The use of charev connects this verse to the actual destruction. Jeremiah is not speaking theoretically about hypothetical ruin; he is addressing the real, present devastation that the people are experiencing as Jerusalem is besieged and destroyed. The promise targets their specific anguish.

word_study.meaning: From ain (אין), meaning 'to be nothing, not exist, be absent.' Me'ein means 'from the non-existence of,' i.e., 'utterly lacking, completely devoid.' The triple repetition of me'ein in this verse creates a cascading emphasis on total absence.
word_study.significance: The theological weight of 'without' language is enormous in Jeremiah. Emptiness is the opposite of God's creative power. Yet the promise is that this emptiness will be filled — that 'without' will become 'with.'

word_study.meaning: From shamah (שׁמע), 'to hear, listen.' But here it means 'to be heard, to sound, to be audible.' The verse is not about the people listening but about sounds being produced — the land becoming alive with sound.
word_study.significance: The promise of restoration centers on sound, on vocal evidence of life. This prepares for verse 11, where sounds of joy, wedding celebrations, and thanksgiving will fill the restored city. The dead land will become vocal.

cross_references.connection: This earlier verse warns that the fields of Judah will become a wasteland, 'desolate without man or beast' — the exact formula quoted and inverted in verse 10.
The covenant curse in Deuteronomy warns that the land will become 'a burning wasteland, without inhabitant or animal' — the judgment formula that Jeremiah now promises will be reversed.
Isaiah promises that the waste places of Jerusalem will 'break forth together into singing' — a parallel vision of the desolate land becoming vocal with joy.

The Book of Mormon promises that the land of promise will be protected and preserved through the righteousness of God's people — reflecting the conditional nature of restoration through covenant faithfulness.

commentary.historical_context: The historical moment is crucial. This prophecy is delivered during the final siege of Jerusalem, when the devastation is not merely predicted but actively occurring. The people are experiencing the fulfillment of covenant curses: cities emptied, land stripped, temple burning. Jeremiah's quote of their despair — 'it will be desolate' — is not a misquotation but an accurate reflection of contemporary perception. Yet here, in the darkest moment, he pronounces that the devastation will not be eternal. This is consistent with the theological theme of Jeremiah's book: judgment is real and severe, but it is not final. God's discipline, while intense, serves restoration. The historical fulfillment, when the exiles did return (538 BCE onwards), vindicated this prophecy. The land that had seemed eternally empty was repopulated; the cities that lay in waste were rebuilt.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Nephi prophesies in 2 Nephi 6:13 that in the latter days, Jerusalem will be restored, its waste places rebuilt, and its inhabitants multiplied — a direct application of Jeremiah's promise to the latter-day covenant people.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 101:17-25 promises that the righteous will inherit the earth and that the desolate places of Zion will be rebuilt and clothed with glory. The promise here in Jeremiah is the foundation for the Restoration's vision of Zion.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The rebuilding of the temple (Zerubbabel's temple in 516 BCE, and later Herod's temple, and in LDS thought, the Salt Lake and other temples) represents the fulfillment of this promise. The temple is the vocal center of the restored land — the place where sounds of worship echo.

commentary.christological_typology: The resurrection of the land from desolation parallels Christ's resurrection from death. Just as Jerusalem was buried in ruin but raised to new life, Christ was laid in the tomb but raised on the third day. The promise that 'sounds will again be heard' in the devastated land prefigures the voice of Christ calling the dead to rise (John 5:28-29).
commentary.application: This verse speaks to moments when personal or spiritual desolation seems absolute and permanent. A broken marriage, a shattered testimony, a wayward child, a moral collapse — these can feel like the 'without inhabitant or animal' devastation of Judah. Yet Jeremiah testifies that God's judgment, however severe, is not final. The land can be restored. Life can return. The first step in restoration is the people's acknowledgment of the desolation — which is what happens in verse 10: the hopelessness is named. But the next step is God's counterword: 'Even though it is desolate now, it will not remain so.' This is the theology of repentance and recovery. For modern covenant members facing personal or ecclesiastical crises, Jeremiah promises that restoration is possible and that God is committed to rebuilding what was destroyed.

text_kjv: The voice of joy, and the voice of gladness, the voice of the bridegroom, and the voice of the bride, the voice of them that shall say, Praise the LORD of hosts: for the LORD is good; for his mercy endureth for ever: and of them that shall bring the sacrifice of praise into the house of the LORD. For I will cause to return the captivity of the land, as at the first, saith the LORD.

commentary.narrative:
This verse fills the desolate silence of verse 10 with a cascade of joyful sounds. Five times the phrase qol ('sound, voice') appears, creating an auditory symphony of restored life. The sounds listed — joy, gladness, bridegroom and bride, thanksgiving — form a comprehensive portrait of covenantal normalcy: family celebration, communal worship, sacrifice in the temple. The verse invokes one of Israel's most sacred liturgical phrases: 'Give thanks to the LORD of Hosts, for the LORD is good, for His faithful love endures forever' (ki tov YHWH, ki le'olam chasdo). This is the refrain of Psalm 136, the great thanksgiving psalm sung at temple festivals, and it appears in the historical record at moments of profound national restoration (2 Chronicles 5:13; Ezra 3:11 at the temple dedication).

The phrase 'faithful love endures forever' (le'olam chasdo) is theologically pivotal. Chesed — covenantal, steadfast love — is not emotion but commitment; olam ('forever') speaks to permanence and eternity. By placing this affirmation in the mouths of the restored community, Jeremiah asserts that God's chesed was operative even during the exile, even when it was invisible. The promise of the verse is not merely that Jerusalem will be repopulated but that the full rhythm of covenantal worship — sacrifice, gratitude, family life, community celebration — will resume. The restoration is not secular but sacred; it is the restoration of a people in right relationship with their God.

word_study.meaning: Qol means 'sound, voice, noise.' In Hebrew thought, a qol is not merely audible vibration; it carries intention and presence. God's own qol ('voice') speaks the cosmos into being (Genesis 1). Here, the sounds of joy become evidence of God's restorative presence.
word_study.significance: The fivefold repetition of qol creates a musical and liturgical effect. Jeremiah is not merely describing restoration but liturgically enacting it through the sounds of his words. This reflects the performative power of prophecy in Israel: the prophet's words participate in bringing about what they announce.

word_study.meaning: Chesed is the signature term of covenant theology in Israel. It denotes not mere kindness but binding loyalty — the faithfulness of one party to another under covenant obligation. Unlike English 'mercy,' which emphasizes pity or clemency, chesed emphasizes persistence and commitment. God's chesed toward Israel is His refusal to abandon the covenant despite Israel's repeated unfaithfulness.
word_study.significance: In the LDS tradition, chesed parallels the term 'mercy' as used in Alma 34:15-16 (the atonement provides both justice and mercy) and the 'lovingkindness' of D&C 88:40 (God's love fills all creation). The affirmation that chesed endures forever (le'olam) is the foundation of restoration theology: judgment passes, but God's covenantal commitment is eternal.

word_study.meaning: From olam (עולם), meaning 'eternal, forever, the distant future.' Le'olam means 'to forever, for eternity.' This is not mere duration but boundlessness — a commitment that transcends time and circumstance.
word_study.significance: The pairing of chesed with le'olam (faithful love + forever) is the kernel of Israel's hope theology. No matter what happens in history, God's fundamental commitment to His covenant people is unchanging. This appears verbatim in Psalm 136 and echoes throughout the Psalms.

word_study.meaning: From yadah (ידה), 'to praise, give thanks.' Todah is both the thanksgiving sacrifice (a specific offering prescribed in Leviticus 7:12-15) and the attitude of gratitude that accompanies it. The todah was not expiatory but celebratory — offered by someone already experiencing deliverance.
word_study.significance: The promise that the restored people will bring todah into the temple is promise not merely of survival but of joy. It is the sacrifice of those who have been saved and are expressing that salvation through worship. In the LDS tradition, sacrament and testimony meeting serve parallel functions.

cross_references.connection: Psalm 136 is built on the refrain 'for His faithful love endures forever' — the exact phrase Jeremiah quotes here, tying his promise to Israel's foundational worship tradition.

These historical passages record that when the temple was dedicated/rebuilt, the people sang 'The LORD is good, for His faithful love endures forever' — the historical fulfillment of Jeremiah's prophecy.
Earlier in Jeremiah, these verses warned that the sounds of joy and bride/bridegroom would cease as judgment; verse 11 reverses this curse entirely.
The Book of Mormon prophesies that in latter days, God's church will bring forth the joy of salvation and gather His people in rejoicing — a parallel to this vision of restored communal worship.
The Lord's promise to gather Israel includes the restoration of full temple worship and the singing of redemptive songs — a latter-day fulfillment of Jeremiah's restoration vision.

commentary.historical_context: The liturgical refrain 'for the LORD is good, for His faithful love endures forever' appears in the historical record at moments of covenant restoration. When Zerubbabel's temple was dedicated in 516 BCE, following the return from exile, Ezra 3:11 records that this exact phrase was sung. The author of Ezra was conscious of Jeremiah's prophecy and recorded the historical fulfillment. The Psalm 136 refrain was sung annually at the Feast of Tabernacles, Israel's great thanksgiving festival, connecting the promise of individual salvation to corporate communal celebration. In the context of ancient Near Eastern religious practice, the restoration of temple sacrifice and worship was not merely religious observance but the restoration of cosmic order — the resumption of the sacred relationship between heaven and earth through Israel's worship.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In 3 Nephi 5:20-26, Christ gathers the Nephite covenant people and they 'lift up their voices to the heavens and praise God' — a direct application of Jeremiah's promise of restored corporate worship. The pattern of gathering, cleansing, and joyful worship repeats across Restoration history.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 59:15-16 promises that 'the spirit of the saints shall rejoice' through gathered worship and commandment-keeping, echoing the vision of restoration through covenant. D&C 133:26-34 prophesies the gathering of Israel with singing and music — the Restoration's vision of the fulfillment of Jeremiah's promise.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The entire LDS temple endowment involves the restoration of worship and covenant relationship through ordinances. The promise of verse 11 — that the people will again bring todah (thanksgiving offerings) to the Lord's house and sing the songs of praise — is central to temple theology. The restoration of the temple in this dispensation fulfills Jeremiah's prophecy in the Latter-day context.

commentary.christological_typology: The restored community singing 'for the LORD is good, for His faithful love endures forever' prefigures the great multitude in Revelation 7:10 who cry out in a loud voice, 'Salvation belongs to our God' — the ultimate restoration of all peoples in worship before God's throne. Christ's atonement is the ultimate expression of chesed — the suffering servant's willingness to bear the burden of covenant judgment, making possible the restoration and eternal thanksgiving of His people.
commentary.application: For modern covenant members, verse 11 teaches that restoration is not merely structural (rebuilt cities, returned exiles) but deeply relational and joyful. It is the restoration of the capacity to celebrate, to worship, to express gratitude. Many who have experienced spiritual crisis or moral failure can relate to the silence of verses 7-10; the promise of verse 11 is that joy can return — not through denial of what was lost, but through the acknowledgment that God's faithful love endures forever and makes new joy possible. This verse also emphasizes that restored faith is not private but communal and vocal: it is expressed in gathering, in worship, in mutual witness. For families recovering from conflict, for communities healing from division, for individuals emerging from depression or shame, the promise of restored joy in communal worship addresses not just the fact of forgiveness but the emotional and relational healing that makes genuine celebration again possible. The todah offering—the sacrifice of thanksgiving—can only be offered by one who has already been saved. This means that the promise of verse 11 is not conditional on moral perfection but on the reality of experienced redemption.

text_kjv: Thus saith the LORD of hosts; Again in this place, which is desolate without man and without beast, and in all the cities thereof, shall be an habitation of shepherds causing their flocks to lie down.

commentary.narrative:
This verse completes the restoration promise by returning from the urban (Jerusalem, temple, worship) to the rural and pastoral. The desolate places that Jeremiah has thrice invoked as 'without man and without beast' will again become 'an habitation of shepherds.' This is not a retreat from civilization but its normalization: shepherds tending flocks in pastures represent the restoration of economic life, agricultural stability, and peaceful prosperity. The verb rabats ('to lie down, rest') suggests not mere existence but comfort and safety — animals at ease, without threat of predation or invasion.

The breadth of the promise — 'in all the cities thereof' — emphasizes that restoration is not limited to Jerusalem but extends throughout the land of Judah. Every city, every district will participate in the return of normal life. The shepherd imagery is particularly resonant in Israel's self-understanding: Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob were shepherds; David was a shepherd before becoming king; and Yahweh Himself is Israel's Shepherd (Psalm 23). Thus, the promise that shepherds will again inhabit the land is a promise that the covenantal order — the patriarchal blessing, the Davidic dynasty's foundation, God's care for His people — will be restored. The pastoral simplicity of verse 12 follows the liturgical grandeur of verse 11, suggesting that restoration encompasses all dimensions of human flourishing: worship and economics, city and countryside, the sacred and the ordinary.

word_study.meaning: From navah (נוה), meaning 'to dwell, settle, inhabit.' Neveh refers to a habitation, dwelling place, or pasture — particularly the place where flocks graze in peace. This is not merely a temporary shelter but an established dwelling.
word_study.significance: The promise is not merely that shepherds will pass through the land but that they will settle there, establish homes, build communities. Restoration entails not nomadic wandering but covenantal inhabitation — the renewal of God's promise to give the land to Israel.

word_study.meaning: From rabats (רבץ), meaning 'to lie down, recline, rest.' Animals that lie down are at ease, chewing cud, unafraid. The verb suggests complete comfort and safety.
word_study.significance: This verb appears in Psalm 23:2 ('He makes me lie down in green pastures') and describes the pastoral peace that is central to Israel's covenantal blessing. The restoration includes not just return but rest — the cessation of threat and warfare.

word_study.meaning: From ra'ah (רעה), 'to shepherd, feed, tend.' A ro'eh (shepherd) is both caretaker and protector of the flock. In Israel's thought, the shepherd metaphor extends from literal shepherding to kingship and to God's relationship with Israel.
word_study.significance: The restoration of shepherds is the restoration of a whole social and economic order. Shepherds represent livelihood, care, responsibility, and covenant relationship. The promise that shepherds will again inhabit the land is a promise that the covenantal order centered on care and fidelity will be restored.

word_study.meaning: Tso'n means 'flocks, herds' — usually sheep but can include goats. Flocks are the principal wealth and sustenance of pastoral peoples.
word_study.significance: The presence of flocks indicates economic recovery and prosperity. In ancient Israel, a man's wealth was measured in flocks and herds (see Abraham in Genesis 12:16, Job in Job 1:3). The restoration of flocks is the restoration of material blessing.

cross_references.connection: The psalmist celebrates the LORD as shepherd who 'makes me lie down in green pastures' — the same pastoral imagery of rest and covenant care that Jeremiah invokes here.
Micah prophesies that the Messianic shepherd will feed His flock in the strength of the LORD, leading to a peaceful restoration — a parallel vision of shepherd-care and restoration.
Zechariah includes pastoral imagery in his eschatological vision of restoration and covenant renewal — showing the persistence of shepherd symbolism in restoration theology.

Peter applies the shepherd metaphor to Christ: 'For you were straying like sheep, but have now returned to the Shepherd and Overseer of your souls' — the New Testament fulfillment of Israel's shepherd theology.
The Lord promises that the President of the Church will be a shepherd over the flock, and that God will support him — applying the shepherd-care theology to the Restoration's leadership structure.

commentary.historical_context: The pastoral imagery of verse 12 would have been immediately resonant to Jeremiah's audience. Pastoral life was not exotic or nostalgic but central to Judah's economy, even in the 6th century BCE. The promise that shepherds would again inhabit the land was a promise of economic recovery and the resumption of normal life. In the Judean highlands, sheep-herding was (and remains) a principal livelihood. The devastation of the siege meant not merely military defeat but economic collapse: flocks were requisitioned or slaughtered, pastures were trampled and burned, shepherds were killed or enslaved. The promise that 'shepherds will again inhabit all the cities' is thus a concrete promise of economic recovery. The historical fulfillment: after the return from exile, pastoral life did resume, and archaeological evidence suggests that the Judean highlands repopulated gradually with pastoral communities.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In 2 Nephi 26:18, Nephi prophesies that in latter days the Lord will 'feed my sheep and will lead them out' — applying the shepherd-care theology to the latter-day covenant people. The Book of Mormon repeatedly uses shepherd imagery for Christ's care over His people.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 21:4-6 applies the shepherd metaphor to Church leadership and promises divine support for those who shepherd the flock. More broadly, D&C 88 promises that in the Millennium, 'the beasts of the field and the fowls of the air shall declare His glory' and all creation will be at peace — the fulfillment of Jeremiah's vision of pastoral restoration.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: While verse 12 is not explicitly about temple worship, it is about covenantal relationship and God's care for His people — the foundation of temple theology. The shepherd metaphor undergirds the sacrament covenant (receiving Christ, the Good Shepherd) and the endowment's teaching about God's covenantal care.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ is explicitly identified as the Good Shepherd in John 10:11-14. The promise that shepherds will again inhabit the land and their flocks will lie down in peace (verse 12) prefigures Christ's role as Shepherd who gathers the scattered sheep and leads them to green pastures (Psalm 23; John 10). The restoration of shepherds to the land is typologically fulfilled in Christ's atonement, which enables the gathering and care of His flock. The imagery of rabats ('lying down in rest') echoes Hebrews 4:9-10, where Christ's rest becomes available to the faithful.
commentary.application: For modern covenant members, verse 12 teaches that spiritual restoration includes material stability and the recovery of livelihood. It counters the false spirituality that divorces salvation from economic flourishing. The promise that 'shepherds will inhabit all the cities' speaks to recovery at all levels: personal (spiritual healing), familial (restored relationships), communal (economic and social recovery), and national (peace and stability). The shepherd metaphor also addresses the need for care and guidance in recovery. One does not shepherd flocks alone; shepherding is a communal, caring activity. Thus, the promise of verse 12 includes the promise of communities rebuilt on patterns of mutual care. For those recovering from crisis, loss, or exile (whether literal or metaphorical), Jeremiah promises that the ordinary rhythms of life — work, livelihood, community, care for others — will be restored. This is not a promise of escape to some ethereal realm but of the restoration of normal, flourishing human life in right relationship with God and community. In the context of Church membership, this verse teaches that spiritual recovery often includes the recovery of purpose, work, and service to others — the restoration of the capacity to 'shepherd' and care for those in one's community.

text_kjv: In the cities of the mountains, in the cities of the vale, and in the cities of the south, and in the land of Benjamin, and in the places about Jerusalem, and in the cities of Judah, shall the flocks pass again under the hands of him that telleth them, saith the LORD.

commentary.narrative: This verse opens the section on restoration with a sweeping geographical survey that encompasses the entire territory of Judah: the hill country (central highlands), the Shephelah (lowland plateau between coast and highlands), the Negev (arid south), Benjamin (immediately north of Jerusalem), the environs of Jerusalem itself, and the cities of Judah proper. The promise that flocks will 'pass again under the hands of him that telleth them' is not merely a statement about resumed pastoral activity—it is a covenantal image invoking Leviticus 27:32, where every tenth animal passing under the shepherd's rod becomes sacred property belonging to the LORD. The verb 'pass' (עבר, 'abar) suggests not haphazard wandering but ordered movement, counted and accounted for. After the destruction of 586 BCE, when Jerusalem lay in ruins and the population was exiled, this image of orderly, countable flocks across every region of the homeland would have resonated as a promise that chaos would give way to restored order and divine oversight.

word_study.meaning: One who counts; the root (מנה, m-n-h) means to number, reckon, or apportion. It carries connotations of both inventory and ownership — to count implies knowing what belongs to you.
word_study.significance: The moneh is not a mere counter but a steward exercising divine authority over the flock. This echoes the shepherd imagery throughout Jeremiah, where care for the flock is a metaphor for proper governance and covenant faithfulness.

word_study.meaning: Plural of yad ('hand'), denoting physical agency, power, and control. Hands represent the active instrument of the shepherd's work.
word_study.significance: The phrase 'under the hands of' (עַל־יְדֵי, 'al yedei) suggests submission to authority, but also care and protection—the flock passes under the watchful oversight of one authorized to count and shepherd them.

word_study.meaning: The adverb od ('still, yet, again') combined with the verb 'abar ('pass, go through') emphasizes restoration—what happened before the exile will happen again. The repetition of the action signals return to normalcy.
word_study.significance: The word 'od' ('yet/again') recurs throughout Jeremiah 30–33 as a refrain of hope. It is the language of re-establishment, not novelty. God is not creating something new but restoring what was disrupted by judgment.

cross_references.connection: The allusion to every tenth animal passing under the rod as belonging to the LORD; Jeremiah's image invokes this law of sacred accounting to suggest that the restored flocks will be under divine scrutiny and care.
An earlier passage condemning shepherds who scatter the flock; this verse promises the reversal—flocks will be gathered and counted, implying restoration of righteous leadership.
Contemporary prophecy of God personally gathering his scattered sheep; like Jeremiah 33:13, it promises divine intervention in shepherding.
Part of the same restoration cycle (chs. 30–33), promising blessing in the land and renewed settlement patterns; verse 13 specifies the geographical scope of that return.

commentary.historical_context: The geographical enumeration—hill country, Shephelah, Negev, Benjamin, Jerusalem environs, and Judah's cities—forms a complete mental map of the Judean kingdom as it existed before the Babylonian siege. This was not mere poetic ornamentation but communicated to exiles a precise, recoverable geography. The mention of flocks passing under a counter's hand reflects the practical concern of a deportation-affected population: how would property be re-established, livestock tracked, and community resources restored? In the ancient Near East, a census of animals was a sign of stable rule; chaos and exile meant loss of such accounting. The promise of resumed pastoral order was thus a promise of restored sovereignty and social stability.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The image of a shepherd numbering and gathering flocks appears in Alma 5:38–40, where Alma applies the shepherd metaphor to spiritual leadership and the need for careful accountability of the covenant community. Like Jeremiah's promise, the Nephite context emphasizes the shepherd's responsibility to know and care for each member of the flock.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 50:40–42 describes the promise that the faithful will be 'crowned with honor and immortality and eternal life.' The restoration motif—return after exile, ordered community, divine oversight—parallels the Latter-day Saint vision of gathering and covenant community building.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The image of ordered, counted flocks under the shepherd's hand relates to the temple concept of a gathered, counted, sealed people. In LDS theology, the gathering of Israel and the sealing of families reflect a cosmic restoration—like Judah's promised return—where chaos gives way to divine order and the bonds of covenant are renewed.

commentary.christological_typology: The shepherd figure counting and caring for the flock points forward to Christ as the Good Shepherd (John 10:11–14), who knows his sheep by name and lays down his life for them. The promise that flocks will be ordered under a counter's hand anticipates the day when all of Christ's gathered, counted, and sealed covenant people will be organized in his fold, never again to be scattered or lost.
commentary.application: For modern covenant members, this verse invites reflection on what it means to be part of a counted, cared-for community. The imagery suggests that God's restoration does not leave individuals anonymous or adrift but involves direct, personal accountability—being 'known' by the shepherd. In practical terms, this speaks to the value of regular engagement with Church community, where members are genuinely known and their progress is tracked not as bureaucracy but as pastoral care. The promise of order after chaos also encourages patience during seasons of disruption or transition; the covenant God's pattern is to restore, to re-establish, and to return people to the security they knew.

text_kjv: Behold, the days come, saith the LORD, that I will perform that good thing which I have promised unto the house of Israel and to the house of Judah.

commentary.narrative: Verse 14 transitions from the image of restored pastoral life to an explicit declaration that God will 'perform' (קוּם, qum—literally, 'raise up' or 'establish') the 'good word' (הַדָּבָר הַטּוֹב, hadavar hatov) he has spoken. The verse does not specify which promises are meant, but its placement here points backward to chapters 30–32, where God detailed his intentions to restore the exiles, rebuild the land, re-establish the Davidic dynasty, and renew the covenant. The phrase 'the days come' (הִנֵּ֛ה יָמִ֥ים בָּאִ֖ים) is a prophetic formula introducing an eschatological moment—a turning point when what has been spoken will become concrete reality. Notably, this verse (along with vv. 15–26) is absent from the Septuagint (LXX), suggesting these verses may represent a later addition to the Hebrew text tradition, possibly added during or after the exile to reinforce the promise at a moment when it seemed most fragile. The inclusion in the Masoretic Text demonstrates the later community's conviction that this specific elaboration was necessary to secure the message of restoration.

word_study.meaning: First-person singular causative form of qum ('stand, rise, establish'). It means to raise up, set in place, bring to fulfillment. The hiphil form emphasizes God's active role in causing the promise to materialize.
word_study.significance: God does not merely announce a future state but actively 'establishes' or 'raises up' that state into reality. This verb appears repeatedly in restoration passages and emphasizes divine agency in rebuilding what has been destroyed.

word_study.meaning: Literally, 'the good word' or 'the good matter.' Davar ('word, matter, thing') here refers to God's spoken promise or decree. Tov ('good') emphasizes that what God promises is not merely functional but beneficent, designed for the well-being of the recipient.
word_study.significance: The phrase recalls the priestly benediction (Numbers 6:24–26) and suggests that God's word brings blessing and shalom. For an exiled community facing devastation, hearing God's promise itself characterized as 'good' would be deeply reassuring—this is not punitive or merely corrective but aimed at restoration and flourishing.

word_study.meaning: First-person singular perfect tense of davar ('speak, say'). The perfect aspect indicates a completed action in the past—the speaking has already occurred; now performance is imminent.
word_study.significance: The contrast between 'I have spoken' (past) and 'I will perform' (future) establishes the reliability of God's word. What he said still stands; now he will back it up with action. This was crucial for exiles who had experienced a catastrophic judgment that seemed to contradict earlier promises.

cross_references.connection: The immediately preceding restoration passage, which outlines specific promises about rebuilding houses, re-establishing Jerusalem, and renewing covenant relationship—these are the 'good words' now referenced in v. 14.

God tells young Jeremiah, 'Thou hast well seen: for I will hasten my word to perform it.' The same verb (natsar, 'watch over; perform') appears, connecting Jeremiah's initial calling to his final message of restoration.
Balaam's declaration that God is not a human who lies; 'hath he said, and shall he not do it?' This verse echoes the conviction that God's word cannot fail.
Part of the exilic prophecies assuring that God will 'raise up' Jerusalem and restore Judah; shares the same vocabulary of establishment (qum) and the same eschatological confidence.
In a Restoration-era parallel, the Lord affirms that his word will not pass away unfulfilled; every covenant word he utters will come to pass—echoing Jeremiah's promise structure.

commentary.historical_context: The absence of verses 14–26 from the Septuagint represents a significant text-critical issue. The LXX was translated from Hebrew manuscripts earlier than the Masoretic Text we possess; its omission of these verses suggests they may have been added to the Hebrew tradition during the later exilic or post-exilic period. However, scholars debate whether this was a later expansion addressing community needs or whether the LXX simply omitted material it considered redundant. What matters for the final canonical text is that the Masoretic tradition—which became authoritative for Judaism and is the basis for most English Bibles—includes these verses, treating them as an integral part of God's restoration promise. For an exilic community, hearing such reassurance repeatedly, in multiple formulations, would have been spiritually vital.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Nephi's vision of the last days (1 Nephi 13–14) includes promises of restoration after scattering; the phrase 'I will perform the good word which I have promised' parallels the Restoration message that God continues to keep his covenants despite periods of apostasy and judgment.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 29:7–11 contains Christ's promise to gather his people and perform his work in the latter days—echoing Jeremiah's formula of spoken promise followed by certain performance. The Restoration fundamentally rests on the conviction that God keeps his word across dispensations.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple is the place where covenants are made and sealed—where God's promises are formally affirmed. The Latter-day Saint concept of 'sealing' (making promises permanent, unchangeable) reflects this Old Testament conviction that God's word, once spoken, will be performed.

commentary.christological_typology: The pattern of God's spoken word preceding its performance is ultimately fulfilled in Christ, the Word (logos) who became flesh and performed the redemption promised since the beginning. The promise 'I will perform the good thing' anticipates Christ's own declaration at the cross: 'It is finished' (John 19:30)—the good word concerning redemption is now performed.
commentary.application: In an age of constant change and broken promises, this verse stands as a counter-cultural affirmation: God's word is not mere rhetoric but bound inevitably to performance. For covenant members experiencing periods of transition or uncertainty—whether personal trials or broader changes in the Church—this verse offers the same comfort it offered exiles: what God has promised, he will establish. The application is not passivity but confident trust. When you have received a promise from God (through scripture, prophetic counsel, or personal revelation), treat it as already established in principle, even if its full manifestation lies in the future.

text_kjv: In those days, and at that time, will I cause the Branch of righteousness to grow up unto David; and he shall execute judgment and righteousness in the land.

commentary.narrative: This verse pivots from general restoration to the specific promise of the Davidic 'branch'—a messianic figure. The phrase 'In those days, and at that time' (בַּיָּמִ֣ים הָהֵ֔ם וּבָעֵ֖ת הַהִ֑יא) formally marks the entrance of the eschatological moment when God's long-delayed promises will crystallize. The word 'branch' (צֶמַח, tsemach) employs an organic metaphor: just as a felled tree sends up a new living shoot, so the Davidic line—cut down by exile and apparent dynastic failure—will sprout again. The verb 'cause to grow' (אַצְמִ֥יחַ, atsmiyach, from the same root as tsemach) emphasizes divine agency; this is not natural political succession or the resumption of human rule, but God's direct intervention to produce a righteous ruler. The phrase 'branch of righteousness' (צֶמַח צְדָקָה, tsemach tsedaqah) recalls Jeremiah 23:5, where a 'righteous branch' (צֶמַח צַדִּיק, tsemach tsaddiq) was promised. The slight variation here—'branch of righteousness' rather than 'righteous branch'—may signal a subtle theological shift: in 23:5 the branch himself embodies righteousness; in 33:15 the branch produces and executes righteousness in the land, emphasizing the relational and cosmic implications of his rule. The promise that he 'shall execute judgment and righteousness' (יַעֲשֶׂה מִשְׁפָּט וּצְדָקָה, ya'aseh mishpat utzedaqah) echoes the covenant ideal that a king rules in perfect alignment with God's own justice and covenant faithfulness.

word_study.meaning: Literally, 'sprout' or 'shoot'—organic growth that emerges from a root system. The root (צ-מ-ח) conveys the idea of vegetation bursting forth from soil, often after a dormant period. In biblical usage, tsemach becomes a technical messianic title for a descendant of David who will restore righteous rule.
word_study.significance: The metaphor of a plant emerging from seemingly dead roots is profoundly consoling to an exilic community. The Davidic dynasty had seemingly ended with the fall of Jerusalem (586 BCE); here God promises that from the 'root' of Jesse or David, a new branch will grow. In rabbinic tradition, tsemach became a messianic designation. In the Restoration, the term appears in the Book of Mormon (Alma 16:12–14) and D&C context where Christ himself is understood as the fulfillment of this promise.

word_study.meaning: Often translated as 'righteousness' or 'justice,' but more precisely denotes right relationship, covenant faithfulness, and the restoration of proper order. It is not abstract moral perfection but relational integrity—governing in accordance with God's covenant and the proper ordering of creation.
word_study.significance: In Jeremiah's context, tsedaqah is what Judah's historical kings failed to maintain. The coming Davidic branch will embody what they did not: absolute alignment between personal character, kingly governance, and divine covenant. The Covenant Rendering's translation 'justice and righteousness' captures both aspects—both the adjudication function (justice) and the relational integrity (righteousness).

word_study.meaning: Hiphil (causative) form of tsemach, meaning 'I will cause to sprout' or 'I will make grow.' The causative voice emphasizes that this is God's direct action, not an emergent political development.
word_study.significance: The causative form is crucial. This ruler will not arise through human political maneuvering or military conquest but through God's intervention. The exiles would have understood this as a supernatural assurance—God himself will plant and nurture this branch.

word_study.meaning: A versatile verb meaning 'do, make, perform, execute.' In the context of judgment and righteousness, it denotes active governance—carrying out the functions of a ruler in alignment with divine covenant.
word_study.significance: The verb emphasizes that the coming Davidic branch will not merely possess righteousness as an internal quality but will actively perform, implement, and execute justice throughout the land. Righteousness will be incarnated in legal and political systems.

cross_references.connection: The earlier messianic promise using similar language; that passage names the branch 'The LORD Our Righteousness' (YHWH Tsidqenu). Verse 15 is a restatement and intensification of this foundational promise.

A shoot from the root of Jesse bearing the spirit of wisdom and understanding; like Jeremiah's branch, Isaiah's messianic figure judges with righteousness and equity. These are closely parallel messianic expectations from contemporaneous prophecy.

Later post-exilic prophecies also use 'Branch' as a messianic title. Zechariah 3:8 promises that God will bring forth his servant 'the Branch.' This indicates the term became a standard messianic designation in later Judaism.

The foundational Davidic covenant, which promised that God would establish David's throne forever and raise up his offspring. Jeremiah 33:15 reasserts this covenant in the face of apparent failure—it has not been annulled by exile.
In Nephite prophecy, Jesus is called 'the Son of David'—the messianic branch who will execute justice and righteousness. The Book of Mormon applies Jeremiah's language to Christ.

commentary.historical_context: The promise of a righteous Davidic branch would have had particular poignancy in the context of Judah's last kings. Zedekiah (597–586 BCE), the final Judean monarch before exile, was a weak ruler who vacillated between resistance to Babylon and submission, ultimately presiding over Jerusalem's catastrophic siege. His predecessor Jehoiakim had pursued exploitative policies and rebelled against Babylon. For an exiled community viewing these failures, the promise of a future branch who would 'execute judgment and righteousness' represented the reversal of everything their recent experience had taught them about failed governance. The metaphor of a 'branch' emerging from David's line also implicitly addressed the question: How can God's promise to David (2 Samuel 7) survive the apparent end of the monarchy? The answer: through a divinely-planted new shoot, not through any human continuation. This reflected a shift in later Jewish messianic expectation toward a more transcendent, divinely-initiated figure rather than a merely political king.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 7:10 explicitly identifies Jesus Christ as the Son of David who would be born of Mary and fulfill this prophecy: 'And behold, he shall be born of Mary, at Jerusalem which is the land of our forefathers, she being a virgin, a precious and chosen vessel.' The Book of Mormon applies Jeremiah's promise directly to Christ's birth and mission.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 113:1–6 contains a revelation where Joseph Smith explains Jeremiah 31:22 in connection with the righteous branch. While not directly addressing 33:15, the framework indicates the Restoration understood Old Testament messianic promises as pointing to Christ and being renewed in the latter-day covenant community.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple ordinances emphasize that Christ is the royal priesthood—both king and high priest. The promise of a righteous branch who executes judgment and righteousness points toward the temple's role as the place where divine justice and order are established on earth. In LDS theology, Christ's role extends to establishing the kingdom of God, which the temple symbolically represents.

commentary.christological_typology: This verse is directly messianic. The 'branch of righteousness' growing up unto David explicitly prefigures Christ, the ultimate son of David who will execute perfect justice and establish an everlasting kingdom. In Christian theology, Jeremiah 33:15–16 stands among the Old Testament's clearest predictions of Christ's coming. The imagery of organic growth from a dead root becomes, in Christian interpretation, the promise of resurrection and restoration through the Messiah. The phrase 'shall execute judgment and righteousness in the land' reaches its fullness when Christ sits at the right hand of God and all judgment is committed to him (John 5:22–27).
commentary.application: For modern covenant members, this verse offers a profound assurance about the nature of true leadership and authority. In a world of compromised leadership and political failure, the image of a ruler who 'executes judgment and righteousness' sets an ideal—one rooted not in human ambition but in divine calling. For those who hold priesthood authority in the Church, this verse invites reflection: Am I exercising authority as a 'branch' of Christ's own rule, or as an independent power? The promise also speaks to hope amid apparent endings. When personal circumstances feel as if a 'dynasty' has ended—a career, a relationship, a season of life—the image of a branch emerging from seemingly-dead roots invites trust that God's purposes are not thwarted by what appears final. New growth, new fruitfulness, is possible through God's direct action.

text_kjv: In those days shall Judah be saved, and Jerusalem shall dwell safely: and this is the name wherewith she shall be called, The LORD our righteousness.

commentary.narrative: Verse 16 shifts the focus from the messianic king (v. 15) to the corporate identity of the restored community. The phrase 'In those days' (בַּיָּמִ֣ים הָהֵ֔ים) places this promise in the same eschatological moment as the appearance of the righteous branch. 'Judah shall be saved' (תִּוָּשַׁ֖ע יְהוּדָ֑ה) uses the verb yasha, which means both 'to save' and 'to deliver/liberate'—Judah will be rescued from exile and destruction, restored to security and restored agency. Most strikingly, Jerusalem itself will be renamed. Instead of bearing a name tied to human geography or history, the city will be called 'The LORD Is Our Righteousness' (יְהוָ֥ה ׀ צִדְקֵֽנוּ, YHWH Tsidqenu). This is the same theophoric name (one incorporating the divine name YHWH) that was applied to the messianic king in Jeremiah 23:6. The shift from masculine (in 23:6, where the king is named YHWH Tsidqenu) to feminine (in 33:16, where Jerusalem is named YHWH Tsidqenu) is theologically stunning. The righteousness that was personified in the individual ruler now becomes the corporate identity of the city itself. This is not a transfer of the name but an expansion of its significance: righteousness becomes not merely the character of a single ruler but the defining reality of the entire restored community. Jerusalem's very identity, its raison d'être, becomes alignment with God's own righteousness. This recalls the Deuteronomic promise that God would place his name in a chosen place (Deuteronomy 12:5, 11, 21)—here, his name (his character, his nature, his righteousness) will dwell in Jerusalem.

word_study.meaning: Third-person feminine singular niphal (passive) form of yasha ('save, deliver, liberate'). The niphal voice implies both that salvation is being done to Judah (passively received) and that Judah itself becomes safe, secure, victorious.
word_study.significance: The verb yasha is fundamental to the theology of deliverance throughout Scripture. It is the root from which Yeshua (Jesus) and Yeshuah (salvation) derive. For an exiled people, the promise that Judah 'shall be saved' meant not merely personal survival but corporate restoration—a return to the status and security of a covenant people.

word_study.meaning: Tishkon (third-person feminine singular imperfect of shakan, 'to dwell, settle') combined with labetach ('in security, safely'). Shakan is the root from which Shekhinah (God's indwelling presence) derives.
word_study.significance: Jerusalem will not merely exist but will dwell 'in trust' or 'in security'—with the confidence that comes from divine protection. The use of shakan (which evokes Shekhinah) suggests that secure dwelling is possible because God's own presence guarantees it.

word_study.meaning: Third-person masculine singular imperfect of qara, 'to call, name.' In Hebrew, to 'call someone by a name' is to assign or proclaim their fundamental identity.
word_study.significance: A change of name in Scripture often signifies a fundamental identity shift (Abram to Abraham, Saul to Paul, Simon to Peter). Jerusalem's renaming as 'The LORD Is Our Righteousness' indicates that her identity, her covenant status, her raison d'être, is being fundamentally redefined through restoration.

word_study.meaning: A theophoric name literally meaning 'The LORD [Is] Our Righteousness.' It is a declarative name asserting that YHWH himself—not human effort, not institutional mechanisms, not historical precedent—is the source of the community's righteous standing and right order.
word_study.significance: This is one of the most profound names of God in Scripture. It asserts that righteousness (tsedaqah—relational integrity, covenant faithfulness, just order) is not something the people achieve but something God provides. For a community facing exile and judgment, being told that their identity is grounded in God's own righteousness (not their own failed works) would be both humbling and liberating. In Christian tradition, this name points to Christ as the source of the believer's righteousness (1 Corinthians 1:30; 2 Corinthians 5:21).

cross_references.connection: The same theophoric name YHWH Tsidqenu is applied to the messianic king. Verse 16's application of the name to Jerusalem itself represents an expansion or corporate application of what was first promised to the individual ruler.
The law that God would choose a place to put his name there. Jeremiah 33:16 fulfills this promise by declaring that God's name (his righteousness, his character) will dwell in Jerusalem.
A promise that Jerusalem will be called 'the city of righteousness' (ʿir hatsedaqah), a parallel vision of the restored city's identity centered on divine justice.

John's vision of the New Jerusalem coming down from heaven, where God dwells with humanity and 'will wipe away every tear'—a New Testament fulfillment of the Old Testament promise of a restored, covenant city where God's presence ensures righteousness and peace.

A Restoration-era revelation identifying the New Jerusalem mentioned in Revelation as Zion, to be built on the American continent. The LDS perspective locates the fulfillment of Jeremiah's promise in the latter-day gathering and establishment of God's kingdom.

commentary.historical_context: The renaming of Jerusalem as YHWH Tsidqenu would have been received by exiles as an extraordinary promise. In cuneiform records from Babylon, exiled Judeans appear in official registers under Babylonian names, stripped of their Hebrew identity. The promise that Jerusalem—the holy city now in ruins, its temple destroyed, its population deported—would not only be rebuilt but renamed with a theophoric name incorporating the divine identity was a radical assertion that exile was not permanent and that God's character and name were not diminished by imperial defeat. The renaming also implicitly addressed the repeated failure of Judah's historical kings to embody righteousness. Rather than trusting in human rulers to maintain justice (as the monarchy had promised), the restored community would ground its identity directly in God's own righteousness. This represented a theological paradigm shift—from hope placed in human institution to hope grounded in divine character.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon anticipates a gathered, covenant people with a restored identity. In 3 Nephi 20:22, Christ promises that the Father will give the Nephite remnant 'a new name' and establish them as his people. The LDS understanding of the latter-day gathering includes the idea of a people whose corporate identity is rooted in covenant with God—paralleling Jeremiah's vision of Jerusalem reidentified as the place where God's righteousness dwells.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 45:66–71 describes the New Jerusalem being built in the latter days and Christ dwelling with his people—echoing Jeremiah's promise that the city will be a place where divine righteousness is embodied and God's presence is manifest. The concept of Zion as a gathered, covenant people with a divinely-ordained identity appears throughout the D&C.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple is the place where God's name dwells (in ancient terminology, God would 'put his name' in the temple—cf. 2 Chronicles 6:14–15). Jeremiah 33:16's promise that Jerusalem will be called YHWH Tsidqenu recalls the temple as the site where God's name and character are most intensely present. In LDS theology, temples are places where covenant community is sealed and where God's presence is particularly manifest.

commentary.christological_typology: The corporate application of the name YHWH Tsidqenu ('The LORD Is Our Righteousness') prefigures the Church as the body of Christ. Just as Jerusalem becomes the bearer of a theophoric name pointing to divine righteousness, so the Church becomes 'the body of Christ' (1 Corinthians 12:27), deriving its identity not from its own merit but from Christ's perfect righteousness. The promise that the city will be renamed and resecured becomes, in Christian theology, the promise of a renovated people—first the Church in this age, ultimately the New Jerusalem (Revelation 21) where God's name and presence are fully realized among his people.
commentary.application: This verse invites a profound reorientation of identity for covenant members. Just as Jerusalem's restored identity was to be rooted not in political power or human achievement but in God's own righteousness, so modern disciples are invited to ground their identity in Christ's righteousness rather than in personal achievement, status, or history. The implications are liberating: You are not primarily your resume, your failures, your ethnic or economic category. Your identity—individually and corporately as a covenant community—is rooted in alignment with God's character and purposes. Practically, this means that renewal and rebirth are always possible. Just as Jerusalem, devastated and deported, was promised a new name and new identity, so anyone can step into a new covenant identity through genuine repentance and reconnection with God. The name YHWH Tsidqenu also challenges the Church itself: Are we, collectively, becoming a community where God's righteousness is visibly embodied? That requires not institutional perfection but authentic covenant alignment.

text_kjv: For thus saith the LORD; David shall never want a man to sit upon the throne of the house of Israel;

commentary.narrative: This verse explicitly restates and reinforces the eternal Davidic covenant. The introductory formula 'For thus saith the LORD' (כִּי־כֹ֖ה אָמַ֣ר יְהוָ֑ה, ki-koh amar YHWH) lends maximum rhetorical weight—this is not speculation or interpretation but a direct proclamation from God. The promise is categorical: 'David shall never want a man to sit upon the throne' (לֹֽא־יִכָּרֵ֣ת לְדָוִ֔ד אִ֕ישׁ יֹשֵׁ֖ב עַל־כִּסֵּ֥א בֵית־יִשְׂרָאֵֽל). The verb lo yikkaret ('will not be cut off') uses language of covenant—the same root (karat, 'to cut') used for 'cutting' a covenant appears here in the promise that the covenant line will not be severed. For an exilic community that had witnessed the deposition and death of the last Davidic king, Zedekiah, this promise was extraordinary. The dynasty appeared to be finished. Yet here God asserts with binding force that the Davidic line will never be permanently cut off—there will always be a successor, a continuation, a 'man' to sit on the throne. The phrase 'throne of the house of Israel' is significant; despite the exile of Judah, the promise extends to 'Israel,' invoking the broader covenant identity of the united people and God's purposes for all of Abraham's descendants. This verse grounds the following promise about the priesthood (v. 18) in the Davidic covenant tradition, establishing that both kingship and priesthood are eternal institutions that will survive exile and judgment.

word_study.meaning: Negative particle + third-person masculine singular niphal imperfect of karat ('to cut, cut off, make a covenant'). The construction means 'will not be cut off' or 'will never be lacking/absent.' Karat as a verb means to cut (used in cutting covenants, circumcision, etc.); the niphal voice indicates the passive state of being cut off.
word_study.significance: The choice of karat ('cut') is theologically loaded. Covenant-making in the ancient world involved cutting animals as a binding ritual. By using this verb, Jeremiah's promise invokes covenant language: the Davidic succession will not be broken because it is covenantally bound. The word appears in the earlier Davidic covenant (2 Samuel 7:15: 'My mercy shall not depart away from him'), reassuring that what God cut/established will not be cut/severed.

word_study.meaning: A single human male; often used for an individual person or heir. In royal succession contexts, it denotes a successor, an heir apparent.
word_study.significance: The promise is concrete and personal: not an abstract dynasty or institution, but a specific 'man'—a living person—will always occupy the throne. This suggests both continuity (the line is never extinct) and renewal (each generation brings a new individual to the throne).

word_study.meaning: Seat of authority; the specific place where a king sits to exercise judgment and rule. Metaphorically, it represents sovereignty, authority, and legitimate power.
word_study.significance: The throne is the symbol of continuity of kingship. As long as the throne is occupied, the dynasty endures. The promise ensures that the throne will never be empty—there will always be a legitimate Davidic heir to occupy it.

word_study.meaning: Literally, 'the house of Israel'; in political contexts, the kingdom or realm of Israel. Here it likely refers to the united people or to the full covenant people encompassing both north and south.
word_study.significance: Even though Jeremiah is addressing the Southern Kingdom of Judah in exile, the invocation of 'the house of Israel' extends the promise beyond the immediate political situation to the full scope of God's covenantal people. This suggests that the Davidic ruler, once restored, will reign over a reunited or fully restored Israel.

cross_references.connection: The foundational Davidic covenant in which God promised David an eternal dynasty and that he would not remove his mercy from David's line. Jeremiah 33:17 directly appeals to this earlier, authoritative covenant promise.

A psalm celebrating the Davidic covenant: 'I have made a covenant with my chosen. I have sworn unto David my servant: Thy seed will I establish forever.' Like Jeremiah, the Psalmist affirms the irrevocable nature of the Davidic promise.

The angel's announcement to Mary concerning Jesus: 'The Lord God shall give unto him the throne of his father David... and of his kingdom there will be no end.' The Davidic covenant is fulfilled in Christ.
A contemporary prophetic description of the coming child born to David's line, whose government and peace will increase forever—consonant with Jeremiah's promise of eternal Davidic succession.

Joseph Smith's revelation explaining Isaiah 52:1–2 in connection with the gathering and sealing of Israel—showing how the Restoration understood Old Testament tribal and dynastic promises in terms of latter-day covenant community.

commentary.historical_context: The promise in verse 17 directly countered the apparent finality of the Babylonian exile. In 597 and 586 BCE, Babylon deported Judean kings and nobility. The last Judean king, Zedekiah, was captured and blinded, and the Babylonian records indicate that subsequent Judean royalty was not restored under Babylonian rule. To an exilic community, the monarchy seemed genuinely extinct. However, Jeremiah's promise insisted that this apparent end was not final. The covenant God made with David (2 Samuel 7) was not annulled by military defeat. Some later Jewish sources indicate that Davidic descendants lived in Babylon (the Davidic line continued through the generations) and returned to Judea with the Persian restoration. In Christian theology, the promise found its ultimate fulfillment in Jesus Christ, understood as the final Davidic heir—the 'son of David' who, though his earthly kingdom was rejected, sits on an eternal throne at the right hand of God.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: 1 Nephi 13:37–42 and Alma 46:22–27 affirm that Christ is the 'son of David' and that the promises made to David are fulfilled in him. The Book of Mormon's witness to Christ as the Davidic heir strengthens the LDS understanding that Jeremiah's promise is ultimately messianic—not merely about human succession but about Christ's eternal reign.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 84:2–4 teaches that the City of Zion will be built as a place of refuge in the latter days; the establishment of this covenant city is linked to the restoration of the gospel and the gathering of Israel. While not explicitly about a Davidic king, the D&C reinforces that God's covenant purposes with Israel are not abandoned but renewed in the Restoration.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: In LDS doctrine, Christ holds all priestly and kingly power. The temple is the place where the covenant is sealed and where Christ's authority (both priestly and kingly) is most fully represented. The promise of eternal Davidic succession is ultimately a promise about Christ's eternal kingship, which is affirmed in temple ordinances and cosmology.

commentary.christological_typology: The Davidic covenant, as stated in 2 Samuel 7 and reiterated here in Jeremiah 33:17, is fundamentally messianic. All subsequent history is read through the lens of awaiting the ultimate Davidic heir—the Messiah who will reign eternally. In Christian tradition, Jesus Christ is this heir. The promise that a man will 'always' sit on David's throne reaches its complete fulfillment in Christ's resurrection, ascension, and eternal kingship. The 'throne' becomes not a physical seat in Jerusalem but Christ's seat at the right hand of God, from which he rules all creation. Hebrews 1:8 applies Psalm 45:6 ('Thy throne, O God, is for ever and ever') to Christ, making the promise of an eternal throne explicitly messianic.
commentary.application: For covenant members, this verse affirms the reliability of God's covenants. In an unstable world where institutions fail and leaders disappoint, Jeremiah's emphatic promise—'David shall never want a man to sit upon the throne'—stands as a counter-cultural assertion: God's word does not fail. More specifically, believers can trust that Christ's kingdom, though often invisible or opposed in this world, is eternally secure and will ultimately triumph. On a personal level, the promise can inspire confidence in one's own spiritual succession and legacy. Just as God promised David an unbroken line, so covenant members are invited to understand their children and descendants as part of an eternal covenant family. Faithfulness to covenant generates a line of righteous descendants (not mechanically, but as a promise rooted in God's faithfulness). Finally, the verse invites reflection on what kind of 'rulers' we become in our own lives and families. If Christ is the eternal Davidic heir who brings true justice and righteousness, how can we, as his disciples, embody righteous stewardship in the spheres we inhabit?

text_kjv: Neither shall the priests the Levites want a man before me to offer burnt offerings, and to kindle meat offerings, and to do sacrifice continually.

commentary.narrative: Verse 18 parallels and completes the promise of verse 17 by extending the covenant guarantee to the priesthood. Just as the Davidic kingship will never lack a successor, so the Levitical priesthood will never lack a minister. The phrase 'the priests the Levites' (הַכֹּהֲנִ֣ים הַלְוִיִּ֔ם, hakkohanim haleviyyim) uses a Deuteronomic designation identifying priests specifically as descendants of the tribe of Levi (cf. Deuteronomy 18:1). This formulation reflects a post-Deuteronomic understanding of priesthood that restricted full priestly functions to Levites and specifically to the descendants of Aaron. The promise that they will 'want' for no man (using the same construction as v. 17, lo yikkaret) means the priestly line will never be cut off. The specific functions listed—'to offer burnt offerings' (עֹ֧ד תַּעֲבֹ֛רְנָה, olah), 'to kindle meat offerings' (מַקְטִ֧יר מִנְחָ֛ה, maktir minchah), and 'to do sacrifice continually' (עֹ֥שֶׂה זֶּ֖בַח כָּל־הַיָּמִֽים, oseh zevach kol hayyamim)—emphasize the perpetual sacrificial function of the Temple. The olah (burnt offering) was entirely consumed on the altar as a complete offering to God; the minchah (grain offering) represented first fruits and agricultural produce; the zevach (fellowship or peace sacrifice) involved a shared meal where priest and worshiper ate together. The promise that these sacrifices will continue 'continually' (כָּל־הַיָּמִֽים, kol hayyamim—literally, 'all the days') suggests not sporadic religious observance but a permanent, uninterrupted covenant relationship maintained through priestly service. For an exiled community separated from the Temple, this promise was profoundly reassuring: the means of atonement, communion with God, and covenant renewal would not permanently disappear. The parallel structure of vv. 17–18 (both using lo yikkaret, both promising eternal continuation) establishes that kingship and priesthood, secular and sacred authority, are both permanent features of the restored covenant order.

word_study.meaning: A double designation: 'the priests, the Levites' or 'the Levitical priests.' Kohen ('priest') and Levi ('member of the tribe of Levi') are joined to specify that priestly authority is restricted to the tribe of Levi.
word_study.significance: This phrasing reflects the post-Deuteronomic tradition (Deuteronomy 17:8–9, 18:1–8) that centralized priestly authority in the Levitical tribe, specifically the house of Aaron. It represents a tightening of priestly qualification—not just anyone could serve as priest, but only a Levite by birth and proper lineage.

word_study.meaning: Literally, 'in front of me' or 'before my face.' In the Temple context, it denotes standing in God's presence, in the sacred space where the divine presence was manifest.
word_study.significance: The priesthood's function is to stand 'before me'—in God's presence—to perform the mediatorial service of sacrifice. This emphasizes the priest's role as one who approaches God on behalf of the people, a function that requires both ritual purity and divine authorization.

word_study.meaning: Literally, 'that which goes up'; the burnt offering was entirely consumed on the altar (hence 'goes up' as smoke), leaving nothing for human consumption. It represented complete dedication or atonement.
word_study.significance: The olah was the most fundamental sacrifice, offered daily (morning and evening) and at all major festivals. Its perpetual offering symbolized constant renewal of covenant and atonement. The promise of perpetual olah means the means of atonement will never cease.

word_study.meaning: Maktir is from katar ('to burn, cause smoke to rise'); minchah is a grain offering, often representing the firstfruits of harvest. To 'kindle the minchah' means to burn the portion designated for God on the altar.
word_study.significance: The minchah represented the people's gratitude for sustenance and their acknowledgment that all produce comes from God. Its perpetual offering symbolized continuous thanksgiving and covenant renewal.

word_study.meaning: To perform or execute sacrifice. Zevach can denote a fellowship offering (peace sacrifice) where the animal is shared between the altar, the priest, and the worshiper—a sacrificial meal establishing covenant communion.
word_study.significance: Unlike the olah (entirely consumed) or minchah (grain), the zevach allowed for a shared meal, emphasizing the relational, communal aspect of covenant. The promise of perpetual zevach guarantees not just formal ritual but ongoing community and communion with God.

word_study.meaning: Literally, 'all the days'; denotes perpetuity or constant, uninterrupted duration.
word_study.significance: The phrase emphasizes that priestly service is not intermittent or subject to interruption but permanent and unbroken. For an exiled community separated from the Temple, this promise of eternal priestly function would be deeply comforting.

cross_references.connection: Establishes the Levitical priesthood and their right to Temple service and support; Jeremiah 33:18 assumes this Deuteronomic framework and promises its perpetuation.
Describes the daily burnt offerings in the Temple—the olah offered morning and evening. Jeremiah's promise of perpetual sacrifice echoes this foundational covenant regulation.

A later post-exilic prophecy envisioning the purified, renewed priesthood offering acceptable sacrifices to the LORD. Like Jeremiah, Malachi promises the continuation and purification of priestly service.

Contrasts the Levitical priesthood (with many priests because death prevented continuity) with Christ's eternal priesthood. The passage uses Jeremiah's premise about priestly succession to argue for Christ's superiority.

A Restoration revelation asserting that the priesthood continues 'even as it was with Adam,' affirming an eternal continuity of priestly authority. Like Jeremiah, the D&C grounds the priesthood in God's unbreakable covenant.

commentary.historical_context: For an exiled Judean community in Babylon (586–539 BCE), separated from Jerusalem and its Temple, the promise of perpetual priestly service was extraordinary. The Temple lay in ruins; sacrifices had ceased; the priestly apparatus was disrupted. Babylonian records show that priests (as well as other skilled professionals) were among those deported. Yet Jeremiah promises that priestly succession will not be permanently broken—that a 'man' will always be available to perform the sacrificial service. Historical records indicate that when the exiles returned under Persian permission (ca. 539 BCE), priestly leadership was indeed restored, and the rebuilt Temple reestablished the sacrificial service. This might be understood as historical fulfillment of Jeremiah's promise. Later Jewish and Christian interpretation saw deeper significance in this passage: rabbinic thought understood it as a promise of perpetual priestly function even without a Temple, and Christian tradition understood it as pointing to Christ as the eternal High Priest whose sacrifice supersedes all Temple sacrifices.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 13:1–19 teaches that the priesthood is eternal and that faithful men in all ages hold authority to perform sacred functions. The Book of Mormon affirms that priesthood authority is divinely conserved across generations—paralleling Jeremiah's promise that the Levitical priesthood will not be severed.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 84:33–34 teaches that the priesthood is 'after the order of the Son of God,' and that the power thereof 'continues in the church of God in all generations.' This directly echoes Jeremiah's promise of priestly perpetuity. D&C 127–128 affirms that saving ordinances are necessary in all dispensations, grounding the practice in the same logic of perpetual priesthood that Jeremiah invokes.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The promise of perpetual priestly service and sacrifice directly connects to the temple. In LDS theology, the temple is the place where covenant ordinances are performed by those holding priesthood authority. The promise that sacrifices will continue 'all the days' is fulfilled, in LDS understanding, through the continuation of saving ordinances in the temple—with modern priesthood holders standing 'before the LORD' to perform sacred rites on behalf of the living and dead.

commentary.christological_typology: In Christian theology, Jeremiah 33:18's promise of perpetual priestly sacrifice finds its ultimate fulfillment in Christ. Hebrews 7–10 explicitly applies this framework: Christ is the eternal High Priest who offered the perfect, perpetual sacrifice (his own death) that supersedes and completes all Temple sacrifices. Hebrews 10:10–14 affirms that 'by one offering he hath perfected for ever them that are sanctified,' meaning Christ's single sacrifice accomplishes what no repetition of animal sacrifices could achieve. The promise that a priest will always stand before God is fulfilled in Christ, who intercedes eternally at the right hand of the Father (Hebrews 7:25). The three sacrifices named—olah (burnt), minchah (grain), zevach (fellowship)—collectively point to Christ's atoning sacrifice as the consummate expression of all Temple worship.
commentary.application: For modern covenant members, verse 18 affirms the reliability and permanence of priesthood authority. In an increasingly secular world where institutions are questioned and religious authority is challenged, Jeremiah's promise—restated through latter-day revelation in the D&C—insists that God's priesthood authority will not be withdrawn from the earth. For members who hold priesthood authority, this is both a solemn affirmation of role and a call to faithfulness. The priesthood exists to mediate between God and people, to perform ordinances, and to build up the covenant community. For all members, the promise ensures that the means of salvation and covenant communion will always be available. You are not living in an era abandoned by God but in a dispensation where priesthood authority is actively exercised. On a deeper level, the verse invites reflection on personal priesthood or covenant responsibility. Whether as a holder of formal priesthood office or as a covenant member, you are called to 'stand before the LORD' and perform sacred service—in your family, your community, your stewardship. This service, like the priestly service, is not temporary but constitutes an eternal calling grounded in God's unbreakable covenant.

text_kjv: And the word of the LORD came unto Jeremiah, saying,

commentary.narrative: This verse marks the opening of a new oracle unit within Jeremiah 33, introducing the theme that will dominate verses 19–26: the unbreakable nature of God's covenants with creation, with David's line, and with the Levitical priesthood. The formula 'the word of the LORD came to Jeremiah' is one of the most significant phrases in prophetic literature, signaling divine communication and the authority of what follows. In the context of Jeremiah's entire ministry—a ministry marked by rejection, siege, imprisonment, and the fall of Jerusalem—this fresh word is crucial. The people are in despair, questioning whether God has abandoned his promises. This oracle arrives to answer that question directly and powerfully.

word_study.meaning: word, utterance, matter, thing; can refer to a divine pronouncement or decree with creative force
