The act of public reading transforms the scroll from a private document into a corporate event—what might have been dismissed as Jeremiah's personal writing becomes a public reading with multiple witnesses. This audible proclamation might explain why the audience later reports the scroll's contents to the king: many people heard it and spread word of its message.
commentary.narrative_continued2: The instruction to read 'in the ears of all Judah that come out of their cities' (be'oznei kol-Yehudah ha'ba'im me'arehem) reveals the scroll's intended scope. It is not merely for Jerusalem's leadership but for the broadest possible audience—representatives from throughout the kingdom. By choosing a fasting day when people from provincial Judah would be present, God ensures that the message reaches beyond the capital's elite circles to the broader population. The scroll thus becomes an act of prophetic communication aimed at the entire nation, not just its rulers.

word_study.meaning: To read, call out, proclaim. The verb can mean silent reading but in context implies public proclamation—calling out loud enough for others to hear.
word_study.significance: Baruch is not to read quietly for his own benefit or small group but to proclaim audibly. The verb emphasizes the public, performative nature of the reading. The scroll becomes an oral event—spoken words from a written document.

word_study.meaning: In the ears of, in the hearing of. Literally 'in the ears of'—emphasizing audible reception.
word_study.significance: The idiom emphasizes that the proclamation is meant to be heard, received through hearing, and internalized. It is not merely vocal but must reach the audience's ears and penetrate their consciousness.

word_study.meaning: Day of fasting, a day of corporate fasting and prayer. Tsom refers to the practice of fasting, often connected to national prayer during crisis or annual observance.
word_study.significance: The TCR notes emphasize that fasting days drew large crowds in a heightened spiritual state. The choice of this moment maximizes both audience size and receptivity. People gathered for fasting were already contemplating national sin and divine judgment—the scroll's message aligns with their spiritual disposition.

word_study.meaning: House of the LORD, the temple. The sacred sanctuary.
word_study.significance: The temple is the divinely authorized space for proclamation. Reading the scroll there (despite Jeremiah's personal exclusion) grants it temple authority and associates it with covenant and divine presence.

word_study.meaning: From the mouth of, at the dictation of. The phrase establishes the source and chain of testimony.
word_study.significance: The phrase appears twice in this section (verses 4 and 6), emphasizing that the scroll contains God's words spoken through Jeremiah and recorded by Baruch. It is not human composition but divine utterance made permanent.

cross_references.connection: After the exile, Ezra 'read in the law of God distinctly, and gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading.' Like Baruch's reading of Jeremiah's scroll, public proclamation of God's word in the temple is meant to cause understanding and response.

Jesus 'stood up for to read' in the synagogue, unrolled the scroll of Isaiah, and read aloud to the congregation. The practice of public reading of prophetic scripture in a place of worship directly parallels Baruch's role.
King Josiah 'read in their ears all the words of the book of the covenant.' Public reading of God's word as a moment of covenant renewal and national response appears in multiple biblical contexts.

John promises blessing on 'he that readeth, and they that hear the words of this prophecy.' The New Testament maintains the practice and principle: prophecy meant to be read aloud and heard by the community.

Paul instructs: 'I charge you by the Lord that this epistle be read unto all the holy brethren.' Apostolic teaching, like prophetic scripture, is meant for public proclamation to the community of believers.

commentary.historical_context: Fasting in ancient Judah was both a private spiritual discipline and a corporate national practice. Public fasts were declared during national crises (drought, siege, international threat) or observed annually on significant dates (such as the Day of Atonement). A fasting day would draw substantial crowds to the temple—not just Jerusalem residents but pilgrims from surrounding towns and villages. The temple courts would be filled with suppliants engaged in prayer and intercession. This setting made it ideal for reaching the broadest audience with maximum receptivity. The practice of reading scripture aloud in the temple was common. The temple was not merely a place of sacrificial worship but also a center for teaching and proclamation. Baruch's task parallels the role of temple functionaries who read the Law and prophets to assembled crowds during festive occasions. By situating the scroll's reading during a national fast, God ensures both large numbers and spiritual openness.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Nephi describes how his record functions: 'And I do this for a wise purpose; for thus it whispereth me, according to the workings of the Spirit of the Lord which is in me' (2 Nephi 4:41). Like Baruch's public reading of Jeremiah's scroll, Nephi's record is meant to be read and heard by future generations. The Book of Mormon is the Restoration equivalent of Jeremiah's scroll—written prophecy meant for broad dissemination and public reception.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 19:36 states: 'His word ye shall receive, as if from mine own mouth.' Written revelation carries the same authority as direct divine speech when received by the faithful community. General Conference, where prophetic teachings are read aloud to the assembled Church, functions as a modern equivalent of Baruch's temple reading.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple setting for the scroll's reading emphasizes that testimony to God's word belongs in sacred space. In Latter-day Saint practice, temples are places where God's word is covenant-sealed and witnessed. The principle suggests that our most important testimonies should be shared in settings of spiritual seriousness and community gathering—family home evening, testimony meeting, temple worship—not merely in casual conversation.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ's mandate to His disciples—'Go ye therefore, and teach all nations' (Matthew 28:19)—parallels God's instruction to Baruch to read the scroll in the ears of all Judah. Both the scroll and the Great Commission aim for universal proclamation. Christ Himself reads scripture aloud in the synagogue (Luke 4), enacting the role Baruch performs. The resurrection and ascension make Christ physically unavailable (like Jeremiah's restriction from the temple), yet His message spreads more widely after His departure through written Gospels and apostolic testimony. The pattern—prophet restricted, message preserved in written form, disseminated through agents, reaching broader audience—flows from Jeremiah through Christ to the Restoration.
commentary.application: This verse highlights the power of strategic public witness. God does not command Baruch to whisper the scroll's contents in private conversations; He commands public proclamation in a setting where it will reach maximum audience with maximum receptivity. For modern disciples, this teaches the importance of seizing opportunities for public testimony and sharing faith in contexts where people are spiritually attentive. A formal testimony in a Church meeting reaches more hearts than private conversation; bearing testimony at a significant life moment (death, birth, marriage) reaches deeper; sharing faith during a time when someone is spiritually seeking reaches more effectively than random attempts. The emphasis on 'reading in the ears of' suggests that hearing testimony aloud—from a trusted witness—carries weight that silent reading or abstract truth cannot match. We live in an age of written communication, yet the verse reminds us that spoken testimony, especially in community settings, remains powerful. Missionary work, family home evening, one-on-one mentoring, public testimony in sacrament meeting—these are modern equivalents of Baruch reading the scroll aloud in the temple. The spiritual receptivity of the audience matters: people gathered for prayer and fasting are more likely to receive testimony than casual audiences. Finally, the instruction to reach 'all Judah that come out of their cities' teaches us that testimony should transcend local boundaries. Our witness should be shared broadly, with strangers, with those unlike us, and with those we might not naturally reach.

text_kjv: It may be they will present their supplication before the LORD, and will return every one from his evil way: for great is the anger and the fury that the LORD hath pronounced against this people.

commentary.narrative:
Jeremiah articulates the theological purpose for the entire scroll-reading enterprise: perhaps—just perhaps—if the people hear God's word read aloud, they might repent and escape the judgment he has announced. The word "perhaps" (ulai in Hebrew) is crucial; it signals not certainty but desperate hope. This is the same word God used in verse 3 when commissioning Jeremiah, suggesting that divine hope itself is conditional and dependent on human response. Jeremiah understands that the scroll exists not to condemn beyond possibility of mercy, but to create one final opening for repentance before judgment becomes irreversible.

The phrase "present their supplication before the LORD" uses the Hebrew techinnah, which comes from the root chanan meaning "to be gracious." A techinnah is not a demand but a plea that throws itself entirely on another's mercy—it acknowledges complete dependence on grace. This is what Jeremiah hopes will happen: that hearing the word will so convict the people that they will abandon their "evil way" (darka hara'ah) individually and collectively. The people are called to turn (shuv), a repentance that involves a complete reversal of direction and allegiance.

Jeremiah's reference to the "anger and fury" (af ve-chemah) that the Lord has "pronounced" (dibber) reminds the audience of what is at stake. This is not Jeremiah's personal anger but God's declared judgment—and it is great (gadol). The pairing of af (anger, literally "nose" in Hebrew, conveying the hot flaring of nostrils in anger) and chemah (fury, heat, the boiling intensity of divine wrath) describes the full spectrum of divine displeasure. The severity of what hangs over the people makes the urgency of the scroll-reading campaign comprehensible: this is a last chance, not a routine exhortation.

word_study.meaning: perhaps, it may be, possibly—a word expressing contingency and uncertain outcome. It admits both the possibility of repentance and the possibility of judgment.
word_study.significance: The same word appears in verse 3, where God uses it to express openness to the people's response. This verbal echo suggests that both divine initiative and human response are necessary for mercy to flow. The word embodies the theological realism of Jeremiah's message: God is not forcing repentance, only offering the conditions under which it becomes possible.

word_study.meaning: a plea for mercy, petition, earnest request—derived from chanan (to show grace, be gracious). A techinnah is fundamentally different from a demand; it acknowledges the supplicant's helplessness and dependence on the other's willingness to grant grace.
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering emphasizes 'plea for mercy' over the more neutral 'supplication,' capturing the nature of what Jeremiah hopes will occur: not bargaining or negotiation, but a throwing of oneself on God's mercy. This word choice shapes the entire enterprise—the scroll's purpose is to create conditions for genuine repentance, not mere compliance.

word_study.meaning: his evil way, path, or course of conduct—darak refers to the way one walks, travels, or lives; it is a metaphor for one's entire mode of life and allegiance. The singular 'his evil way' emphasizes individual responsibility even within collective judgment.
word_study.significance: The phrase calls for a turning away not from a single sin but from a fundamental orientation toward evil. This echoes covenant language (turning from the way that leads away from God) and anticipates New Testament concepts of metanoia (complete reversal of direction).

word_study.meaning: af (anger) literally refers to the nose or nostril, conveying the image of hot breath or flaring nostrils—a visceral expression of divine wrath. Chemah (fury, heat, rage) describes the intense burning quality of anger. Together, they describe the full spectrum of divine displeasure.
word_study.significance: These terms are paired frequently in biblical literature to express the totality and intensity of God's judgment. The use of both terms here emphasizes that this is not a mild disapproval but a comprehensive and serious judgment that demands response.

cross_references.connection: God uses the same word 'ulai' ('perhaps') to express the contingent hope that the people might repent and escape judgment, establishing that both divine initiative and human response are necessary for mercy.

Even though King Josiah turned from evil completely, God's anger toward Judah remained because of previous generations' sins—a reminder that individual repentance may not avert collective judgment, yet Jeremiah still appeals for it.
Another prophet calls the people to 'return...with all your heart' and appeals to God's graciousness and mercy, echoing Jeremiah's hope that repentance might turn away judgment.
Modern revelation teaches that when we repent of our sins and 'confess them,' God will forgive—a principle Jeremiah's scroll presupposes: repentance opens the door to divine mercy.

commentary.historical_context: The scroll is written in the fourth year of Jehoiakim (605 BCE, after the battle of Carchemish), when Babylonian threat was becoming increasingly urgent. Jeremiah's appeal assumes that the people still have time to change course—that God's judgment, while announced, remains conditional on response. In the context of ancient Near Eastern treaty language, judgment could be averted if the vassal people returned to covenant fidelity. Jeremiah frames the scroll-reading as an act of covenant renewal, appealing to the people's status as God's chosen people and reminding them that mercy remained available if they would turn.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon repeatedly illustrates the principle that prophets are sent to warn people of judgment, giving them opportunity to repent. King Benjamin's address (Mosiah 2-5) similarly seeks to turn hearts to righteous living by exposing the consequences of sin. Alma's mission to the Zoramites (Alma 31-35) shows a prophet grieving over a people's refusal to hear God's word despite earnest preaching.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 1:4-5 describes the Lord's purpose in giving latter-day revelation: 'Wherefore, I the Lord, knowing the calamity which should come upon the inhabitants of the earth, called upon my servant Joseph Smith, Jr., and spake unto him from heaven.' Like Jeremiah's scroll, modern revelation is offered as a merciful warning before judgment falls. D&C 112:24 teaches 'Let him that is unfaithful be removed, and let my servant John be appointed in his place'—suggesting that turning away from covenant is the true danger.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The scroll-reading in the temple setting (verse 10) echoes the principle that God's house is a place of covenant renewal and a locus where heaven speaks to earth. In modern temple language, covenants are presented as conditions for eternal life, requiring that we 'turn from' our evil ways—precisely Jeremiah's call.

commentary.christological_typology: Jeremiah's scroll, read aloud as a final appeal before judgment, prefigures the gospel of Jesus Christ—a word of judgment on sin but also an offer of mercy to all who turn and believe. Christ himself will become the final appeal, the living word that calls people to repentance (Hebrews 1:1-2). The contingency Jeremiah expresses ('perhaps they will...') is resolved in Christ, who makes repentance and return genuinely possible through atonement.
commentary.application: This verse challenges us to recognize that warning and appeal precede judgment. God does not punish without offering opportunity for change. When we encounter difficult scriptural messages or prophetic warnings in our own time, we should ask: Is God calling me to repent and turn from something? What 'evil way' in my own life needs to be abandoned? Like the people in Jeremiah's day, we live in a time of warning and opportunity—the question is whether we will hear and respond before the window of grace closes.

text_kjv: And Baruch the son of Neriah did according to all that Jeremiah the prophet commanded him, reading in the book the words of the LORD in the LORD'S house.

commentary.narrative:
The narrative moves from theological purpose (verse 7) to practical obedience (verse 8): Baruch performs exactly what Jeremiah has commanded. This verse establishes Baruch as the faithful instrument through whom the word will reach the people. The phrase "did according to all that Jeremiah the prophet commanded him" echoes covenant obedience language and recalls the Rechabites of the preceding chapter (35:10, 18), who also obeyed fully the commands of their father Jonadab. The connection is deliberate: both the Rechabites and Baruch serve as models of faithfulness in a culture of widespread disobedience.

Baruch's action is described as reading "the words of the LORD in the LORD'S house." The scroll contains divine speech—it is not Jeremiah's private opinion but YHWH's declared word. That it is read in the temple emphasizes the sacred nature of the act; the temple is the proper venue for encountering God's word, the place where heaven and earth intersect. The phrase "in the book" (ba-sepher) is significant: the scroll is not loose oracles or fragmentary utterances but an organized, written collection that can be read coherently to an audience. This represents a formal, authoritative presentation of God's word, not casual rumor or individual prophecy.

Jeremiah is called "the prophet" (ha-navi) here—the same title used to identify him as the authentic voice of God in verse 8b. This title matters: it distinguishes his words from the false prophets who proliferate in Jeremiah's day. Baruch is not merely Jeremiah's servant but the scribe of the prophet—one who preserves and transmits the prophet's words faithfully. The obedience described here becomes the model for scribal responsibility throughout Jewish tradition: the duty to preserve, transmit, and present divine words without alteration.

word_study.meaning: did/performed according to everything that—a phrase emphasizing complete, unqualified obedience. The word kekhol ('according to all') stresses comprehensiveness; nothing was omitted or modified.
word_study.significance: This is covenantal obedience language, echoed repeatedly in Scripture when servants or people are called to fulfill divine commands perfectly. The phrase creates an implicit comparison with those who do NOT obey 'according to all'—implicitly condemning the widespread partial obedience or disobedience of Judah.

word_study.meaning: the prophet—one who speaks for God, receives divine revelation, and communicates God's will to the people. The article 'the' (ha) suggests singularity and specificity: THE prophet, implying Jeremiah's unique role.
word_study.significance: The title 'ha-navi' distinguishes Jeremiah from false prophets and establishes his authority as the authentic conduit of God's word. In the context of Jeremiah's disputes with false prophets throughout the book, this title is a claim about legitimacy and truth.

word_study.meaning: the words/utterances of the LORD—YHWH's speech, commands, and revealed will. These are not human words attributed to God but the direct speech of the covenant God.
word_study.significance: This phrase appears dozens of times in the Hebrew Bible and designates Scripture as authoritative divine speech. The scroll Baruch reads is not commentary or interpretation but the words of God themselves—this is why it carries such power and why its rejection or destruction becomes so consequential.

word_study.meaning: the house of the LORD—the Jerusalem temple, the central sanctuary where God's presence dwells and where covenant was renewed, sacrifices offered, and God's word encountered.
word_study.significance: The temple as the venue for reading God's word emphasizes that this is not a private or marginal act but a central religious action. The temple is where the community gathers and where God's will is most directly accessible.

cross_references.connection: The Rechabites also obey 'according to all that' their father Jonadab commanded them, creating a literary and moral parallel: both Baruch and the Rechabites exemplify faithful obedience in an unfaithful generation.

Moses promises that God will raise up a prophet like himself; the standard for recognizing a true prophet is that God puts his words in the prophet's mouth—exactly what Jeremiah claims and what his words in the scroll represent.
Samuel tells Saul 'to obey is better than sacrifice'—a principle embodied in Baruch's obedience, which requires no elaborate ritual but simple faithfulness to the prophet's command.

Paul instructs Timothy to entrust what he has heard to 'faithful men who will be able to teach others also'—a New Testament principle of faithful transmission of God's word that Baruch exemplifies in his scribal role.

Modern revelation establishes that the Lord's servant (in this case, the prophet) speaks the words of the Lord, and the people should 'hear him as if from my own mouth'—a principle that authorizes Jeremiah's words as divine and validates Baruch's faithful transmission.

commentary.historical_context: Baruch son of Neriah is a historical figure attested in extra-biblical sources. He came from a prominent Judean family with administrative connections (his brother Seraiah held high office, Jeremiah 51:59). Scribes in the ancient world were not merely copyists but trusted officials who preserved, transmitted, and sometimes interpreted important texts. Baruch's role as Jeremiah's scribe placed him in the dangerous position of being associated with an unpopular prophet—a position that required courage and conviction. The action described here (reading in the temple) was itself a deliberate, public act of advocacy that marked Baruch as aligned with Jeremiah's message.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Nephi serves as a faithful transmitter of God's word, writing on plates and preserving records for future generations (1 Nephi 19:1-6). Like Baruch, Nephi is called to preserve and transmit prophetic words, and his obedience ensures that God's word survives and reaches those who will receive it.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 21:4-6 establishes the principle of faithful transmission: 'Wherefore, meaning the church, thou shalt give heed unto all his words and commandments which he shall give unto you as he receiveth them, walking in all holiness before me.' Baruch's complete obedience ('according to all that Jeremiah commanded') models this principle of receiving and transmitting revelation without alteration.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The reading occurs 'in the house of the LORD,' establishing the temple as the proper venue for encountering God's word and renewing covenant. In modern temple experience, we similarly encounter God's word and will in a sacred setting designed to bring us into alignment with divine purposes.

commentary.christological_typology: Baruch's role as the faithful scribe who transmits the prophet's words prefigures the role of the apostles and Gospel writers, who faithfully record and transmit Jesus' words and deeds. As Baruch's obedience ensures that Jeremiah's message reaches the people, the evangelists' obedience preserves Christ's message for the Church. Both exemplify faithful scribal ministry in service of God's revealed word.
commentary.application: Baruch's complete obedience to Jeremiah's command—'did according to all'—challenges us to examine our own relationship to God's word. Do we receive it fully and without reservation? Do we transmit it faithfully to others, or do we edit and qualify it according to what we think will be well-received? In an age of individualism and selective belief, Baruch's example of simple, complete obedience to the prophet's word stands as a rebuke to cafeteria spirituality. Our task, like Baruch's, is not to judge which parts of God's word are worth obeying, but to obey all that we have been commanded.

text_kjv: And it came to pass in the fifth year of Jehoiakim the son of Josiah king of Judah, in the ninth month, that they proclaimed a fast before the LORD to all the people in Jerusalem, and to all the people that came from the cities of Judah unto Jerusalem.

commentary.narrative:
The temporal setting shifts forward: nearly a year has passed since the scroll was written in the fourth year of Jehoiakim (verse 1). Now, in the fifth year, in the ninth month (Kislev, approximately November-December), a fast is proclaimed "before the LORD." This is not a private act but a public religious gathering, a call to the entire population of Jerusalem and people coming from the surrounding cities of Judah. The fast appears to have been called in response to the Babylonian threat, particularly after the battle of Carchemish (605 BCE), which had dramatically shifted the geopolitical situation in the Near East. Babylon's emergence as the dominant power meant that Judah's security was in acute jeopardy.

The proclamation of a fast is significant: it signals a collective acknowledgment that something is gravely wrong and that the people need to seek divine intervention. A fast was an act of humiliation before God, an attempt through self-denial and prayer to arouse God's attention and mercy. The phrase "before the LORD" (lipnei YHWH) emphasizes that this is fundamentally a religious act, not merely a political necessity—the fast is directed toward heaven, an appeal for divine favor. The broad scope of participation—"all the people in Jerusalem" and people traveling from "the cities of Judah"—suggests a coordinated, official action, possibly initiated by religious authorities or the king himself.

The timing is providential for Baruch's mission: the fast creates a gathering when the maximum number of people will be present in the temple precincts, precisely where Baruch is about to read the scroll. The narrative thus demonstrates how God coordinates circumstances—the scroll is completed, the scroll-reading opportunity is planned, and now conditions are created (through the fast) that will gather the precise audience needed to hear the message. This is not coincidence but theological providence: God arranges the stage for his word to be heard.

word_study.meaning: a fast, abstinence from food—an act of self-denial and humiliation before God, typically undertaken during times of crisis, grief, or urgent prayer. Fasting was believed to make prayer more effective and demonstrate sincerity of repentance.
word_study.significance: In the Hebrew Bible, fasting is a covenantal act: the people demonstrate their need for God and their willingness to submit themselves to his will. That a fast is proclaimed at this moment suggests official recognition of danger and a collective appeal for divine mercy—making the subsequent reading of Jeremiah's scroll a form of answer to that prayer.

word_study.meaning: they called, proclaimed, summoned—the verb carries the sense of making an official, public announcement. The fast was not voluntary but officially declared.
word_study.significance: The use of the passive form leaves ambiguous who declared the fast (king, religious authorities, or a combination), but the formality of proclamation emphasizes that this is an official, binding act affecting the entire religious community.

word_study.meaning: before/in the presence of the LORD—a phrase emphasizing that the act is directed toward God and performed in consciousness of God's presence. This is not merely a social practice but a religious act with vertical orientation.
word_study.significance: The phrase reiterates the religious nature of the fast and reminds readers that all action in this narrative is ultimately directed toward God and responsive to God's will and declared judgment.

word_study.meaning: in the fifth year—the ordinal 'fifth' establishes chronological precision. This is Jehoiakim's fifth regnal year, approximately 601 BCE if Jehoiakim's reign began in 609 BCE.
word_study.significance: The specific dating anchors the narrative in historical reality and indicates that Jeremiah operated within a known historical framework. The delay between the scroll's composition and its public reading (about a year) suggests that God's word operates on its own timeline, not necessarily with immediate effect.

cross_references.connection: During King Josiah's reign, the discovery of the scroll of the law triggered a similar crisis response: Josiah tore his clothes and ordered a fast and sacrifice, recognizing that God's judgment threatened the nation. Jehoiakim's fast echoes that earlier moment of religious urgency.

The people of Nineveh proclaimed a fast and turned from their evil ways in response to Jonah's prophetic warning—exactly the outcome Jeremiah hoped for in verse 7. Here, too, a fast creates the context for receptiveness to prophetic word.

Joel also calls for a public fast, summoning priests and people to gather and cry out to God—using identical language of official proclamation ('qar'u tsom') to mobilize collective religious response to crisis.

Modern revelation teaches that 'he who is faithful and wise in time is accounted worthy to inherit the glories of a celestial kingdom'—suggesting that responding to divine warning with genuine repentance (of which fasting is one sign) opens the way to blessing rather than judgment.

commentary.historical_context: The ninth month (Kislev) falls in late autumn/early winter in the Hebrew calendar, corresponding roughly to November-December. This timing is significant for two reasons: First, it explains why a winter brazier appears later in the narrative (verse 22), indicating the cold season; second, it suggests that the fast was called in response to the deteriorating military situation following Babylon's victory at Carchemish (605 BCE). That victory had eliminated Egyptian power in the Levant and left Judah exposed to Babylonian expansion. Nearly a decade into Jehoiakim's reign, the threat was becoming undeniable. A public fast would have been a natural response from religious and political authorities seeking to align the nation with God's will in a moment of acute danger. The gathering of people "from the cities of Judah" suggests a high-traffic period in Jerusalem, making the temple precincts an ideal venue for reading the scroll.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 5:50-51 describes Alma calling the people to covenant renewal and asking them to 'awake and arouse your faculties.' Similarly, the proclamation of a fast is a call to awaken to religious reality and recognize the need for divine intervention. The fast functions as a collective 'awakening' to crisis and the need for repentance.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 88:118-119 teaches that 'in that day the Lord shall know that his church is alive' when members are united in faith and purpose. The proclamation of the fast and the gathering it creates is an attempt to unify Judah religiously and to demonstrate collective commitment to seeking God's favor—a principle that operates in the Church through united faith and obedience.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The fast creates a context for religious renewal and the renewal of covenants, and it gathers the people at the temple—the locus of God's presence and the place where covenant is renewed. The timing ensures that the maximum number will be present in the temple when the scroll is read, making the temple the natural gathering place for encountering God's word.

commentary.christological_typology: The fast proclaimed before the LORD prefigures Jesus' teaching on fasting and prayer as disciplines that align us with God's purposes (Matthew 6:16-18). Christ himself fasted before his temptation and ministry (Matthew 4:1-2), modeling the discipline of seeking God's will through self-denial. The response Jeremiah hopes for—that the people will turn from evil through encountering God's word—is ultimately made possible through Christ's atonement, which removes the barrier between divine word and human capacity to respond.
commentary.application: This verse reminds us that God often provides the circumstances and opportunities for his word to be heard, even when we don't fully recognize them. The fast gathered the people precisely when the scroll would be read—divine providence coordinating the messenger, the message, and the audience. In our own lives, we should recognize that crises, uncertainties, and seasons of struggle often create spiritual openness and receptiveness to God's word. When we face difficulty or urgency, rather than merely seeking human solutions, we should ask: Is this a moment when God is calling me to fast, pray, and genuinely seek his will? The proclamation of the fast invites us to consider whether we use life's difficulties as opportunities for deeper spiritual engagement or merely as problems to be solved.

text_kjv: Then read Baruch in the book the words of Jeremiah in the house of the LORD, in the chamber of Gemariah the son of Shaphan the scribe, in the higher court, at the entry of the new gate of the LORD'S house, in the ears of all the people.

commentary.narrative:
The moment of reading arrives: Baruch performs his public action in the temple during the fast. The precision of the geographical description—the chamber of Gemariah in the upper court at the entrance of the New Gate—indicates a high-traffic location where Baruch could reach maximum audience. Gemariah son of Shaphan is not a random official but a member of a family deeply connected to prophetic history. His father Shaphan was the scribe who read the discovered scroll of the law to King Josiah nearly a century earlier (2 Kings 22:8-10), prompting one of the great religious reforms in Judah's history. Now Shaphan's son provides a chamber in which Jeremiah's scroll is read—a remarkable continuation of familial involvement with prophetic texts across generations.

The use of Gemariah's chamber suggests his sympathy with Jeremiah's message. That he allows Baruch to read in his space, in a prominent location within the temple, indicates tacit support. Later in the narrative (verse 25), Gemariah and others will attempt to prevent the king from destroying the scroll, demonstrating that this family remained committed to preserving God's word. The location itself—not a hidden corner but the entrance to the New Gate in the upper court—was deliberately public. This was not a clandestine reading but a bold, open proclamation. The phrase "in the ears of all the people" emphasizes that this was a public address intended for everyone present.

The temporal and spatial coordinates matter theologically: the reading occurs during a religiously charged moment (the fast) in the sacred space of the temple, at a point of maximum visibility. The scroll that had been written in a chamber (verse 4) is now read in a chamber; the written word becomes spoken word, encountering living listeners. For many in that audience, this will be their first exposure to the full, coherent collection of Jeremiah's prophecies. The public reading transforms what might have remained a private text into a confrontation with God's word that demands response.

word_study.meaning: to read, recite, call out—in the context of public proclamation, to read aloud in a formal manner, ensuring that all present hear the text. Reading in ancient contexts was typically oral and audible, not silent.
word_study.significance: The shift from written to oral, from private composition to public proclamation, makes the word embodied and present. Qara emphasizes the performative, audible nature of the reading—this is not information transfer but confrontation with living speech.

word_study.meaning: a chamber, room, or cell—often used to designate rooms in the temple precincts where officials worked or where materials were stored. Gemariah's chamber appears to have been an official room within the temple complex.
word_study.significance: The chamber is situated between private (Gemariah's own office space) and public (the court and temple precincts). This location allows Baruch to read in a semi-protected space while remaining audible to all who pass through or gather in the court—a strategic position balancing boldness with some measure of safety.

word_study.meaning: the upper court, the higher court—distinguished from the inner court closer to the sanctuary. This court would have been accessible to all who entered the temple and was likely a high-traffic area.
word_study.significance: The upper court represents a semi-public space within the temple, accessible to ordinary worshippers but not the innermost sanctuary. This location ensures broad access to the scroll-reading while maintaining appropriate boundaries regarding sacred space.

word_study.meaning: the New Gate of the house of the LORD—an entrance to the temple complex, probably so named because it had been recently constructed or renovated. Its exact location is debated by scholars, but it was clearly a prominent entry point.
word_study.significance: The gate serves as a marker of a specific, identifiable location within the temple geography. The entrance or gateway of a structure is typically a point of maximum traffic and visibility. Reading at the entrance ensures that no one entering or leaving the temple could miss the proclamation.

word_study.term_english: in the ears of all the people
word_study.meaning: in the ears of all the people—a Hebrew idiom emphasizing audible, public proclamation directed toward the entire assembled community. To read 'in the ears' of someone is to ensure they hear.
word_study.significance: This phrase underscores that the reading is intentionally public and comprehensive. No one in the vicinity could claim they didn't hear; the word confronts the entire people. This echoes the covenant-renewal formula, where God's word is spoken 'in the ears' of all Israel (cf. Deuteronomy 31:28).

cross_references.connection: Shaphan (Gemariah's father) brought the scroll of the law to King Josiah and read it aloud, triggering Josiah's reform. Now his son Gemariah provides a space for Jeremiah's scroll to be read—demonstrating that this family's role in transmitting God's word to Judah's leaders spans generations.

Earlier in Jeremiah, Ahikam son of Shaphan (Gemariah's brother) protected Jeremiah from execution—showing that the Shaphan family consistently advocated for the prophet and his message despite political pressure.

Ezra reads the law 'in the ears of all the people' with interpretation and clarity, causing the people to weep and repent—establishing the pattern of public, formal reading of God's word as an instrument of spiritual renewal and covenant recovery.

Moses commands that the law be read aloud before all Israel at the Feast of Booths 'that they may hear, and that they may learn to fear the LORD'—a covenant-renewal principle that Baruch's reading enacts in Jeremiah's context.

Modern revelation establishes that God's word should be 'proclaimed abroad, as with the sound of a trump'—emphasizing public, audible proclamation as the proper mode of communicating God's will to a community.

commentary.historical_context: The temple precincts during a proclaimed fast would have been crowded with worshippers from Jerusalem and surrounding regions. The upper court was a semi-public space where officials conducted business and where ordinary worshippers could gather—making it an ideal venue for reaching a broad audience. Gemariah's family had long-standing connections to both Jeremiah and to the prophetic tradition (through his father Shaphan's role in Josiah's reform). His willingness to provide his chamber suggests that at least some members of the Judean elite recognized Jeremiah's legitimacy, even if they could not prevent his rejection by the king and majority of officials. The strategic placement 'at the entrance of the new gate' maximized visibility: anyone entering or leaving the temple would encounter the reading.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 26:22-23 describes Alma and his companions preaching 'in every congregation' and in 'every place,' bringing God's word to all who would hear. Similarly, Baruch's reading 'in the ears of all the people' seeks to maximize the reach of the prophetic message. The Book of Mormon repeatedly emphasizes the importance of publicly proclaiming God's word, not hiding it away.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 88:103 teaches 'That faith also by works is dead, being alone; wherefore it is manifest that faith without works is dead'—and similarly, faith in prophetic word requires public witness and proclamation. The scroll must be read aloud, not merely preserved in private; revelation requires transmission.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The reading occurs in the temple, the house of the Lord, establishing the temple as the proper place for encountering God's word and experiencing religious revival. In the Restoration, temples similarly serve as places where heaven communicates with earth and where covenant is renewed.

commentary.christological_typology: Baruch's public reading of the scroll prefigures the Great Commission, where the gospel must be proclaimed "to all nations" and "in the ears of all people." As the scroll confronts Judah with God's word and demand for response, so Jesus' message confronts all humanity with the offer of salvation and the call to repentance. The public, audible nature of the proclamation (in the ears of all the people) reflects Christ's teaching that what is whispered in secret should be proclaimed on the housetops (Matthew 10:27).
commentary.application: This verse challenges us to consider how God's word is made public and accessible in our own lives. The scroll was not hidden but proclaimed 'in the ears of all the people'—it was available to anyone willing to listen. In our modern context, God's word is abundantly available through scripture, conference addresses, and the teaching of the Church, yet many do not truly hear it. The question for us is: Are we positioning ourselves to hear God's word clearly? Do we attend to it with the openness and attention the Judean people should have shown? Additionally, Baruch's willingness to read publicly, despite potential opposition from the king, invites us to consider: Am I willing to bear witness to God's word, even when it might be unpopular or costly? The public nature of the reading made Baruch identifiable and potentially vulnerable—yet he proceeded anyway, trusting in the importance of the message.

text_kjv: When Michaiah the son of Gemariah, the son of Shaphan, had heard out of the book all the words of the LORD,

commentary.narrative:
The narrative now traces the transmission of the scroll's message up the chain of authority. Micaiah (also spelled Michaiah), son of Gemariah, hears the scroll being read in his father's chamber. The genealogy—Micaiah son of Gemariah son of Shaphan—situates him in a family deeply invested in prophetic history and God's word. His grandfather Shaphan read the scroll of the law to King Josiah; his father Gemariah provided the chamber where Jeremiah's scroll is now being read; and Micaiah himself becomes the messenger who will carry the news to the officials, setting in motion the final confrontation between the king and the prophet's word.

The phrase "had heard out of the book all the words of the LORD" is crucial. Micaiah does not merely catch fragments or partial truths; he hears "all the words," the complete message. The verb "heard" (shama in Hebrew) carries connotations not merely of auditory perception but of attentive listening and receiving. To shama God's words is to accept them, to be moved by them. The text implies that Micaiah's hearing was transformative—the complete message had an impact sufficient to move him to action. The phrase "out of the book" emphasizes that these are written, preserved, and now publicly proclaimed words, not rumor or hearsay but God's declared judgment read from a text.

Micaiah becomes the pivotal figure in a chain of transmission: Jeremiah commanded the writing of the scroll (verse 1-4); Baruch wrote it (verse 4-5); Jeremiah commanded Baruch to read it (verse 6); Baruch read it to all the people (verse 8, 10); Micaiah heard it and moved to report it (verse 11-12); the officials heard it from Micaiah (verse 16); the king heard about it (implied in verse 16-17). Each link in this chain represents both a faithful transmission and a potential point of failure. Micaiah's response—to carry the message to higher authorities—suggests that he recognized the weight and importance of what he had heard and felt obligated to ensure that decision-makers knew what Jeremiah was proclaiming.

word_study.meaning: to hear, listen, obey—in Hebrew, shama can mean simply to perceive sound, but often carries a deeper meaning of receptive listening and accepting what is heard. To 'hear' God's word is to be accountable to it.
word_study.significance: The verb shama is not mere passive auditory experience but involves engagement and responsibility. Micaiah didn't just hear words; he heard words that demanded response. This is why his next action (reporting to the officials) follows naturally—he has truly heard and therefore must act.

word_study.meaning: from/out of the book, scroll—the preposition me-al suggests reading from or derived from a written text. The scroll is the source and authority for what Micaiah heard.
word_study.significance: The specification 'out of the book' emphasizes the textual, formal, authoritative nature of the proclamation. This is not Baruch's personal interpretation but God's recorded word, read from a preserved text.

word_study.meaning: all the words, every word—the adjective kol (all) emphasizes comprehensiveness and totality. Micaiah heard the complete message, not selected portions.
word_study.significance: The emphasis on 'all' suggests that the full scope of Jeremiah's judgment is what moved Micaiah to action. He grasped the total weight of what God was saying through the prophet, not just a single isolated utterance.

word_study.meaning: the words of the LORD—God's own utterance, the divine speech contained in the scroll. These are not human words about God but God's direct address.
word_study.significance: The designation 'words of the LORD' establishes the ultimate source and authority of what Micaiah heard. He is hearing God speak through the prophet, which is why the message carries such weight that he must report it to officials.

cross_references.connection: Elnathan son of Achbor is mentioned here as one of the officials who will oppose the scroll; he was also the one sent to Egypt to extradite the prophet Uriah for execution, showing his enmity toward prophetic voices that condemn the king.

Shaphan reads the scroll of the law to King Josiah and reports what he has heard; his grandson Micaiah now performs a similar function, reporting Jeremiah's scroll to the officials—showing that faithful transmission of God's word across generations can occur within families.

'The prudent see danger and take refuge, but the simple keep going and pay the penalty'—Micaiah's immediate action upon hearing the scroll demonstrates prudence in recognizing danger and attempting to alert those in authority.

Modern revelation teaches that when we hear God's word, we become accountable to act on it: 'Nevertheless, I will send upon you all the blessings of the Father, if ye continue faithful'—suggesting that hearing is inseparable from the obligation to respond and transmit what we have learned.

commentary.historical_context: Micaiah represents the educated elite of Judah—the family connection and his access to the temple precincts indicate social standing. That he immediately grasps the significance of what he has heard and acts on it suggests both intelligence and conscience. The speed with which the message moves from Baruch (reading aloud) to Micaiah (hearing) to the officials (being informed) to the king (learning about it) demonstrates how information flowed through Judah's administrative structures. In ancient societies, oral report by trusted family members was a primary mechanism of communication among the elite. Micaiah's willingness to report what he has heard, even though it might displease the king, shows a conscience aligned with God's word rather than with political expediency.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Lehi hears God's word through a vision and immediately gathers his family and flees, recognizing the urgency and authority of what he has been told (1 Nephi 2:1-2). Similarly, Micaiah hears God's word and immediately moves to inform those who need to know—demonstrating that authentic hearing of God's word produces urgent, faithful action.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 21:5-6 teaches that when the Lord's servant speaks the Lord's words, 'the power of my Spirit carrieth them unto all parts of the land.' Micaiah's hearing of the scroll and his movement to report it is an example of how God's word, once proclaimed, carries an energy that moves people to action and spreads through the community.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: Micaiah hears God's word in the temple, the house of the Lord, suggesting that the temple is the proper place for receiving divine communication and being moved to faithful action. The temple creates the conditions (sacredness, gathering, attentiveness) in which hearing God's word can occur.

commentary.christological_typology: Micaiah's hearing of the complete word of God and his consequent movement to transmit it prefigures the disciples' experience of hearing Jesus and being commissioned to preach the gospel to all nations. As Micaiah carries the message to officials, the apostles are sent to carry Christ's message to all people. Both exemplify the principle that authentic hearing produces movement and transmission.
commentary.application: Micaiah's story invites us to examine what we do when we hear God's word with clarity and power. Hearing 'all the words of the LORD' from Baruch's reading moved Micaiah to action—he didn't sit passively but took steps to ensure that those in authority heard and responded to the message. In our lives, when we encounter God's word through scripture, prophetic voice, or the Spirit, are we moved to action? Are we willing to share what we have learned with others, even if it might be unpopular? The phrase 'all the words' suggests that Micaiah received not just isolated proof-texts but the full scope of God's message—a reminder that we should seek comprehensive understanding of God's will, not just the parts that comfort us. Finally, Micaiah's immediate response challenges us to consider: When God's word confronts us, do we delay, or do we move with urgency to act on what we have learned?

text_kjv: Then he went down into the king's house, into the scribe's chamber: and, lo, all the princes sat there, even Elishama the scribe, and Delaiah the son of Shemaiah, and Elnathan the son of Achbor, and Gemariah the son of Shaphan, and Zedekiah the son of Hananiah, and all the princes.

commentary.narrative:
Micaiah's report immediately precipitates a meeting of Judah's highest officials in the royal palace. The phrase "went down" (vayered) signals movement from the temple (on higher ground) to the king's house (lower topographically and, in the narrative's symbolic geography, representing political rather than religious authority). The setting is the scribe's chamber in the palace, where official business was conducted. The gathering of "all the princes" indicates a formal assembly, likely convened either because of Micaiah's urgent report or because these officials happened to be meeting when he arrived with his news.

The list of officials names five individuals by name and then adds "and all the princes," suggesting these five were the most significant or most directly involved. Each name requires attention. Elishama is the royal scribe, the chief official responsible for written communication in the kingdom—his presence signals the official nature of what is about to occur. Delaiah son of Shemaiah appears sympathetic (verse 25 will show him attempting to prevent the king from burning the scroll), suggesting that opinion among the officials was divided regarding how to respond to Jeremiah's message. Elnathan son of Achbor, by contrast, presents a contrast: earlier in Jeremiah's narrative (26:22), Elnathan was the official sent to Egypt to capture the prophet Uriah and bring him back for execution. His presence here foreshadows the hostility the scroll will face. Gemariah son of Shaphan—the same Gemariah in whose chamber Baruch read—now appears among the officials, positioned to defend the scroll from destruction.

The gathering represents the political center of Judah's power. These are the men who advise or influence the king, and they are about to hear, for the first time through official channels, what Jeremiah has proclaimed. The dramatic irony is profound: the same officials who sat in Gemariah's chamber (where Baruch read) or heard reports of the reading are now assembling to decide how the king should respond. The moment of truth is approaching—God's word, transmitted through Jeremiah and Baruch and reported by Micaiah, now reaches the seat of political power. What will happen next will determine whether the scroll survives or is destroyed, and whether Judah will have the opportunity to respond to God's warning with repentance.

word_study.meaning: he went down, descended—suggesting both physical movement down in elevation and a descent from sacred to secular space. The verb often carries implications about direction and spiritual significance.
word_study.significance: The movement 'down' from the temple to the palace symbolically represents a shift from religious to political authority. It also foreshadows the ultimate rejection of the scroll by political power—the trajectory is downward, toward destruction rather than implementation.

word_study.meaning: the king's house, the royal palace—the seat of political and administrative authority in Judah. This is where official decisions affecting the entire kingdom are made.
word_study.significance: The shift from the temple (bet YHWH) to the king's house (bet ha-melech) represents a fundamental tension in Jeremiah's theology: political power and religious authority are not always aligned. Jehoiakim's house will ultimately reject God's word, while the temple had at least been the venue for hearing it.

word_study.meaning: the chamber of the scribe—an official room where royal scribes conducted writing and record-keeping business. This is where official documents were composed, reviewed, and preserved.
word_study.significance: The irony is profound: the scribe's chamber in the palace, where official records were made and kept, becomes the venue where the officials will first formally confront Jeremiah's scroll. The chamber represents the bureaucratic apparatus of the state—precisely the structure that will ultimately oppose and attempt to suppress the prophetic word.

word_study.meaning: princes, officials, leaders—high-ranking members of the government and royal administration. These were the chief advisors and administrators of the kingdom.
word_study.significance: The word sarim emphasizes that these are not minor functionaries but major power-holders in Judah. Their decision about how to respond to the scroll will significantly influence the king's response. The gathering of all the sarim indicates the significance of the moment—nothing less than the official recognition and response to Jeremiah's prophetic testimony.

word_study.meaning: behold, lo, there—a particle drawing attention to what is being revealed or observed. It conveys immediacy and often marks a moment of revelation or recognition.
word_study.significance: Hinneh creates narrative immediacy: Micaiah arrives and finds the officials already assembled. This suggests providential timing—the right people are in the right place at the right moment to receive the crucial report about the scroll. The word invites readers to pay close attention to what is about to unfold.

cross_references.connection: Elnathan son of Achbor, mentioned here as one of the officials, was previously sent to Egypt to extradite the prophet Uriah for execution—his presence among those hearing about the scroll foreshadows opposition to Jeremiah's message.

Delaiah and Gemariah, both named here, will later attempt to persuade King Jehoiakim not to burn the scroll—showing that even within the circle of officials gathered in verse 12, opinion was divided regarding the scroll's treatment.

When the scroll of the law was found during Josiah's reign, it was brought to the king through his officials and scribes, who read it to the king, initiating a religious reform—a parallel narrative showing how kingship and prophetic word could intersect productively.

David flees before Saul, and reports are brought to Saul by those who have seen David's movements—like Micaiah's report of the scroll to the officials, highlighting how information flows up through chains of command to reach centers of power.

Modern revelation states that God's warnings come 'that every man may partake according to his condition,' suggesting that God speaks to nations through their leaders—the gathering of officials to hear about the scroll represents the moment when judgment reaches kingship itself.

commentary.historical_context: The scribe's chamber in the royal palace was where official documents were reviewed, and where decisions about significant matters were deliberated. The rapid assembly of the officials suggests either that Micaiah's report was urgent enough to interrupt ongoing business, or that these officials were already meeting and received the news during their session. Elishama as the royal scribe had responsibility for preserving royal records; Delaiah and Elnathan held significant administrative positions; Gemariah maintained his connection to both religious and political spheres; Zedekiah son of Hananiah is less well-documented but clearly held rank among the officials. The diversity of opinion among these men (some would later defend the scroll, others would not) reflects the complexity of Judean politics: there was no monolithic opposition to Jeremiah, but rather a spectrum of responses, with some officials recognizing his legitimacy even when the king rejected it.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: King Benjamin assembles his people to hear a proclamation before his death (Mosiah 1-2); similarly, this assembly of officials gathers to hear about Jeremiah's proclamation. Both scenarios place decision-makers in the position of having to respond to a message of significant consequence for their people's spiritual condition.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 1:38 teaches that God's word, whether spoken by the Lord or by his servants, is equally binding: 'Whether by mine own voice or by the voice of my servants, it is the same.' The assembly of officials in verse 12 gathers to determine how to respond to God's word spoken through Jeremiah—a decision with eternal consequences.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The movement from the temple (where the scroll was read) to the palace (where officials gather) represents a transition from receiving God's word to making decisions about responding to it. In modern context, this mirrors the movement from worship and learning to covenantal action and obedience.

commentary.christological_typology: The gathering of officials to confront the prophetic word prefigures the gathering of the Sanhedrin to judge Jesus, who is himself the ultimate fulfillment of prophetic testimony. As Judah's officials must decide how to respond to Jeremiah's scroll, so later leaders must decide how to respond to the Prophet of prophets. Both scenarios center on the fundamental question: Will political power align itself with God's truth, or resist it?
commentary.application: Verse 12 raises a profound question for our own time: When God's word reaches us, do we gather seriously to hear and weigh it, or do we dismiss it without careful consideration? The assembly of officials represents a moment when political power is forced to confront prophetic truth. In our lives, prophetic messages (whether from scriptures, conference talks, or the still small voice of the Spirit) constantly confront us with calls to repentance and course correction. Do we take time to assemble (metaphorically) our best thinking, our most honest assessment, and truly hear what God is saying through his servants? Or do we—like officials who have already made up their minds—go through the motions of hearing while our hearts remain fixed in resistance? The diversity of opinion among the officials (Gemariah defended the scroll; Elnathan opposed it) reminds us that godly officials can disagree on how to respond to prophetic word. Yet all must take it seriously. What matters is not agreement but sincere, prayerful engagement with the message. Finally, Micaiah's urgency in bringing the news to the officials invites us to ask: When we recognize important spiritual truth, do we treat it with urgency and work to ensure that those in positions of influence understand and respond?

text_kjv: Then Michaiah declared unto them all the words that he had heard, when Baruch read the book in the ears of the people.

commentary.narrative:
Micaiah serves as a critical link in a five-stage chain of transmission: God → Jeremiah → Baruch → the people → Micaiah → the officials. This verse introduces the mechanism by which prophetic words reach the political leadership—not through direct contact with the prophet, but through layers of intermediaries. Micaiah's formal report (higgid in Hebrew) carries authority; he is not gossiping but officially relaying what he witnessed. The fact that he attended the public reading in the temple court (v. 10) positions him as a credible eyewitness to the words' content and delivery.

The verb 'declared' (higgid) denotes a formal, deliberate communication, not casual conversation. This is significant because the officials are hearing a filtered, second-hand account of the scroll's contents. Yet the power of Jeremiah's words survives transmission through multiple voices—the message retains enough force that it compels the officials to act. This chain of transmission also reflects how prophecy functioned in ancient Israel: the prophet's original spoken words were not always immediately available to all; they had to be memorized, recited, and circulated through trusted intermediaries before reaching the wider circles of power.

word_study.meaning: to tell, report, declare formally; from nagad, meaning to make known or reveal
word_study.significance: Unlike casual speech (dabar), higgid emphasizes formal, deliberate communication of weighty information. Micaiah is making an official report to the officials, establishing the credibility and gravity of what he witnessed. The same root appears in 'nagid' (prince/official), suggesting that this mode of speech is appropriate to formal court proceedings.

word_study.meaning: to hear, listen, obey; can mean both auditory perception and faithful response
word_study.significance: Micaiah positions himself as a 'shomer' (one who listens and keeps)—he has heard the words and now reports them faithfully. In Hebrew thought, true hearing includes obedience; Micaiah's report demonstrates that he has internalized the message enough to transmit it accurately.

cross_references.connection: This verse references the public reading where Micaiah heard the scroll—the event that enables his report to the officials and sets the entire chain of escalation in motion.

During Josiah's reign, the Book of the Law is discovered and read aloud; scribes then report it to the king, establishing a parallel pattern of prophetic texts reaching leadership through intermediary witnesses.

The prophet distinguishes between those who 'have a dream' (direct revelation) and those who 'have my word' (transmitted speech), emphasizing that Micaiah's report faithfully carries Jeremiah's word to the officials despite the mediation.

commentary.historical_context: In ancient Near Eastern courts, official business was conducted through formal channels of communication. A subordinate like Micaiah would not approach the officials casually; he would request an audience and deliver a formal report. The chain of transmission visible here—public reading → eyewitness → official report → royal audience—reflects standard administrative practice. The officials' reliance on intermediaries rather than direct access to the prophet is typical of monarchic bureaucracy, where the king's advisors managed information flow and filtered what reached the ruler.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In Mosiah 12:25-28, King Noah's priests try to suppress the prophet Abinadi's message by preventing it from reaching the people; the contrast here shows how Jeremiah's words, despite efforts at suppression, cascade through multiple witnesses and cannot be contained.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 21:4-6 describes the role of those who hear and transmit the Lord's word faithfully, drawing a parallel to Micaiah's function as a reliable conduit of prophetic speech. The Lord values both the speaker and the faithful hearer-and-reporter.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The public reading in the temple court (v. 10) establishes the sanctuary as the proper place for God's word to be proclaimed; Micaiah's report from the temple to the palace shows how the sacred word moves outward from the holy place to influence secular power.

commentary.christological_typology: The chain of transmission of prophetic words—God's message passing through multiple faithful witnesses to reach those in power—foreshadows how Jesus Christ, the ultimate Word of God (Logos in John 1:1), would be proclaimed by faithful witnesses (the apostles and disciples) to all nations. The reliability of transmission depends on the faithfulness of each link; Christ entrusted His gospel to disciples who would carry it faithfully to the world.
commentary.application: In modern covenant life, members often receive prophetic truth not directly from Church leaders but through Sunday School teachers, seminary instructors, family members, or friends who have heard and are retransmitting the word. Like Micaiah, we have a responsibility to report and share what we have heard faithfully and accurately, without distortion or dilution. The verse also invites reflection on how we serve as intermediaries of truth in our families and communities—are we reliable links in the chain that brings God's word to those who need it?

text_kjv: Therefore all the princes sent Jehudi the son of Nethaniah, the son of Shelemiah, the son of Cushi, unto Baruch, saying, Take in thine hand the roll wherein thou hast read in the ears of the people, and come. So Baruch the son of Neriah took the roll in his hand, and came unto them.

commentary.narrative:
This verse marks a crucial escalation: the officials, alarmed by Micaiah's report, act decisively to summon Baruch and the scroll itself. They do not arrest him or seize the text; they send an intermediary (Jehudi) with a respectful summons. The inclusion of Jehudi's genealogy—tracing him through three generations (son of Nethaniah, son of Shelemiah, son of Cushi)—is unusual for a minor figure and suggests either that he holds an official position or that his ancestry is notable. 'Cushi' means 'the Cushite' or 'the Ethiopian,' indicating possible African heritage, which points to the ethnic and cultural diversity of Jehoiakim's court.

Jehudi functions throughout this chapter as an intermediary: he carries messages between the officials and Baruch (v. 14), then reads the scroll to the king (v. 21). His role demonstrates how palace business operated through chains of official messengers. Notably, the officials' tone is formal but not hostile—they ask Baruch to 'take the roll in your hand and come,' which is a civil request, not a commandment. This courtesy is significant because it shows that at this stage in the process, the scroll and its bearer have not yet become targets of royal wrath. The officials are functioning as interested listeners seeking to understand the source and authenticity of what they have heard. The narrative builds tension through this gradual escalation from public reading to official audience to royal presence.

word_study.meaning: officials, princes, leaders; from sar (chief, ruler, captain)
word_study.significance: The sarim were the king's advisors and administrators—a powerful inner circle below the monarch. Their alarm at the scroll's contents (v. 16) carries weight because they represent the bureaucratic and military establishment of Judah. They are the ones positioned to influence the king, but they also fear his reaction.

word_study.meaning: to send, dispatch, release; can indicate commissioning someone for a formal task
word_study.significance: The officials do not go themselves but formally dispatch Jehudi, which shows the hierarchical protocols of palace communication. Each step in accessing the scroll involves proper channels.

word_study.meaning: scroll, rolled manuscript; from galal (to roll)
word_study.significance: The physical scroll is treated as an object of significance—something to be carefully requested, transported, and eventually presented to the king. The megillah is not dismissed as mere parchment but handled with ceremonial weight.

cross_references.connection: Jehudi later reads this same scroll to King Jehoiakim, showing how the chain of transmission continues from officials to monarch, with Jehudi as the key messenger throughout.
Ahikam son of Shaphan protects Jeremiah from death, showing that some court officials were sympathetic to the prophet; the sarim in chapter 36 may represent a similar divided court.
The king is commanded to keep a copy of the Torah and read it all his life; the scroll of Jeremiah is presented to Jehoiakim in a similar formal manner, though with different consequences.
Similar genealogical details for messengers and the practice of formal court communications through appointed intermediaries reflect standard Near Eastern administrative procedure.

commentary.historical_context: In Judean palace administration, messengers like Jehudi were trusted functionaries who carried official business between departments and officials. The dispatch of such a messenger to retrieve Baruch and the scroll shows that the officials regarded this matter as requiring formal handling, not informal investigation. The fact that Baruch complies without resistance suggests that being summoned by the sarim (not yet by the king himself) was not immediately dangerous—he goes willingly, bringing the scroll. The genealogical detail about Jehudi's ancestry may indicate his credentials: a man of known family, appointed to this task. The diversity suggested by 'Cushi' (Cushite/Ethiopian) reflects how ancient Near Eastern courts, including Judah's, drew personnel from various ethnic backgrounds, particularly in administrative and military roles.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In Alma 14:8-10, Alma and Amulek are brought before the magistrates and judges after their preaching disturbs the city; like Baruch, they are summoned by official channels and comply with the legal process, trusting that truth will prevail.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 88:77-78 counsels Saints to share knowledge freely and not to hide their faith; Baruch's willingness to bring the scroll to the officials and testify to its source demonstrates this openness to sharing prophetic truth, even when uncertain of the reception.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The scroll moves from the temple (where it was publicly read, v. 10) to the palace (where it will be read before the king). This horizontal movement of scripture mirrors how the truth of the Restoration moves from the temple (as the center of revealed knowledge) outward to influence all institutions.

commentary.christological_typology: Baruch's willingness to bring the scroll before the officials, even though he cannot control their response, parallels the disciples' willingness to present Jesus (the Living Word) before the authorities, knowing that His message would be both rejected and upheld. Like the scroll, which is neither destroyed nor ignored but handled and transmitted, Christ is neither eliminated nor contained by earthly powers.
commentary.application: When we are called upon to testify or to share our faith (whether in a formal setting like a disciplinary council or an informal one like a family discussion), we can follow Baruch's example: respond respectfully to the summons, bring the full truth without editing or withholding, and trust the process. We are not responsible for how others receive the message, only for faithfully presenting it. The verse also teaches that authority—whether of officials or of family members—does not diminish the truth we carry; we remain responsible for honest transmission.

text_kjv: And they said unto him, Sit down now, and read it in our ears. So Baruch read it in their ears.

commentary.narrative:
The officials extend a polite but commanding invitation to Baruch: 'Sit down, please, and read it to us.' The addition of 'please' (the particle na in Hebrew) softens what is fundamentally an official order. This is the second formal reading of the scroll (the first was to the public in v. 10); each successive reading amplifies the scroll's impact and brings its message closer to ultimate power. The physical act of Baruch sitting and reading in the presence of the officials creates an intimate, formal setting—more deliberate and focused than the public reading at the temple gate.

What Baruch reads to the officials is the complete text; nothing is omitted or paraphrased. The narrative's repetition of 'read it in their ears' underscores that this is an oral performance, not a silent distribution of the text. The sound of the words, the weight of each phrase, and the cumulative force of the prophecies are experienced directly by the listeners. The officials are not skimming a summary; they are hearing the full prophetic judgment against Judah, against the false prophets, and against the king himself. This reading will trigger their fear (v. 16) precisely because they grasp the complete scope of the judgment and understand its implications for the monarchy.

word_study.meaning: sit, dwell, remain; can be a command (imperative) or a gentle invitation depending on context
word_study.significance: Paired with the particle 'na' (please, I pray), 'shev na' becomes a polite command—the officials are asking Baruch to make himself comfortable and settle in for the reading. This phrasing shows respect for the scribe while maintaining their authority. The invitation to sit also suggests that the reading will take time; this is not a hurried recitation but a full performance.

word_study.meaning: to read, call out, proclaim; in the qal stem, to read aloud
word_study.significance: The Hebrew verb qara emphasizes oral performance and proclamation. Reading in the ancient world was almost always oral; the reader's voice and delivery carried meaning. The same verb is used for Baruch's public reading (v. 10), emphasizing the continuity of the same text being transmitted through different audiences.

word_study.meaning: in their ears, in their hearing; a prepositional phrase emphasizing auditory reception
word_study.significance: The phrase 'in the ears' appears throughout chapter 36 (vv. 6, 10, 13, 15), creating a refrain that emphasizes how the word of God travels from mouth to ear, from speaker to hearer. It highlights the embodied, sensory experience of receiving prophetic speech. The Covenant Rendering's use of 'in their hearing' captures this auditory intimacy.

cross_references.connection: This verse parallels the first reading of the scroll in the temple court; the repetition of the full text to different audiences creates a pattern of escalating impact.

Ezra and the Levites read the Law to the people 'and gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading,' showing how formal public reading of scripture involved both performance and comprehension.
Jesus sits to read from Isaiah in the synagogue, following the custom of formal, seated reading of scripture; the practice is continuous from Jeremiah's era to the first-century synagogue.
Moses commands that the Law be read to all Israel at the Feast of Tabernacles; formal public reading of divine word is commanded in Torah and practiced throughout the Old Testament.

commentary.historical_context: In ancient Israel, reading was predominantly a public, performative act. Scrolls were not distributed individually for silent reading; instead, a skilled reader would recite the text aloud while others listened. The posture of sitting while reading (as opposed to standing) may indicate a formal, authoritative position—the reader commands attention while seated, often with others standing or seated before him. The officials' request that Baruch sit and read suggests a formal hearing, similar to a legal proceeding or a royal audience. The intimacy of this setting—a small group of powerful men gathering to hear prophetic words against their own interests—adds psychological weight to the moment. Each hearer must confront the scroll's message in real time, with no opportunity to skip passages or dismiss what is being said.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In Alma 31:5, the sons of Mosiah travel to preach, and 'the word which was preached was powerful' because it was proclaimed with conviction and received by hearts prepared to hear. Baruch's reading to the officials mirrors this power of direct, formal proclamation.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 68:25-28 emphasizes the duty of parents (and leaders) to teach the word of God diligently and to share it with rising generations. Baruch's faithful reading fulfills this principle—he is transmitting God's word to those in authority, trusting that it will be received and acted upon.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The careful, ceremonial reading of scripture in the temple parallels Baruch's formal performance before the officials. Both contexts treat the word of God as something to be approached solemnly, with full attention.
