commentary.christological_typology: The seated reading of the Word—with listeners gathering to hear—foreshadows how Jesus would teach His disciples, sitting on mountainsides or in houses and proclaiming the kingdom of God. The scroll read by Baruch is a type of the Living Word (Christ), whose message convicts hearers and demands response. The officials' reaction (fear and resolve to act, v. 16) models the proper response to divine truth.
commentary.application: In our modern covenant life, we participate in similar formal readings when we gather for sacrament meeting, stake conference, or even family home evening to hear scripture and doctrine. Like the officials before Baruch, we are invited to 'sit and listen' with full attention to God's word. This verse invites us to approach scripture and prophetic proclamation with the same seriousness the officials showed—not as background noise or casual reading, but as a formal encounter with divine truth that demands our full engagement and expects to change us.

text_kjv: Now it came to pass, when they had heard all the words, they were afraid both one and other, and said unto Baruch, We will surely tell the king of all these words.

commentary.narrative:
The officials' reaction to the scroll is decisive: fear strikes them, and they recognize immediately that the king must be informed. The phrase 'they were afraid both one and other' (pachadu ish el re'ehu—literally, 'they feared, each toward his neighbor') suggests a shared, corporate dread. This is not individual panic but a collective realization of the scroll's gravity. The officials grasp that the message—warnings of judgment, accusations against false prophets, condemnation of the king's policies—represents an existential threat to the regime. Their fear is appropriate religious fear, the kind that should trigger obedience; it is exactly the reaction the prophetic word is designed to produce.

Crucially, the officials' response demonstrates moral courage. Despite their own fear and the knowledge that the king does not welcome such messages, they commit to inform him. The emphatic construction 'we will surely tell' (hagged naggid) expresses resolved determination. These officials understand their duty: a message of such magnitude cannot be suppressed or hidden from the monarch. They are showing the kind of integrity that Jeremiah himself exemplifies—the willingness to speak truth even when the audience will not receive it gladly. Their action stands in stark contrast to what follows: King Jehoiakim, hearing the same words, will respond not with repentance but with rage and destruction. The officials' fear leads to action; the king's fear leads to denial and defiance.

word_study.meaning: to fear, tremble, be afraid; can denote both terror and reverent fear
word_study.significance: Pachad is not a weak or shameful emotion in biblical theology; it is the proper response to encountering the word of the Lord. The officials' fear indicates that they recognize the prophetic message as authoritative and binding. Their fear demonstrates spiritual discernment—they grasp the reality of divine judgment in a way the king will refuse to do.

word_study.meaning: infinitive absolute followed by imperfect—'we will certainly, truly, definitely tell'; emphatic construction expressing resolved purpose
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering captures this as 'we must certainly report.' The doubling of the root creates emphasis and finality. The officials are not merely considering whether to tell the king; they are declaring their certain intention to do so. No hesitation, no debate—just resolved action.

word_study.meaning: each to his neighbor, one to another; a phrase emphasizing mutual or reciprocal action
word_study.significance: This construction emphasizes the corporate, shared nature of their fear and reaction. They are not isolated in their response; each official reinforces the fear and resolution of his peers. This communal dynamic strengthens their commitment to report to the king.

cross_references.connection: King Jehoiakim hears the same words but shows no fear; instead, he burns the scroll. The contrast between the officials' reverent fear and the king's defiant contempt illustrates two opposite responses to prophetic truth.

The apostles are arrested and brought before the council; like Jeremiah's officials, they fear but remain resolute in reporting what they have witnessed, showing that faithfulness to truth transcends era and culture.
The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom; the officials' appropriate fear of God's judgment stands in contrast to Jehoiakim's foolish dismissal of the prophetic word.

Jeremiah himself is told not to fear those who oppose him because the Lord is with him; the officials show similar courage by facing the king's probable displeasure rather than suppressing the message.

commentary.historical_context: In the ancient Near East, court officials occupied a precarious position: they were expected to serve the king's interests, yet they also bore responsibility for the kingdom's spiritual and political welfare. A message like Jeremiah's, which threatened the regime, placed officials in an impossible position. Yet the account shows them choosing faithfulness over self-preservation. Their willingness to report the scroll to the king, knowing his temperament, demonstrates both courage and a proper understanding of hierarchy: important matters must be brought before the monarch, regardless of the likely reaction. The officials' fear also reflects the psychological impact of hearing such comprehensive judgment; the scroll likely contained material about specific abuses, false prophets, and divine wrath—enough to shake even hardened administrators.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In Mosiah 11:20-29, King Noah's priests and officials try to suppress Abinadi's prophetic message, but Abinadi's courage and their lack of spiritual fear contrast sharply with Jeremiah's officials, who show proper reverence for the divine word.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 121:4-6 describes how the Lord's word 'shall go forth from you when I command it, and not before; and ye shall be made free.' The officials' recognition that the king must be told reflects an understanding that prophetic truth has its own authority and cannot be contained.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The fear of the Lord, central to temple covenant, is demonstrated by the officials' reverential response to the scroll. They understand that to suppress God's word is to defy God Himself, not merely to defy a prophet.

commentary.christological_typology: The officials' fear at hearing the complete word of judgment parallels the fear that grips the disciples when Jesus speaks of His impending death and resurrection. Just as the officials resolve to transmit the message despite its grim content, the disciples will ultimately choose to proclaim Christ's message despite its cost to them. The scroll becomes a type of Christ—a complete, embodied message of judgment and mercy that demands response and cannot be ignored.
commentary.application: When we encounter prophetic truth in General Conference, in the scriptures, or in personal revelation, we should examine our response. Do we, like the officials, feel appropriate reverence and resolve to act, or do we rationalize and dismiss what makes us uncomfortable? The verse challenges us to move beyond personal fear to corporate responsibility: if we have heard the word of God, we have a duty to share it with those for whom we bear responsibility—our families, our callings, our communities. Our fear should drive us toward action, not toward silence.

text_kjv: And they asked Baruch, saying, Tell us now, How didst thou write all these words at his mouth?

commentary.narrative:
The officials' next question probes the fundamental issue of prophetic authenticity: how was this text produced? Their inquiry is not hostile but investigative. They want to establish the chain of transmission and verify that these words come from Jeremiah himself, not from Baruch's own composition or editorial work. The question 'How did you write all these words at his mouth?' seeks to understand the mechanism: Did Jeremiah dictate directly to you? Did you transcribe his spoken words? Is this a direct, unmediated recording of prophetic speech, or is it interpreted/paraphrased?

This verse contains one of the few direct references in the Hebrew Bible to the actual process of how prophecy was preserved in written form. The phrase 'at his mouth' (mippiv) can be understood both literally (from his mouth = his dictation) and theologically (the word proceeds from the Lord's mouth through the prophet's mouth). The officials are asking about both the mechanics of composition and the theological chain of authority. Their question anticipates modern scholarly interest in oral versus written transmission, prophetic composition, and textual stability. Baruch's response (v. 18) will clarify that this is direct dictation, not interpretation—the scribe was a faithful recorder, not an author. The officials' investigation shows that even in the ancient world, people understood the importance of verifying the authenticity and provenance of prophetic texts.

word_study.meaning: to ask, inquire, question; often implies seeking information or clarification
word_study.significance: Shaal suggests a formal inquiry, not casual conversation. The officials are conducting an investigation into the text's authenticity. Their use of this verb shows they take the matter seriously enough to pose deliberate questions.

word_study.meaning: to write, inscribe, record; the fundamental verb for all written composition and transcription
word_study.significance: Katav is the core term in this chapter for all writing activities. The officials are asking about Baruch's act of writing—what was his role, what was his method, how much of what appears on the scroll is his own work versus faithful transcription.

word_study.meaning: from his mouth, at his dictation; a phrase that can mean both literal oral speech and authoritative pronouncement
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering notes that mippiv is both literal and metaphorical. Literally, it means Jeremiah spoke the words aloud; metaphorically/theologically, it indicates that these words proceed from divine authority channeled through the prophet's speech. The phrase establishes the connection between oral proclamation and written record.

cross_references.connection: The Lord commands Jeremiah to 'write in a book all the words that I have spoken unto you,' establishing the divine command for prophetic words to be written down and preserved.
The Lord tells Moses to 'write these words' of the covenant; like Baruch, scribes were tasked with recording divine speech exactly as spoken.

Paul writes to Timothy about entrusting reliable teaching 'to faithful men, who shall be able to teach others also,' echoing the chain-of-transmission principle and the importance of faithful, accurate transmission of the word.

Peter affirms that prophecy 'came not in old time by the will of man: but holy men of God spake as they were moved by the Holy Ghost,' establishing that prophetic speech originates in divine inspiration, not human composition.

commentary.historical_context: In the ancient Near East, the authenticity of written texts was a matter of serious concern, especially for official and religious documents. Scribes were trained to copy texts faithfully, and the question of whether a scribe merely transcribed or actively composed was significant for establishing a text's authority. The officials' question reflects an understanding that someone had to record Jeremiah's oral prophecies; the method of that recording affected whether the text could be trusted as a faithful record of the prophet's words. Ancient Near Eastern practice shows that when prophecies were written down, scribes often added explanatory material or editorial comments. The officials' question suggests they want to know whether Baruch added such material or stuck strictly to Jeremiah's dictation. This concern for textual fidelity appears in Egyptian and Mesopotamian sources as well—the question 'Is this the exact word of the original speaker, or interpretation?' was perennially important.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In Mormon 8:16-17, Moroni emphasizes that the Book of Mormon record is a faithful account of what was spoken, establishing the chain of witness and the principle that scripture is a reliable transmission of divine speech.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 18:34-36 describes how the Lord's word is transmitted through ordained servants and preserved faithfully; the question here parallels modern concerns about how doctrines are accurately conveyed through authorized channels.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: In temple contexts, covenants are transmitted through specific language and performance; just as Baruch's faithful transcription of Jeremiah's words ensures their fidelity, temple practice ensures that sacred ordinances and teachings are preserved exactly as the Lord has ordained them.

commentary.christological_typology: The officials' inquiry into the chain of transmission from Jeremiah to the written text foreshadows questions about how Christ's words were preserved in the Gospels: Did the evangelists transcribe His exact words, or did they interpret and paraphrase? The dual authorship—the prophet's voice channeled through the scribe's hand—parallels how divine truth (Christ's teaching, which comes from the Father) is recorded through human witness (the evangelists). The scroll becomes a type of the Gospel account, both seeking to faithfully transmit divine speech through written record.
commentary.application: In our covenant community, we grapple with similar questions about authenticity and fidelity. When we read a General Conference talk, we want to know: Is this the speaker's exact words or an edited summary? When we study scripture, we depend on the faithful transmission of the text from original languages to our current translations. This verse invites us to appreciate the faithful scribes, scholars, and record-keepers who have preserved God's word through centuries and cultures. It also challenges us to be faithful transmitters ourselves: When we share a testimony or teach a lesson, are we faithfully conveying what we have heard, or are we inserting our own interpretations? Like Baruch, we bear responsibility for accurate transmission.

text_kjv: Then Baruch answered them, He pronounced all these words unto me with his mouth, and I wrote them with ink in the book.

commentary.narrative:
Baruch's response is precise, authoritative, and definitive. He establishes that the scroll contains Jeremiah's direct dictation, not his own composition or interpretation. The phrase 'He pronounced all these words unto me with his mouth' (mippiv yiqra elai—literally, 'from his mouth he called out to me') describes an ongoing process of oral dictation. The iterative sense of yiqra (he would call out, he kept calling out) suggests that this was not a one-time transcription but a repeated, extended process in which Jeremiah spoke and Baruch recorded. The introduction of physical details—'I wrote them with ink in the book'—grounds the narrative in material reality. This is one of only two references in the Hebrew Bible to ink (deyo), establishing a concrete witness to the means by which the prophetic word was preserved.

Baruch's statement addresses the officials' concern about authenticity and fidelity. He is claiming, in effect: 'I was a faithful recorder. The words are not mine; they came from Jeremiah's mouth. I did not add, subtract, or interpret; I wrote them down as he spoke them.' The mention of ink is not merely incidental—it emphasizes the permanence of the written word. Ink, unlike erasable materials, creates a permanent record. Carbon-based ink, made from soot and gum arabic, cannot be easily washed away; once written, it is fixed. This detail becomes theologically significant later when King Jehoiakim burns the scroll (v. 23)—the king can destroy the physical parchment, but he cannot unmake the words that were written. The word of God, once spoken and recorded, has a reality independent of the physical medium. This verse provides the clearest biblical description of how prophetic texts were physically produced: through the direct dictation of the prophet and the faithful recording of the scribe, using permanent writing materials.

word_study.meaning: to call out, proclaim, read aloud; in the qal imperfect (yiqra), suggests an iterative or repeated action
word_study.significance: The iterative sense indicates that this was an ongoing process: Jeremiah repeatedly called out words to Baruch for transcription. The same verb (qara) was used for the public and official readings of the scroll (vv. 10, 15), creating a verbal connection: the words Jeremiah called out to Baruch are the same words read publicly and officially. Continuity is maintained through the verb's repetition.

word_study.meaning: ink, writing fluid; likely a mixture of carbon soot and gum arabic
word_study.significance: This is only one of two occurrences of deyo in the Hebrew Bible (the other is in Ezekiel 9:2-3, where a scribe with an inkhorn marks the foreheads of the righteous). The word is rare but significant: it emphasizes the physical reality of the inscription. Ancient ink was not erasable; it was permanent. This detail becomes crucial when Jehoiakim burns the scroll—the ink's permanence foreshadows the permanence of the word even when the scroll is destroyed. The Covenant Rendering notes in its key term definition that ink was 'a carbon-based mixture of soot and gum' that would not dissolve but burn with the parchment.

word_study.meaning: scroll, book, written document; from the root safar (to count, narrate, or record)
word_study.significance: The sefer is not just a random piece of parchment but a formal, bounded record—'the book' (with the definite article) emphasizes that this is THE authoritative scroll containing Jeremiah's prophecies. The term appears throughout chapter 36, creating a sense of the scroll as a unified, authoritative text.

word_study.meaning: to write, inscribe, record; the fundamental Hebrew verb for all writing activity
word_study.significance: Baruch's use of the first-person 'I wrote' establishes his agency and responsibility for the act of transcription. He is not claiming authorship of the words but ownership of the writing process itself. His action—the physical act of writing—makes him a crucial link in the chain of transmission: the word moved from Jeremiah's mouth to Baruch's hand to the parchment to the readers' ears.

cross_references.connection: The Lord commands Jeremiah to 'write in a book all the words that I have spoken,' establishing divine sanction for the writing process and for Baruch's role as recorder.

Jeremiah buys a field and has the deed written 'in the sight of witnesses,' creating a parallel to how Baruch's writing serves as witnessed, authoritative proof of the transaction between God's word and written record.
The Lord tells Moses to 'write this for a memorial in a book,' establishing the principle that significant divine communications are to be preserved in writing for future generations.

The apostle John writes, 'I had many things to write unto you, but I will not write them with pen and ink; but I trust to come unto you, and speak face to face,' showing the contrast between oral communication and written word—both valued but distinct.

The psalmist writes, 'My heart is inditing a good matter: I speak of the things which I have made touching the king: my tongue is the pen of a ready writer,' establishing that the written word flows from the heart through the tongue to the pen.

commentary.historical_context: The process Baruch describes—sitting with a prophet, hearing his dictation, and writing it down with ink on parchment—reflects the standard method of producing prophetic literature in ancient Israel. Prophetic utterances were oral; they had to be captured in writing by someone trained in scribal arts. Baruch, as Jeremiah's scribe, would have been educated in writing, familiar with the materials (parchment, ink), and trained to record accurately. The use of ink (deyo) is particularly significant: ancient writing materials included incised clay tablets (cuneiform) and papyrus with various inks, but parchment with carbon ink (as used here) created durable, permanent records. The mention of ink emphasizes not just the physical act but the permanence intended—these words were not meant to be temporary. The rarity of ink (deyo) in biblical text suggests that the narrator is underlining the materiality and significance of the written record. For ancient readers, the invocation of ink would have evoked the sensory reality of writing: the smell of soot-based ink, the scratch of pen on parchment, the gradual accumulation of words that become permanent only as the ink dries.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In 1 Nephi 1:16-17, Nephi records his own experience: 'I make a record of my proceedings in my days,' and later Nephi carefully transcribes the plates of brass. Like Baruch, Nephi functions as a faithful recorder of sacred words and history, using the best available materials to ensure permanence.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 21:4-5 describes the role of the Church president in receiving the Lord's word, with the implication that such words are to be preserved and transmitted faithfully. The principle of faithful transmission through appointed servants—prophet to scribe to reader—continues in modern revelation.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The careful recording and preservation of sacred texts parallels the temple principle of sealed, preserved ordinances and covenants. Just as Baruch's ink permanently fixes the prophetic word, temple sealings 'bind on earth and in heaven.' Both involve the faithful transmission and preservation of binding divine speech through authorized means.

commentary.christological_typology: Baruch's role as faithful recorder of Jeremiah's words foreshadows the role of the apostles and evangelists as recorders of Jesus' words and actions. Just as Baruch did not compose the words but faithfully transcribed them, the Gospel writers understood themselves as witnesses and recorders of the Living Word, not as authors creating new doctrine. The mention of 'ink'—permanent, unchangeable—suggests the permanence of prophetic and divine speech: once spoken and recorded, the word cannot be unmade. Christ, the Word made flesh, similarly establishes a permanent reality that history cannot erase, even if specific physical records are destroyed.
commentary.application: Baruch's straightforward answer—'He spoke; I wrote faithfully'—models integrity and accountability. In our modern context, when we are entrusted with communicating God's word or another's message, we bear the responsibility Baruch accepted: faithful transmission without addition, subtraction, or interpretation. This applies to teachers sharing doctrine, parents teaching children, or any believer bearing testimony. We are not the authors of the truth we proclaim; we are the recorders and transmitters. Our responsibility is accuracy, not originality. The verse also invites appreciation for the scribes, scholars, and keepers of texts who have preserved God's word for us. We hold in our hands the product of countless Baruks throughout history—faithful scribes who chose accuracy over convenience, permanence over profit. Finally, the mention of ink—permanent and irreplaceable—challenges us to consider the weight of what we say and write: once spoken or written, our words have reality and consequence. Like ink, they cannot be wholly taken back.

text_kjv: Then said the princes unto Baruch, Go, hide thee, thou and Jeremiah; and let no man know where ye be.

commentary.narrative:
After hearing the scroll read aloud, the officials recognize the danger they and Jeremiah now face. Their command to hide is not cowardice but clear-eyed assessment: they have heard prophetic judgment against Judah and the king, and they know Jehoiakim's temperament. The word 'princes' (שָׂרִים, sarim) refers to high officials in the royal court — men with access to the king but not immunity from his wrath. These are the same officials who, moments before, were deeply alarmed by the scroll's contents (v. 16). Their protective instruction to Baruch and Jeremiah reveals a profound tension in their position: they take God's word seriously enough to be genuinely afraid, yet they lack the courage or power to stand openly against the king.

The command to hide (הִסָּתֵר, histater, 'to conceal oneself') carries urgency and practicality. The officials do not tell Baruch and Jeremiah to flee Judah or to go public with the scroll — they tell them to disappear, to go underground. This reflects their understanding that the king will seek to destroy both the messengers and the message. The Covenant Rendering's emphasis — 'No one must know where you are' — captures the absolute nature of the concealment required. The officials are buying time and preserving lives, perhaps hoping the king's initial rage will pass or that circumstances will change.

word_study.meaning: Rulers, officials, commanders; members of the royal court with administrative authority. The term can refer to military commanders, regional governors, or high-ranking courtiers. Here it denotes the king's closest advisors.
word_study.significance: These officials occupy an ambiguous position throughout the narrative — they hear the word, fear it, attempt to buffer the king from it, yet ultimately cannot protect the prophet. Their fear of the scroll's message (v. 16, pachadu) contrasts with the king's fearlessness (v. 24, lo fachadu), showing that proximity to God's word produces fear in some hearts and hardness in others.

word_study.meaning: From the root סתר (s-t-r), 'to conceal, hide, cover.' The hifil form here is reflexive — 'to hide oneself, to go into hiding.' The root carries connotations not just of physical concealment but of refuge and protection.
word_study.significance: This command echoes the protective pattern of Jeremiah's ministry — he will be hidden, protected by allies, concealed from the king's reach. The word suggests refuge rather than mere escape; it implies finding a place of safety where one can continue God's work. The Covenant Rendering emphasizes the totality of concealment required in this moment.

cross_references.connection: Ahikam son of Shaphan protects Jeremiah from death, echoing this pattern of officials who take the prophet's side despite royal hostility.

King Josiah's response to hearing God's word — tearing his garments in repentance — provides a stark contrast to his son Jehoiakim's contemptuous response, which will be explicitly mentioned in verse 24.
The principle that God reveals His secrets to His servants the prophets; Jeremiah and Baruch are fulfilling this prophetic function by recording and reading God's word.
Michal hides David from Saul's wrath, establishing the Old Testament pattern of covert protection for those pursued by hostile rulers for prophetic faithfulness.

commentary.historical_context: The 'princes' or 'officials' (sarim) would have included the king's cabinet — military commanders, administrators, scribes, and counselors. Many served at the pleasure of the king and could be removed, exiled, or executed at his whim. The structure of the royal court meant these men had enough access to know dangerous information but not enough power to openly oppose the king without risking their positions and lives. Their instruction to Jeremiah and Baruch to hide reflects the reality of political vulnerability in the ancient Near East, where a king's mood could rapidly shift from favor to fury. The scroll's reading in the presence of these officials made them witnesses and, by extension, potential targets if the king believed they sympathized with the prophetic message.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 36:22-24 describes Alma's fear when confronted with the word of God, similar to the officials' alarm; however, Alma responds with repentance while these officials respond with protective hiding rather than transformation. The Book of Mormon repeatedly shows that hearing God's word produces a choice — to harden or to soften the heart.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 21:4-6 emphasizes the Lord's protection of the bearer of His word; Jeremiah and Baruch, like the Joseph Smith whose writings the D&C preserves, are protected by allies even when hunted by powerful enemies. The pattern of hiding the Lord's word and His servants reappears throughout Restoration history.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The protection and concealment of sacred records — a theme central to Jeremiah 36 — finds its fullest expression in the hiding and preservation of temple records, priesthood ordinances, and sacred knowledge, which are concealed from the profane and revealed only to the covenant community.

commentary.christological_typology: Jeremiah and Baruch, hunted by the king for bearing God's word, prefigure the persecution of Christ and His apostles. The necessity to hide in order to preserve the message foreshadows Jesus's instruction to His disciples to be 'wise as serpents' (Matthew 10:16) and the early Church's use of catacombs and hidden meeting places. The scroll itself — God's written word destined to be destroyed yet preserved — points to Christ, the Living Word, whose death was intended to end His message but whose resurrection and continued witness have proven indestructible.
commentary.application: Modern members face pressure, though rarely lethal, to hide or minimize their testimony of God's word. This verse teaches that there are times when discretion and protection of sacred things are not cowardice but wisdom. The officials recognize a fundamental truth: some hearts are closed to the message, and pursuing confrontation with those bent on destruction serves no purpose. Yet this verse also teaches that the hiding must be strategic and temporary, not a permanent silence. Jeremiah and Baruch will not stay hidden; they will eventually record the scroll again. The lesson is that covenant members must discern when to speak boldly and when to preserve themselves and the message for a future season when it may be received.

text_kjv: And they went in to the king into the court, but they laid up the roll in the chamber of Elishama the scribe, and told all the words in the ears of the king.

commentary.narrative:
This verse reveals a crucial strategic decision by the officials. They do not bring the scroll directly to the king; instead, they place it in safe-keeping first, then go to Jehoiakim with only an oral report. Elishama the scribe occupies a significant position in this narrative — he is a trusted officer (likely the keeper of records) whose chamber can serve as a secure repository. The officials' tactic appears designed to buffer the king's first encounter with the word: let him hear the content orally, gauge his reaction, and perhaps retain control of access to the physical document. However, this strategy reveals their misunderstanding of the king's character. Jehoiakim will not be satisfied with a summary; he will demand the scroll itself.

The phrase 'told all the words in the ears of the king' emphasizes oral transmission. In ancient court culture, being heard 'in the ears' of the king meant speaking directly to his person, with intimacy and authority. But words spoken in ears can be dismissed or forgotten; Jehoiakim will not be satisfied with ephemeral speech. The officials' decision to lodge the scroll with Elishama is an act of protective instinct — they are trying to preserve it from immediate destruction. Yet they underestimate both the king's determination and his willingness to summon the document. Their precaution, though well-intentioned, proves futile.

word_study.meaning: Hifil form of פקד (p-q-d), meaning 'to entrust, deposit, commit to safekeeping.' The root carries connotations of careful placement under someone's care or watch. It implies both security and custody — the scroll is being placed in trusted hands for preservation.
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering's 'deposited' captures the deliberate, careful nature of this action. The officials are not merely setting the scroll aside; they are entrusting it to Elishama with an implicit understanding that it will be protected. This term, used elsewhere for trusting valuables or children to a guardian's care, reveals the officials' sense that they are protecting something of great worth. Ironically, they are protecting God's word from a king who wants to destroy it — an act that honors the word even as it reflects political powerlessness.

word_study.meaning: A room, chamber, or storehouse. The term refers to a dedicated space, often in a palace or temple, used for specific purposes — administrative offices, treasure storage, or record-keeping. Elishama's chamber would be an official space within the palace complex.
word_study.significance: That the scroll is placed in a scribe's chamber — the very space where documents are created, preserved, and kept — suggests an appropriate place of safekeeping. Yet even the official record-room is not safe from a determined king. This detail underscores the vulnerability of the written word when a ruler opposes it: no institutional protection, no bureaucratic safety, can ultimately shield God's message from a king bent on its destruction.

word_study.term_original: וַיַּגִּ֙ידוּ֙ בְּאָזְנֵ֣י הַמֶּ֔לֶךְ אֵ֖ת כָּל־הַדְּבָרִֽים׃ (vayyaggidu be'oznei hammelekh et kol-haddebarim)
word_study.meaning: They reported, announced, or made known all the words/matters in the ears/hearing of the king. 'In the ears' is an idiom for direct, personal communication to someone's presence.
word_study.significance: The phrase emphasizes oral, face-to-face communication. In ancient Near Eastern court culture, to speak 'in the ears' of a ruler meant to address him directly, often with respectful access. Yet this intimacy does not translate into influence over the king. The officials can report the contents, but they cannot control how the king receives or responds to what he hears.

cross_references.connection: The earlier reading before the officials in the scribe Gemariah's chamber, which prompted their alarm and led to this cautious approach to the king.
The law requiring the king to write out and read the law; Jehoiakim's rejection of this scroll violates the covenantal obligation of the king to receive God's word with reverence.
Josiah's scribes bring the scroll of the law to him, and he hears it with fear and repentance — the inverse of Jehoiakim's response to the same scenario of a king hearing God's word via officials.

The principle of officials and scribes bearing the word of God and the king's authority (even when the king is receptive); Artaxerxes receives the law through his officials, though his response is dramatically different from Jehoiakim's.

commentary.historical_context: Elishama the scribe (סֹפֵר, sofer) would have been a high administrative official, likely responsible for royal correspondence, record-keeping, and perhaps the royal archives. In the ancient Near East, scribes held considerable power and prestige; they were the literate elite who preserved and transmitted official documents. The 'chamber of Elishama' would be an official office within the palace, marked by its access to the scribe's authority and the security provided by the palace structure itself. However, even this institutional authority could not protect against the king's will. The officials' strategy reveals an understanding of palace politics: officials could sometimes buffer the king from immediate confrontation with information, manage his access to documents, and preserve things in neutral spaces. Yet this system of checks and balances breaks down entirely when the king is determined to act.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 37:2-5 describes the preservation of records by placing them in the care of trusted individuals; Alma entrusts records to his son Helaman, paralleling the officials' entrusting the scroll to Elishama. Both cases involve the protection of sacred text through careful placement in trustworthy hands.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 42:15 emphasizes that words once spoken cannot be recalled, yet written words can be preserved; the officials' strategy of oral report plus written preservation reflects the principle that God's word in written form has greater staying power than mere speech.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple veil separates sacred space and protects sacred ordinances from the profane; similarly, the officials attempt to create a buffer (Elishama's chamber) between the sacred scroll and the profane king. Yet just as the veil can be penetrated, physical barriers cannot protect God's word if a ruler is determined to destroy it.

commentary.christological_typology: The scroll placed in safekeeping and then forcibly retrieved foreshadows the resurrection and vindication of Christ. Though Jehoiakim attempts to destroy the scroll, it cannot be permanently destroyed — Jeremiah and Baruch will rewrite it, adding more (v. 32). Similarly, though Christ was crucified and entombed, His resurrection and the preservation of His message through the Gospels show that no power can ultimately destroy the Living Word.
commentary.application: This verse teaches about the limits of human strategy in preserving divine truth. The officials do what they can — protect the scroll, report carefully, manage access — but ultimately they cannot control the outcome. Modern members sometimes labor under the assumption that perfect planning, wise strategy, or careful management will protect their faith or their families from hostile forces. This verse suggests humility: we do our best to preserve sacred things and teach them wisely, but we cannot guarantee that all hearers will receive the message with reverence. Our responsibility is to protect and transmit faithfully; the reception belongs to God and to the receiver's free choice. The officials' failure also teaches that institutional safeguards — even the authority of scribes and the security of official chambers — cannot ultimately shield the word from those bent on its destruction. Only God's promises of preservation can be trusted absolutely.

text_kjv: So the king sent Jehudi to fetch the roll: and he took it out of Elishama the scribe's chamber. And Jehudi read it in the ears of the king, and in the ears of all the princes that stood beside the king.

commentary.narrative:
The king's summons of Jehudi represents the shattering of the officials' carefully laid plan. Jehoiakim does not accept the oral report; he demands the physical scroll. Jehudi (יְהוּדִי, Yehudi) is identified as a court official, likely a servant or attendant to the king, and his task is to retrieve the document from Elishama's protective custody. The verb 'sent' (שָׁלַח, shalach) indicates royal command — this is not a request but a demand backed by royal authority. The officials' protective strategy of hiding the scroll in Elishama's chamber bought a brief window of time but no permanent refuge. Once the king asks for the document, no official can refuse without risking his position or life.

The scene that follows is the third public reading of the scroll — first to Baruch and Jeremiah in private (v. 4), second to the officials in Gemariah's chamber (v. 12-13), and now before the king and his entire court. Each reading is more public and more dangerous than the last. Jehudi reads aloud (יִקְרָאֶ֤הָ, yiqra'eha) while the king sits and the officials stand beside him. The formality of court protocol — standing officials, seated king, an official reader — heightens the solemnity of the moment. Yet this same protocol will prove irrelevant when Jehoiakim decides to destroy the scroll. The presence of all the officials means multiple witnesses to both the word and the king's response, though their presence cannot sway the king's will.

word_study.meaning: To send, dispatch, or command to go. The verb carries the force of royal authority — when a king 'sends' someone, it is a command, not a request. The root is fundamental to describing the dispatch of messengers, servants, or military forces.
word_study.significance: The use of shalach emphasizes that Jehoiakim is exercising kingly prerogative. He does not ask for the scroll; he commands its delivery. This verb echoes the sending of officials in verse 12 and will recur in the pattern of Jeremiah being 'sent' by God — yet here it describes the king's power to command, not God's authority.

word_study.meaning: A name meaning 'the Judean' or 'the Jew.' The name is likely that of a court official, though little else is known about him. The text gives him no character development; he is simply an instrument of the king's will, summoned to retrieve and read the scroll.
word_study.significance: Jehudi is a neutral figure — not hostile to the prophet, but simply carrying out the king's command. His neutrality makes his role particularly tragic: he is the one who will read God's word, section by section, as the king systematically destroys it. He becomes, unknowingly, a witness to the word's destruction.

word_study.meaning: To take, seize, or retrieve. The infinitive form emphasizes the action of retrieval. Laqach ('to take') is a simple, direct action — fetch the scroll.
word_study.significance: The plainness of the language contrasts with the ominous implications. The king's command is stated matter-of-factly: go get the scroll. Yet the reader knows what will follow. The Covenant Rendering's 'fetch' captures the casual tone that masks the catastrophic intent.

word_study.meaning: To read, proclaim, or call. The qal imperfect form indicates ongoing or repeated action. The scroll is read aloud in the ancient mode — not silently by the listener, but vocally by the reader, heard by all present.
word_study.significance: The verb yiqra connects to the qeriah ('calling' or 'reading') of scripture in ancient Israel. Reading is a public, audible act. Yet in this case, the reading is accompanied by the king's act of slicing and burning. The word is simultaneously proclaimed and destroyed.

word_study.meaning: 'Standing over/beside the king.' The preposition me'al ('from over/beside') describes officials standing in positions of attendance near the seated king. In court protocol, standing while the king sat demonstrated respect and readiness to serve.
word_study.significance: The spatial arrangement reinforces hierarchy: the king is seated (in a position of authority and comfort), while officials stand (in positions of service and attention). This physical arrangement will intensify the tragedy of the scene — the standing officials will be powerless to prevent what the seated king does.

cross_references.connection: The first reading, in private, to Baruch and Jeremiah, establishing the baseline for how the scroll should be received — with attention and faithfulness.
The second reading to the officials, which provokes genuine fear; this contrast with their inability to prevent the third reading emphasizes their political powerlessness.
The parallel scene in which Josiah hears the scroll and responds with reverence and fear, providing the sharp contrast to Jehoiakim's response.
The law requires public reading of God's word to the people; Jeremiah's scroll is being read, but to a king who will respond with destruction rather than covenant renewal.

The sealed scroll in John's vision, which no one is worthy to open except the Lion of Judah, is the inverse of Jeremiah's scroll, which a king opens and destroys without any sense of its sacred character.

commentary.historical_context: Court protocol in the ancient Near East prescribed precise arrangements for royal audiences. Kings received petitioners and listened to reports while seated, often on a throne, with officials and courtiers standing nearby in positions of deference. The reading of an important document before a king was a formal act, typically performed by a designated official or scribe. Jehudi's role as the reader suggests he held an official position, perhaps as a clerk or herald. The gathering of 'all the princes' (the full court) to hear the reading indicates its importance and, from the officials' perspective, perhaps their hope that numbers and formality would impress the king with the seriousness of the scroll's content. However, formal protocol proved irrelevant to Jehoiakim's will.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 32:28-29 describes the word as a seed planted; the scroll's reading before the king is like planting seed, but on the hardest ground — a heart closed to growth. The Book of Mormon emphasizes that the word takes root and grows only in hearts prepared to receive it.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 76:5-7 describes receiving truth through revelation; the officials and even Jehudi receive the word through hearing, yet it does not take root in Jehoiakim's heart. The Restoration teaches that truth received must be received by a willing heart or it produces no covenant fruit.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The reading of the scroll before the assembled court mirrors the reading of scriptures and the teaching of covenants in the temple, where gathered saints hear sacred words. Yet this scene is a dark inversion — sacred words are heard but rejected, destroyed rather than internalized.

commentary.christological_typology: The reading of God's word before a hostile king prefigures Christ's declaration of His mission in the synagogue (Luke 4:16-30), where He reads from Isaiah and the crowd's initial curiosity turns to rage and the desire to kill Him. The process is reversed — Christ is the Living Word being rejected — yet the principle is the same: the word of God, once spoken, creates division and either reception or violent rejection. Jehudi, the neutral instrument of the king's will, foreshadows the soldiers and officials who execute Christ's crucifixion; neither recognizes the cosmic significance of what they are doing.
commentary.application: Modern members often assume that if the truth is simply presented clearly enough, people will receive it. This verse suggests otherwise. The officials presented the scroll well; Jehudi read it professionally; the context was solemn and formal. Yet the king's heart remained closed. This teaches humility about our power to convince. Our role is to faithfully present God's word, as Jehudi faithfully reads it. The reception belongs to the hearer. Furthermore, the verse teaches that even formal, institutional settings — the royal court with all its dignity and order — cannot compel righteousness. Modern religious institutions and structures have value, but they cannot force a hardened heart to soften. Only God's grace can transform the will.

text_kjv: Now the king sat in the winterhouse in the ninth month: and there was a fire on the hearth burning before him.

commentary.narrative:
This verse performs the crucial narrative function of establishing the physical setting and, implicitly, the means of destruction. The 'winterhouse' (בֵּ֣ית הַחֹ֔רֶף, beit hachoref) was the palace's winter quarters, used during the cold months. The ninth month (Kislev, roughly November-December) indicates the season when heating was necessary. The brazier (אָח, ach) — a portable metal or ceramic container burning with charcoal — was common in ancient Near Eastern homes and palaces for warmth. Yet in this verse, the brazier's innocuous function as a source of warmth becomes charged with ominous significance. The reader has not yet learned that the scroll will be destroyed; but the narrative's specific attention to the fire's presence tells us exactly how it will happen.

The verse is a masterpiece of narrative restraint. It does not say 'the king sat in the winterhouse preparing to destroy the scroll'; it simply reports physical facts. Yet those facts contain the tragedy in miniature. The king is seated for comfort, warming himself by a fire. The scroll is about to be brought in, page by page. Each page will be cut from the scroll and cast into the very fire meant for warmth, turning an instrument of comfort into an instrument of destruction. The phrase 'before him' (לְפָנָֽיו, lefanav) emphasizes the proximity of the fire to the king — it is within arm's reach, available, ready to be used. The verse's apparent simplicity masks profound irony: the very comfort and ease of the royal situation enables and facilitates the destruction of God's word.

word_study.meaning: The 'house of cold' or 'winter house'; a dedicated section of a palace used during the colder months. Beit ('house') refers to a room or building; choref ('cold' or 'winter') indicates its seasonal purpose. Wealthy households in the ancient Near East maintained separate quarters for different seasons, with summer houses for ventilation and winter houses for insulation and heating.
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering's 'winter quarters' captures the sense of a designated space. This detail is not merely atmospheric; it indicates that the king is at ease, in his comfort zone, warmed and secure. Yet it is precisely in this place of comfort that he will enact his violence against God's word. The verse suggests that evil often flourishes not in moments of crisis or hardship, but in moments of ease and power.

word_study.meaning: The ninth month in the Hebrew calendar, corresponding to Kislev (roughly November-December). In the biblical calendar, months are numbered from Nisan (spring), making the ninth month fall in late autumn/early winter.
word_study.significance: The specific temporal marker places the scene in a season of cold and darkness. In later Jewish tradition, Kislev becomes the month of Hanukkah, a festival of light. The tragic irony is that in this dark season, the light of God's written word will be deliberately snuffed out. The winter setting also emphasizes the inhospitality of the time; Jeremiah and Baruch are fleeing into the cold months ahead.

word_study.meaning: And the brazier was burning/blazing before him. Ach ('brazier') is a rare word in Hebrew, appearing only in this chapter (vv. 22-23). Mebo'eret ('burning, blazing') is the feminine participle of ba'ar, meaning 'to consume by fire, to burn.' The phrase literally means 'the brazier was burning before him.'
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering's specificity here is crucial: 'a fire burning in the brazier before him,' not merely 'a fire' but a specific, contained fire in a specific vessel, positioned within the king's immediate vicinity. The redundancy of 'before him' emphasizes accessibility. The fire is not across the room; it is right there, ready to be used. The verb mebo'eret ('burning') is in the durative state — the fire is already going, not being lit for the first time. It is an established fire, constant and present.

word_study.meaning: A portable container for burning charcoal, used for heating rooms in ancient homes and palaces. The ach was typically made of metal (bronze or copper) or ceramic, with a wide mouth to hold burning charcoal and sometimes handles for carrying. It served the practical purpose of providing localized warmth without the need for a built-in fireplace.
word_study.significance: As noted in the TCR translator notes, ach is a rare term, appearing only in Jeremiah 36:22-23. The word's rarity makes its introduction here significant — it is not a common hearth or fireplace but a specific, portable vessel. This detail matters because a portable brazier can be moved, refilled, adjusted. It is an intimate fire, not a distant architectural feature. In the context of this narrative, the ach becomes the instrument of the scroll's destruction. The tool meant for comfort becomes the tool of annihilation.

cross_references.connection: Amos condemns the wealthy who have 'winter houses and summer houses,' pointing to the luxury and excess often associated with spiritual hardness; Jehoiakim's ease in his winterhouse mirrors the complacency condemned by the prophets.

The Psalmist describes God's judgment: 'Thou shalt make them as a fiery oven in the time of thine anger'; here, the king uses fire not as God's instrument of judgment but as his own instrument of rebellion against God's word.

The prophecy that 'all the proud, yea, and all that do wickedly, shall be stubble: and the day that cometh shall burn them up'; the fire that warms Jehoiakim in his comfort foreshadows the divine fire that will ultimately consume him and his house.
Paul describes Christ being 'revealed from heaven with his mighty angels, In flaming fire'; in ultimate contrast to this scene, God's word will be vindicated by divine fire, not destroyed by it.

commentary.historical_context: Winter houses in the ancient Near East were a luxury of the wealthy and royal. The palace of a Judean king like Jehoiakim would have included multiple suites of rooms designed for different seasons. The ninth month (Kislev) in Jerusalem can be quite cold, with temperatures dropping to near freezing at night and substantial chill during the day. A brazier would provide essential warmth in an interior room without requiring central heating. The use of charcoal (from wood burned in special conditions to produce a long-lasting, high-heat fuel) indicates a relatively sophisticated heating method, available only to the wealthy and royal. The specific detail that the brazier is 'burning' suggests a fresh or well-maintained fire, not a dying ember. In ancient palace settings, maintaining the king's comfort was the constant work of servants; the fire would be kept going throughout the day and evening.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: 2 Nephi 28:21-23 describes how the devil leads people to comfort in sin, suggesting that ease and comfort are often the conditions under which spiritual hardness develops. Jehoiakim's comfort in his winterhouse parallels the Nephites' descent into pride and spiritual blindness while materially comfortable.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 95:7-8 uses the image of a refiner's fire to describe God's judgment upon His people; here, the fire is not God's refining instrument but man's destructive force. The contrast between fire that refines (God's) and fire that destroys (man's) is central to Restoration theology.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple contains sacred altars where fire burns as a sign of God's presence and acceptance of offerings. The king's brazier, by contrast, is an instrument of sacrilege, not sacred worship. The contrast suggests the perversion of religious symbols and objects when used in service to rebellion against God.

commentary.christological_typology: The fire about to destroy the scroll prefigures the trial of Christ. Just as the scroll (God's written word) will be consumed in flames, Christ (God's Living Word) will be subjected to crucifixion and the cross (sometimes described metaphorically as fire testing). Yet in both cases — the scroll and Christ — the intention is destruction, but the ultimate outcome is preservation and vindication. The scroll will be rewritten, fuller and richer. Christ will rise and reign eternally. The fire that was meant to destroy becomes the very means by which the word's eternal significance is demonstrated.
commentary.application: This verse reminds modern members that moral and spiritual danger often does not announce itself. Jehoiakim is not in a moment of crisis, under pressure, or facing urgent temptation. He is comfortable, warm, at ease in his winterhouse. It is precisely in such moments that vigilance is required. Comfort and abundance can soften moral sensibility and harden the heart against God's word. The verse teaches that times of ease are times to draw closer to God's word, not times to drift from it. Furthermore, the verse teaches that the instruments of blessing (warmth from the fire) can become instruments of destruction when used in rebellion against God. Our talents, resources, and positions — all meant to be used in service to God and good — can be perverted to destructive purposes if we allow our hearts to harden against truth.

text_kjv: And it came to pass, that when Jehudi had read three or four leaves, he cut it with the penknife, and cast it into the fire that was on the hearth, until all the roll was consumed in the fire that was on the hearth.

commentary.narrative:
This verse is the narrative climax of the entire chapter — the moment of destruction itself. The verb 'came to pass' (וַיְהִ֣י, vayehi) marks the transition from setting to action. Jehudi reads not the entire scroll at once, but section by section. After reading three or four 'columns' (דְּלָתוֹת, delathot — the visible 'doors' or panels of text on an unrolled scroll), Jehoiakim interrupts. He does not wait to hear the complete message; he does not contemplate or debate; he acts with immediate and deliberate violence.

The king takes the scribe's knife (תַּעַר הַסֹּפֵ֗ר, ta'ar hasofer) — the very tool used to prepare, trim, and repair scrolls — and uses it to cut the section from the scroll. This is not a moment of uncontrolled rage; it is systematic, even ritualistic. He cuts after every few columns, slices away the parchment, and casts it into the brazier. The iterative construction in the verse ('three or four columns, then cut, then throw') repeated until 'all the roll was consumed' indicates a prolonged, deliberate, methodical destruction. The king is performing a ritual of annihilation, not a momentary outburst. The repetition of 'the fire that was on the hearth' at both the beginning and end of the verb phrase hammers home the image: this fire is the instrument of destruction, and it consumes everything.

The phrase 'until all the roll was consumed' indicates that Jehoiakim persists until nothing is left. This is total destruction. There is no moment where he has second thoughts, no officials who successfully intercede, no divine intervention. The scroll is utterly burned. Yet the narrative arc of the chapter ensures that the reader knows this destruction is not final — Jeremiah and Baruch will rewrite it, and what is rewritten will be longer and richer than the original (v. 32). The king's attempt to silence God's word will fail.

word_study.meaning: Literally 'doors'; in the context of scrolls, the word refers to the visible columns or panels of text visible when a scroll is unrolled to reading position. The metaphor compares the columns of writing to doors — perhaps suggesting the architectural panels of a building, or perhaps understood as 'openings' or 'sections' through which the text is accessed.
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering's 'columns' makes the meaning clearer to modern readers, though the Hebrew 'doors' carries the ancient metaphor. When a scroll was unrolled, the text would appear in columns, and 'three or four doors' would mean a manageable portion to read aloud, perhaps thirty to fifty lines of text. The use of delathot (a plural form suggesting multiple, discrete sections) emphasizes that the destruction is sectional, not all at once. The king allows Jehudi to read, then slices off a section, then throws it into the fire. This gives the illusion of a process, a sequence, when in fact each step seals the same fate.

word_study.meaning: To tear, rip, cut. The qal imperfect form indicates an ongoing or repeated action. The root q-r-a relates to tearing or ripping apart. This is not a careful cutting with precision but a violent tearing of the parchment.
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering's 'cut off' suggests a decisive action. The verb emphasizes violence — tearing, not neatly separating. This is an act of destruction, not of careful handling. The same root (q-r-a) is used for tearing garments in grief or mourning (see verse 24, 'they did not tear their garments'). The king tears the scroll as a gesture of utter rejection; it is the inverse of tearing garments in mourning for death. He tears the scroll, mourning nothing, regretting nothing.

word_study.meaning: A blade used by scribes (soferim) for cutting and trimming parchment, scraping away errors, and shaping the edges of scrolls. The ta'ar is a sharp instrument, necessary for the craft of creating and maintaining written texts.
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering notes the deep irony here: the instrument created for the production and preservation of texts becomes the instrument of destruction. The scribe's knife is meant to be used in service to the word; Jehoiakim uses it to unmake the word. This inversion of purpose is central to the verse's tragic power — the tools of literacy itself are turned against the text. The choice to mention the scribe's knife specifically (not just 'a knife' or 'a blade') emphasizes the perversion: this tool belongs in the hands of someone preserving text, not destroying it.

word_study.meaning: To throw, cast, or hurl into. The verb hashlekh means to throw forcefully, to cast away, to discard. The preposition el ('into') indicates direction — the action is toward the fire, into its consuming flames.
word_study.significance: The verb conveys violence and contempt. Jehoiakim is not carefully placing the pieces in the fire; he is throwing them, casting them aside. The action mirrors the theological gesture of complete rejection — not just refusing the message but violently repudiating it, casting it away as worthless. Each throwing is an act of defiance against God.

word_study.meaning: The completion or ending of the entire scroll; tom means 'to be finished, completed, consumed.' The phrase emphasizes totality — nothing of the scroll remains. This is not partial destruction but the total annihilation of the physical document.
word_study.significance: The repetition of 'all the roll' (kol-hamegillah) and the final phrase 'in the fire in the brazier' (al-ha'esh asher ba'ach) creates a hammering insistence on total consumption. The rhetoric of the verse emphasizes that the king leaves nothing standing, no remnant of the original scroll. Yet this very totality will lead to the rewriting. Had the king allowed even part of the scroll to survive, Jeremiah might not have felt compelled to dictate it again, enriched and expanded.

cross_references.connection: King Josiah tears his garments in repentance upon hearing God's word; his son Jehoiakim tears (cuts) the scroll itself in contempt, showing the contrast between a king who receives God's word and a king who rejects it.
Immediately following the destruction, Jeremiah dictates the scroll to Baruch again, with additional words — demonstrating that God's word cannot be destroyed by human hands, only multiplied.
Though Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego are cast into a fiery furnace, they are preserved; similarly, the words of God, though cast into fire by the king, will be preserved and vindicated.

Jesus declares that not one jot or tittle shall pass away from the law; the destruction of Jeremiah's scroll stands as an attempt to prove Christ's words false, yet history proves Him right — the word endures.
John receives a revelation that must be written and witnessed; despite persecution, the written word of God persists through time, as Jeremiah's rewritten scroll persists.

commentary.historical_context: The systematic destruction of a scroll by a ruler was a known instrument of suppression in the ancient Near East. However, the total destruction of Jeremiah's scroll was unusual in its completeness — few rulers would spend the time and focus to ensure that every column of a lengthy scroll was burned. The act was theatrical as well as destructive; the king's actions were witnessed by his entire court. This public destruction served as a statement: the king was declaring to everyone present that he rejected not only the content of the scroll but its very right to exist. The use of the scribe's knife adds a level of craft and deliberation to the act — this is not the violence of a mob but the considered action of a ruler executing his will. In the context of ancient literacy, scrolls were valuable objects, both economically and intellectually. A scroll of this length would represent many hours of scribal labor and the cost of parchment. That the king would deliberately destroy such an object indicates both his power (he could afford the loss) and his contempt for what it contained.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 14:8-10 describes the burning of believers and their records by a persecuting mob; yet despite this violence, the truth endures and is eventually vindicated. The Book of Mormon itself is a parallel: records were hidden and preserved despite attempts to destroy them. The principle that God's word cannot be destroyed, only hidden and later revealed, appears throughout the Book of Mormon.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 123:1-7 describes the persecution of the early Church and commands the Saints to keep records 'for your own exaltation and for the exaltation of your posterity.' Jeremiah's scroll, though burned, will be rewritten; similarly, the records of the Restoration, though persecuted, endure. The Doctrine and Covenants itself exists because, like Jeremiah, the Lord's servants were commanded to record the word.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The destruction of the scroll by fire stands in contrast to sacred fire in the temple — fire that was meant to consume offerings as a sign of God's acceptance. The king's fire consumes God's word in a gesture of rejection. In the temple, fire symbolizes purification and transformation; in Jehoiakim's brazier, it symbolizes destruction and contempt. The contrast underscores the perversion of sacred symbols when used in rebellion.

commentary.christological_typology: This verse prefigures the crucifixion of Christ, the Living Word. Just as the written scroll is methodically cut apart and cast into fire, Christ's body is methodically tortured and offered up on the cross. Yet in both cases, the intent to destroy fails — the scroll is rewritten, fuller and richer; Christ is resurrected, glorified and eternal. The verse also echoes the spiritual principle that attempts to destroy God's word paradoxically confirm its importance. The very fact that Jehoiakim felt compelled to burn the scroll demonstrates his awareness of its power and significance. Similarly, the fact that the world persecuted and crucified Christ demonstrates the threat the world sensed in Him. The reaction of the persecutor reveals the reality of what is persecuted.
commentary.application: This verse teaches that hostility to God's word is real and has real power in the immediate term. The scroll was genuinely destroyed; no copy existed immediately after the burning. Jeremiah and Baruch could not walk back into the palace and retrieve it. In modern life, covenant members may face attempts to destroy or suppress truth — through mockery, institutional pressure, family opposition, or the subtler pressure of a culture that gradually makes faith uncomfortable. The verse acknowledges that these attempts can cause real damage in the short term. However, the narrative are of Jeremiah 36 teaches that human attempts to destroy God's word ultimately fail. The rewriting of the scroll, enriched and expanded, testifies that God's word, once given, cannot be unmade. Modern members who find their faith threatened by opposition can take comfort in this principle: truth may be hidden, suppressed, or temporarily lost from view, but it cannot be permanently destroyed. The task of believers is to have faith that truth, like Jeremiah's scroll, will be vindicated and preserved.

text_kjv: Yet they were not afraid, nor rent their garments, neither the king, nor any of his servants that heard all these words.

commentary.narrative:
This final verse of the reading functions as a devastating conclusion to the episode and, by implication, to the entire spiritual condition of Judah's leadership. It is constructed entirely as negation — what did not happen. The double negative structure ('they were not afraid, nor rent their garments') is emphatic: neither fear nor mourning occurred. This verse is the narrative opposite of what happened when the scroll was read in verse 16, when 'all the princes were afraid.' Here, after the scroll has been burned, neither the king nor his servants show any sign of the spiritual crisis that should accompany the destruction of God's word.

The language here deliberately recalls 2 Kings 22:11-13, where King Josiah heard the scroll of the law read: 'And it came to pass, when the king had heard the words of the book of the law, that he rent his clothes' and showed profound alarm and repentance. The contrast between Josiah's response and Jehoiakim's could not be more stark. Josiah tears his garments (קָרַע אֶת־בְגָדָיו, qara'a et-begadav) as an expression of horror at the judgment pronounced on his nation; Jehoiakim tears (cuts) the scroll itself in contempt. Where Josiah humbles himself before God's word, Jehoiakim exalts himself against it. The verse concludes the spiritual trajectory of Jerusalem's leadership: the king and his entire court are so hardened that the destruction of God's word produces no visible reaction — no fear, no grief, no repentance.

The phrase 'that heard all these words' is crucial. They heard the complete message. They were not ignorant of its content; they knew what God was saying through the prophet. Their lack of fear is not due to misunderstanding but to willful rejection. The scroll's entire message was proclaimed to them, and they responded with a kind of spiritual numbness — not even the emotional response of anger or defiance, but the absence of any spiritual response whatsoever.

word_study.meaning: They did not fear, were not afraid. Pachad means 'to fear, be afraid, be in awe.' The negation creates the opposite: the absence of fear. Notably, this is the inverse of verse 16, where the officials 'were afraid' (pachadu) upon hearing the same message.
word_study.significance: The contrast between the officials' fear and the king's fearlessness reveals a spiritual distinction. The officials' fear indicates they recognize God's voice and the gravity of judgment. The king's lack of fear indicates either spiritual blindness or deliberate hardness. The word pachad also carries the connotation of reverent awe before God; its absence here means the king shows no reverence, no recognition of the divine authority behind the scroll.

word_study.meaning: They did not tear/rip their garments. Qara'a means 'to tear, rend, rip.' Bigdim refers to garments or clothes. Tearing one's garments was a gesture of grief, mourning, distress, and repentance in ancient Hebrew culture.
word_study.significance: The absence of garment-tearing is the absence of mourning. In ancient Israel, tearing garments was an expected response to death, calamity, or awareness of divine judgment. The phrase deliberately echoes Josiah's response to hearing the law, which included tearing garments (2 Kings 22:11). Jehoiakim's failure to tear his garments is his failure to mourn, to grieve, or to repent. The same root word (qara'a) is used in verse 23 for the king cutting the scroll; Jehoiakim tears the scroll but not his garments — an ironic inversion that shows his hardness.

word_study.meaning: His servants, his attendants, those who serve the king. Avadim refers to servants or slaves in a general sense, but in the context of the royal court, it refers to officials, courtiers, and attendants who serve at the pleasure of the king.
word_study.significance: The phrase 'neither the king, nor any of his servants' emphasizes the totality of spiritual hardness. It is not just the king; it is his entire entourage. This suggests that the hardness is not individual but systemic — the entire court has been corrupted by the king's will or is so aligned with his worldview that none of them break ranks to express alarm or grief. The phrase also suggests that the servants mirror the king's attitude, showing the corrosive effect of leadership hardness on an entire institution.

word_study.term_original: הַשֹּׁ֣מְעִ֔ים אֵ֥ת כָּל־הַדְּבָרִ֖ים הָאֵֽלֶּה׃ (hashomedim et kol-haddebarim ha'elleh)
word_study.meaning: Those who heard all these words/matters. Shema'a means 'to hear, listen, obey.' Debarim means 'words, matters, events.' The phrase emphasizes that they heard completely — all the words, not just a portion.
word_study.significance: The emphasis on 'all these words' reinforces that ignorance is not an excuse. They heard the entire message. They were not kept in the dark; they were fully informed of God's judgment and summons to repentance. Their lack of fear, therefore, is not based on misunderstanding but on willful hardness. The phrase echoes the covenant principle that those who hear the word bear responsibility for their response to it.

cross_references.connection: Josiah's response to hearing the scroll of the law — tearing his garments, repenting, seeking the Lord — stands in vivid contrast to Jehoiakim's response of contempt and hardness.
The officials earlier were genuinely afraid when they heard the scroll read; the king's fearlessness after hearing it shows the depth of his rejection of God's word.
Pharaoh's repeated refusal to humble himself before God's word and signs; like Pharaoh, Jehoiakim refuses to acknowledge God's authority or the gravity of judgment.

Paul describes those who are hardening 'their hearts after thy hardness and impenitent heart, treasurest up unto thyself wrath'; Jehoiakim's hardness is storing up judgment for himself and his nation.
The warning against hardening one's heart when hearing the voice of God; Jehoiakim exemplifies the hardened heart that refuses to listen, repent, or respond to divine summons.

commentary.historical_context: The court of Jehoiakim (608-597 BCE) was characterized by political instability and resistance to the Babylonian threat. Jehoiakim had been placed on the throne by the Egyptian Pharaoh and later submitted to Babylon, creating a volatile diplomatic situation. The king's defiant response to Jeremiah's scroll may have been partly political — an assertion of independence and power at a moment when Judah's sovereignty was compromised. In such circumstances, a king might be especially resistant to prophetic warnings that acknowledged Babylon's inevitability or that criticized the king's own conduct. The court's collective lack of fear may have reflected the king's own attitude or may have indicated court members' awareness that expressing alarm or dissent would endanger them. The cultural practice of tearing garments as a response to bad news was deeply embedded in ancient Near Eastern practice, making its absence all the more striking. An observer from the ancient world would have been shocked by a court that heard divine judgment without the expected emotional and physical responses.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels:
2 Nephi 28:27-28 describes the progression of deception and hardness in the latter days, including 'there shall also be many which shall say, Eat, drink, and be merry . . . and there is no harm in this.' The Book of Mormon repeatedly describes how societies gradually lose the capacity to respond to truth; Jehoiakim's hardness is an ancient example of spiritual sclerosis. The Book of Mormon also teaches in Alma 9:31-32 that 'And now behold, I say unto you, that if this people, who have received so many blessings from the hand of the Lord, should transgress contrary to the light and knowledge which they have received, I say unto you that if this be the case, that if they should fall into transgression, it would be far more tolerable for the Lamanites than for them.'

Jehoiakim and his court have received clear knowledge of God's will through the scroll, yet they respond with hardness rather than repentance. The Book of Mormon teaches that those given much light and rejecting it incur greater judgment.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 1:14-16 describes the Lord's word coming to the latter-day Church: 'And the voice of warning shall be unto all people, by the mouths of my disciples, whom I have chosen in these last days... Wherefore, I the Lord, knowing the calamity which should come upon the inhabitants of the earth, called upon my servant Joseph Smith, and spake unto him from heaven, and gave him commandments.' The Doctrine and Covenants itself exists because the Lord commands His word be recorded and shared. Jehoiakim's destruction of Jeremiah's scroll stands as a warning of what happens when people reject God's recorded word; the preservation and expansion of the Doctrine and Covenants testifies that God's word ultimately cannot be destroyed.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple is a place where covenants are made and spiritual sensitivity is cultivated. Those who receive temple ordinances are expected to develop the capacity to hear and respond to God's voice with reverence, fear, and willingness to change. Jehoiakim's hardness — his inability or unwillingness to fear God's word — represents the spiritual state of those who resist covenant and remain outside the saving ordinances. The temple is designed, in part, to soften hearts hardened by the world.

commentary.christological_typology: Jehoiakim's hardness prefigures the hardness of those who rejected and crucified Christ. The Gospels describe how even miracles and clear testimony failed to produce repentance in hostile crowds. Yet Christ's response to rejection was not to withdraw His message but to fulfill His mission completely, accepting even death. The contrast between Josiah's and Jehoiakim's responses also prefigures the contrast between two responses to Jesus: some (like the disciples and Mary Magdalene) responded with spiritual sensitivity and transformation; others (like the Pharisees and the high priest) responded with hardness and ultimately sought His destruction. The burning of the scroll by Jehoiakim foreshadows the crucifixion — an attempt to destroy God's word that paradoxically demonstrated its power and led to its vindication through Jeremiah's rewriting and through the Resurrection and the Gospels.
commentary.application: This verse is a sober warning about spiritual hardness. It teaches that it is possible to hear God's word clearly, repeatedly, and completely, yet remain unchanged. Mere exposure to truth does not guarantee response. The officials heard the same scroll and were afraid (v. 16); Jehoiakim heard it and showed no fear. The difference lay in the state of their hearts before hearing, not in the clarity or completeness of the message. Modern covenant members face a similar choice. Every General Conference, every sermon, every scripture study is an opportunity to have the heart softened or hardened. The verse suggests that failure to respond with fear, humility, and willingness to change is itself a choice — and a dangerous one. The phrase 'neither the king, nor any of his servants' warns that collective hardness is contagious.
