When a leader hardens his or her heart, others follow; when leadership resists truth, entire communities can become resistant. Yet the verse also teaches that the time of opportunity is limited. Jehoiakim's destruction of the scroll was not immediately punished, but his nation would fall to Babylon within a generation. The lack of immediate consequence is not a sign of impunity but a prelude to ultimate judgment. Modern members should take seriously the summons to soften their hearts, to fear God's word, and to repent while there is yet time.

text_kjv: Nevertheless Elnathan and Delaiah and Gemariah had made intercession to the king that he would not burn the roll: but he would not hear them.

commentary.narrative: In the immediate aftermath of Jeremiah's scroll being read aloud in the king's presence, three court officials attempt what should have been an obvious intervention: they urge Jehoiakim not to burn it. This moment reveals the complexity of opposition to Jeremiah in the royal court. These men were not prophets themselves, but they recognized something troubling about the king's impulse to destroy the written word. Gemariah, who appears here, is the same official in whose chamber Baruch had originally read the scroll to the people (verse 10)—his consistency in opposing its destruction suggests he understood the gravity of what was about to happen. Yet Jehoiakim refuses to listen. The verb shama ('to listen, hear') carries weight here: the king will not even grant his own advisors an audience. This refusal parallels the central accusation of Jeremiah's entire ministry—that Judah refuses to listen to God's word.
commentary.narrative_continued: The three names—Elnathan, Delaiah, and Gemariah—were real historical figures in Judah's court, and their advocacy here raises an important question about resistance to tyranny within power structures. Elnathan, notably, is the same official who had tracked down the prophet Uriah and brought him back from Egypt for execution (26:22). Yet here he intercedes to save a scroll. This is not a story of heroic rebels, but of officials attempting to operate within the system, to counsel restraint, to preserve something they sensed was worth preserving. That they fail is the point. Their failure sets up the entire theological claim of verses 26-30: when human intervention within existing power structures fails, God acts directly.

word_study.meaning: From the root פגע (p-g-'), meaning 'to meet, encounter, strike, intercede.' The Hiphil form intensifies the sense to 'to make strong intercession, to plead urgently.' The term suggests not merely a polite request but insistent, personal advocacy—these men threw themselves into the argument.
word_study.significance: This word appears elsewhere in contexts of prophetic intercession (e.g., 1 Samuel 2:25). By using it here, the text grants these officials a quasi-prophetic role—they are pleading, interceding, doing what the prophets do. Yet even this fails. The Covenant Rendering captures the intensity: 'urged' conveys the sense of urgent, passionate advocacy.

word_study.term_english: would not hear / would not listen
word_study.meaning: The root שמע (sh-m-') means 'to hear, listen, obey.' It is the verb that echoes through Jeremiah's prophecies—God calls and Judah does not listen. The negation velo shama ('he did not listen') is decisive: not merely that he disagreed, but that he refused to hear the voices of counsel.
word_study.significance: This verb creates a theological mirror. God sent Jeremiah to speak, and the people would not listen (7:24-26). Now the king will not listen to his own advisors. The refusal to listen is the foundational sin in Jeremiah, and it compounds itself through every level of society.

cross_references.connection: The repeated pattern: God speaks through the prophets, and the people refuse to listen (velo shamu). Jehoiakim's refusal to hear his own counselors echoes Judah's refusal to hear God.
Elnathan's earlier role in bringing the prophet Uriah back from Egypt for execution establishes the context for his later advocacy—he has witnessed the consequences of ignoring warnings before.

Another use of hifgi'u in the context of intercession: 'If one man sin against another, the judge shall judge him, but if a man sin against the LORD, who shall intreat for him?' The same word, the same impossibility when human mediation fails.
Modern revelation on forgiveness: 'Nevertheless, he that forgives shall be forgiven.' The refusal to listen, like the refusal to forgive, has spiritual consequences that cascade through history.
Book of Mormon theology on hardening the heart: those who resist the word experience a gradual spiritual decline. Jehoiakim's refusal to listen leads to inevitable judgment.

commentary.historical_context: The court of Jehoiakim (r. 609-598 BCE) was a center of conflicting political pressures. Egypt and Babylon competed for control of the Levant. Jehoiakim initially ruled as an Egyptian vassal but eventually submitted to Babylon. Jeremiah's prophecies of Babylonian invasion threatened the stability the king was attempting to maintain through diplomacy and military preparation. The king's advisors—particularly those involved in the reading and reception of the scroll—would have been deeply concerned about how prophecies of doom could affect morale and political strategy. Yet their concern was practical, not theological. They were not defending the scroll on grounds of divine authority but on grounds of prudence: 'Do not burn this thing.' That prudence failed because the king's commitment to denying the prophecy superseded even his advisors' counsel. This reveals a deep dysfunction in Jehoiakim's court: the king has isolated himself even from his own officials.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon records similar patterns of leadership rejecting counsel. Lehi's sons, though not prophets, sense something true about Lehi's words (1 Nephi 2:11-12) and eventually soften. By contrast, Zerahemnah and Amalickiah refuse to listen to any counsel of peace. Jehoiakim's refusal mirrors the hardening of hearts that precedes destruction in the Book of Mormon narrative.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 121:36-37 speaks of unrighteous dominion: those who exercise authority through coercion rather than persuasion lose the Spirit. Jehoiakim's refusal to hear his own counselors is a type of unrighteous dominion—he silences even those within his own administration. The principle applies: 'He is the greatest who is the servant of all' (D&C 50:26).
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple covenant includes the principle of listening—to God, to prophets, to witnesses. Jehoiakim's refusal to listen is a covenant violation, a turning away from the divine word even when delivered through mortal servants and officials.

commentary.christological_typology: Jehoiakim's refusal to listen anticipates the rejection of Christ. The officials urge the king to hear; the disciples urge the scribes and Pharisees to accept the true word; Christ himself comes with the message of the kingdom and is rejected. The pattern of refused intercession—mortal attempts to mediate truth that fail—points to the eventual necessity of divine intervention, which comes through Christ's atonement.
commentary.application: This verse invites modern readers to examine whether we listen to counsel, especially when that counsel runs counter to our desires or our preferred interpretations. The three officials are not heroic figures—they are ordinary men with normal authority trying to prevent a mistake. Yet their failure to move the king suggests that some hearts are simply closed. The modern application is twofold: (1) If we are in positions of authority or influence, do we listen to those who bring us difficult truth? (2) If we sense something wrong in our community or institution, do we attempt intercession, knowing that our attempt may fail but trusting that God sees it?

text_kjv: But the king commanded Jerahmeel the son of Hammelech, and Seraiah the son of Azriel, and Shelemiah the son of Abdeel, to take Baruch the scribe and Jeremiah the prophet: but the LORD hid them.

commentary.narrative: Rejected by his own advisors, Jehoiakim moves directly to violent suppression. He orders the arrest of both Baruch (the scribe who physically wrote the scroll) and Jeremiah (the prophet whose words were written). This escalation is significant: the king has moved from destroying the object to destroying the people. The three officers named—Jerahmeel, Seraiah, and Shelemiah—are the king's instruments of force. We know nothing more about them from the text; they function as faceless executors of the king's will. Their names appear, they receive orders, and they disappear into the narrative. What matters is what they do not accomplish: they are sent to seize Baruch and Jeremiah, but the text states with stunning simplicity that 'the LORD hid them.' No chase scene, no dramatic escape, no human intervention. God acts. The parallelism is crucial: the officials in verse 25 urged the king to spare the scroll; the king ignored them. Now the king orders arrest; God silences the arrest.
commentary.narrative_continued: This is one of the most theologically dense verses in the chapter. The verb 'hid' (yastur) echoes backward to verse 19, where the officials command Baruch and Jeremiah to 'hide yourselves' (histater). What begins as human advice becomes divine action. The officials whisper, 'Hide!' God hides them completely—beyond the reach of the king's officers, beyond the reach of the narrative itself. We are not told where they went or how they escaped. The text refuses to provide the machinery of deliverance because the point is not the how but the who. God, not circumstance, not clever planning, not the intervention of sympathetic officials, but God hid them. This verse encapsulates the entire theological claim of Jeremiah's ministry: God's word cannot be extinguished by human force, and God's servants are preserved not by earthly power but by divine protection.

word_study.meaning: Literally 'son of the king.' This could denote a literal prince (a son of Jehoiakim) or could be a court title applied to other officials. The phrase is ambiguous in ancient Near Eastern administration—'king's son' could be birth or office.
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering clarifies: 'Jerahmeel the king's son.' Whether literal or titular, he holds high authority. He is sent first in the list, suggesting primacy. That even a member of the royal family is a tool of the king's violence underscores how thoroughly Jehoiakim has bent the apparatus of power to his will.

word_study.meaning: From the root סתר (s-t-r), meaning 'to hide, conceal, cover.' The verb yastur appears in contexts of divine hiddenness (God's face hidden, Psalm 104:29) and divine protection (hidden by God, Psalm 27:5). The Hiphil form here emphasizes God as the active concealer.
word_study.significance: The verb appears in Exodus 2:2-3, where Jochebed hides baby Moses. The language of deliverance in the Bible often uses this verb. But here, God is the subject—not parents, not officials, but God himself 'hid them.' The perfect tense (vayyastirem) is decisive: the action is complete and authoritative. They were hidden. The matter is settled.

word_study.meaning: The root means 'to take, grasp, seize, capture.' The infinitive construct form laqach is used in command: 'to take.' It is neutral—the same verb is used for 'taking' a wife or 'taking' a prisoner.
word_study.significance: The verb emphasizes forceful action. This is not an invitation or a summons but a seizure. Yet what is seized is not Baruch or Jeremiah but empty air. Their absence is absolute—not hidden in a cave where they might be found, but hidden by God in a way that transcends physical location.

cross_references.connection: The officials' counsel to 'hide yourselves' (histater) is echoed and fulfilled when 'the LORD hid them' (yastirem YHWH). Human advice becomes divine action.
In the day of trouble, he will hide me in his pavilion, in the secret of his tabernacle shall he hide me. The same theology of divine hiddenness as protection.
Jochebed hides baby Moses to preserve him from Pharaoh's decree. The pattern of hiding the covenant messenger from hostile power recurs throughout Scripture.

Nephi records that Lehi was 'led by the Spirit, driven forth before the wind.' Divine protection often works beyond rational explanation or discernible mechanism—the Lord's way of preserving his servants.

God's promise to Joseph Smith: 'If thou art called to pass through tribulation... know thou, my son, that all these things shall give thee experience, and shall be for thy good.' God's hiddenness from human threat does not mean abandonment but rather divine oversight of deliverance.

commentary.historical_context: Ancient Near Eastern monarchs maintained secret police and internal security forces. Jehoiakim's order to arrest Baruch and Jeremiah would have been understood immediately by his court as a standard mechanism of political control. The Babylonian and Egyptian empires both employed such forces. What is remarkable in this historical context is not the king's order but the text's refusal to explain the escape. In contemporary royal inscriptions, a king who fails to capture his enemies typically omits the incident from the record or attributes it to supernatural opposition from the enemy's gods. Here, the text is candid: the king ordered the arrest, and God prevented it. No propaganda, no exaggeration—simply a statement of divine intervention into human politics. The Judean scribal tradition that preserved this account clearly understood that Jeremiah and Baruch's survival and eventual legacy were facts of historical and theological significance.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma and Amulek are hidden from their enemies (Alma 14:28-29) in a way that transcends natural explanation. Nephi is led away from Laban's men. The Book of Mormon records multiple instances of divine hiddenness protecting prophets and righteous people from state violence. The pattern is consistent: when human authorities seek to silence God's word, God preserves the messenger.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 76:1-2 records that Joseph Smith and Sidney Rigdon received a vision while the door was locked and no one else could enter. Spiritual protection and divine concealment often work by mechanisms not visible to earthly agents. The hiding of Jeremiah and Baruch is analogous—God's means of protection transcend physical barriers.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple teaches that God's power is beyond the reach of earthly hostility. Those who possess covenantal relationship with God are under his protection, even when visible circumstances suggest vulnerability. The verse prefigures the principle that no power on earth can ultimately thwart God's purposes for his covenant people.

commentary.christological_typology: Jeremiah's hiding foreshadows the concealment and resurrection of Christ. Like Jeremiah, Christ is seized by those who oppose God's word; like Jeremiah, Christ is protected and preserved through death itself. The verb 'hid' takes on Christological significance when read forward through history: Christ's hiddenness in death is temporary; his resurrection reveals that God's protection of his messenger transcends even the grave.
commentary.application: In modern life, this verse speaks to the reality that covenant protection works according to God's timeline and means, not ours. We live in an age where information cannot be completely suppressed; Jeremiah and Baruch would have had the advantage of twentieth-first century communications technology. Yet the principle remains: those who serve God's purposes are preserved by him, not by circumstance or technology. This does not mean immunity from suffering, but rather that the ultimate purposes of God's word cannot be frustrated. For those facing pressure to compromise convictions or suppress truth, this verse offers a radical reassurance: God hides his people. Not always visibly, not always in the way we expect, but with absolute certainty.

text_kjv: Then the word of the LORD came to Jeremiah, after that the king had burned the roll, and the words which Baruch wrote at the mouth of Jeremiah, saying,

commentary.narrative: After the dramatic events of verses 25-26—the failed intercession, the order for arrest, the divine hiddenness—the text pivots to the most important development: God speaks to Jeremiah again. This verse uses the classic prophetic reception formula, 'the word of the LORD came to Jeremiah,' which appears throughout the prophetic books and signals a direct divine communication. The timing is crucial: 'after that the king had burned the roll.' The king's destruction of the scroll might have been interpreted as a victory—the prophecy has been physically annihilated. The written word is ash. But immediately, before Jeremiah can even process what has happened, God communicates again. This is theology acting itself out in narrative. The Covenant Rendering notes that 'the scroll and the words' are mentioned as two distinct things: the physical object and its verbal content. The king burned one; he cannot burn the other. The narrative structure itself enacts the theological claim: destruction of the medium does not extinguish the message.
commentary.narrative_continued: The phrase 'the words which Baruch wrote at the mouth of Jeremiah' requires careful attention. Baruch is the scribe, the physical writer, but the words are Jeremiah's—they came from Jeremiah's mouth. The verb 'to write' (katab) is passive in the sense that Baruch's role is transcriptive, not creative. He is the instrument; Jeremiah is the source. Yet both are significant. Jeremiah could not have reached the temple assembly without Baruch's literacy and willingness to serve as his voice. Baruch could not have written authentic prophecy without Jeremiah's prophetic call. The collaboration matters, but so does the distinction of roles. This verse sets up verses 28-32, where God will command that all these words be written again. The repetition will not be a diminishment but a vindication: the word of God is so powerful that its re-inscription is not a loss but a reaffirmation.

word_study.term_english: the word of the LORD came
word_study.meaning: The standard prophetic reception formula, appearing hundreds of times in the Hebrew Bible. 'Devar' (word) means both the utterance and its content—the word is thing-like, powerful, generative. It comes (ba) to the prophet—the word is active, not passive.
word_study.significance: This formula authenticates what follows. When the reader sees 'vayhi devar-YHWH,' they know a direct divine communication is about to be reported. By using this formula immediately after the king's act of destruction, the text claims that Jeremiah's subsequent commands have the same authority as all other prophetic utterances in Scripture. The king's fire cannot alter that authority.

word_study.meaning: Literally 'from the mouth of.' The phrase indicates direct verbal transmission—the words came from Jeremiah's mouth to Baruch's quill. The 'mouth' (peh) in Hebrew often represents the source of speech, the seat of verbal authority.
word_study.significance: This phrasing establishes the prophetic chain: God spoke to Jeremiah; Jeremiah spoke to Baruch; Baruch wrote. Each link is necessary. The words are God's (carried by Jeremiah), but they are transmitted through Baruch's scribal skill. This matters for understanding how prophecy was preserved in Israel—not by direct inscription from heaven but through the collaboration of prophet and scribe.

cross_references.connection: The same reception formula opens the entire book of Jeremiah. That this communication appears here, after the scroll's destruction, signals continuity: Jeremiah's prophetic ministry is unbroken by external assault.

The word that goes forth from God's mouth shall not return to him empty but will accomplish that which he purposes. Jehoiakim's burning of the scroll is an attempt to make the word return empty; this verse asserts that it will not.
In the New Testament, Paul writes: 'The word of God is not bound.' Even in persecution and imprisonment, the message spreads. The same principle: human efforts to silence God's word ultimately fail.

Nephi writes of seeking to understand the words of Isaiah: the process of copying, studying, and transmitting sacred text is central to covenant community. Baruch's role as scribe connects to the larger LDS understanding of how revelation is preserved.

Modern revelation on the authority of prophetic word: 'Whatsoever they shall speak when moved upon by the Holy Ghost shall be scripture.' Jeremiah's words, now being transmitted through Baruch, carry that kind of authority.

commentary.historical_context: In the ancient Near Eastern world, the burning of written documents was a recognized method of political suppression. Hittite kings burned records to erase the memory of their predecessors; Egyptian pharaohs defaced inscriptions to deny the legitimacy of predecessors. Yet the practice revealed a fundamental misunderstanding of how meaning works: destroying the physical object does not destroy the idea, especially when that idea has been transmitted orally or through copies. In Jeremiah's case, the scroll had already been read aloud in the temple; its contents were known to many. The king's burning of the scroll was a symbolic act of defiance against the prophecy itself, not a practical erasure of it. The immediate divine response—God speaks again—suggests that such symbolic gestures are ultimately powerless against God's purposes. The historical context makes clear that this is not a story about the indestructibility of books (though it has implications for that) but about the indestructibility of God's word.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon itself is a text repeatedly threatened with destruction—first by those who wished to suppress Joseph Smith's claims, later by those who sought to discredit the book. Yet the text survives and multiplies. The Book of Mormon teaches the principle enacted here in Jeremiah: the word of God cannot be permanently suppressed. The very fact of the Book of Mormon's existence is analogous to Jeremiah's words being re-written.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 21:4-6 promises that the word of the Lord, spoken through prophets, 'shall all be fulfilled, whether by mine own voice or by the voice of my servants, it is the same.' The Lord stands behind his word, guarantees it, and brings it to pass. Jeremiah's words, now being re-spoken through God's command, carry that same guarantee.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple teaches the principle of restoration and renewal. Just as temple worship involves repeated covenants and recommitments, the re-writing of Jeremiah's words is a temple-like act: what was destroyed is restored, what was lost is recovered. This foreshadows resurrection and renewal of all things.

commentary.christological_typology: The destruction and restoration of the scroll prefigures the death and resurrection of Christ. Like the scroll that is burned but whose words persist, Christ's body is destroyed but his word continues and multiplies through the Church. The resurrection is the ultimate assertion that no human force can permanently suppress God's word or God's messenger.
commentary.application: This verse offers comfort to anyone who has experienced the suppression or dismissal of truth they hold dear. In academic, professional, or personal contexts, ideas and truths are sometimes attacked, marginalized, or officially denied. This verse teaches that the fundamental reality is not the immediate reception or acceptance of truth but the persistence of truth itself. Jeremiah does not despair at the burning of the scroll because he understands that the word comes from God, not from the scroll. For modern members of the Church, this verse suggests that our faith does not depend on the favorable reception of our testimony in the culture around us. The word has been spoken; it persists; God will bring it to pass in his own time.

text_kjv: Take thee again another roll, and write in it all the former words that were in the first roll, which Jehoiakim the king of Judah hath burned.

commentary.narrative: God's first command to Jeremiah is direct and simple: take another scroll and write it all again. The verb 'shuv qach' (again take) is the key phrase, using the verb 'return' (shuv) in the command form—'again take.' This is the theological response to destruction: not grief, not resignation, but repetition. The Covenant Rendering captures this perfectly: 'Take another scroll and write on it all the previous words.' God does not promise a different message or an abbreviated version or a stronger pronouncement. He commands the exact same words: 'all the former words that were in the first roll.' This is striking. Jehoiakim has just destroyed the scroll precisely because the words offended him—prophecies of Babylonian invasion that he finds politically intolerable. God does not respond by softening the message or finding a more palatable way to express the same idea. He commands the exact repetition. This is a direct confrontation: the king tried to silence this word; now it will be written again, identically. The command to re-write is itself a prophecy fulfilled—it proves the word's resilience.
commentary.narrative_continued: The command also serves a practical function in the narrative. Jeremiah and Baruch have been hidden; they cannot openly move about Jerusalem. Yet God commands them to reproduce the scroll. How this actually occurred is left unexplained, but the command itself asserts that the prophet's access to materials and writing space will be preserved. Implicitly, God is saying: Yes, I have hidden you; yes, you are fugitives; yet you will find the means to accomplish this task. The re-writing becomes an act of faith and obedience, grounded in the promise that God's purposes will be accomplished. The repetition of 'all the former words' also establishes an important principle for understanding prophetic revision. When God commands Jeremiah to rewrite, the content does not change. Yet in verse 32, we are told that Jeremiah did write again, and 'there were added besides unto them many like words.' The second scroll is not identical in length; it contains additions. This raises a profound question about how prophetic corpora grow: does God add new material because the situation has worsened, or does the scribe naturally expand as events unfold? The text leaves this ambiguous, suggesting that both the preservation of original words and the addition of new prophecies are legitimate expressions of God's ongoing communication.

word_study.meaning: The verb 'shuv' means 'to return, turn back, again.' Combined with the imperative 'qach' (take), it forms a command structure: 'return and take' or more idiomatically 'take again.' Shuv is central to Jeremiah's theology—repentance is shuvah, a returning to God.
word_study.significance: The use of shuv here is not accidental. The same verb that calls for repentance is now used to command the return-and-renewal of the scroll. God's response to destruction is to return to the task, to begin again. This connects to the larger theological message of the second half of Jeremiah (chapters 30-33), where restoration and return become dominant themes. The scroll's destruction prompts its renewal through the same verb (shuv) that promises Judah's ultimate restoration.

word_study.meaning: Megillah means 'scroll, roll'—a rolled manuscript. The word 'acheret' (another, different) emphasizes material replacement. A new physical object must be obtained and used.
word_study.significance: The text is precise: not the same scroll (which has been destroyed) but another one. This materiality matters. God is not commanding a purely spiritual repetition but an actual, physical re-inscription on a new scroll. The distinction between the word (which is immaterial and indestructible) and the scroll (which is material and can be burned) runs through this entire passage.

word_study.meaning: The adjective 'rishon' means 'first, former, earlier.' The phrase 'kol-hadevarim hariszhonim' means 'all the former/first words'—the complete original content.
word_study.significance: The emphasis on 'all' and 'former' establishes continuity and completeness. Nothing is to be omitted, nothing revised. The word is to be re-transmitted exactly as it was originally spoken. This integrity of transmission is crucial for prophetic authority.

cross_references.connection: God commands Jeremiah to write promises of restoration: 'Write thee all the words that I have spoken unto thee in a book.' The pattern of written restoration appears again—God's word is recovered through writing.
The word of God stands forever; it does not fade like grass or flowers. Though heaven and earth pass away, God's word remains. The scroll may be burned; the word persists.

God promises to raise up a prophet like Moses, and put his words in the prophet's mouth. Jeremiah's words, now being re-written, are understood as God's words placed in Jeremiah's mouth—a fulfillment of this promise.
Nephi ponders the words of his father Lehi and desires to know their meaning. The Book of Mormon emphasizes the importance of written and spoken word being studied, repeated, and transmitted.
Revelation on restoration: after tribulation comes the blessing. The command to re-write the scroll is a form of blessing after the tribulation of its destruction.

commentary.historical_context: In ancient scribal practice, texts were copied and re-copied, with each new generation of scribes producing fresh manuscripts. The production of a scroll required significant resources: papyrus or leather, ink, skill in writing. For Jeremiah and Baruch to produce another scroll while in hiding would have required either the assistance of sympathetic allies or a miraculous provision of materials. The text does not explain the logistics, which suggests that the focus is theological rather than practical. Historically, the preservation of Jeremiah's prophecies through multiple versions and editions is well-documented in the textual tradition. The Dead Sea Scrolls contain multiple text-types of Jeremiah, some longer and some shorter than the Masoretic text. This verse is consistent with what we know about how prophetic texts were actually preserved in ancient Judah: through deliberate copying and re-inscription, with variations and expansions occurring as the text circulated. The command to re-write is thus not fictional but reflects actual scribal practice.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In the Book of Mormon, Nephi is commanded to keep a record and to preserve the teachings of his father. The principle of restoring and re-inscribing sacred word through scribal action is central to Nephite theology. When Nephi decides to make the large plates, he is essentially obeying this same principle: record the sacred word anew for future generations.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 21:4-5 promises that the Lord will 'support [the Church president] by the virtue of my word, which shall not pass away, though heaven and earth shall pass away.' The re-writing of Jeremiah's scroll is an enactment of this principle: the word outlasts all physical threats and can be renewed at God's command.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple involves ritualized repetition—the same covenants renewed again and again, the same ordinances performed for generation after generation. The re-writing of the scroll is a kind of textual temple act: the sacred word is renewed, repeated, and made present again through the scribe's action.

commentary.christological_typology: The destruction and renewal of the scroll prefigures Christ's death and resurrection. The scroll is 'destroyed' but renewed in identical form—so Christ dies but is raised in bodily reality, the same person but restored. The command to re-write echoes God's commitment to restoration: nothing is lost that belongs to God's purposes; all will be recovered in the end.
commentary.application: This verse speaks to anyone who has experienced the loss of something they have worked to create or preserve—a destroyed manuscript, a lost work, a betrayed project. God's command to Jeremiah is to begin again. The re-creation will not diminish the value of what was lost; it will vindicate the original work by proving its worth and its durability. For modern readers, this verse offers permission to start again after failure, knowing that repetition and renewal are not signs of defeat but of fidelity to purpose. If the message matters, it is worth delivering again. If the truth is true, it can be re-stated as many times as necessary.

text_kjv: And thou shalt say to Jehoiakim king of Judah, Thus saith the LORD; Thou hast burned this roll, saying, Why hast thou written therein, saying, The king of Babylon shall certainly come and destroy this land, and shall cause to cease from thence man and beast?

commentary.narrative: God now provides the actual content of what Jeremiah is to say to Jehoiakim. The message begins by quoting the king's own objection back to him. Jehoiakim burned the scroll 'saying, Why hast thou written therein'—the king's own justification for destroying the text is that it contained an intolerable prediction: 'The king of Babylon shall certainly come and destroy this land.' This is the core of Jehoiakim's offense: not that the scroll existed, not that it was read aloud, but that it prophesied his loss of power to Babylon. By burning the scroll, Jehoiakim imagined he could prevent the prophecy. This reflects a magical understanding of causation: if the written prediction is destroyed, the predicted event will not occur. God's response is to quote this reasoning back to the king, exposing its futility. The king tried to unwrite history, to use fire against fate. The prophecy he burned was not random speculation but prediction of what would actually come to pass—historical reality that no amount of burning could alter.
commentary.narrative_continued: The phrase 'The king of Babylon shall certainly come' uses the emphatic infinitive absolute construction (bo yavo), which intensifies certainty. Not 'might come,' not 'could come,' but 'will certainly come.' The Covenant Rendering notes that this is 'the very prediction the king tried to annul by burning.' The prophecy is specific: the king of Babylon (presumably Nebuchadnezzar II, who would indeed conquer Judah in 586 BCE) will come and 'destroy this land' and 'cause to cease from thence man and beast'—total depopulation. This is comprehensive judgment: not merely military defeat but the emptying of the land of all inhabitants. The phrase 'man and beast' (hishbit adam ubhemah) is a merism—a way of saying 'everything living.' The severity of the judgment reflects the severity of Judah's rebellion. Jehoiakim's act of burning the scroll is thus not merely an attack on the medium but a rejection of the message itself—a refusal to acknowledge Babylon's inevitable victory. God's response is not to negotiate with the king but to reassert the prophecy and add judgment for the king's defiance.

word_study.meaning: The imperfect form of 'amar' (to say, speak). The imperfect can function as a future command: 'you shall/must say.' It places Jeremiah in the position of messenger, repeating God's words verbatim.
word_study.significance: The prophetic role is primarily that of speaker—the one who takes God's word and delivers it to the people. Jeremiah is not to compose or interpret but to speak exactly what he is commanded. The use of the future tense here (tomar) is a command that places responsibility on Jeremiah to transmit this message.

word_study.meaning: An emphatic infinitive absolute construction, using the root בוא (ba, to come) in both infinitive and imperfect forms. This doubled form intensifies the action, creating emphasis and certainty.
word_study.significance: In Hebrew, the infinitive absolute placed before the finite verb of the same root creates emphasis. 'Bo yavo' ('coming he comes,' or 'will certainly come') is a way of expressing absolute certainty and inevitability. This is not a conditional prophecy; it is a statement of what will definitely occur. The construction appears frequently in legal and prophetic texts to denote binding, unalterable declarations.

word_study.meaning: From the root שחת (sh-h-t), meaning 'to destroy, corrupt, ruin, devastate.' The Hiphil form intensifies the action—'to cause destruction.' The root appears in contexts of military ruin and total devastation.
word_study.significance: This is not gentle judgment but catastrophic destruction. The same root appears in descriptions of the Flood and other acts of comprehensive divine judgment. Jehoiakim's Babylon is understood as an instrument of utter destruction.

word_study.meaning: From the root שבת (sh-b-t), meaning 'to cease, desist, stop.' The Hiphil form means 'to cause to cease, bring to an end.' It suggests the cessation of activity, life, and productivity.
word_study.significance: The prophecy promises not merely defeat but the end of human presence in the land. The verb 'cause to cease' (hishhbit) is used in Psalm 46:9 ('He maketh wars to cease unto the end of the earth'). But here it is applied to the cessation of human and animal life—an end to all activity, all productivity.

cross_references.connection: An earlier prophecy against Jehoiakim: 'He shall be buried with the burial of an ass, drawn and cast forth beyond the gates of Jerusalem.' The present verse adds to the judgment: not merely an ignoble burial but the king's inability to prevent Babylon's invasion.
Historical record of Jehoiakim's reign and submission to Babylon. The chapter is satisfied with condensed history; Jeremiah provides the prophetic dimension of these events.
The covenant curses for disobedience include invasion, destruction, and exile. The prophecy of Babylon's invasion is not arbitrary but flows from covenant violation.

God's word will accomplish what he purposes: 'Calling a ravenous bird from the east, the man that executeth my counsel from a far country.' Nebuchadnezzar, though he does not know it, is God's instrument for accomplishing his purposes.
Latter-day revelation prophecying conflict and judgment on nations. The pattern of divine warning followed by judgment if the warning is rejected recurs in modern revelation as it does in Jeremiah.

commentary.historical_context: Jehoiakim ruled Judah from 609-598 BCE, initially as an Egyptian vassal and later as a Babylonian tribute-payer. Babylon's conquest of the Levantine states was a gradual process, with repeated campaigns and revolts. Jehoiakim's burning of the scroll likely occurred early in his reign when Babylon's threat seemed distant or when he was still confident in Egyptian support. Historically, Babylon did indeed come and did indeed destroy Judah, deporting most of the population in 586 BCE. Jeremiah's prophecy, though made decades before the final destruction, proved accurate in every particular. The king's attempt to prevent this future through burning a scroll was thus not merely futile but absurdly futile—the very events he sought to prevent through sympathetic magic actually occurred, almost exactly as prophesied. The historical reality validates the prophecy and exposes Jehoiakim's action as worse than useless: it was an act of rebellion against announced divine judgment.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon records similar patterns where rulers attempt to suppress prophecy and face judgment as a result. King Noah burns Abinadi, and the kingdom is destroyed (Mosiah 17-19). The principle is consistent: the attempt to suppress God's word through violence leads not to success but to judgment.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 1:37-38 states: 'What I the Lord have spoken, I have spoken; and I excuse not myself; and though the heavens and the earth pass away, my word shall not pass away, but shall all be fulfilled.' Jehoiakim's burning of the scroll is an attempt to make God's word pass away; the revelation asserts the impossibility of that attempt.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple teaches that God's word is binding and eternal. Covenants made before God cannot be unbound by mere human action. Similarly, Jeremiah's prophecy, once spoken, cannot be unsaid or unwritten. Its status as God's word makes it immutable.

commentary.christological_typology: Jehoiakim's defiant rejection of divine warning foreshadows humanity's rejection of Christ. Like Jehoiakim trying to prevent the inevitable through burning a scroll, the scribes and Pharisees try to suppress the resurrection through guards and seals. In both cases, the attempt reveals the futility of human resistance to God's purposes. Christ's resurrection, like Babylon's invasion, was announced in advance and cannot be prevented by human action.
commentary.application: This verse confronts modern readers with a hard question: Are there prophecies or truths we are trying to suppress or silence? Do we refuse to hear unwelcome messages because they threaten our preferred future? Jehoiakim's sin was not merely resistance to Jeremiah but refusal to listen to the message because it threatened his political survival. We may do the same with spiritual truths that threaten our comfort or convenience. The verse teaches that such suppression never ultimately works. The truth persists, and the attempt to silence it often becomes itself a form of judgment—Jehoiakim's act of defiance is recorded forever as a sign of his blindness and rebellion. We are invited to listen to unwelcome prophecies not out of political calculation but out of faith that God speaks truth, and truth, once spoken, cannot be unspoken.

text_kjv: Therefore thus saith the LORD of Jehoiakim king of Judah; He shall have none to sit upon the throne of David: and his dead body shall be cast out in the day to the heat, and in the night to the frost.

commentary.narrative: This final verse of the chapter delivers the divine judgment on Jehoiakim for his act of burning the scroll. The judgment has two parts: dynastic and personal. First, dynastic termination—'He shall have none to sit upon the throne of David.' This is a judgment on his line, not merely on himself. Jehoiakim's son Jehoiachin did briefly reign for three months (2 Kings 24:8-12) before being deported to Babylon. This raises a question about how this prophecy was understood to be fulfilled. One answer is that the brevity of Jehoiachin's reign was so insignificant that it did not constitute real rule. Another is that the prophecy refers to lasting, sustained rule on the throne—and indeed, no descendant of Jehoiakim ever ruled again after the exile. The prophecy proved accurate in its ultimate sense: Jehoiakim's line did not continue to rule. The second part of the judgment is intensely personal and visceral: 'his dead body shall be cast out in the day to the heat, and in the night to the frost.' This denies Jehoiakim the basic dignity of proper burial. His corpse will be exposed to the elements, neither covered nor collected, subject to the extremes of weather.
commentary.narrative_continued: The phrase 'cast out' (mushlekhet) suggests violence and degradation—not laid to rest but thrown away. The pairing of 'heat by day' and 'frost by night' (chorev... qerach) creates a merism—his body will be exposed to every extreme, every hardship, with no one to gather it. This connects directly to Jeremiah 22:18-19, where the prophet earlier promised that Jehoiakim would 'be buried with the burial of an ass—dragged and thrown beyond the gates of Jerusalem.' The prophecy of undignified disposal is one of the harshest judgments in the biblical corpus. Burial was crucial to ancient Judean understanding of human dignity and the proper ending of life. To deny burial, to leave a body exposed and uninterred, was a fate reserved for the worst offenders. The historical record is somewhat ambiguous about Jehoiakim's actual death and burial, but the prophecy stands in Scripture as a permanent record of divine judgment. What is clear is that this judgment is presented as a direct consequence of burning the scroll. Jehoiakim's act of destruction is answered not with more words (God could have simply warned him again) but with a pronouncement of personal ruin. The text treats the physical destruction of the scroll as a transgression grave enough to warrant the king's own destruction.

word_study.term_english: He shall have none to sit
word_study.term_original: לֹא־יִהְיֶה־לוֹ יוֹשֵׁב עַל־כִּסֵּא (lo yihyeh-lo yoshev al-kisse)
word_study.meaning: Literally 'there will not be to him one sitting on the throne.' The phrase emphasizes the absence of a successor—not that Jehoiakim will not sit, but that no heir of his will sit after him.
word_study.significance: In ancient Near Eastern thought, the permanence of a dynasty was the highest honor. To promise the absence of an heir was to pronounce the end of a name and line. The formula 'sitting on the throne of David' echoes the Davidic covenant, implying that Jehoiakim's rejection of God's word has disqualified him from the promises made to the house of David.

word_study.meaning: From the root שלך (sh-l-k), meaning 'to throw, cast, hurl.' The passive form indicates that someone (unspecified) will throw him. The action is violent and dismissive.
word_study.significance: The verb mushlekhet appears in contexts of deliberate disrespect or rejection. To be 'thrown' is the opposite of being 'placed' or 'laid to rest.' The word choice emphasizes the violence and disrespect inherent in the judgment.

word_study.meaning: The term can mean 'heat,' 'drought,' or 'dryness.' It refers to the harsh, desiccating heat of the day in a Middle Eastern climate—extreme and destructive.
word_study.significance: The word choice is specific to arid climate. The body will dry and desiccate under the sun, exposed and unprotected.

word_study.meaning: Frost, ice, cold. The word refers to the freezing temperatures of night in the Judean highlands, where temperatures drop significantly after sunset.
word_study.significance: The merism of chorev (heat) and qerach (frost) communicates total exposure to all weather extremes. No shelter, no protection, no burial—only the natural elements working on the corpse in their cycles.

cross_references.connection: Earlier prophecy against Jehoiakim: 'He shall be buried with the burial of an ass, drawn and cast forth beyond the gates of Jerusalem.' This verse echoes and confirms that earlier judgment.
Historical account of Jehoiakim's reign and death. The text notes his death but provides no details of burial, leaving ambiguity about whether the prophecy was literally fulfilled.
Covenant curses for disobedience: 'Thy carcase shall be meat unto all fowls of the air.' The denial of burial is listed as a covenant curse for those who break covenant.
Samuel pronounces judgment on King Agag: 'As thy sword hath made women childless, so shall thy mother be childless among women.' Both judgments connect the king's deeds to his personal fate.

Modern revelation on divine justice: 'Wherefore, I, the Lord, have said that the wicked shall not have power, and it shall be so, and all things contrary to my law tend downward and their end is to be burned up.'

commentary.historical_context: In ancient Near Eastern royal ideology, the continuation of one's line and the honor of one's burial were the highest concerns of a king. To prophesy both the end of the dynasty and denial of proper burial was to invoke the absolute nadir of judgment. Jehoiakim's actual historical fate is somewhat obscured by the biblical sources, but the Egyptian historian Manetho records that he died in captivity (though in Egypt, not in Babylon). The uncertainty of the historical record may itself be part of the judgment's fulfillment—his death is not commemorated with dignity or detail; it is obscured by history. The prophecy's insistence on his body being 'cast out' and exposed reflects ancient anxieties about the fate of the dead. In the ancient Near Eastern worldview, a proper burial ensured a peaceful afterlife; denial of burial was believed to doom the dead to restless wandering. The prophecy thus pronounces not merely physical degradation but spiritual consequences. Archaeological and historical research suggests that Jerusalem did experience devastation and depopulation following Babylon's siege in 586 BCE, confirming the general accuracy of the Babylonian invasion prophecy even if the specific details of Jehoiakim's death and burial remain uncertain.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon records similar judgments on kings who reject prophecy. King Amalickiah's death is recorded with a kind of shadow over it—the record notes his death almost in passing, denying him the dignity of full commemoration. The principle is consistent: those who reject God's word face judgment that includes loss of honor and legacy.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 121:37 warns: 'That they may be conformed to the image of the Son of God, that he may be the firstborn among many brethren.' By contrast, those who reject this process face a different outcome. Jehoiakim's judgment—no heir, no dignity, no legacy—is what comes to those who set themselves against God's purposes.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple teaches that all things are accountable before God, and all actions have consequences. Jehoiakim's act of burning the scroll, though it occurred in his palace, is known to God and judged by God. No act against God's word escapes divine notice. The promise of judgment for transgression is as much a part of temple theology as the promise of reward for faithfulness.

commentary.christological_typology: Jehoiakim's judgment prefigures the judgment of those who reject Christ. Like Jehoiakim, who had the opportunity to hear and respond to the prophetic word but refused, those who know of Christ and reject him face judgment. The denial of honor and legacy in Jehoiakim's judgment echoes Christ's teaching that whoever loses his life for Christ's sake will gain it (Matthew 16:25)—but the converse is also implied: whoever refuses to lose his life for Christ's sake will lose everything. Jehoiakim's end, unrecorded and undignified in history, contrasts with the promise of eternal life and honor given to those who accept God's word.
commentary.application: This verse brings the chapter's theological drama to a personal and terrifying conclusion. Jehoiakim was not evil in an abstract sense; he was a political pragmatist trying to maintain his kingdom in a dangerous time. His burning of the scroll was a rational response to a threat—or so he thought. Yet the chapter reveals that by taking that rational action, he set himself against God. The judgment pronounced here is severe: loss of dynasty, loss of honor, loss of proper ending. For modern readers, the verse poses a question: Are there moments when our 'rational' choices, our 'necessary' decisions, are actually acts of rebellion against God's word? The application is not to become a political naif or to ignore real dangers, but to recognize that there are some things—God's truth, God's prophetic word—that cannot be fought without fighting against God himself. Jehoiakim's choice to burn the scroll was not merely a political miscalculation; it was a spiritual catastrophe, and it cost him everything. The verse teaches that the true security lies not in suppressing difficult truths but in listening to them and adjusting our lives accordingly.

text_kjv: And I will punish him and his seed and his servants for their iniquity; and I will bring upon them, and upon the inhabitants of Jerusalem, and upon the men of Judah, all the evil that I have pronounced against them; but they hearkened not.

commentary.narrative:
Jeremiah 36:31 contains the Lord's pronouncement of judgment against King Jehoiakim and extends across concentric circles of culpability — from the king himself, to his offspring and servants, to all of Jerusalem, and finally to all the men of Judah. This verse is the divine response to Jehoiakim's act of burning the scroll in verse 23. The destruction of the written word does not nullify the spoken word; instead, it seals the judgment. The phrase 'but they hearkened not' echoes a refrain that runs through the entire book of Jeremiah — Israel's persistent refusal to listen has consequences that cannot be erased by burning paper. The judgment here is not arbitrary punishment but the inevitable outcome of sustained disobedience.

What makes this verse theologically significant is that Jehoiakim's burning of the scroll becomes the final act of rebellion that triggers comprehensive judgment. Throughout Jeremiah's ministry, the king and people have refused to repent. But the burning of the scroll is symbolic — it represents rejection not merely of words on parchment, but of the word of God itself. The Lord's response through Jeremiah demonstrates that such rejection has real consequences. The structure of the judgment (individual king → family → city → nation) shows that sin radiates outward; the king's disobedience brings judgment on those under his authority and those in his sphere of influence.

word_study.meaning: to visit upon, to reckon with, to hold accountable; carries the sense of divine reckoning and inspection. The root implies God's attentive gaze and deliberate judgment. In the Covenant Rendering, it is rendered 'I will punish,' but the Hebrew suggests more precisely 'I will visit upon' — God marking, noting, and acting in response to sin.
word_study.significance: This is not passive judgment but active divine accountability. The same word is used when God 'visits' in mercy (Exod. 13:19) or in judgment (Jer. 9:25). Here it denotes God's authoritative examination and response to Jehoiakim's defiance.

word_study.meaning: evil, harm, disaster, calamity. In the context of divine speech, it refers to the threatened judgment — the concrete consequences Jeremiah has been proclaiming throughout his ministry. The Covenant Rendering renders it 'disaster,' which captures the concrete, historical dimension rather than abstract moral evil.
word_study.significance: The specific 'evil' Jehoiakim rejected is not vague but concrete — the destruction of Jerusalem and exile that Jeremiah announced. By burning the scroll, Jehoiakim attempted to destroy the word describing this judgment, but the judgment itself remains in effect.

word_study.meaning: to hear, to listen, to obey. In Hebrew thought, hearing and obeying are inseparable. To hear the word of God is to be bound by it; to refuse to hear is to refuse to obey. The negative form here — 'they did not listen' — is the terminal indictment of the entire episode.
word_study.significance: This verb encapsulates the central theme of Jeremiah: Israel's stubborn refusal to hear God's word through the prophet. The repetition of this failure throughout the book makes it clear that judgment is not arbitrary but the natural consequence of sustained inattention to God's voice.

cross_references.connection: Jehoiakim's officials earlier sought to kill Jeremiah for speaking the same words of judgment; the consistent rejection of the prophetic word sets the stage for this final act of defiance through burning the scroll.
The catalogue of curses for disobedience parallels the comprehensive judgment Jeremiah pronounces; the Lord is executing the covenant curse through historical events.
The historical fulfillment of this judgment: Jehoiakim was placed under Babylonian tribute and eventually died in captivity, fulfilling the Lord's pronouncement in this verse.
Jeremiah is assured at the outset that he will face opposition but that the Lord will deliver him; verse 31 shows the judgment falling not on the prophet but on those who reject his message.

This verse illustrates the Old Testament pattern of God speaking through prophets; the New Testament fulfillment brings final revelation through Christ, against which all refusal is ultimate rebellion.

commentary.historical_context:
King Jehoiakim reigned during the transitional period when Babylon's power was rising and Egypt's was waning in the ancient Near East. His act of burning the scroll (verses 20-23) was an act of political and religious defiance — a rejection not only of the prophet's message but of the very notion that God controlled the political future. In ancient Near Eastern royal ideology, a king's authority was absolute; the idea that a mere prophet could speak words that superseded the king's will was intolerable to Jehoiakim. His burning of the scroll was thus an assertion of royal prerogative over divine authority.

The punishment formula in verse 31 reflects covenant language familiar in the ancient Near East, where treaties and agreements often included curses pronounced on those who violated them. Jehoiakim, in burning the scroll, was in effect violating the covenant relationship between the Lord and Judah. The judgment extends to his seed and servants because in ancient Near Eastern thought, a king's actions had consequences for his entire household and administration. The destruction of Jerusalem and exile of Judah would indeed vindicate Jeremiah's words: Jehoiakim died in captivity (2 Kings 24:6), his son was removed from power after a brief reign, and the city fell to Babylon in 586 BCE.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Lehi's vision and prophecy of Jerusalem's fall (1 Nephi 1:13-14) parallels Jeremiah's message; both prophets faced rejection when delivering unpopular warnings of judgment. The Book of Mormon emphasizes that the Lord's word cannot be thwarted by human opposition, a theme central to this chapter.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 1:35-37 teaches that the Lord's word shall be fulfilled; no one can hinder the accomplishment of God's purposes. This principle is illustrated here: Jehoiakim's attempt to silence the word through fire proved futile.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The destruction of the Jerusalem temple in 586 BCE, which Jeremiah foresaw and Jehoiakim rejected, represents the breaking of the covenant relationship. In Latter-day Saint thought, the temple is the center of covenant making; its destruction signifies covenant breaking on Israel's part.

commentary.christological_typology: Jeremiah's role as a suffering prophet who delivers unpopular truth parallels the role of Christ, who was rejected by religious and civil authorities. Christ's resurrection and the spread of the gospel after his death mirrors the principle demonstrated in verse 32: the word of God cannot be permanently silenced. Those who reject the word face judgment; those who receive it find redemption.
commentary.application: For modern covenant members, this verse teaches that there are real consequences to persistent refusal to hear God's word — whether through living prophets, scripture, or personal revelation. Jehoiakim did not deny the Lord's existence; he refused to take God's word seriously. The destruction that followed was not arbitrary punishment but the inevitable result of ignoring reality as God has revealed it. In our own lives, the temptation to minimize or discard prophetic counsel — to 'burn the scroll' through selective listening or rationalization — carries real spiritual consequences. The focus here is not on feeling guilty but on recognizing that God's word describes reality accurately; rejecting it does not change what is true.

text_kjv: Then took Jeremiah another roll, and gave it to Baruch the scribe, the son of Neriah; who wrote therein from the mouth of Jeremiah all the words of the book which Jehoiakim king of Judah had burned in the fire: and there were added besides unto them many like words.

commentary.narrative:
Jeremiah 36:32 is the theological triumph of the chapter and one of the most profound statements in scripture about the nature of God's word. After Jehoiakim burns the scroll, Jeremiah does not abandon his task or concede defeat. Instead, he immediately takes 'another roll' and gives it to Baruch to rewrite — not from memory, but 'from the mouth of Jeremiah,' indicating a new dictation, a fresh speaking of the word. The initial burning of the scroll might have been an act of royal defiance, but what follows is an act of divine restoration and expansion.

The crucial theological point comes in the final clause: 'and there were added besides unto them many like words.' The king's attempt to silence the prophetic word resulted not in its diminishment but in its multiplication. The scroll that was burned contained specific words of judgment; the new scroll contains all of those words restored, plus additional words of similar content and weight. In the Covenant Rendering, the verb 'added' (nosaf) is in the passive voice, suggesting that this expansion was not merely Jeremiah and Baruch's editorial decision but a divine initiative — God ensured that the word would not only be preserved but amplified.

This verse establishes a principle that becomes foundational to biblical theology and to the Restoration: the word of God is indestructible. Fire cannot burn it away. Persecution cannot silence it. Human opposition cannot diminish it. Instead, every attempt to destroy it becomes an occasion for it to grow and multiply. This is not merely a historical account of what happened in Jerusalem around 605 BCE; it is a theological statement about the nature and power of God's word.

word_study.meaning: a scroll or roll of parchment; the physical medium on which God's word is inscribed. The term emphasizes that God's word, while eternal and spiritual, is communicated through physical means — writing, speech, text — that enter human history and culture.
word_study.significance: The image of the scroll is crucial throughout this chapter; it represents the bridge between the eternal word of God and the temporal, historical realm. The burning of the scroll is a direct assault on that bridge — an attempt to destroy the means by which God's word reaches humanity.

word_study.meaning: to write, to inscribe, to record. The verb here indicates that Baruch is not paraphrasing or summarizing but recording the exact words that Jeremiah speaks. Writing is the medium through which the prophetic word becomes permanent and communicable across time and space.
word_study.significance: This act of dictation and writing establishes the pattern for how God's word is preserved and transmitted. Baruch becomes the scribe through whom God's word is fixed in writing, making it available to future generations.

word_study.meaning: to add, to append, to increase. The verb is in the Niphal (passive) form, suggesting that these words were added not by human decision alone but through divine action. The same word is used when God 'adds' years to Hezekiah's life (Isaiah 38:5) and when God 'adds' to the church in Acts 2:47.
word_study.significance: The passive voice is theologically significant: it indicates divine initiative. The expansion of the scroll is not a human cover-up or editorial invention but evidence of God's continuing speech and insistence. The word grows because God wills it to grow. This principle permeates the theology of Restoration: latter-day revelation does not replace earlier revelation but adds to it, expands it, clarifies it.

word_study.meaning: many similar words; words of the same character, weight, and purpose as those already written. The phrase emphasizes both quantity (many) and quality (similar in kind and authority). These are not filler words but words of genuine prophetic significance.
word_study.significance: The fact that similar words were added suggests that God's message through Jeremiah was not exhausted in the first scroll. There is inexhaustible depth and breadth to the prophetic word. Each new utterance adds to the portrait of God's character and purposes without contradicting what came before.

cross_references.connection: Isaiah promises that God's word shall not return empty but will accomplish what God purposes; this principle is vindicated in Jeremiah's scroll, which cannot be destroyed and continues to work its purpose.
Paul writes that 'the word of God is not bound' even though he is imprisoned; like Jeremiah's restored scroll, the word persists despite human attempts to silence or confine it.

The Lord assures Jeremiah at the beginning that though he will face opposition, the Lord will deliver him and make him 'an iron pillar'; verse 32 shows this promise fulfilled as Jeremiah continues his prophetic work despite the king's hostility.
Nephi sees in vision that many plain and precious things are removed from the Bible, but the Lord promises they will be restored; like Jeremiah's scroll, what is lost will be returned and clarified.

The Lord promises that His word shall be fulfilled and that the words the Lord gives are spirit and life; this eternal principle is illustrated in the indestructibility and multiplication of Jeremiah's scroll.
Jesus teaches that 'heaven and earth shall pass away, but my words shall not pass away'; Jeremiah's scroll demonstrates this principle — human attempts to destroy God's word prove futile.

commentary.historical_context:
The writing of scrolls in ancient Judah was a meticulous process. Parchment or papyrus had to be prepared, and scribes like Baruch were highly trained professionals. A scroll of significant length would have taken considerable time to produce. The fact that Jeremiah and Baruch immediately undertook to rewrite the scroll demonstrates remarkable courage and faith — they were publicly contradicting the king's action and risking further retaliation. In ancient Near Eastern royal courts, such defiance would typically result in severe punishment.

The burning of written documents was a recognized form of censorship and protest in the ancient world. By burning the scroll, Jehoiakim was sending a message: this document has no authority, it is null and void, it is literally reduced to ashes. Yet Jeremiah's response — to rewrite it — was equally powerful as political theater. It demonstrated that the king could not erase the prophetic word. The very act of rewriting, in full view of the court, was a proclamation that God's word transcends royal power.

Historically, this chapter is dated to around 605 BCE, during Jehoiakim's reign. The Babylonian threat was real; Nebuchadnezzar's forces would eventually surround Jerusalem. Jeremiah's words about exile and destruction would prove devastatingly accurate. When the scroll was rewritten with additional words, it contained not only the original judgment but expanded explanation of why judgment was coming and what it would entail.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon itself represents a modern parallel to Jeremiah's scroll: a record that preserves words similar to but distinct from the Bible, 'that you may know that the covenants of the Lord which he made unto the house of Israel have not been cast away' (Book of Mormon title page). Like Jeremiah's expanded scroll, the Book of Mormon adds to and clarifies the message of the standard works.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 27:5 teaches that many important things pertain to the kingdom of God but were taken from the Bible; D&C sections represent modern expansion and clarification of God's word, paralleling the principle demonstrated in verse 32 that God's word grows and is multiplied across dispensations. The principle of continuing revelation in the Doctrine and Covenants is rooted in this ancient principle that God does not exhaust His word in one utterance.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The restoration of the scroll parallels the restoration of temple ordinances and covenants in the Latter-day Restoration. What was lost or obscured is recovered and clarified through God's continuing work with His people. The temple represents the fullness of God's word; the restoration of temple worship in the latter days mirrors Jeremiah's restoration of the scroll.

commentary.christological_typology: Jeremiah becomes a type of Christ in his suffering, rejection, and the vindication of his word. Just as Jehoiakim attempted to silence Jeremiah through burning the scroll, the religious and civil authorities attempted to silence Christ through crucifixion. Yet just as Jeremiah's word multiplied and spread after the burning of the scroll, Christ's teaching spread throughout the world after His resurrection. The principle is identical: the word of God cannot be permanently silenced or destroyed; attempts to destroy it only result in its wider dissemination and greater power. The scroll restored with added words prefigures Christ's completion and fulfillment of all law and prophecy — not their abolishment but their expansion and clarification.
commentary.application: For modern Latter-day Saints, verse 32 teaches a principle crucial to understanding the Restoration: God does not merely repeat Himself but continually expands and clarifies His word. The Doctrine and Covenants is 'many like words' added to the words of prophets like Jeremiah. When critics argue that Latter-day revelation contradicts or unnecessarily expands upon the Bible, they misunderstand the principle demonstrated here. Just as Jehoiakim could not stop God's word through the scroll by burning it, and just as Jeremiah and Baruch responded not with defeat but with restoration and expansion, the Restoration responds to centuries of lost truths not by returning to the original but by expanding, clarifying, and adding. The principle also encourages believers to trust that God's word will survive and flourish despite opposition. In a world increasingly hostile to religious faith and truth, this verse anchors the believer's hope: the word of God is not fragile or dependent on human approval. It grows, multiplies, and accomplishes God's purposes regardless of opposition.

text_kjv: And king Zedekiah the son of Josiah reigned instead of Coniah the son of Jehoiakim, whom Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon made king in the land of Judah.

commentary.narrative:
Jeremiah 37 opens with a stark political reality: Zedekiah sits on Judah's throne not by divine right or legitimate succession, but as a puppet installed by Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon. The mention of Coniah (a shortened form of Jeconiah/Jehoiachin) is particularly significant—this previous king reigned only three months before being deported to Babylon in 597 BCE with the first wave of exile. Zedekiah, Josiah's youngest surviving son, became king in his place, but his kingship carried a fundamental weakness: it was granted by a foreign power, not legitimized by the people or by God.

This verse establishes the political prison within which Jeremiah must operate. Zedekiah is caught between his vassal obligations to Babylon and the pressure from his own court and people to resist. The Hebrew term himlikh ('installed') emphasizes that Nebuchadnezzar actively *caused* Zedekiah to reign—he is not a sovereign monarch but an appointee whose authority derives entirely from Babylonian sufferance. This relationship will create the tragic dynamic of chapter 37: a weak king who sends to the prophet for intercession but lacks the moral courage to act on divine counsel.

The genealogy—"son of Josiah"—also carries weight. Josiah was Judah's great reforming king, beloved by the people and remembered for his covenant renewal (2 Kings 23). His sons, by contrast, represent a catastrophic collapse of royal virtue. The contrast between father and son underscores the spiritual decline that has made Judah vulnerable to conquest.

word_study.meaning: From the root MLK ('to reign, to be king'). The simple form means 'he reigned,' but in context requires understanding that this reign was established by external authority, not indigenous legitimacy. The Covenant Rendering's 'installed' captures the Babylonian agency more precisely than the KJV's 'reigned.'
word_study.significance: The verb emphasizes Zedekiah's dependent status. He does not seize the throne or inherit it legitimately; Nebuchadnezzar establishes him in power. This explains why Zedekiah will later be unable to fully commit to the prophet's counsel—his authority is too fragile to withstand the opposition of his own court.

word_study.meaning: Causative form of MLK: 'he caused to reign, installed.' This is the active choice of Nebuchadnezzar, not the passive result of circumstance. It underscores that Babylon, not Judah or heaven, determines who sits on Judah's throne.
word_study.significance: The shift from yimlokh (simple reign) to himlikh (caused to reign) shows that Zedekiah's kingship is a Babylonian construct. This legal-political reality frames the entire conflict of chapter 37 and 38: Zedekiah cannot act decisively because he is answerable to Babylon, not to his own conscience or God.

word_study.meaning: Literally 'under,' but in the context of royal succession means 'in place of, instead of.' It indicates substitution or replacement in an office or role.
word_study.significance: Tachath signals that Zedekiah is not a continuation of his brother Coniah's legacy but a replacement—an alternative the Babylonians imposed when Coniah proved inconvenient. This emphasizes discontinuity and foreign control over Judah's royal line.

cross_references.connection: Provides the historical background of Coniah's deportation and Zedekiah's installation as Babylon's vassal king in 597 BCE, confirming the political circumstances alluded to in Jeremiah 37:1.

Summarizes Zedekiah's reign and notes that 'he did that which was evil in the sight of the LORD his God, and humbled not himself before Jeremiah the prophet speaking from the mouth of the LORD,' foreshadowing the tension between king and prophet in this chapter.

Contrasts Coniah (Jeconiah) with the 'good figs' (the exiles who accept their fate), using royal deportation as the background for understanding Zedekiah's precarious position and compromised authority.
An earlier oracle against Coniah: 'Is this man Coniah a despised broken idol?' This context makes Zedekiah's role as replacement-king even more fraught with political and theological instability.

Modern revelation on the limits of authority obtained through coercion: 'Behold, there are many called, but few are chosen... because their hearts are set so much upon the things of this world.' Zedekiah's dilemma—power without legitimacy—parallels the principle that authority without righteousness cannot endure.

commentary.historical_context: Zedekiah ascended to Judah's throne in 597 BCE following the first Babylonian siege and the deportation of his brother Coniah. The political landscape of the ancient Near East at this time was dominated by the rising power of Nebuchadnezzar II, who ruled Babylon from 605–562 BCE. Judah, along with other Levantine kingdoms, had become tributaries of Babylon. The vassal-king system was common in the ancient Near East: a great king (like Nebuchadnezzar) would install a local ruler who was expected to maintain order, pay tribute, and remain loyal. The arrangement was mutually beneficial in theory—the vassal gained internal authority; the suzerain gained a stable region. In practice, vassal kings were constantly caught between pressure from their own populations (who chafed under foreign domination) and the demands of their overlord. Zedekiah's weakness in this chapter reflects a historical reality: a vassal king could not easily defy his suzerain without risking deposition or worse. The mention of Pharaoh's army in verse 5 shows why—when Hophra of Egypt sent forces northward, it created a moment of hope in Jerusalem that Babylon might be distracted or weakened. But Zedekiah's inability to commit fully to rebellion, or to listen decisively to Jeremiah, stems from his fundamentally precarious position.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon contains multiple instances of kings who inherit or receive power but lack the moral authority to govern effectively—most notably in Mosiah 11-29, where weak kings lead their people into bondage. The principle that political power without spiritual integrity leads to destruction is central to both Jeremiah and the Book of Mormon.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 121:36-37 teaches that 'all influence obtained without righteousness is ephemeral.' Zedekiah's kingship, obtained through Babylonian appointment rather than through covenant with God, will prove to have no lasting foundation. His inability to act decisively in behalf of God's prophet (Jeremiah) and God's people stems from this fundamental lack of righteous authority.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The installation of a king not of God's choosing echoes the principle that true authority derives from temple covenant and divine appointment, not from external power. Zedekiah sits on David's throne, but his reign violates the Davidic covenant—he is a king without the Spirit, a symbol of exile and separation from the temple.

commentary.christological_typology: Zedekiah represents, in negative type, the kingship that fails to honor God's word through the prophet. Christ, by contrast, is the King who perfectly submits to the Father's will and fulfills the prophetic word. Where Zedekiah cannot act on Jeremiah's counsel because of his political weakness, Christ acts decisively to accomplish redemption despite worldly pressure. The contrast also prefigures the rejection of God's spokesman: just as Zedekiah hears Jeremiah but does not obey, the world hears Christ but refuses to honor His kingship.
commentary.application: Zedekiah's situation invites reflection on how external pressure and compromised authority can paralyze good intentions. In modern covenant life, we may find ourselves in positions where cultural, social, or professional pressure tempts us to half-measures in discipleship. The lesson is stark: a throne built on anything other than righteousness—whether it be social status, wealth, approval-seeking, or compromise—will collapse. The strength to act on prophetic counsel comes not from the approval of the world but from the conviction that God's word is true, regardless of worldly consequence. For those in positions of leadership, Zedekiah's failure is a warning: authority that rests on external validation rather than inner righteousness will eventually betray you and those you lead.

text_kjv: But neither he, nor his servants, nor the people of the land, did hearken unto the words of the LORD, which he spake by the prophet Jeremiah.

commentary.narrative:
This verse is the theological lynchpin of chapter 37. It moves from political description (who Zedekiah is) to moral indictment (what Zedekiah failed to do). The three-tier structure of disobedience—king, officials, and common people—shows that responsibility for Judah's catastrophe is not confined to one person but is systemic, cultural, and collective. Every level of society had the opportunity to hear God's word through Jeremiah and chose not to.

The phrase "by the prophet Jeremiah" is not incidental. It emphasizes that this was not Jeremiah's private opinion or political agenda; this was the word of the LORD, mediated through an authorized messenger.
