In Hebrew covenant thinking, to reject the prophet's word is to reject God Himself (see Deuteronomy 18:18-19, where God promises to hold accountable those who do not listen to His prophet). The use of the simple past tense—"did not hearken"—is particularly devastating because it describes a habitual pattern throughout Zedekiah's reign, not a single incident.

This verse also explains why Zedekiah, despite his later request for Jeremiah to pray (verse 3), is already under judgment. He has already demonstrated willful disobedience to the word of God. His later desperate appeal for intercession will come too late—not because God cannot forgive, but because the political and spiritual trajectory has already been set. The disobedience of verse 2 creates the circumstances of imprisonment and siege that dominate the rest of the chapter.

word_study.meaning: Root meaning 'to hear, to listen, to obey.' In Hebrew covenant language, shamah encompasses not merely hearing sound but hearing with obedience—genuine listening that results in action. The negative form 'did not hearken' means either did not listen or listened but refused to act.
word_study.significance: Shamah is the foundational covenantal verb of faithfulness in the Old Testament. The failure to shamah is the failure of the covenant relationship itself. This explains why Zedekiah's disobedience is not merely political error but theological betrayal.

word_study.meaning: Literally 'by the hand of.' This is the standard Hebrew idiom for prophetic mediation—God's word reaches the people through the prophet's hand, mouth, and agency. The preposition be marks instrumental causation: the prophet is the instrument through which God speaks.
word_study.significance: Be-yad establishes that Jeremiah is not an independent voice but a conduit. To reject Jeremiah's word is not to reject one man's politics but to reject God's authoritative speech. This is why the disobedience carries such weight—it is not merely disagreement with a political figure but defiance of God.

word_study.meaning: Plural of eved (servant). In royal contexts, avadim refers to court officials, advisors, and administrators—those who serve the king and bear responsibility for his decisions. The term carries the sense of both subordination and agency.
word_study.significance: The inclusion of the king's servants in the indictment shows that institutional resistance to prophecy is not merely the king's personal failing. His court, his advisors, his bureaucracy all conspired in the rejection of God's word. This mirrors the institutional idolatry condemned throughout Jeremiah.

word_study.meaning: Literally 'the people of the earth/land.' This phrase can mean the common populace, but in this context refers to the landed gentry and ordinary citizens who constituted Judah's society below the royal court. They were not passive spectators but active participants in the resistance to Jeremiah's message.
word_study.significance: The inclusion of am ha-arets shows that the disobedience to God's word was not a top-down imposition but had popular support. The people did not want to hear Jeremiah's message of submission to Babylon because it contradicted their national pride and survival instincts. This is why Jeremiah faced such fierce opposition—he was calling for something the entire society actively resisted.

cross_references.connection: Establishes the principle that rejection of a prophet sent by God is rejection of God Himself: 'whoever will not hearken unto my words which he shall speak in my name, I will require it of him.' This is the theological framework that makes Zedekiah's disobedience in Jeremiah 37:2 not merely political but covenantal betrayal.

Jeremiah's commissioning, where God warns him that the king, priests, and people will oppose him. Jeremiah 37:2 is the fulfillment of that warning—the entire society, as predicted, resists the prophet's word.

Describes Israel's fall to Assyria with language strikingly similar to Jeremiah 37:2: 'Yet the LORD testified against Israel... by all the prophets and seers, saying, Turn ye from your evil ways... Notwithstanding they would not hear, but hardened their necks.' Judah is repeating Israel's fatal pattern.

Jeremiah's earlier summary of his own ministry: God 'hath sent unto you all his servants the prophets... saying, Return ye now every one from his evil way... but ye have not hearkened.' This shows the long, persistent pattern of disobedience that culminates in chapter 37.

In the Book of Mormon, Nephi rebukes the people for rejecting prophetic counsel: 'ye have sought all the days of your lives for that which ye could not obtain; and ye have sought for happiness in doing iniquity, which thing is contrary to the nature of that righteousness which is in our great and eternal Head.' The principle that covenant violation stems from preferring worldly security over obedience appears in both Jeremiah and the Book of Mormon.

commentary.historical_context: By the time Jeremiah began his ministry (around 627 BCE), Judah had experienced decades of religious reform under Josiah (640–609 BCE) but had quickly regressed spiritually after his death. Multiple short-lived kings followed Josiah, each making political deals and military alliances that compromised Judah's covenant status. By Zedekiah's reign (597–586 BCE), the society was fractured: some advocated submission to Babylon as the will of God; others championed Egyptian alliance and continued resistance. Jeremiah stood almost alone in calling for submission to Babylon as the divinely appointed judgment. His message was politically toxic because it contradicted the national desire for independence and the nationalist propaganda promoted by other prophets and priests. The resistance to Jeremiah was not ignorant rejection but calculated suppression of an inconvenient truth. This is what makes verse 2 so damning—the disobedience was willful, not accidental.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The pattern of institutional resistance to prophetic word pervades the Book of Mormon. In 2 Nephi 26-27, Jacob describes a future day when people 'heap up treasures upon the earth, and seek their own will, and enlarge the borders of their garments, that they may not hear the words of the Holy One of God.' The people of Judah in Jeremiah 37:2 do exactly this—they construct a society oriented toward their own desires and national independence, which blinds them to prophetic truth.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 1:14 states: 'They seek not the Lord to establish his righteousness, but every man walketh in his own way, and after the image of his own god, whose image is in the likeness of the world.' This describes Zedekiah, his servants, and the people of Judah exactly—they have collectively chosen a path that honors their own will and Babylon's power, rather than submitting to God's word through Jeremiah.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: Judah's refusal to hear the prophet is ultimately a refusal of the temple covenant and the Deuteronomic law that bound them to the LORD. They are functionally severing themselves from the covenant community, which is why exile (separation from the temple) becomes inevitable.

commentary.christological_typology: Jeremiah's rejection by the entire society—king, officials, and people—is a type of the rejection Christ would face. Matthew 23:37 captures this: 'O Jerusalem, Jerusalem, thou that killest the prophets, and stonest them which are sent unto thee, how often would I have gathered thy children together, even as a hen gathereth her chickens under her wings, and ye would not!' The pattern of rejected prophets culminates in the rejection of the Prophet par excellence. The disobedience to Jeremiah prefigures the greater tragedy of disobedience to Christ.
commentary.application: Verse 2 confronts us with a question every member of the covenant community must face: Am I truly listening to the servants of God, or am I listening selectively—hearing only what aligns with my preferences? Zedekiah had access to prophetic counsel but filtered it through his political interests. In our day, we have prophets and apostles whose words are preserved in written form and made universally accessible. The question is whether we truly hearken—not just hear, but obey. Verse 2 suggests that selective listening is a form of disobedience. We cannot claim to sustain the prophets while ignoring their counsel when it cuts against our preferences or plans. True listening to the prophet means allowing his word to redirect our desires and choices, even when it costs us something.

text_kjv: And Zedekiah the king sent Jehucal the son of Shelemiah and Zephaniah the son of Maaseiah the priest to the prophet Jeremiah, saying, Pray now unto the LORD our God for us.

commentary.narrative:
Here begins the tragic irony that defines chapter 37-38: Zedekiah, who has refused to hearken to the word of the LORD spoken through Jeremiah (verse 2), now sends a delegation to ask Jeremiah to pray on behalf of the kingdom. The king recognizes that prayer and prophetic intercession matter, but only when national crisis threatens. The delegation itself is carefully composed—Jehucal, a court official, paired with Zephaniah, a priest. This is not a casual errand but an official diplomatic mission, suggesting that Zedekiah is taking the request seriously, at least performatively.

The verb "sent" (yishlach) indicates formal delegation, not a request made informally or humbly. Yet the phrase "Pray now unto the LORD our God for us" carries the polite particle na (rendered as "now" or "please"), which softens the command and acknowledges Jeremiah's spiritual authority. This is the language of desperation dressed in diplomatic courtesy. Zedekiah is willing to ask the prophet for prayer but not to obey the prophet's counsel—a distinction that exposes the hollowness of his piety.

The phrase "our God" is particularly poignant. Zedekiah claims the LORD as his God only in extremity, not in obedience. The verb "pray" (hitpallel) refers to intercession, the prophet's mediatorial function. Zedekiah wants Jeremiah to stand between him and God's judgment, but he himself refuses to stand with God and His prophet against the crowd. This will become the central failure of Zedekiah's character—he will repeatedly seek Jeremiah's counsel in secret (38:14-28) but lack the courage to act upon it publicly.

word_study.meaning: From the root SHL, meaning 'to send.' The past tense indicates a deliberate action by the king. This is not a spontaneous request but an official communication, underscored by the fact that Zedekiah chooses two high-ranking emissaries to carry it.
word_study.significance: The verb emphasizes that Zedekiah is taking the step deliberately and with full knowledge of what he is asking. He knows Jeremiah is a prophet; he knows prayer matters. Yet he delays this action until national crisis forces his hand (the Egyptian army's arrival in verse 5 is the trigger). This shows Zedekiah's tendency to seek spiritual help only when political solutions fail.

word_study.meaning: Reflexive form of PLL, meaning 'to pray, to intercede.' The reflexive form suggests mutual or reciprocal prayer—the prophet speaking to God on behalf of the people. This is the classic prophetic function of intercession, as seen in Abraham's prayer for Sodom (Genesis 18:23-32) or Moses' intercession for Israel.
word_study.significance: Hitpallel emphasizes that Zedekiah is asking Jeremiah to assume a mediatorial role—to stand between heaven and earth and plead for Judah's deliverance. Ironically, Jeremiah will do exactly this (see 37:3b and following), but his intercession will not produce what Zedekiah expects, because prayer cannot overturn the judgment that disobedience has earned.

word_study.meaning: A particle expressing polite request, entreaty, or urgency. It softens an imperative into a plea. The Covenant Rendering's use of 'Please' captures this more effectively than the KJV's 'now,' which sounds more temporal than respectful.
word_study.significance: The particle na indicates that Zedekiah is not commanding Jeremiah to pray but begging him. This reveals the king's awareness of his spiritual powerlessness and his recognition that Jeremiah, the despised prophet, has access to the divine that Zedekiah himself lacks. It is an admission of Zedekiah's bankruptcy—he cannot secure his kingdom through politics or military might, and now must resort to prayer, which he has previously rejected.

cross_references.connection: A more extended version of this same pattern: Zedekiah secretly asks Jeremiah for God's word, Jeremiah gives honest counsel that contradicts the king's desires, and Zedekiah lacks courage to act on it. Chapter 37:3 establishes the pattern that chapter 38 repeats and intensifies.

Pharaoh begs Moses to pray for him, asking God to remove the plagues: 'Intreat the LORD, that he may take away the frogs from me.' Like Zedekiah, Pharaoh seeks prophetic intercession only when afflicted, not out of genuine repentance or obedience.

Saul asks Samuel to pray with him and honor him before the people after his disobedience: 'I have sinned... I feared the people, and obeyed their voice.' Like Zedekiah, Saul seeks the prophet's support while lacking the courage to obey the prophet's word.

Alma is cast out by the people, and later the king asks Alma to pray for the land. The pattern of leaders seeking prophetic intercession only in crisis—not in obedience—is a recurring theme in both the Old Testament and Book of Mormon.

Modern revelation on prayer: 'He that is ordained of God and sent forth, the same is appointed to be the judge of this people... And no one can assist in this work except those who are clean before God.' Jeremiah's intercession can only be effective if he stands in righteousness, which Zedekiah's court does not.

commentary.historical_context: The delegation of Jehucal and Zephaniah son of Maaseiah likely reflects the actual political structure of Zedekiah's reign. Jehucal appears again in Jeremiah 38:1 as one of the officials who press Zedekiah to execute Jeremiah, showing a shift from supplicant to prosecutor—a common pattern when a leader's desperation passes and political opposition reasserts itself. Zephaniah son of Maaseiah, a priestly official, appears again in 38:1 and later in 52:24 as 'the second priest,' indicating his high rank in the religious establishment. His inclusion in this delegation suggests that even the priestly class, though representing religious authority, was part of the resistance to Jeremiah's word. The timing of this request is crucial: Zedekiah sends it only after hearing of Pharaoh's approach (implied by the sequence of verses 3-5), showing that the king's piety is entirely circumstantial—he seeks divine help only when natural resources (military alliance) become available.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon contains multiple episodes of kings and peoples who seek prophetic counsel only in crisis. In Helaman 11:1-6, the people cry repentance to the prophet Nephi when famine strikes, though they had previously rejected his word. The principle is consistent: genuine repentance requires obedience before crisis, not merely prayer during affliction.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 63:32 teaches: 'Wherefore, let all men beware how they take my name in their lips... he that doeth this shall be answerable unto me saith the Lord.' Zedekiah invokes 'the LORD our God' and asks the prophet to pray, but he himself has not repented or changed course. His piety rings hollow before the Lord who searches hearts.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The request for prophetic intercession should have led Zedekiah to the temple, to repentance, and to covenant renewal. Instead, it becomes a transaction—seeking prayer without seeking to change his life. This reflects a corruption of the covenantal relationship where one approaches the temple or the prophet seeking blessing while refusing to obey the commandments.

commentary.christological_typology: Zedekiah's delegation to Jeremiah, asking for prayer without willingness to obey, parallels the attitude of those who came to Jesus demanding signs and wonders while rejecting His gospel. Matthew 12:39 records Christ's response: 'An evil and adulterous generation seeketh after a sign.' The petition for prayer without repentance, for divine intervention without obedience, reflects a fundamental misunderstanding of how God works. True intercession requires a change of heart in the intercessor and in those for whom he intercedes.
commentary.application: This verse exposes a form of spiritual shallow-rooting that many in covenant communities face: we seek God's blessing and the prophet's prayer in times of crisis while resisting the prophet's counsel in times of stability. This is spiritual opportunism, not genuine faith. True faith requires that we align ourselves with prophetic direction before we face consequences, not after. For modern members, this means: sustaining the prophets is not merely a formal action at General Conference but a commitment to follow their counsel in real life, even when it requires sacrifice. When we face difficulty, we should ask ourselves whether we have been living according to the words of the prophets in our prosperous times. Prayer for deliverance from consequences, without willingness to obey the word that prevents those consequences, is not prayer that God is bound to answer.

text_kjv: Now Jeremiah came in and went out among the people: for they had not put him into prison.

commentary.narrative:
This brief verse functions as a crucial temporal and biographical marker. It establishes that at this moment—when Zedekiah sends his delegation—Jeremiah still enjoys freedom of movement. He can "come and go" among the people, a Hebrew idiom (ba vayotse) for unrestricted daily activity. This freedom is about to change. The verse serves as a hinge between Jeremiah's pre-imprisonment ministry and the suffering that begins in the next verse.

The emphasis that "they had not put him into prison" suggests that imprisonment is a known threat, something that is already being contemplated or feared. The negative statement—what has *not yet* happened—casts a shadow forward. We know from chapters 36-39 that Jeremiah faces multiple imprisonments, beatings, and threats of execution. Verse 4 captures the brief window before that persecution intensifies. It is a moment of precarious freedom, the last moment before the prophet's physical suffering becomes acute.

The phrase "among the people" is also significant. Jeremiah has been operating as a public prophet, speaking openly in the streets and in the temple, bearing witness to Judah's sin and calling them to repentance. This open ministry is about to be restricted. Once imprisoned, Jeremiah will speak less to the masses and more to the king in private—a shift in his prophetic mode that reflects the narrowing of his sphere of influence as political pressure mounts.

word_study.meaning: A Hebrew idiom meaning to move about freely, to have unrestricted access and mobility. The pair of verbs (entering and exiting) together convey a sense of continuous, unobstructed movement through the community.
word_study.significance: Ba vayotse is the language of freedom and public presence. Its use here emphasizes that Jeremiah, though despised, still has the legal right to move in Jerusalem. This changes once he is imprisoned; his voice becomes confined to the dungeon or the courtyard of the guards. The idiom underscores the shift from public prophet to silenced witness.

word_study.meaning: Literally 'in the midst of the people.' This phrase emphasizes Jeremiah's presence within the community, not above or apart from it. He is moving among them, accessible to them, sharing their space even though they reject his word.
word_study.significance: Be-tokh ha-am shows that Jeremiah's ministry is incarnational—he does not prophesy from a distance but lives among the people he seeks to call to repentance. This makes his ministry more powerful (he witnesses to them in their daily lives) and more dangerous (he is always visible to his opponents).

word_study.meaning: Literally 'house of confinement.' Keli can refer to various types of imprisonment, from dungeon to courtyard-prison to stocks. The term appears frequently in Jeremiah 37-38 to describe the various places where Jeremiah is held.
word_study.significance: The word keli anticipates the imprisonments that follow. Each appearance of beyt ha-keli in this chapter marks a stage in Jeremiah's suffering. Verse 4 uses the negative—'not yet imprisoned'—to mark the transition from freedom to bondage that is about to occur.

cross_references.connection: Jeremiah's earlier lament: 'The word of the LORD was made a reproach unto me, and a derision, daily... I am in derision of all my people.' This verse echoes that tension between public presence and public rejection.

A later description of Jeremiah's imprisonment: 'For Zedekiah king of Judah had shut him up in the court of the prison, saying, Wherefore dost thou prophesy?' The imprisonment mentioned implicitly in 37:4 becomes explicit reality in 32:2 and beyond.

An earlier episode where Jeremiah prophesies in the temple and is immediately seized by the people and threatened with death. This provides background for why Jeremiah's continued public presence is remarkable and increasingly dangerous.

The companion text for this week: 'All our enemies have opened their mouths against us.' Lamentations, traditionally attributed to Jeremiah, contains the prophet's reflection on his suffering during the siege and aftermath.

Paul's catalog of his own sufferings includes imprisonment, beatings, and danger, echoing the pattern of prophetic persecution that Jeremiah enters in this chapter. Both prophetic figures move freely in public only until opposition coalesces.

commentary.historical_context: The statement that Jeremiah has not yet been imprisoned is historically significant. We know from Jeremiah 20:1-6 that Jeremiah had been beaten and confined by Pashhur the priest earlier in his ministry. Yet by the time of chapter 37 (the final siege, 588-586 BCE), Zedekiah has allowed Jeremiah more freedom than the previous regime. This may reflect either Zedekiah's uncertainty about his authority or his recognition that executing a prophet would be dangerous. However, as the siege tightens and pressure from the court officials (including the very men sent in verse 3) increases, the king's tolerance wears thin. The transition from freedom to imprisonment reflects the political dynamics of a weakening regime under increasing stress. Zedekiah, already compromised by his vassal status, becomes increasingly subject to the will of his officials and war party, who see Jeremiah's call for surrender as treason.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon contains similar patterns of prophets who enjoy freedom until their message becomes politically threatening. Abinadi was killed when he challenged King Noah's regime (Mosiah 17), and Samuel the Lamanite was imprisoned while prophesying to the Nephites (Helaman 16:1-11). The pattern suggests that religious opposition to political power eventually leads to physical persecution.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 121:7-9 addresses Joseph Smith's imprisonment in Missouri with the promise: 'My son, peace be unto thy soul; thine adversity and thine afflictions shall be but a small moment; And then, if thou endure it well, all these things shall give thee experience, and shall be for thy good.' Jeremiah's coming imprisonment will be a 'small moment' in terms of eternity, and his witness will not be destroyed by it.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: Jeremiah's freedom to move among the people and his later imprisonment reflect the principle that the Lord's prophets are never truly imprisoned—their voice cannot be bound. Even in the dungeon, Jeremiah will continue to prophesy and receive revelation (37:11-15, 38:1-28).

commentary.christological_typology: Verse 4 foreshadows Christ's freedom in movement before His arrest, and then His imprisonment and passion. Christ moved freely among the people during His ministry, as Jeremiah does here. Yet like Jeremiah, He faced increasing opposition and was ultimately seized and confined. The freedom of verses 1-4 of Jeremiah 37 parallels the freedom of Christ's ministry; the imprisonment of later verses parallels His passion.
commentary.application: This verse is a reminder that freedom to live according to conscience and to speak truth is not guaranteed and often temporal. For members of the Church, this verse raises the question: When do we use our freedom to speak truth? Are we willing to bear witness to God's word in our workplaces, schools, and communities while we still have freedom to do so? Or do we wait until circumstances force us into a corner? Jeremiah uses his freedom in verse 4 to move among the people—presumably continuing his prophetic ministry even as his imprisonment looms. The lesson is to use the freedom and platform we have while we have it. Procrastinating 'till we are imprisoned' by circumstance is not an option for a true witness.

text_kjv: Then Pharaoh's army was come forth out of Egypt: and when the Chaldeans that besieged Jerusalem heard tidings of them, they departed from Jerusalem.

commentary.narrative:
This verse marks a dramatic turn in the historical situation and explains the timing of Zedekiah's request for prayer. Pharaoh's army—sent by Hophra (Apries), Pharaoh of Egypt (589-570 BCE)—has marched northward, creating a military threat that diverts Babylonian attention from Jerusalem. The Chaldean siege forces, faced with a new danger from Egypt, withdraw from Jerusalem to meet this threat. For the inhabitants of Jerusalem, this withdrawal appears to be a miraculous deliverance—the siege is lifted, the enemy retreats.

This is precisely the false hope that Jeremiah was sent to destroy. While ordinary citizens and even the king might view this military reprieve as divine intervention or confirmation that resistance to Babylon is justified, Jeremiah will interpret it very differently. The withdrawal is tactical, not strategic. Nebuchadnezzar, not defeated, has merely repositioned his forces. The Chaldeans will return—in fact, historically they did so and conducted an even more devastating siege in 588-586 BCE. The false hope created by Pharaoh's army is dangerous because it will harden hearts against Jeremiah's message of submission.

Note the sequence: Zedekiah asks for prayer (verse 3), Jeremiah is free to move (verse 4), and *then* the military reprieve arrives (verse 5). The king might interpret this sequence as Jeremiah's prayer being answered, leading him to believe that resistance to Babylon is sanctioned by God. Yet God has not granted deliverance; God has merely allowed political circumstance to create temporary relief. This is precisely the kind of ambiguous situation where discerning between true and false hope becomes critical—and where Jeremiah's prophetic clarity will prove invaluable.

word_study.meaning: Cheil means 'army, force, military power.' Par'oh is the title for the Egyptian king. Pharaoh's army refers to the military forces sent by Hophra of Egypt (589-570 BCE), the reigning Pharaoh at this time.
word_study.significance: The mention of Pharaoh's army highlights the geopolitical complexity: Judah is caught between two superpowers (Egypt and Babylon), and hopes that one will counterbalance the other. However, Jeremiah will make clear that trusting in Egypt or in this military alliance is exactly the kind of faithlessness he condemns.

word_study.meaning: From the root YTZ, meaning 'to go out, to come forth, to emerge.' Yatzah can indicate a military movement or expedition. In military contexts, it often means to muster or deploy forces.
word_study.significance: Yatzah emphasizes the active initiation of Pharaoh's military campaign. Egypt is not responding to a Judean request (though they may have coordinated); Egypt is acting on its own strategic interests, which happen to create temporary advantage for Judah.

word_study.meaning: A cognate accusative construction (hearing the hearing, or more idiomatically, 'heard the report'). Yishmeu comes from SHM (to hear); shimam is a noun derived from the same root meaning 'report, news, fame.' The construction emphasizes the transmission of intelligence—the Chaldeans received news of Pharaoh's approach.
word_study.significance: This construction highlights communication and intelligence in ancient warfare. Armies depended on scouts and messengers to relay information about enemy movements. The Chaldeans' withdrawal was prompted by tactical intelligence, not by military defeat—a distinction that will matter for understanding how false hope develops.

word_study.meaning: The Chaldeans, the people of Babylon's heartland (southern Mesopotamia). In the late 7th and 6th centuries BCE, Chaldean dynasties ruled Babylon. The term is used in Jeremiah for Nebuchadnezzar's forces.
word_study.significance: The term Chaldeans/Kasdim is consistent throughout Jeremiah for Babylon's military forces. Their withdrawal is presented as a tactical repositioning, not as a defeat or a change in Babylon's strategic goal of conquering Judah.

word_study.meaning: From the root TZR, meaning 'to besiege, to press, to confine.' Tzar carries a sense of constriction and threat. Those who besiege (tzarim) apply military pressure to a city.
word_study.significance: Ha-tzarim emphasizes the hostile military situation. The Chaldeans are not merely camping; they are actively besieging Jerusalem, which makes their withdrawal even more significant (and apparently hopeful) to the inhabitants.

word_study.meaning: From the root ALH, meaning 'to go up, to ascend, to withdraw.' In military contexts, ye'alu often means to lift a siege or to withdraw from a position. The term suggests a disengagement, not a rout or defeat.
word_study.significance: Va-ye'alu is a neutral term describing a tactical withdrawal, not a victory or defeat. The Chaldeans are repositioning to deal with Egypt, not abandoning their ultimate goal of conquering Judah. This distinction is crucial to Jeremiah's prophetic interpretation.

cross_references.connection: A passage later in this siege sequence where Jeremiah predicts: 'The Chaldeans shall come again, and fight against this city... for though ye have made a covenant with me to let you go free... yet ye turned, and polluted my name.' This directly confirms that Pharaoh's withdrawal is temporary, and the Chaldeans will return.

Historical background: 'And the king of Egypt came not again any more out of his land: for the king of Babylon had taken from the river of Egypt unto the river Euphrates all that pertained to the king of Egypt.' This shows that despite Hophra's intervention, Egypt ultimately could not save Judah from Babylon.
cross_references.connection2: Jeremiah's entire message about the futility of depending on Egypt is grounded in the historical reality that Egypt simply did not have the military capacity to overcome Babylon long-term.

cross_references.connection: The following verses contain Jeremiah's prophetic response to Pharaoh's arrival, interpreting it not as deliverance but as a temporary reprieve before greater suffering.

An earlier oracle: 'And now what hast thou to do in the way of Egypt, to drink the waters of Sihor? or what hast thou to do in the way of Assyria, to drink the waters of the river?' Jeremiah has long warned against trusting in Egypt as a military or political ally.

A summary description of Zedekiah: 'He also rebelled against king Nebuchadnezzar, who had made him swear by God: but he stiffened his neck, and hardened his heart from turning unto the LORD God of Israel.' The arrival of Pharaoh's army will only harden Zedekiah's neck further as he entertains false hope.

commentary.historical_context:
Hophra (Apries in Greek sources) ruled Egypt from 589 to 570 BCE and faced constant pressure from the rising power of Babylon. His decision to send an army northward to support Judah was likely prompted both by the traditional Egyptian interest in preventing any single power from dominating the Levantine corridor and by appeals from Judean envoys. However, as 2 Kings 24:7 notes, Hophra's intervention could not ultimately counter Babylonian dominance. This is a well-documented historical moment: ancient sources (including Josephus and the Babylonian Chronicles) confirm that the Chaldeans did withdraw from Jerusalem to confront Hophra's forces, and then returned to complete the siege and destruction of the city in 586 BCE.

The geography of this confrontation is significant: Egypt was to the southwest of Judah, Babylon to the northeast. An Egyptian army marching toward the Levant would have to cross through the Sinai and southern Judah. The Babylonian withdrawal was a prudent military decision to consolidate forces against this new threat. However, it was also temporary. Hophra's forces could not sustain their northern campaign, and within a matter of months, the Chaldeans returned with greater ferocity.

This historical sequence makes Jeremiah's prophetic clarity even more remarkable. While the entire political establishment of Jerusalem was celebrating what appeared to be a miraculous deliverance, Jeremiah saw through to the future and correctly predicted that the reprieve was false.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon contains multiple episodes where temporary military relief leads to false hope and spiritual hardening. In Alma 51-52, when the Nephites receive military aid from the Lamanite king, some among them grow proud and begin to trust in military power rather than in God. The pattern is consistent: outward deliverance can harden hearts if not properly interpreted through the prophetic lens.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 87:6 warns: 'Thus with the sword and by bloodshed the inhabitants of the earth shall mourn; and with famine, and plague, and earthquake, and the thunder of heaven, and the fierce and vivid lightning also, shall the inhabitants of the earth be made to feel the wrath, and indignation, and chastening hand of an Almighty God.' The appearance of Pharaoh's army might seem like a reprieve from judgment, but it does not change the underlying judgment that Babylon will conquer Judah.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The false hope created by Pharaoh's arrival parallels the spiritual danger of seeking God's approval through worldly means rather than through covenantal obedience. True deliverance comes through the temple covenant and submission to God's word, not through military alliances with Egypt.

commentary.christological_typology: This verse illustrates the difference between worldly solutions and divine solution. Pharaoh's army offers temporary military relief; Christ offers eternal redemption. The temporary reprieve from the Chaldean siege is precisely the kind of false hope that keeps people from seeking true salvation. Christ's teaching about taking up the cross (Matthew 16:24-26) is similar to Jeremiah's call to accept Babylon's conquest—both require accepting a hard truth rather than grasping at worldly salvation.
commentary.application: This verse challenges us to discern between genuine deliverance and false hope. In our own lives, we encounter many circumstances that appear favorable or appear to be answers to prayer, yet may actually be distractions from what God is calling us to do. The question is: Do we have the spiritual discernment to distinguish between worldly relief and divine guidance? Pharaoh's army brings military relief, but it does not change the fundamental judgment on Judah. Similarly, in our lives, external circumstances may shift, obstacles may temporarily clear, or opportunities may arise—but these do not necessarily indicate that we are following God's will. True guidance comes through the prophetic word, not through circumstance. The modern application is to ask: Am I trusting in worldly signs of success and approval, or am I seeking and following prophetic direction even when it contradicts what appears to be favorable circumstance?

text_kjv: Then came the word of the LORD unto the prophet Jeremiah, saying,

commentary.narrative:
This verse opens Jeremiah's prophetic response to the military crisis that has just unfolded. The formula "the word of the LORD came unto the prophet Jeremiah, saying" is the standard prophetic reception formula in Hebrew Scripture, appearing dozens of times in Jeremiah. This formula establishes that what follows is not Jeremiah's private political opinion or strategic analysis, but a message from God Himself, mediated through the prophet.

The timing is crucial: immediately after the Chaldeans withdraw (verse 5), God speaks to Jeremiah. The king and people are celebrating, interpreting the withdrawal as deliverance. In this moment of false hope and potential spiritual blindness, God gives Jeremiah a word to speak. The verses that follow (37:7-10, not included in this passage but crucial context) will contain Jeremiah's interpretation of events: the Chaldeans will return, and Jerusalem will fall. This is not the message the king wants to hear, but it is the word of the LORD.

The formula itself—"came the word"—uses the Hebrew construction "vayehi debar-YHWH," which emphasizes the reception of divine speech. It is not that Jeremiah thought up this interpretation or made a clever political analysis. God actively communicated to him. This distinction is vital because it shields Jeremiah from the accusation that he is merely expressing anti-war sentiment. He is speaking God's word, even though it contradicts the political consensus.

The phrase "to the prophet Jeremiah" also matters. Throughout chapter 37, Jeremiah is repeatedly identified as "the prophet"—ha-navi in Hebrew. This title establishes his formal office and authority. He is not a private citizen offering opinions; he is the LORD's prophet, functioning in an official capacity. When the word of the LORD comes to "the prophet Jeremiah," it comes to someone who has a recognized role in Judean society, even if that role is despised.

word_study.meaning: Debar means 'word, speech, thing, matter.' YHWH is God's covenantal name. Debar-YHWH is the standard Hebrew term for a divine utterance or message. It refers not merely to sound or information but to God's active communication and the substantive content of that communication.
word_study.significance: Debar-YHWH is the fundamental term for prophetic authority in the Old Testament. When Jeremiah speaks 'the word of the LORD,' he is not expressing opinion but conveying divine intention. This is why resistance to Jeremiah's word constitutes resistance to God (see Deuteronomy 18:18-19).

word_study.meaning: From the root HYH ('to be, to happen, to become'). Va-yehi is the narrative past tense: 'it happened, it came to pass.' In prophetic formula contexts, va-yehi introduces a significant event—the reception of divine speech.
word_study.significance: Va-yehi emphasizes that the coming of God's word is an event, something that happens in the prophet's experience. Jeremiah does not generate this word; it comes to him. This is the classic Old Testament understanding of prophetic inspiration as receptive rather than generative.

word_study.meaning: A preposition indicating direction, recipient, or target. In the formula 'the word of the LORD came el the prophet,' el indicates that the prophet is the recipient of divine address.
word_study.significance: The preposition el establishes the prophet as the addressee of God's speech. God is not speaking about Jeremiah but *to* Jeremiah. This direct address makes Jeremiah the authorized messenger who must communicate what he has received.

word_study.meaning: From the root NVB, meaning 'to call, to announce, to speak forth.' A navi is one who speaks for God, who announces God's will. The article ha ('the') indicates a specific office or known figure—'the prophet' (Jeremiah) is a recognized title in this narrative.
word_study.significance: Ha-navi appears repeatedly in chapter 37 (verses 2, 3, 4, 6) and establishes Jeremiah's formal status. Despite his unpopularity, Jeremiah is acknowledged as 'the prophet'—the authorized spokesman for God. This title gives his word its binding authority, even when people refuse to obey.

word_study.meaning: An infinitive form meaning 'to say.' In prophetic formula, le'mor introduces the direct speech that follows—the actual content of the divine message. It is rendered as a colon in modern translations.
word_study.significance: Le'mor signals that what follows in verses 7-10 (in the full chapter) is the verbatim or near-verbatim content of God's word to Jeremiah. The divine speech is about to be directly quoted or paraphrased.

cross_references.connection: The very opening of the book of Jeremiah: 'The words of Jeremiah... To whom the word of the LORD came in the days of Josiah.' This establishes the fundamental structure of Jeremiah's ministry: he speaks the word of the LORD, not his own words.

A principle of prophecy: 'Surely the Lord GOD will do nothing, but he revealeth his secret unto his servants the prophets. The lion hath roared, who will not fear? the Lord GOD hath spoken, who can but prophesy?' The word of the LORD coming to a prophet compels speech and constrains the prophet to communicate it.

God's promise to Moses: 'I will raise them up a Prophet from among their brethren, like unto thee, and will put my words in his mouth; and he shall speak unto them all that I shall command him. And it shall come to pass, that whosoever will not hearken unto my words which he shall speak in my name, I will require it of him.' Jeremiah 37:6 shows this principle in operation: God puts words in Jeremiah's mouth; Jeremiah must speak them.

Nephi's record: 'And it came to pass that the Spirit of the Lord came upon my father; and he was carried away even unto an exceedingly high mountain.' The Book of Mormon uses similar language for the reception of revelation. The formula 'the word came' or 'the Spirit came' establishes the divine origin of what the prophet is about to communicate.

Modern revelation on prophetic office: 'And whatsoever they shall speak when moved upon by the Holy Ghost shall be scripture, shall be the will of the Lord, shall be the mind of the Lord, shall be the word of the Lord, shall be the voice of the Lord, and the power of God unto salvation.' Jeremiah 37:6, by the formula it uses, establishes that what follows from Jeremiah's mouth is 'the will of the Lord' and 'the voice of the Lord.'

commentary.historical_context: The prophetic reception formula "vayehi debar-YHWH el..." appears extensively in the prophetic books of the Old Testament (Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Hosea, Joel, etc.) and reflects the understood mechanism of prophetic inspiration in ancient Israel. The formula itself does not provide narrative detail about *how* the prophet received the word (through vision, audible voice, internal impression, etc.); it simply asserts that the word came—that is, was received and now must be communicated. In Jeremiah's case, he experiences both visions and auditions, and references both types of revelation. What matters here is that the formula asserts the divine origin of the message. In the ancient Near Eastern context, both Egyptian and Mesopotamian sources contain similar formulas asserting that kings and rulers received divine communication. The biblical formula serves a similar function: to claim authentic divine authorization for the prophet's speech. In the specific historical moment of verse 6, with the Chaldeans withdrawing and the city in a mood of false hope, the word of the LORD coming to Jeremiah represents God's correction of the false interpretation of events that is about to dominate Jerusalem's thinking.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon contains multiple parallels to this reception formula. Alma 5:46 records: 'And it came to pass that he said unto me: If thou desirest a further witness, cast thy mind upon the night that thou didst hear me.' 2 Nephi 32:3 states: 'Angels speak by the power of the Holy Ghost; wherefore, they speak the words of Christ.' The principle that authentic divine speech comes to prophets through the Holy Ghost is consistent in both the Old Testament and the Book of Mormon.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 21:4-6 describes the role of the president of the Church (parallel to the prophet Jeremiah's role): 'Wherefore, meaning the church, thou shalt give him power and authority over the interpreting of the scriptures... And he shall be ordained of me and set apart to hold the keys of this ministry... And he shall keep all the commandments and statutes of the church of Christ.' The formula in Jeremiah 37:6 establishes Jeremiah as the authorized voice through which God directs His people—the same function described in D&C 21 for the modern prophet.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The word of the LORD coming to the prophet is the mechanism by which God maintains His covenant with His people. The prophet serves as the mediatorial voice maintaining the temple covenant relationship. When Jeremiah receives the word of the LORD (verse 6) and communicates it to Zedekiah (verses 7-10), he is functioning as a temple mediator, calling the king back to covenant obedience.

commentary.christological_typology: Jeremiah receiving the word of the LORD is a type of Christ, the ultimate Word of God. John 1:1 identifies Christ as 'the Word' (Logos) who was 'with God, and the Word was God.' Where Jeremiah receives the word of the LORD and must communicate it, Christ *is* the Word—God's complete and final communication to humanity. Jeremiah is the voice crying in the wilderness; Christ is the Word made flesh. The formula in verse 6 prefigures the Incarnation: God's will and intention finding expression through a human instrument.
commentary.application: For modern Latter-day Saints, this verse raises the question of prophetic voice and testimony. When we sustain prophets and apostles, we are asserting our belief that 'the word of the LORD' comes to them, just as it came to Jeremiah. The question is: Do we allow that word to shape our lives, even when it contradicts the conventional wisdom of our time? Verse 6 is simple, understated—just the formula that the word came. Yet it is also the foundation of everything that follows. If we truly believe that God speaks through His prophets, then when their word comes to us, we must receive it as Jeremiah's contemporaries should have: with reverence, attention, and the willingness to change our course. The verse invites reflection: Are we truly listening for the word of the LORD, or are we listening only for those prophetic words that align with what we already think? True prophetic faith means openness to correction, just as Jeremiah's contemporaries should have been open to his correction in this moment.

text_kjv: Thus saith the LORD, the God of Israel; Thus shall ye say to the king of Judah, that sent you unto me to enquire of me; Behold, Pharaoh's army, which is come forth to help you, shall return to Egypt into their own land.

commentary.narrative:
Jeremiah's response to Zedekiah's desperate plea arrives with crushing finality. The king has sent a delegation to consult the prophet, apparently hoping for a word of encouragement. Instead, God delivers a message that systematically dismantles Judah's political calculation. The Egyptians have indeed mobilized — Pharaoh's army is marching toward Jerusalem to relieve the siege. By all human reckoning, this should reverse the military situation. But Jeremiah announces what seems politically impossible: Egypt will retreat to its own land, and the Chaldeans will return to finish their conquest.

The structure of the message is significant. God addresses the delegation directly rather than the king — the answer must pass through the same mediators who brought the question. This emphasizes that the word comes through the prophet, not through back-channel hope or wishful thinking. Zedekiah's act of sending emissaries to 'enquire' of the LORD (Hebrew lidrosheni, 'to seek a prophetic oracle') represents a formal appeal to divine guidance. But the guidance offered contradicts his political hopes entirely.

This verse captures a recurring Jeremianic theme: God's sovereignty over human political arrangements. Egypt's military intervention is not irrelevant to the outcome — it will indeed cause a temporary Chaldean withdrawal. But it changes nothing about Jerusalem's ultimate fate. The prophet's role is to see what political actors cannot: that divine decree transcends military strategy.

word_study.meaning: To seek, to inquire, to consult; specifically, to seek a prophetic oracle or divine guidance through established means. The root carries the sense of searching out or investigating earnestly.
word_study.significance: This verb establishes the formal prophetic context. Zedekiah is not making a casual request but performing a ritualized act of seeking divine oracle. God answers that request, but not with the answer the king wanted. In Latter-day Saint understanding, this reflects the principle that God answers prayers according to His will, not according to human preference.

word_study.meaning: To turn back, to return, to come back. Often used for military withdrawal or repentance. The Covenant Rendering emphasizes the finality: Egypt's army will return to Egypt — the retreat is not temporary pause but decisive withdrawal.
word_study.significance: The verb appears twice in this oracle (verse 7 and verse 8), creating a frame: Pharaoh's army returns home, then the Chaldeans return to finish the siege. This creates theological inevitability — both retreats and returns are part of God's decreed sequence.

word_study.meaning: Pharaoh's force, military power, or army. Chayil denotes military strength or manpower; Paroh is the Egyptian ruler. The phrase appears multiple times in this passage, emphasizing the external military intervention that offers false hope.
word_study.significance: For Judah in 588 BCE, Egypt represents the only potential superpower ally against Babylon. But God reveals that this alliance is ephemeral and strategically insignificant against the decree of destruction.

cross_references.connection: Describes the actual withdrawal of the Chaldean army when news of Pharaoh's approach reaches them — the event Jeremiah now predicts will be reversed.
Records the actual return and siege of Jerusalem by Nebuchadnezzar's army, confirming Jeremiah's prediction.
Isaiah's contemporary oracle against trusting in Egypt and horses rather than the Lord — shares Jeremiah's theme of the futility of political alliances against God's decree.
Modern revelation distinguishing between God's decrees (immutable) and human calculations (mutable) — echoes Jeremiah's prophetic principle that divine will supersedes political strategy.

commentary.historical_context: In 588 BCE, Jerusalem faced siege by Nebuchadnezzar's Chaldean forces. Egypt, under Pharaoh Hophra (also called Apries), mobilized military forces to relieve the siege. This Egyptian intervention did indeed cause a temporary Chaldean withdrawal (verse 5). However, the Chaldeans soon returned and completed the siege. Jeremiah's oracle accurately predicted this sequence. From a military standpoint, the Egyptians could not compete with Babylonian military power at this stage. Babylon had become the dominant imperial force in the ancient Near East, and Judah's hope that Egypt could reverse the military balance was politically unrealistic. Jeremiah's role was to articulate what political observers might have seen but did not wish to acknowledge: the military equation was already decided.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Nephi's prophecies in 1 Nephi 19:10 similarly use specific historical predictions to validate the prophet's authority — God reveals what will happen so that when it comes to pass, believers will trust His word. Jeremiah's prediction about Egypt's retreat and the Chaldeans' return serves this same function.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 1:37-38 establishes that God's word does not return void — what He speaks comes to pass. Jeremiah's oracle functions as a test case of this principle.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: Jeremiah speaks from within the siege — the temple still stands but is under threat. His role as prophet is to testify that physical structures and human political arrangements cannot supersede divine decree. This prefigures how the Restoration emphasizes the covenant over the building.

commentary.christological_typology: Jeremiah stands as a type of a prophet rejected by his political superiors. Zedekiah appeals to him not out of faith but desperation. Christ similarly was sought by Pilate not for genuine spiritual direction but for political legitimacy. In both cases, the prophet/Messiah offers truth that contradicts the seeker's desires, and the seeker ultimately rejects the message.
commentary.application: This verse teaches that genuine seeking of God's will requires willingness to accept answers that contradict our preferences. Zedekiah consulted Jeremiah hoping for reassurance; instead, he received warning. Modern covenant members face similar tests: when we 'enquire' of the Lord through prayer and revelation, are we prepared to accept direction that undermines our political or personal calculations? The verse challenges us to seek God's will for its own sake, not instrumentally to validate plans already decided.

text_kjv: And the Chaldeans shall come again, and fight against this city, and take it, and burn it with fire.

commentary.narrative:
Verse 8 intensifies the prophetic word by detailing the inevitable sequence that will follow Egypt's retreat. The three verbs — return, fight, capture, burn — create a compressed military narrative that admits no deviation. In Hebrew, the rapidity of these actions (all in relatively short form) heightens the sense of inexorability. The prophet is not merely predicting a military defeat but describing an act of divine judgment that will unfold through military means.

The specificity of 'burn it with fire' carries profound theological weight. This is not merely destructive violence; it is the execution of a divine sentence. Fire in biblical imagery often represents purification through judgment, or divine wrath. That Jerusalem itself — the city where the temple stood, the seat of Davidic kingship — will be burned suggests a radical recalibration of Israel's place in God's plan. The nation that had received covenant promises through David now faces covenant judgment through conquest and destruction.

The phrase 'this city' appears three times in verses 8-10, with increasing emphasis on the finality of the decree. Each repetition narrows focus: from the armies and general warfare, to the city itself, to the act of burning specifically. By verse 10, even a hypothetically wounded enemy would still accomplish this burning. The city's destruction is not contingent on military circumstances but on the firm decree of God.

word_study.meaning: To turn back, to return. This verb also carries connotations of returning to a previous state or resuming a previous action. Here: the Chaldeans will return to the siege.
word_study.significance: The repetition of this verb (shab) from verse 7 creates structural unity — first Egypt returns, then the Chaldeans return, establishing the sequence of events that will prove Jeremiah's prophetic accuracy.

word_study.meaning: To wage war, to engage in battle, to fight against. A Niphal form suggesting the action is engaged or undertaken against an object.
word_study.significance: The verb emphasizes active, sustained conflict — not a single skirmish but the full weight of military assault against the fortified city.

word_study.meaning: To capture, to seize, to take possession. Often used for military conquest, particularly the taking of fortified cities.
word_study.significance: This verb appears frequently in descriptions of Babylon's military campaigns. The city's capture is presented as inevitable consequence of the siege.

word_study.meaning: To burn, to incinerate, to consume with fire. The verb carries the sense of total destruction. The Covenant Rendering notes that this verb foreshadows 52:13, where the actual burning of the temple and city is recorded.
word_study.significance: Fire in biblical judgment language represents both purification and destruction. That Jerusalem will be burned signals the thoroughness of its judgment — not merely conquered, but consumed. This prefigures the later burning of the Second Temple in 70 CE and resonates with Latter-day Saint understanding of God's judgments working through historical processes.

cross_references.connection: The historical fulfillment of this prophecy — Nebuzaradan burns the house of the Lord and all the houses of Jerusalem, bringing to pass what Jeremiah predicted.
Parallel historical account of the burning of Jerusalem and the temple by the Chaldeans, confirming the fulfillment of Jeremiah's oracle.
Lamentations, written after the destruction, reflects on how 'the Lord hath swallowed up all the habitations of Jacob' — Jeremiah's prediction now lamented as accomplished fact.
The Lord declares that His judgments are sure and will come to pass — echoes the inevitable unfolding of Jeremiah's prophecy.

commentary.historical_context: The burning of Jerusalem in 586 BCE was a catastrophic event in ancient Near Eastern history. Assyrian and Babylonian military practice typically involved the burning of rebel cities as demonstration of power and as punishment. Babylon, under Nebuchadnezzar II, conducted systematic destruction campaigns against cities that resisted. Archaeological evidence from Jerusalem shows evidence of intense burning in the 6th century BCE, consistent with this account. The Chaldean (Babylonian) military machine was the dominant force in the Levant at this time, and Jerusalem's resistance was ultimately futile. Jeremiah's prophecy, however, frames this military outcome as divine judgment rather than mere geopolitical inevitability.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Mormon's prophecies about the destruction of the Nephite civilization (Ether 9:26, Mormon 8:37) use similar language of burning and destruction as consequences of rejecting prophetic counsel. The Book of Mormon repeatedly illustrates that military might cannot resist God's judgment when righteousness is absent.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 97:26-27 speaks of fire as an instrument of God's judgment, coming upon the wicked. Jeremiah's image of burning aligns with this later revelation about the nature of divine judgment.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The burning of the temple in 586 BCE raised profound questions about God's covenant promises to David and about the security of the temple itself. Later, in Restoration history, the burning of temples and temples threatened paralleled this experience (Nauvoo Temple), reminding the Saints that buildings are not permanent — the covenant is. Joseph Smith taught that the place of the temple could change, and in 1832 a revelation in D&C 97:15-16 indicates that even the temple would face trials.

commentary.christological_typology: The destruction of Jerusalem and its temple by fire parallels the trial of the Son of Man through fire (the Passion). Yet Christ's burning is redemptive — it accomplishes salvation. Jerusalem's burning accomplishes judgment. Both involve fire as a refining or purifying force, but with different outcomes based on righteousness and the nature of the covenant.
commentary.application: This verse confronts modern readers with the reality that God's judgments work through history and are not averted by political alliance or military might. For Latter-day Saints, it teaches that prophetic warnings are meant to be heeded before judgment falls, not consulted after consequences arrive. It also invites reflection on how our own spiritual 'cities' (habits, practices, compromises) may be subject to God's fire if we do not repent. The inevitability of the three verbs — return, fight, capture, burn — suggests that once judgment is decreed, it unfolds inexorably. The time to change course is before the decree, not after.

text_kjv: Thus saith the LORD; Deceive not yourselves, saying, The Chaldeans shall surely depart from us: for they shall not depart.

commentary.narrative:
Verse 9 directly addresses the self-deception that grips Jerusalem at this moment. The people, seeing Pharaoh's army approach and the Chaldean siege temporarily lifted, have convinced themselves that the crisis has passed. 'The Chaldeans shall surely depart from us' — this is the false confidence Jeremiah targets. The people misinterpret the tactical withdrawal caused by Egypt's mobilization as a permanent retreat. They have allowed military success (however temporary) to override prophetic warning.

The verb translated 'deceive' (Hebrew tashshi'u, from nasa, 'to lift up') literally means 'do not lift up your souls' or 'do not raise your hearts/hopes.' It describes the act of creating false hope, of self-deception. The Covenant Rendering captures this well: 'Do not deceive yourselves by thinking...' The people are not merely victims of Egyptian propaganda or military miscalculation; they are actively deceiving themselves. They choose to believe what they want rather than what the prophet announces.

The counter-assertion is absolute: 'They shall not depart.' This is stated twice in the verse — first as the false belief the people harbor ('surely depart'), then as the divine contradiction ('shall not depart'). The repetition emphasizes the finality of God's word against the people's wishful thinking. Jeremiah's message amounts to a call to reality: stop believing comfortable lies and acknowledge the truth of what is coming.

word_study.meaning: Literally, 'do not lift up your souls.' The idiom nasa nephesh means to raise hopes, to entertain false expectations, to delude oneself. The plural 'yourselves' indicates the warning addresses the entire delegation or the entire people.
word_study.significance: This phrase identifies the spiritual/psychological mechanism of the people's error. They are not merely mistaken; they are actively self-deceiving. In Latter-day Saint terms, this echoes the warning against becoming 'past feeling' (1 Nephi 17:45) — a state where one chooses false comfort over truth.

word_study.meaning: To say, to speak, to utter. Here introduces the reported speech — the thoughts/words of the self-deceived people.
word_study.significance: This grammatical device lets the people's own reasoning condemn them. God reports what they are saying to themselves, showing that the error originates in their own wishful thinking, not in external propaganda.

word_study.meaning: The construction halokh + future verb is Hebrew's infinitive absolute construction, expressing certainty, inevitability, or emphasis. Literally: 'going they will go' or 'they will certainly/absolutely go.' Here, the people's expression of confident expectation.
word_study.significance: The same grammatical form that expresses God's certainty in verse 7 ('surely shall ye say') is now used to express human false certainty. This creates irony: the people use the language of divine inevitability to express their false hope, not realizing that only God's word carries true inevitability.

word_study.meaning: They shall not go, they will not depart. The simple negation contradicts the people's expectation.
word_study.significance: God's final word on the matter is stated with stark simplicity — not with the infinitive absolute construction (which would be redundant after the people's false claim), but with clear negation. The people's speculation ends here.

cross_references.connection: Describes the actual Chaldean withdrawal when they heard of Pharaoh's army — the event the people have misinterpreted as permanent.
Jeremiah elsewhere prophesies against false prophets who tell people 'Ye shall have peace' — this verse continues that theme of people preferring comforting lies to prophetic truth.
Book of Mormon warning that the devil 'pacifieth, and telleth them there is no hell' — describes the same mechanism of self-deception Jeremiah confronts.

The Lord warns that spirits at variance with God will not be sent to faithful saints, and that self-deception about spiritual matters has consequences — echoes Jeremiah's warning about deceiving oneself.

commentary.historical_context: The military situation in 588 BCE was genuinely ambiguous to observers without prophetic insight. The Chaldean withdrawal was a fact — visible to all, potentially encouraging to the hopeful. Pharaoh's army had indeed mobilized and was approaching Jerusalem. From a purely military analysis, one might reasonably expect that the Chaldeans would negotiate a withdrawal rather than fight a two-front war (with Pharaoh's forces and Jerusalem simultaneously). But Jeremiah's prophetic claim is that this military analysis, however reasonable, does not account for divine decree. The Babylonian empire under Nebuchadnezzar was on a trajectory of regional dominance, and Jerusalem's resistance was ultimately futile. Yet the people, clinging to the tactical withdrawal, convinced themselves that the crisis had passed.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 34:41 warns against procrastination of repentance, using the metaphor of waiting until death. The Nephites similarly deceived themselves about military security and divine judgment — thinking that fortifications and temporary victories meant safety (Jacob 2:28-30). Moroni's letters to Pahoran (Alma 59-60) show frustration with leadership that chose comfortable illusions over prophetic warnings about military realities.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 63:16 warns 'They who believe in me and are baptized, the same shall be saved.' The inverse — those who will not believe are not saved — applies to Jeremiah's audience. Their self-deception prevents them from receiving the truth that could lead to survival.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple was viewed by many Jerusalemites as a guarantee of safety (Jeremiah 7:4 addresses this explicitly). Verse 9 challenges the assumption that physical structures or military alliances can substitute for covenantal righteousness.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ's warnings to Jerusalem about its coming destruction (Matthew 24, Luke 21) parallel Jeremiah's warnings — both prophets call people to face reality and repent before judgment falls. Both are rejected by those who prefer false comfort. Both experience sorrow that their people refuse to gather (Matthew 23:37, Jeremiah 13:17).
commentary.application: This verse penetrates the psychology of denial. When external circumstances seem to support our preferred outcomes, we are tempted to dismiss prophetic warnings as alarmism. Jeremiah challenges the people — and challenges us — to distinguish between what we wish to believe and what God has declared to be true. For modern Latter-day Saints, this raises questions about self-deception in our own time: Do we choose comfort over truth? Do we interpret temporary reversals as permanent victories? Do we silence prophetic counsel that contradicts our political or social preferences? The verse invites deep honesty about where we are deceiving ourselves, individually or collectively.

text_kjv: For though ye had smitten the whole army of the Chaldeans that fight against you, and there remained but wounded men among them, yet should they rise up every man in his tent, and burn this city with fire.

commentary.narrative:
Verse 10 contains one of the most startling hyperbolic statements in the prophetic literature. It expresses the absolute irresistibility of God's decree through an extreme hypothetical: even if Judah defeated the entire Chaldean army and left nothing but wounded men in their tents, those wounded men would still rise up and burn Jerusalem. This is not rational military prediction; it is theological assertion in hyperbolic form.

The verse functions as an anti-military argument. It is not merely saying 'Jerusalem will fall.' It is saying that no amount of human military victory can prevent what God has decreed. The hypothesis — winning a complete victory against the Chaldeans — is militarily absurd. Judah has no such capacity. Yet even in this absurd scenario, the outcome remains fixed. The wounded — those barely clinging to life, pierced through with weapons (Hebrew meduqqarim) — would still accomplish God's judgment.

This hyperbolic form is meant to penetrate the people's confidence in their military capacity and their reliance on Egypt. It is Jeremiah's most forceful way of saying: your calculations about military outcomes are irrelevant. God has determined this city will burn. The question is not whether, but how the people will respond — will they flee, will they surrender, will they choose the path that preserves lives? The decree cannot be changed, but the manner of its unfolding can be influenced by human choice.

word_study.meaning: A conditional form (if/though) with the past tense, expressing a counterfactual condition. 'If you had struck/smitten.' This sets up the hypothetical scenario that will be contradicted.
word_study.significance: The conditional form is crucial — it establishes that this is not a prediction of military outcome but a theological statement about what God's decree means. The military scenario is hypothetical; the divine outcome is actual.

word_study.meaning: The entire Chaldean military force or military might. Chayil can mean both army and strength/power. Kasdim is the Hebrew term for Chaldeans/Babylonians.
word_study.significance: The word 'whole' emphasizes totality — not just defeating one legion or detachment, but defeating the entire Babylonian force arrayed against Jerusalem.

word_study.meaning: Men who are pierced through, stabbed, mortally wounded. Meduqqarim is from the root daqar, meaning to pierce or stab. These are not merely injured but essentially annihilated — men run through with swords, barely alive.
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering emphasizes this: 'only wounded men remained among them, each lying in his tent.' These are the most helpless imaginable combatants — yet even they would execute God's judgment. The point is not military but theological: God's decree needs no mighty army to accomplish it.

word_study.meaning: To rise, to stand up, to get up. Often used of getting up from lying down or from death itself. Here: even from a state of mortal wounding, they would rise.
word_study.significance: The verb suggests an impossible action — wounded men rising from their tents to accomplish a military objective. This underscores the hyperbolic, almost miraculous nature of what Jeremiah is claiming: the Chaldeans will accomplish this not through normal military power but through the force of God's decree.

word_study.term_original: sarafu et hair hazot ba-esh (שרפו את העיר הזאת באש)
word_study.meaning: They will burn this city with fire. The same verb and object as in verse 8, now in the context of this hypothetical. The prepositional phrase 'with fire' emphasizes the totality of the destruction.
word_study.significance: The repetition of this phrase from verse 8 creates a closure — whether through normal military conquest or through miraculous divine enforcement, the city will burn. The outcome is fixed; only the means remains variable.

cross_references.connection: Jeremiah's call narrative promises him that God will make him 'a defenced city' while he himself will face opposition — illustrating the same principle that human protection comes from God, not from military might.
Jehoshaphat's experience where God tells Judah 'the battle is not yours, but God's' — expressing the same principle that divine decree supersedes military calculation.
The psalmist declares that 'no king is saved by the multitude of an host' but by trust in the Lord — captures the same theological claim about the futility of military reliance.
The temple is consecrated by God's word; no human power can ultimately prevail against God's house — parallels Jeremiah's claim about the fixedness of God's decree.

commentary.historical_context: This verse reflects the reality that by 588 BCE, Babylon was militarily supreme in the ancient Near East. Even Judah's best military scenario — a decisive victory over the Chaldean army — would merely delay the inevitable Babylonian response. Nebuchadnezzar had resources to field multiple armies and would not abandon the siege of Jerusalem. The verse also reflects the cultural context of ancient prophecy: hyperbolic forms were understood as ways of expressing absolute certainty about what God had decreed. The point was theological and rhetorical, not a literal military prediction of what would happen if exactly the hypothetical scenario came to pass.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Lehi's prophecy to his sons (1 Nephi 2:20-22) establishes the Restoration principle: 'if ye keep the commandments of the Lord, ye shall prosper in the land; but if ye keep not the commandments of the Lord, ye shall be cut off from his presence.' Like Jeremiah, Lehi announces a fixed outcome conditional on obedience or disobedience, though the specific historical path may vary.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 136:36 teaches that those who break covenants place themselves under condemnation 'that they cannot be sanctified by the law of consecration.' Similarly, Jeremiah announces that Jerusalem's breach of covenant puts it under judgment that no military action can reverse.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple in Jerusalem was believed by many to be inviolable (Jeremiah 7:4, 'The temple of the Lord, the temple of the Lord'). Verse 10 challenges this belief — no sacred place is exempt from judgment if covenant is broken. This connects to Latter-day Saint understanding that temples must be defended and sustained through righteousness, not merely by their existence.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ's statement in Matthew 24:34-35 ('This generation shall not pass till all these things be fulfilled... but my words shall not pass away') parallels Jeremiah's hyperbolic assertion that God's word will accomplish what He has spoken, regardless of human capacity to prevent it. Both prophets announce decrees that will come to pass.
commentary.application: Verse 10 invites Latter-day Saints to examine what we trust in for protection and security. Do we rely on military might, political alliance, economic power, or physical fortifications? Or do we recognize that genuine security comes only through covenantal relationship with God? The hyperbolic form invites us to consider scenarios where everything in which we trust fails — and asks whether our faith in God remains. For individuals, the verse might prompt: What would happen if my job, my family security, my health, my status all collapsed? Would I still trust God's purposes? The verse calls us to a faith that is not contingent on favorable external circumstances.

text_kjv: And it came to pass, that when the army of the Chaldeans was broken up from Jerusalem for fear of Pharaoh's army,

commentary.narrative:
Verse 11 marks a narrative turn. The temporal clause sets the stage for Jeremiah's arrest by introducing the specific moment when the Chaldean army withdrew from Jerusalem due to the approach of Pharaoh's forces. This verse is not merely informational; it is the historical context for the events that follow. After delivering the oracle that contradicts the people's hopeful expectations, we now see the apparent confirmation of their false hope: the Chaldeans have indeed withdrawn.

The verb 'was broken up' (Hebrew he'alot, 'went up' or 'withdrew') is the same term used in verse 5, creating narrative cohesion. The people, upon seeing this withdrawal, would have felt vindicated in their self-deception. 'See? Jeremiah was wrong. The Chaldeans are leaving. Our faith in Pharaoh was justified.' The dramatic irony is that they are witnessing exactly what Jeremiah predicted in verse 7 — not a permanent Egyptian salvation, but a temporary respite before the Chaldeans' inevitable return.

For Jeremiah, this moment creates a specific vulnerability. With the immediate threat lifted, tensions in Jerusalem ease. The desperation that led to consulting the prophet diminishes. And at precisely this moment, as the oracle's credibility seems undermined by events, Jeremiah leaves the city. The timing is crucial: he departs during the period of false security, when his prophetic warnings seem irrelevant.

word_study.meaning: And it came to pass, and it happened. This is the standard narrative connector in Hebrew biblical prose, marking transitions and introducing new scenes.
word_study.significance: The phrase signals that we are moving from divine oracle to historical narration. The prophecy has been delivered; now we see it begin to unfold.

word_study.meaning: The Chaldean military force. This is the same phrase used throughout the chapter to refer to Nebuchadnezzar's besieging army.
word_study.significance: The specific reference to the military force (rather than the people or nation of Chaldet generally) emphasizes that the withdrawal is military/tactical, not political or permanent.

word_study.meaning: Went up from, withdrew from, lifted up from. The verb alah can mean to go up geographically or to withdraw/lift (as in lifting a siege). Here: the army withdrew from Jerusalem.
word_study.significance: This is the Niphal passive form — the army is described as withdrawing rather than being actively commanded to withdraw by Nebuchadnezzar. The focus is on the observable fact: the siege has been lifted.

word_study.meaning: From before the face of, from the presence of, because of, for fear of. Literally 'from before the face of.'' This preposition indicates cause: the reason for the withdrawal.
word_study.significance: The phrase clarifies that the withdrawal was tactical — caused by the news or presence of Pharaoh's army. It was not a choice to abandon the siege but a response to external military pressure.

cross_references.connection: The parallel account that introduces this same withdrawal — provides the initial context that verse 11 now references.
Jeremiah's prediction that 'Pharaoh's army...shall return to Egypt into their own land' — verse 11 begins to narrate the fulfillment of this prediction.
Historical record of Jerusalem's siege by Babylon — provides external historical context for understanding the military situation in 588 BCE.

Joseph Smith's experience in Liberty Jail, asking God why tribulation continued despite faith — shares the theme of apparent relief from persecution (the Chaldean withdrawal) being temporary, with deeper trials ahead.

commentary.historical_context: The withdrawal of the Chaldean army in 588 BCE is historically attested in both biblical and extra-biblical sources. Pharaoh Hophra (Apries) did indeed send military forces northward in response to Babylon's siege of Judah.
