The fact that it is mentioned only in Jeremiah underscores the historical memory preserved in this text. During normal times, the Bakers' Street would have been a bustling commercial area. During the siege, it represented the shrinking supply of bread available to the city.

word_study.term_english: until all the bread in the city were spent (ad-tom kol-ha-lechem min-ha-ir)
word_study.meaning: A conditional phrase: 'until the completion/exhaustion of all the bread from the city.' Tom (from tamam) means 'to be complete, to be finished, to be consumed.' The preposition min (from) indicates source — bread coming from the city's reserves.
word_study.significance: This phrase is historically significant because it records the progression of famine in Jerusalem. Initially bread was available (Jeremiah received his daily ration). Eventually, the supply was exhausted, leading to the catastrophic hunger described in Lamentations and the final historical records (2 Kings 25:3). The text is tracking not just Jeremiah's imprisonment but the city's slow starvation.

cross_references.connection: A fuller narrative of Jeremiah's imprisonment in the court of the guard, where the Lord also appears to him with a message of hope — the court of the guard becomes not just a place of captivity but of revelation.

Later, Jeremiah is cast into a miry dungeon by other officials but rescued by Ebed-melech, an Ethiopian eunuch; he is then returned to the court of the guard, showing that this courtyard became his place of relative safety.

The famine in Jerusalem reaches its peak after the final siege, with children starving and mothers unable to feed their young — the 'until all the bread in the city were spent' of verse 21 finds its tragic fulfillment in these laments.

The historical parallel account recording that the siege lasted two years and that 'the famine prevailed in the city' — providing independent confirmation of the siege conditions reflected in Jeremiah.

While still imprisoned in the court of the guard, Jeremiah receives the divine word announcing restoration and hope — showing that the court of the guard, though a place of imprisonment, was also a place where God continued to speak to His prophet.

commentary.historical_context: The siege of Jerusalem in 588-586 BCE was a prolonged military campaign by Nebuchadnezzar's forces. Ancient Near Eastern siege warfare typically involved surrounding a city, cutting off supply lines, and waiting for the population to exhaust its reserves or surrender. Jerusalem had significant grain storage capacity (2 Kings 20:6 records Hezekiah's storage), but a two-year siege would deplete even substantial reserves. The mention of 'Bakers' Street' as a source of bread rations reflects the reality that even during siege, some food production or distribution continued — the bakeries may have been operating on rationed flour. The 'court of the guard' within the palace would have been a protected space, with priority access to the king's remaining supplies. Jeremiah's transfer there was a form of privilege within imprisonment — better conditions than those available to ordinary citizens starving outside the palace walls. The detail about bread 'until all the bread in the city were spent' foreshadows the final phase of the siege when even the palace's supplies were exhausted (2 Kings 25:3), at which point Zedekiah fled the city in desperation.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In Alma 36:27-29, Alma describes his anguish when imprisoned in Ammonihah, bound with cords and unable to speak the word of God. Like Jeremiah, Alma was imprisoned by those opposed to his message. However, Alma was delivered by divine power in a single night. Jeremiah was not similarly delivered but instead endured long imprisonment and witnessed the fulfillment of his prophecies. Both texts show that the righteous may face extended confinement, yet God preserves them for His purposes. The Book of Mormon emphasizes miraculous deliverance; Jeremiah emphasizes faithful endurance and God's providential protection through natural means (the king's decision to move him).
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 121:7-9 records Joseph Smith's prayer from Liberty Jail, appealing to God during his unjust imprisonment: 'My son, peace be unto thy soul; thine adversity and thine afflictions shall be but a small moment; And then, if thou endure it well, God shall exalt thee on high.' The principle is clear: imprisonment and affliction are temporary, and those who endure faithfully are exalted. Zedekiah's decision to improve Jeremiah's conditions through a human mechanism (transfer to the court of the guard) echoes the principle that God can work through earthly authorities to preserve His servants.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The court of the guard, though a military space, became a place where Jeremiah received temple-like revelation from God (see 32:2-3, 33:1). This foreshadows New Testament understanding that God's presence is not confined to a physical building but dwells where His covenant people are faithful. Though separated from the temple, Jeremiah continued to receive God's word in the courtyard. This principle extends into latter-day understanding: the Lord's communication with His prophets is not dependent on location but on covenant faithfulness.

commentary.christological_typology: Jeremiah's imprisonment in the court of the guard, where he remains alive but confined, prefigures aspects of Christ's passion. Jesus was also imprisoned (John 18:3-24), also experienced both cruelty and surprising kindness (Simon of Cyrene, the centurion who acknowledged His innocence), and also endured to the point of death. Both Jeremiah and Jesus spoke truth that challenged the authorities, were arrested despite their innocence, and faced the real possibility of death. Yet both trusted that God's purposes would be fulfilled through their faithful witness. Jeremiah's survival through the siege (he was eventually liberated when the city fell) parallels Christ's resurrection — vindication beyond the point of apparent defeat.
commentary.application: Verse 21 presents a nuanced view of how God's purposes advance even through imperfect human decisions. Zedekiah did not act from pure motives; he was seeking to ease his conscience and maintain a degree of political flexibility. Yet his command to transfer Jeremiah had divine significance — it preserved the prophet's life. For modern believers, this teaches that God can work through and even around human weakness. We do not need perfect circumstances or perfect people to carry out God's will. Jeremiah accepted the court of the guard as his place of confinement and there received revelation (32:2-3, 33:1). He did not demand immediate freedom or complete vindication. He accepted the partial mercy offered by Zedekiah and continued his prophetic work within those constraints. We too may face situations where we do not receive everything we ask for but receive something — a partial answer, a compromise solution, a way through difficulty rather than around it. The application is to accept God's providential care through imperfect means, to remain faithful even in constrained circumstances, and to trust that God's plans will be fulfilled. The narrative of verse 21 also demonstrates that political powers, even when they oppose God's prophets, are ultimately instruments in God's hands. Zedekiah's decisions do not frustrate God's purposes but serve them.

text_kjv: Now when Ebedmelech the Ethiopian, one of the eunuchs which was in the king's house, heard that they had put Jeremiah in the dungeon; the king then sitting in the gate of Benjamin;

commentary.narrative: This verse introduces Ebed-Melech (Hebrew: 'servant of the king'), a Cushite court official whose foreign origin and moral courage will transform the tragedy of Jeremiah's imprisonment. While the nobles and princes have already cast the prophet into the cistern to die (37:15; 38:6), this unnamed official hears what has happened. The detail that the king sits at the Benjamin Gate — a public judicial setting — is crucial: it means Zedekiah is accessible and performing his role as judge, yet he has allowed Jeremiah to be thrown into a mud cistern without water or food. Ebed-Melech's knowledge comes through the palace information network, and his conscience compels him to act. The Covenant Rendering clarifies that 'saris' need not mean 'eunuch' in the physical sense but designates a high-ranking court official with real access and authority — essential to his ability to mount a rescue.
commentary.narrative_continued: The placement of this verse at the narrative turning point is theologically significant. In Jeremiah's ministry, he has been rejected by kings, priests, and the people. Yet it is a foreigner — a Cushite from the distant region south of Egypt — who recognizes injustice and acts. This pattern recurs throughout Scripture: foreigners often exhibit greater faith and obedience than the covenant people (the centurion in Matthew 8:10; the widow of Zarephath in 1 Kings 17). The political context matters: Jerusalem is under siege, the city is starving, and Zedekiah is weak, pressured by his nobles who want Jeremiah silenced. Ebed-Melech's intervention occurs within this crucible of famine and fear. His foreign status may even be an advantage—he is not entangled in the internal politics that silenced the king's better impulses.

word_study.meaning: Literally 'servant of the king.' This was not necessarily a name given at birth but a title indicating high rank in the royal administration. In the Restoration, we learn that names often carry prophetic or covenant significance; here, Ebed-Melech's very name declares his loyalty to the crown, yet his actions show he is ultimately loyal to a higher authority—God and His prophet.
word_study.significance: The name frames his entire character: he is the king's servant, yet he serves the king by rescuing God's prophet, demonstrating that true loyalty to earthly rulers lies in honoring God's representatives.

word_study.meaning: An inhabitant of Cush, the region south of Egypt encompassing modern Sudan and parts of Ethiopia. Cushites had a long history in Egypt and the Levant, serving as soldiers, administrators, and traders. The term emphasizes Ebed-Melech's foreign, non-Israelite identity.
word_study.significance: His Cushite origin underscores the irony and challenge of the narrative: a foreigner shows the moral courage that Judah's own leaders lack. This foreshadows how the nations will execute God's judgment on Jerusalem, and how God's purposes extend beyond the boundaries of the covenant people.

word_study.meaning: Literally 'the cistern' or 'the pit.' In biblical usage, a bor could be a storage cistern for water, a natural sinkhole, or, in this context, a prison pit. The same term appears in the story of Joseph (Genesis 37:20-24) and Jonah (2:6). Unlike a dungeon with a door and guards, a bor is a deep hole from which escape is nearly impossible.
word_study.significance: The use of bor rather than a more conventional prison intensifies the horror: Jeremiah is entombed, effectively, in a place designed for storage. This deepens the typological foreshadowing of resurrection—entombment in a pit that appears to be a tomb.

word_study.meaning: One of the major gates of Jerusalem, on the northern side of the city, leading toward the tribal territory of Benjamin. Gates in ancient cities served as judicial centers where the king heard cases and administered justice.
word_study.significance: That Zedekiah sits 'at the Benjamin Gate' places him in a liminal space—he is the judge and representative of order, yet he has allowed injustice to occur. The gate itself, leading to Benjamin's territory, may carry subtle theological weight in Jeremiah's narrative, as Benjamin's tribe held both Jerusalem and significance in the post-exilic restoration.

cross_references.connection: Joseph is cast into a bor (pit/cistern) by his brothers, and later rescued—a typological pattern of entombment and deliverance that parallels Jeremiah's situation and points to resurrection themes.
Elijah is sustained by a foreign widow (the woman of Zarephath) during famine—like Ebed-Melech, a non-Israelite shows greater faith and compassion than Israel's own people.
Jesus commends the faith of a Roman centurion, noting that he has found greater faith in a foreigner than in Israel—directly paralleling the moral pattern of Ebed-Melech's intervention.
The previous imprisonment and release of Jeremiah from the dungeon in Jonathan's house; this verse marks the second imprisonment in the cistern, a darker crisis requiring rescue.
The speaker cries from the pit and his voice is heard; God draws near in answer—a parallel to Jeremiah's cry from the cistern and his rescue through Ebed-Melech.

commentary.historical_context: Cushites served in various administrative and military roles throughout the ancient Near East. Archaeological evidence and Egyptian records document Cushite soldiers and officials in the Levantine court systems. Ebed-Melech's position as a high-ranking official gave him direct access to the king—he could bypass intermediaries to appeal directly to Zedekiah. The Benjamin Gate was a real topographical and administrative feature of Jerusalem's defensive structure. During the final siege of Jerusalem (588-586 BC), famine conditions were severe; the city's food supplies were cut off, and starvation became a weapon of siege warfare. The detail that 'there is no more bread in the city' (verse 9) reflects this historical reality. Zedekiah's weakness and vacillation are consistent with later historical records and his character as depicted throughout Jeremiah and in 2 Kings 24-25. The presence of foreign officials in the royal administration reflects the cosmopolitan nature of ancient Near Eastern courts, where diplomatic ties and trade partnerships often placed nationals of client kingdoms in service roles.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In the Book of Mormon, Abinadi is martyred by King Noah's court, and later Limhi's people suffer under oppressive rule—yet divine deliverance comes through God's providential raising up of righteous individuals (Alma 17-18). Ebed-Melech's role as an unlikely savior parallels how the Lord raises up unexpected instruments of salvation. The theme of a righteous minority standing against institutional corruption appears throughout the Book of Mormon (Alma 35:13-15; Helaman 13:34-35), where few listen to prophets yet God preserves a remnant.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 121:7-8 addresses those who suffer wrongfully, assuring them that God 'seeth the end from the beginning' and that suffering is not permanent. Jeremiah's entombment in the cistern echoes this—though cast down, he is raised up. Additionally, D&C 58:2-4 teaches that the righteous are blessed even in tribulation, and that those who serve God without complaint receive greater reward—reflecting Ebed-Melech's courageous faithfulness despite personal risk.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The cistern—a pit, a descent into darkness, a place of death—prefigures both the crucifixion and the passage through the veil. The rescue from the cistern mirrors the resurrection and ascension from the grave. In temple ordinance language, the movement from darkness to light, from death to life, reflects the endowment pattern. Ebed-Melech's role as rescuer prefigures the role of Christ, who raises the dead and brings forth life from the grave.

commentary.christological_typology: Jeremiah cast into the cistern and rescued from death foreshadows Christ's entombment and resurrection. The cistern is a tomb—dark, deep, apparently final. Ebed-Melech's rescue prefigures the Father's raising of Christ from the grave. More subtly, Ebed-Melech—whose name means 'servant of the king'—acts as a type of the Holy Spirit or the Father's agent in accomplishing deliverance. The detail of rags and ropes (verse 11-12) prefigures the 'grave clothes' from which Christ is resurrected (John 20:6-7). The ultimate reversal—that a foreigner, not the king or nobles, rescues the prophet—points to how Christ's salvation came not through the established religious order but through one 'despised and rejected of men' (Isaiah 53:3).
commentary.application: Modern covenant members face pressure from institutional forces—cultural, professional, political—that may oppose prophetic truth or righteous principles. Like Zedekiah, we may feel torn between social pressure and conscience. Ebed-Melech's example teaches several principles: (1) Conscience is not bound by rank or nationality; what is right is right, regardless of whether the powerful acknowledge it. (2) Immediate action matters—Ebed-Melech 'went out' without delay, without committee meetings or political calculations. (3) Compassion precedes rescue—he gathers soft rags to protect Jeremiah, showing that saving lives includes alleviating suffering. (4) Foreigners and outsiders may possess greater moral clarity than those embedded in corrupt systems. In our time, standing with prophetic truth may require us to risk social status or professional standing. Ebed-Melech's courage should embolden us to act decisively when we see injustice, regardless of whether powerful institutions support us.

text_kjv: Ebedmelech went forth out of the king's house, and spake to the king, saying,

commentary.narrative: Verse 8 captures the moment of Ebed-Melech's decision to act. The verb 'went forth' (vayyetse) carries connotation of urgency and resolve. He does not summon the king through intermediaries; he leaves the palace compound and goes directly to find Zedekiah at the Benjamin Gate. This is a calculated risk: he is about to interrupt the king at a public judicial setting and raise a matter that contradicts the will of the nobles and princes who have just secured the king's acquiescence to Jeremiah's death sentence. The simple structure of this verse—mere action and intention to speak—emphasizes the directness of Ebed-Melech's approach. He is not performing elaborate courtly ritual; he is moving with purpose. The Covenant Rendering brings this out: 'Ebed-Melech left the royal palace and spoke to the king,' capturing the immediacy without intervening explanations.
commentary.narrative_continued: The shift in geography matters: Ebed-Melech must leave the safety of the palace to reach the king in public. This makes his mission more exposed—anyone could witness his appeal and report it back to the hostile nobles. His willingness to be seen and heard publicly, advocating for the prophet, demonstrates that this is not a private petition delivered with plausible deniability. He is willing to attach his name and reputation to the cause of justice. The fact that he speaks (vaydabber) is foregrounded—he has something to say, a message that will reframe the situation for Zedekiah. In ancient Near Eastern court protocol, such an approach required either extreme confidence in one's standing or extreme moral conviction (or both). Ebed-Melech's subsequent words (verse 9) will bear out that he is motivated by conscience.

word_study.meaning: Third person masculine singular past (consecutive) of yatsa, meaning 'to go out, to exit, to depart.' The consecutive form vav-yetse links this action to the preceding statement ('when Ebed-Melech heard'), indicating a direct causal sequence: upon hearing, he went out.
word_study.significance: The verb choice emphasizes immediacy and resolve. In contrast to Zedekiah's passivity and the nobles' aggressive scheming, Ebed-Melech's going forth represents active moral agency. Throughout Scripture, going forth is often associated with answering a calling or undertaking a mission (Abraham in Genesis 12:4; Moses in Exodus 3:10).

word_study.meaning: Literally 'and he spoke unto the king.' The verb dibber (to speak) in this context implies not mere idle words but purposeful address, often used of prophetic speech or formal communication. The preposition el ('to, unto') indicates direct address.
word_study.significance: Ebed-Melech's speech is not a whisper or indirect suggestion but a formal address to the throne. He is claiming the right and duty to be heard on a matter of justice.

cross_references.connection: Micaiah hears the words of Jeremiah read aloud and immediately goes to the princes to report them; similarly, Ebed-Melech hears of injustice and immediately acts, showing that receptive ears and conscience compel action.
Abigail intercedes with David by going out to meet him and speaking directly to him, bypassing normal protocol; like Ebed-Melech, she risks the king's displeasure to prevent a grave injustice.
Esther approaches the king at a public banquet and speaks directly to intercede for her people; both she and Ebed-Melech risk their position by speaking truth to power in a public setting.

Alma encounters opposition in Ammonihah but is sustained by an angel and commanded to return; like Ebed-Melech's courage, Alma's return represents the willingness to face hostility in pursuit of righteousness.

commentary.historical_context: In ancient Near Eastern court protocol, direct approach to a seated king was typically mediated through officials or formalized through ritual. Ebed-Melech's going forth and speaking directly required either official sanction or considerable courage (or both). The gate setting, where the king sat in judgment, was a public forum where ordinary subjects might petition; however, the matter of a condemned prophet was not routine business. Ebed-Melech's willingness to interrupt judicial proceedings suggests either that he had significant standing or that he deemed the matter sufficiently urgent to override protocol. The social distance between a Cushite foreigner and the king of Judah would normally be substantial; yet Ebed-Melech's title (saris—high official) indicates he had regular access and could address the king. His public approach also means that his advocacy will become known to the nobles, which will later require the king to hide their transaction from public view (see 38:24-28).

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In Alma 8, Alma is driven out of the city but returns to preach repentance despite opposition. In Helaman 13, Samuel the Lamanite stands on the wall and addresses King Jacob directly, despite being a foreigner and not invited. These Book of Mormon prophets and witnesses share Ebed-Melech's willingness to address authority figures directly and publicly, regardless of personal risk.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 1:24 speaks of the Lord's servants being 'persecuted' yet continuing their message; D&C 123:15-17 counsels the Saints to 'call upon the Lord in mighty prayer' and to 'lay this matter before the Lord.' Ebed-Melech's action fulfills this principle—he does not murmur or withdraw but brings the injustice to the attention of the authority who can remedy it.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The approach to the king parallels the approach to the throne of God in the temple—a descent through veils and gates toward the center of authority and judgment. Ebed-Melech's willingness to approach Zedekiah openly and honestly mirrors the covenant of directness before God in the temple.

commentary.christological_typology: Ebed-Melech's going forth to speak truth to power prefigures Christ's public ministry, in which He addresses rulers and authorities directly (John 18:19-24; Mark 14:61-62). Christ's refusal to remain silent before the Sanhedrin and before Pilate parallels Ebed-Melech's refusal to remain silent before Zedekiah. Both act despite knowing their intervention will create powerful enemies.
commentary.application: In our own time, conscience may compel us to speak truth in uncomfortable settings—to leaders, peers, or institutions. Ebed-Melech's example teaches that we need not wait for permission or a 'convenient moment' to raise matters of justice and righteous principle. However, his approach is not reckless; he speaks to the person with actual authority to remedy the situation (the king, not the nobles). Modern application suggests that we should (1) identify who has the authority to act, (2) go directly to that person if necessary, (3) speak with clarity and directness, and (4) be prepared for the consequences of being publicly associated with a righteous cause. Like Ebed-Melech, we may find that our willingness to be seen and heard inspires others and creates accountability.

text_kjv: My lord the king, these men have done evil in all that they have done to Jeremiah the prophet, whom they have cast into the dungeon; and he is like to die for hunger in the place where he is: for there is no more bread in the city.

commentary.narrative: Ebed-Melech's speech is a masterpiece of moral rhetoric. He opens with the formal address 'My lord the king' (Adoni ha-melekh), affirming Zedekiah's status and authority. Then he pivots to a moral judgment: 'these men have done evil' (here'u ha-anashim ha-elleh). He does not report events neutrally; he interprets them morally. The 'men' he condemns are the nobles and princes who convinced the king to surrender Jeremiah. His appeal is structured in layers: (1) moral judgment on the officials' action, (2) identification of the victim as 'Jeremiah the prophet'—restoring his prophetic status after the nobles tried to reduce him to a criminal, (3) description of the place of death (the cistern), and (4) the cause of death (starvation due to city-wide famine). Each layer is meant to move Zedekiah from passive acquiescence to active rescue.
commentary.narrative_continued: The phrase 'he is like to die for hunger' (vayyamet tachtav mi-pnei ha-ra'ab, literally 'he will die beneath him from famine') conveys both the physical reality—Jeremiah is sinking in mud at the bottom of a cistern with no food—and the urgency of action. Ebed-Melech does not ask the king to reverse the nobles' order; he asks the king to prevent a death that is now imminent. This reframes the issue: no longer is this about politics or the nobles' vendetta against the prophet; it is about whether the king will permit a man to starve to death while he sits at the gate of judgment. The final phrase, 'for there is no more bread in the city,' establishes that the starvation is not accidental but systematic—the siege has cut off all supply. The old ration Jeremiah received (37:21) has ceased. Ebed-Melech is saying: the city is starving, and you, my lord, know this. Will you allow your prophet to die of starvation in a pit while you deliberate?

word_study.meaning: Third person masculine plural perfect of ra'a, meaning 'to do evil, to act wickedly, to harm.' The verb carries moral weight—it is not a neutral description but a judgment. The root ra ('evil') appears throughout the Hebrew Bible in contexts of moral transgression.
word_study.significance: By using here'u, Ebed-Melech does not frame the nobles' action as a political decision or a strategic move; he names it as moral evil. This language elevates the appeal above political calculation—he is appealing to the king's moral conscience. In the Covenant Rendering, this is rendered as 'done a terrible thing,' capturing the moral gravity.

word_study.meaning: Literally 'the prophet.' This is Jeremiah's essential identity—not a criminal, not a political enemy, but a navi, one who speaks God's words. The definite article ('the') suggests a recognized status.
word_study.significance: By calling Jeremiah 'the prophet,' Ebed-Melech restores the prophetic title that the nobles had stripped from him through their actions. In Israel's theology, the prophet is God's voice; to imprison a prophet is to oppose God. This language may have resonated with Zedekiah's nominal faith—he may still have believed (however weakly) that prophets were instruments of God.

word_study.meaning: Third person masculine plural perfect of shala, meaning 'to cast, to throw, to hurl.' The verb is violent and aggressive, not a neutral term for imprisonment. It conveys the brutality of Jeremiah's detention.
word_study.significance: The verb choice makes the nobles' action sound less like judicial punishment and more like mob violence. They 'hurled' the prophet into the pit—an act of aggression, not law.

word_study.meaning: A cistern, pit, or deep hole—not a formal prison. The same word used for Joseph's pit in Genesis 37.
word_study.significance: The cistern is not a place of confinement designed for holding prisoners; it is an ad hoc grave. Ebed-Melech's use of this term emphasizes that Jeremiah has been placed in a death-trap, not a prison. This detail heightens urgency.

word_study.term_original: יָמוּת תַּחְתָּיו מִפְּנֵי הָרָעָב (Yamut tachtav mi-pnei ha-ra'ab)
word_study.meaning: Literally 'he will die beneath him/in his place from famine.' The phrase tachtav ('beneath him,' i.e., 'where he is') emphasizes both location and entrapment—he will die in the place where he is stuck, unable to escape. The phrase mi-pnei ha-ra'ab ('because of famine,' literally 'from the face of famine') personifies famine as an advancing force.
word_study.significance: The construction makes death appear imminent and certain. Ebed-Melech is not asking the king to avert a distant possibility; he is warning that death is advancing like an enemy toward a helpless man.

word_study.term_original: אֵין הַלֶּחֶם עוֹד בָּעִיר (Ein ha-lehem od ba-ir)
word_study.meaning: Literally 'there is no more bread yet in the city.' The word lehem (bread) can mean literal bread or, metonymically, food in general. The particle od ('still, yet') emphasizes that the supply has been exhausted—what bread there was is gone.
word_study.significance: This detail establishes the siege conditions and the universal crisis. It is not that Jeremiah alone is being starved; the entire city is starving. But while the nobles and king can still access resources (as shown by their relative comfort), Jeremiah has been denied even the meager ration he previously received. Ebed-Melech is pointing out the injustice: the city starves equally, but only Jeremiah has been sentenced to death by starvation in a pit.

cross_references.connection: In his previous imprisonment, Jeremiah's ration was secured by the king's order; now that ration has ceased due to famine, demonstrating how even the king's mercy can be overridden by circumstances and the hostility of the nobles.
Jeremiah laments the persecution he endures for speaking God's word; Ebed-Melech's defense of him as 'the prophet' affirms the divine nature of his ministry despite the nobles' rejection.
Describes the famine in Jerusalem during the final siege, paralleling the historical context of Jeremiah 38—the 'no more bread in the city' reflects the desperate food shortage of 588-586 BC.
Calls on leaders to 'open thy mouth for the dumb' and 'plead the cause of the poor and needy'; Ebed-Melech embodies this principle by speaking on behalf of the voiceless prophet.
Alma is driven out of the city, yet the Lord tells him to return and preach repentance; similarly, Jeremiah is rejected by the city's leaders, yet God ensures his message and life are preserved.

commentary.historical_context: The famine 'in the city' reflects the historical reality of Jerusalem's final siege (588-586 BC). Archaeological and textual evidence indicates severe food shortage; Lamentations 1:11 and 4:9-10 attest to starvation during this period. The Babylonian siege lasted approximately 18 months, during which Jerusalem's food supplies dwindled. Ebed-Melech's mention of 'no more bread' is not hyperbole but a description of documented conditions. The nobles' control over the king's decisions regarding Jeremiah is historically consistent with the patterns of dynastic conflict in Judah's final years—high officials often wielded power over weak monarchs. Zedekiah's passivity and the nobles' hostility toward the prophet are confirmed in 2 Kings 24:17-25:7 and in historical records of the period. Ebed-Melech's status as a high-ranking official gave him both access and responsibility—he was in a position to know the conditions in the cistern and to take action.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In Alma 8:7-16, Alma is driven out of Ammonihah by hostile people, yet returns to warn the city of God's judgment. Like Ebed-Melech advocating for Jeremiah, righteous individuals in the Book of Mormon stand with prophets despite widespread rejection. In Alma 34:38-40, Amulek instructs the people to 'cry out in your houses, and your fields, and your closets'; the principle is that the righteous must vocally oppose injustice and unbelief.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 136:31 teaches that 'it is the duty of the Church to instruct all Saints in all things pertaining to the gospel.' Ebed-Melech, though not a member of the covenant people, shows the principle of bearing witness to truth. D&C 58:26-29 instructs that the righteous should 'seek to bring forth and establish the cause of Zion,' standing against injustice. Ebed-Melech's advocacy exemplifies this duty.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The accusation of the nobles' 'evil' and the appeal for justice before the king parallels the concept of accountability before God in the temple—the throne of judgment where all deeds are known and judged. Ebed-Melech's moral appeal invokes Zedekiah's role as judge, prefiguring the universal judgment before God's throne.

commentary.christological_typology: Ebed-Melech's defense of Jeremiah as 'the prophet' whom wicked men have cast down prefigures how Christ, the Prophet (Deuteronomy 18:15), was rejected, condemned, and cast into the grave by the official religious establishment. Like Jeremiah, Christ is condemned by those in power; like Ebed-Melech's appeal, the Father's raising of Christ is an act of justice and vindication. The starvation theme also carries typological weight: Christ's words in John 6:35 ('I am the bread of life') invert the starvation motif—whereas Jeremiah faces death by hunger, Christ offers eternal sustenance. The cistern as a place of death prefigures the tomb; the rescue prefigures resurrection.
commentary.application: Ebed-Melech's speech teaches modern believers how to advocate for justice: (1) Address authority respectfully while maintaining moral clarity. He honors the king while condemning the officials' evil. (2) Name injustice plainly without equivocation or false neutrality. He does not say 'there is a disagreement' but 'these men have done evil.' (3) Restore dignity to the victim by affirming their true identity and status. He calls Jeremiah 'the prophet,' not a criminal or troublemaker. (4) Ground the appeal in shared reality and shared values. He invokes the famine that everyone knows about—a universal condition—to show the particular injustice of Jeremiah's starvation. (5) Create urgency by emphasizing imminent death, not distant consequences. He says Jeremiah will die 'in the place where he is,' not someday. Modern covenant members who must advocate for justice in institutional, professional, or family settings should follow Ebed-Melech's model: respectful but clear, dignified but urgent, rooted in shared facts and shared values.

text_kjv: Then the king commanded Ebedmelech the Ethiopian, saying, Take from hence thirty men with thee, and take up Jeremiah the prophet out of the dungeon, before he die.

commentary.narrative: Ebed-Melech's appeal succeeds. The word 'then' (vayyetzav, literally 'and he commanded') marks the turning point: Zedekiah moves from passive acquiescence to active rescue. The king commands Ebed-Melech to take 'thirty men' and extract Jeremiah from the cistern. The number thirty is significant. On the surface, it may seem excessive for a rescue operation—why would a cistern extraction require thirty men? Possible explanations: (1) the cistern is extremely deep or the mud extremely thick, requiring many hands to pull Jeremiah out safely, (2) the king provides an armed detail to prevent the nobles from interfering with the rescue, or (3) the number itself carries symbolic weight, as 'thirty' appears throughout Scripture in contexts of covenant, judgment, and redemption (thirty pieces of silver for Judas, the thirtieth year of Ezekiel's vision, etc.). The king's phrase 'before he die' (beterem yamut) intensifies the urgency—this is not a leisurely retrieval but a race against imminent death.
commentary.narrative_continued: Critically, the king does not publicly reverse the nobles' decision or apologize for having agreed to Jeremiah's imprisonment. Zedekiah acts, but carefully: he gives a command that can appear to be a prudent preservation of the king's prisoner (after all, a dead prophet is of no use) rather than a repudiation of the nobles' judgment. This reflects Zedekiah's character throughout Jeremiah: he sympathizes with the prophet but lacks the courage to openly defy the pressure group that surrounds him. Ebed-Melech's appeal has moved Zedekiah to do what is right, but the king does so in a way that minimizes confrontation with the nobles. The phrase 'take from hence' (qach be-yadekha mi-zeh) gives Ebed-Melech command over the thirty men ('under your hand/authority'), entrusting the operation entirely to him. This is a sign of trust and confidence—Zedekiah is not sending a supervising official but giving Ebed-Melech full authority.

word_study.meaning: Third person masculine singular past (consecutive) of tzavah, meaning 'to command, to ordain, to charge with instructions.' The consecutive vav indicates this action follows directly from Ebed-Melech's speech.
word_study.significance: The shift from the nobles' pressure on the king (in verses 4-6) to the king now commanding is dramatic. Zedekiah's moral will, however weak, is activated by a righteous appeal. The verb tzavah is often used of God's commands (e.g., 'God commanded Abraham'); Zedekiah's command here, though limited in scope, enacts a microcosm of justice.

word_study.term_original: קַח בְּיָדְךָ מִזֶּה שְׁלֹשִׁים אֲנָשִׁים (Qach be-yadekha mi-zeh shloshim anashim)
word_study.meaning: Literally 'take in your hand from here thirty men.' The phrase be-yadekha ('in your hand,' i.e., 'under your authority/command') grants Ebed-Melech command over the men. The number shloshim (thirty) is precise and specific.
word_study.significance: The phrase be-yadekha emphasizes that Ebed-Melech has been granted executive authority by the king—he is not merely requesting men but is authorized to command them. The Covenant Rendering captures this: 'Take thirty men from here under your authority.'

word_study.meaning: Second person masculine singular perfect of alah, meaning 'to cause to go up, to bring up, to extract.' In this context, it means to pull or hoist out of the cistern.
word_study.significance: The verb alah has connotations of ascent, deliverance, and resurrection in biblical usage (e.g., aliyah, ascent to the temple, or God causing Israel to 'go up' from Egypt). Jeremiah's extraction from the cistern is described with the same verb used for liberation and redemption.

word_study.meaning: Literally 'before he dies'; the word terem ('before that, prior to') introduces a temporal clause. The subjunctive form yamut ('he should/would die') expresses the threat of death that must be prevented.
word_study.significance: The construction creates urgency: death is imminent and must be forestalled. The king is not ordering a leisurely retrieval but a desperate rescue against the approach of death. The phrase echoes the language Ebed-Melech used in his appeal.

cross_references.connection: Obadiah, a righteous official in Ahab's house, uses his position to protect God's prophets (Elijah) from the queen's persecution; similarly, Ebed-Melech uses his position to rescue Jeremiah.
The king commands the hanging of Haman to prevent an injustice; Zedekiah similarly commands action to prevent Jeremiah's death.

Joseph of Arimathea, a member of the council, uses his standing to request the body of Jesus and provide an honorable tomb; a figure of authority acts against prevailing institutional hostility to the prophet.
An angel delivers Alma and Amulek from prison in Ammonihah; both miraculous and human rescue of prophets occurs in the Book of Mormon, paralleling Jeremiah's rescue.
Ahikam son of Shaphan protects Jeremiah from being executed by the people; this establishes a pattern of protection by righteous officials despite popular and noble hostility.

commentary.historical_context: The provision of thirty men by a royal command reflects ancient Near Eastern court procedure. When a king entrusted a sensitive task to a trusted official, providing guards or workers was standard protocol. The number thirty may indicate a military contingent—enough to prevent interference by hostile nobles or to handle a difficult extraction. The urgency of the operation is historically plausible: if Jeremiah had been in the cistern for an extended period (even days), with water/mud conditions and starvation, death could indeed be imminent. Ancient cisterns were often 20-30 feet deep or deeper; extracting a man from such depths would be extremely difficult and dangerous. The ropes and rags mentioned in verse 11-12 were likely necessary equipment. The king's command grants operational authority to Ebed-Melech rather than a senior military officer or prince, suggesting that the nobles are not to be informed or given a role in the rescue—this keeps the operation covert and prevents sabotage.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In Alma 8:14-16, the Lord tells Alma to return to Ammonihah with the command to preach repentance. While the context is different, both passages show that righteous individuals are given divine or lawful authority to accomplish deliverance. In Helaman 5:21, the servants of the Lord are filled with power to escape danger—Ebed-Melech's receipt of authority and thirty men parallels the empowerment given to righteous doers of God's will.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 121:34-36 teaches that 'only by persuasion, by long-suffering, by gentleness and meekness, and by love unfeigned; by kindness, and pure knowledge' can we become effective instruments of God. Ebed-Melech's persuasion has moved Zedekiah to act righteously. Additionally, D&C 41:11 states that the righteous 'shall be filled with joy and gladness'; Ebed-Melech's faithful obedience to conscience brings him to an act of joy—the rescue of the prophet.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The king's command, granting authority to Ebed-Melech to effect deliverance, parallels the bestowal of priesthood power and authority in the temple. The thirty men who assist in the extraction prefigure the collective power of covenant communities united in righteous purpose.

commentary.christological_typology: Zedekiah's command to rescue Jeremiah from the cistern prefigures the Father's command to raise Christ from the grave (Romans 6:9, 'Christ being raised from the dead dieth no more'). The thirty men who assist in the extraction prefigure the angels who attend the resurrection (Matthew 28:1-7). The cistern as a place of death and the command to 'bring up' the prophet from it is a type of resurrection. More broadly, the king's command, though imperfect and given for less-than-perfect motives, still effects justice and deliverance—prefiguring how God's justice and mercy operate through imperfect human instruments to accomplish divine purposes.
commentary.application: This verse teaches that moral conviction, when expressed clearly and respectfully, can move even weak or pressured leaders to do what is right. Zedekiah is not a righteous man; he is weak and vacillating. Yet Ebed-Melech's appeal activates his conscience and his capacity for justice. For modern believers, this suggests: (1) When advocating for justice, address the highest authority with the clearest moral appeal—Ebed-Melech went to the king, not the nobles. (2) Be prepared for leaders to act correctly for mixed or imperfect motives; Zedekiah rescues Jeremiah partly to avoid his death, not out of sudden repentance. (3) Trust that even limited or guarded actions toward justice can be effective; the king's secret command to Ebed-Melech succeeds in the rescue. (4) When given authority by leadership to accomplish a righteous task, act with full confidence and speed—Ebed-Melech does not hesitate or second-guess but moves forward 'under his authority.' In family, institutional, and professional contexts, sometimes we must appeal to leadership to do what is right; this verse teaches that such appeals can succeed and that leaders, even imperfect ones, can be moved to execute justice when the case is clearly made.

text_kjv: So Ebedmelech took the men with him, and went into the house of the king under the treasury, and took thence old cast clouts, and old rotten rags, and let them down by cords into the dungeon to Jeremiah.

commentary.narrative: Verse 11 depicts Ebed-Melech moving from moral appeal to practical action with remarkable efficiency and compassion. He takes the thirty men 'under his command' (as authorized by the king) and enters the royal palace, going to a storage area beneath the treasury. The phrase 'under the treasury' (tachat ha-otsar) indicates a basement or cellar—a place where discarded items were stored. What Ebed-Melech does next is both mundane and profound: he gathers 'worn-out rags and tattered scraps of cloth' (beloyei sechabot u-beloyei melachim). These are not valuable items; they are castoffs, worn beyond use. Yet Ebed-Melech's purpose is urgent: he needs material to protect Jeremiah's body when the ropes lift him from the cistern. This detail reveals Ebed-Melech thinking ahead, anticipating that bare ropes under a weakened man's armpits would cause injury. He is not merely rescuing Jeremiah from death but also preserving his dignity and minimizing his suffering. The care taken in selecting soft materials for a condemned, starving man demonstrates Ebed-Melech's profound compassion. He then 'let[s] them down by cords into the dungeon,' using multiple ropes and the cushioning materials to create a means of extraction.
commentary.narrative_continued: The physicality of this verse is striking. Ebed-Melech is literally descending into the dark infrastructure of the royal palace (the storage area) to find materials for an extramarital rescue of a man his masters want dead. His willingness to touch 'old, rotten rags'—items of minimal value—shows that he does not concern himself with status or cleanliness concerns. He is focused entirely on practical mercy. The verb 'let them down' (vayshlach-hem) suggests care in lowering—not dropping hastily but controlled descent by cords. The Covenant Rendering clarifies: 'lowered them down to Jeremiah in the cistern by ropes.' Each element of the procedure is deliberate. Furthermore, Ebed-Melech has managed to do all this—gather materials, descend into storage, and lower them—without drawing attention or resistance from the hostile nobles. The operation is covert enough to succeed, yet organized enough to be effective.

word_study.meaning: Third person masculine singular past (consecutive) of lakach, meaning 'to take, to seize, to grasp.' The verb indicates firm, purposeful action. Ebed-Melech takes the men immediately; there is no hesitation or committee formation.
word_study.significance: The urgency and decisiveness of Ebed-Melech's action is striking. He does not delay or equivocate but acts immediately upon receiving the king's command. The verb lakach conveys both authority (he takes charge) and dispatch (he does not dawdle).

word_study.term_english: went into the house of the king
word_study.meaning: Third person masculine singular past (consecutive) of bo, meaning 'to enter, to come in.' Literally 'entered the house of the king.' The 'house of the king' (veit ha-melekh) is the royal palace complex.
word_study.significance: Ebed-Melech's access to the royal palace is immediate and unquestioned—he is a high official with regular right of entry. No guard stops him; no delay obstructs him.

word_study.meaning: Literally 'to/under the treasury' (tachat = beneath, under; otsar = treasury, storehouse). The phrase indicates a basement or cellar area, likely a subterranean storage chamber.
word_study.significance: The treasurer's office typically oversaw valuables and supplies for the palace. The chamber beneath it would hold both valuable goods (scrolls, records, precious items) and, logically, worn-out items discarded from daily use. Ebed-Melech's knowledge of this space suggests he is familiar with the palace infrastructure—further evidence of his high status.

word_study.meaning: Literally 'worn-out rags' or 'worn castoff cloths.' The word beloyei means 'worn out, tattered, worn to tatters'; sechabot likely refers to cloth scraps or old garments. The Covenant Rendering renders this as 'worn rags.'
word_study.significance: The specificity of this description—'worn-out' twice (verse 11 uses 'beloyei sechabot u-beloyei melachim') emphasizes that these are not fine linens or valuable cloth but discarded materials. Yet their worn, soft texture makes them ideal for protecting bare skin under rope. Ebed-Melech's solution is resourceful: he uses what is at hand, what no one values, to serve his purpose of mercy.

word_study.meaning: Literally 'worn-out pieces' or 'tattered scraps.' The word melachim may derive from a root meaning 'to wear away' or 'to rend.' The term emphasizes deterioration and uselessness.
word_study.significance: The repetition of 'worn-out' (beloyei) twice in this verse emphasizes that Ebed-Melech is using the most humble, discarded materials. Yet these materials, despised in themselves, become instruments of salvation for the prophet.

word_study.meaning: Third person masculine singular past (consecutive) of shalach, meaning 'to send, to let down, to lower.' In this context, it indicates controlled descent by rope.
word_study.significance: The verb shalach suggests care and intentionality rather than mere dropping. Ebed-Melech is not throwing the materials down but lowering them deliberately, perhaps with the help of the thirty men.

word_study.meaning: Plural of chabel, meaning 'rope, cord, rope.' The plural indicates multiple ropes used for the operation.
word_study.significance: The use of multiple cords suggests a sophisticated rescue procedure—probably requiring pulleys or mechanical advantage to lift a man from a deep pit. The materials are already in place for extraction; Ebed-Melech's operation is coordinated and well-planned.

cross_references.connection: Jesus commends the righteous who clothed the naked, visited the prisoner, and helped the hungry; Ebed-Melech's actions prefigure these acts of mercy—he provides clothing (rags) and attends to a prisoner's suffering.
Teaches that every person has been given gifts to use for one another; Ebed-Melech's gifts of compassion and practical intelligence are deployed to save a life.
States that 'he that hath pity upon the poor lendeth unto the LORD'; Ebed-Melech's mercy toward the prophet, who is poor and suffering, is counted as mercy toward God.
Alma, though persecuted and driven from Ammonihah, is comforted by an angel and empowered to return; likewise, Jeremiah, though cast down, is lifted up by Ebed-Melech's faithfulness.
Teaches that charity 'suffereth long, and is kind, and envieth not, and is not puffed up, seeketh not her own'; Ebed-Melech's gathering of rags for a stranger's comfort exemplifies this charity.

commentary.historical_context: The storage of worn-out palace materials in a basement chamber is historically plausible. Ancient palaces generated continuous amounts of discarded textiles, broken tools, and refuse. Systematic storage of such items was practical. The use of ropes and pulleys for extracting objects or persons from deep pits is attested in ancient Near Eastern art and literature. Egyptian tomb paintings show scenes of workers using ropes and pulleys to move heavy objects; similar technology would have been used in rescue operations. The depth and diameter of ancient cisterns varied; many were 20-30 feet deep. Extracting a man from such depths, especially if he were weak, injured, or stuck in mud, would indeed require multiple men and careful procedure. The use of padding under ropes reflects practical knowledge of the dangers of rope friction on skin—a reality known to anyone who has handled ship ropes or heavy loads. Ebed-Melech's familiarity with the palace infrastructure and his access to these materials without question confirms his high status and the trust placed in him by the royal household.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In Mosiah 11:26-27, King Limhi helps his people escape from the Lamanites through a narrow pass—an act requiring practical knowledge and careful leadership. In Helaman 5:17-20, Nephi and Lehi call upon God and are surrounded by fire that protects them; while supernatural, the passage illustrates the principle that God delivers His servants through both natural and miraculous means. Ebed-Melech's rescue of Jeremiah through natural, practical means parallels how God works through His servants to accomplish deliverance.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 64:33 teaches that we should 'lift up [our] hearts and rejoice' and 'be not afraid' because the Lord will 'go before [us]' and shall 'fight [our] battles'; Ebed-Melech's confidence in proceeding with the rescue reflects a quiet faith that God's work will prosper. Additionally, D&C 42:31 instructs the Saints to 'impart of your substance unto the poor, every man according to that which he hath,' and Ebed-Melech uses his resources (his position, knowledge, the materials at hand) to save a life.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The descent into the palace basement to retrieve humble materials for a sacred purpose parallels the temple's descent through veils and chambers to the center. Ebed-Melech's willingness to work with materials others have discarded—worn rags—reflects the temple principle that all things, however humble, can be consecrated to sacred purpose. The lifting up of Jeremiah from the cistern mirrors the ascent through temple ordinances toward exaltation.

commentary.christological_typology: Ebed-Melech's gathering of worn, humble materials to cushion and protect Jeremiah prefigures how Christ, the son of God, 'emptied himself' (Philippians 2:7) and took on humble form to lift humanity from the pit of death and separation from God. The rags, despised in themselves but made useful for mercy, are types of Christ's humanity—seemingly ordinary, yet the instrument of salvation. The descent into a cellar to retrieve materials for rescue prefigures Christ's descent into hell/Sheol (1 Peter 3:19) to rescue the faithful dead. More broadly, Jeremiah's entombment in the cistern and his lifting up by another's hands is a type of resurrection through another's power—Christ's resurrection accomplished by the Father's power, not by Christ's own will (John 10:17-18).
commentary.application: Verse 11 teaches that practical mercy requires both foresight and humility. Ebed-Melech does not simply begin pulling on ropes but thinks through the consequences: rough ropes would harm a weakened man. So he goes to the effort of gathering padding. For modern believers, this suggests: (1) When helping those in distress, think ahead about unintended harm and how to mitigate it. A rescue is not complete if the process of rescue causes additional suffering. (2) Use what is at hand, however humble or despised. Ebed-Melech does not demand that fine linens be brought from storage; he uses old rags, which are actually more suitable for his purpose (soft, flexible, disposable). (3) Accept that mercy often requires us to touch things others consider 'dirty' or unworthy. Ebed-Melech handles 'old, rotten rags' without apparent disgust. In caring for the sick, poor, or marginalized, we may be required to work with things others avoid. (4) Coordinate practical action with decisiveness. Ebed-Melech does not overthink or hesitate; he gathers what is needed and executes the plan. In family, professional, and ecclesiastical contexts, we are often called to show mercy in practical ways that require forethought, humility, and swift action.

text_kjv: And Ebedmelech the Ethiopian said unto Jeremiah, Put now these old cast clouts and rotten rags under thine armholes under the cords. And Jeremiah did so.

commentary.narrative: The final verse of this rescue narrative crystallizes the themes of compassion, cooperation, and deliverance. Ebed-Melech, hovering above the cistern with the ropes and materials in hand, gives a specific instruction to Jeremiah below. He does not merely drop the materials or shout commands; he explains clearly what Jeremiah must do: 'Put the worn rags and scraps of cloth under your arms, beneath the ropes.' The phrase 'under thine armholes' (tachat atsilot yadekha, literally 'beneath the hollows of your arms') shows that Ebed-Melech has considered the anatomy of extraction—the armpits are where a human body naturally supports weight. Without padding, the rough ropes would cut into bare skin and cause injury to an already weakened man. Ebed-Melech's instruction is not a barked command but a piece of practical wisdom, almost a gift of knowledge alongside the material gift of rags. The response, 'And Jeremiah did so' (vayyaas Yirmeyahu ken), is profoundly simple. After weeks of imprisonment, starvation, and abandonment, Jeremiah trusts Ebed-Melech and obeys his instruction immediately and completely. There is no hesitation, no suspicion, no refusal. Jeremiah does exactly what the foreigner tells him to do, and in that act of trust, he becomes the agent of his own deliverance.
commentary.narrative_continued: This verse shows the cooperation of rescuer and rescued in a moment of ultimate vulnerability. Jeremiah cannot save himself; he depends on Ebed-Melech's strength and knowledge. Yet Jeremiah also plays an active role—he must position himself correctly, must place the rags precisely, must prepare himself for the lifting. There is no passivity here on either side, but rather a choreography of trust and cooperation. The simplicity of the closing phrase ('And Jeremiah did so') belies its profundity. After chapters of Jeremiah being manipulated by kings and nobles, interrogated and mistrusted, it is a radical simplicity that he trusts the foreigner. The Covenant Rendering captures this perfectly: 'Ebed-Melech the Cushite called down to Jeremiah, "Put the worn rags and scraps of cloth under your arms, beneath the ropes." And Jeremiah did so.' The word 'called down' suggests that Ebed-Melech is speaking from above, from daylight, to Jeremiah below in darkness—a spatial metaphor for the movement from death to life that is about to occur.

word_study.term_original: וַיֹּאמֶר עֶבֶד מֶלֶךְ הַכּוּשִׁי אֶל־יִרְמְיָהוּ (Va-yomer Eved-Melekh ha-Kushi el-Yirmeyahu)
word_study.meaning: Third person masculine singular past (consecutive) of amar, meaning 'to say, to speak.' The construction 'said unto' (vayyomer el) indicates direct address.
word_study.significance: The verb amar is used for all forms of human speech in biblical Hebrew, but in this context, it is intimate and personal communication between rescuer and rescued. Ebed-Melech speaks directly to Jeremiah, not about him or for him, but to him.

word_study.meaning: Imperative of sim (to put, to place) with the particle na, which is a polite, almost pleading marker. Literally 'put, please' or 'put now, I pray.' The particle na softens the command, making it a request.
word_study.significance: Despite Ebed-Melech's authority, he addresses Jeremiah with courtesy and respect. He does not command harshly but makes a respectful request. This is remarkable: Ebed-Melech is in the position of rescuer and has authority over the operation, yet he treats Jeremiah with deference. The particle na reflects a deep respect for Jeremiah's autonomy and dignity, even in his helplessness.

word_study.meaning: Literally 'beneath the hollows/cavities of your hands' or 'under the armpits.' The word atsilot refers to the hollow spaces of the body, specifically the armpits where arms connect to the torso. Yadekha is 'your hands' (possessive form), though in this context it refers to the arm/shoulder area.
word_study.significance: This is anatomically precise. Ebed-Melech knows that the armpits are the natural point of weight distribution when a person is lifted by rope. By instructing Jeremiah to place padding there, he is ensuring that the extraction will be as painless as possible. This shows both knowledge and care—Ebed-Melech is not simply conducting a mechanical rescue but is thinking about Jeremiah's comfort and safety.

word_study.meaning: Literally 'from beneath the ropes' or 'under the ropes.' The phrase clarifies that the padding goes between Jeremiah's body and the ropes, not above them.
word_study.significance: The instruction is precise and practical. The rags must be positioned to serve as a barrier between the rope and skin. This instruction ensures that Jeremiah understands exactly what is needed and in what sequence it must happen.

word_study.meaning: Third person masculine singular past (consecutive) of asah, meaning 'to do, to make, to act,' with the adverb ken meaning 'thus, so, in this manner.' Literally 'and Jeremiah did thus/in this way.'
word_study.significance: The simplicity of this verb and its object conveys absolute obedience and trust. Jeremiah does not question, does not hesitate, does not negotiate. He does exactly what Ebed-Melech instructs. This single sentence encapsulates the transformation from despair to hope, from abandonment to rescue, from isolation to connection with another human being.

cross_references.connection: When Jesus calls Lazarus from the tomb, Lazarus 'came forth, bound hand and foot with graveclothes'; similarly, Jeremiah emerges from the cistern with rags and ropes—grave-clothes that become instruments of resurrection.

States that 'faith cometh by hearing, and hearing by the word of God'; Jeremiah's trust in Ebed-Melech is activated by hearing his voice and instructions from above—a microcosm of faith in response to God's word.

Alma speaks of 'calling upon his holy name day and night' and receiving deliverance; Jeremiah's rescue through Ebed-Melech's voice parallels how the righteous are delivered through God's voice speaking through His servants.
Jesus teaches that those who take upon them His name must keep His commandments; Jeremiah takes upon himself the risk of trusting Ebed-Melech and, in obedience, is lifted to safety.

Teaches that we should 'be clothed with humility,' for God 'resisteth the proud, but giveth grace unto the humble'; Jeremiah's act of humility—following the foreigner's instruction without pride or resistance—opens the way for his deliverance.

commentary.historical_context: The instruction to pad the armpits reflects practical knowledge of the dangers of rope burn and pressure injury. Anyone who has handled heavy ropes knows that bare skin under tension is subject to severe abrasion and bruising. For a man who has been starving and weakened in a cistern, such injury could be life-threatening (opening wounds to infection during a period without medical care). Ebed-Melech's attention to this detail shows both technical knowledge and compassion. The act of Jeremiah obeying immediately reflects trust that would have been earned through reputation or previous relationship. There is no indication that Jeremiah and Ebed-Melech had met before, yet Jeremiah trusts him. This may reflect the reputation of Ebed-Melech among the palace staff as a person of integrity and good will, or it may reflect Jeremiah's spiritual insight into character. The simplicity of the final phrase also reflects the brevity with which ancient texts often recorded the resolution of crisis—once the key decision has been made and agreed upon, the narrative moves forward with dispatch.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In Alma 34:32-35, Amulek teaches that in this life is the time to prepare to meet God, and to 'cry unto [the Lord] with faith' in all circumstances. Jeremiah's trust in Ebed-Melech, despite his desperation, mirrors the principle that the righteous should trust in God's servants and instruments of deliverance. In 2 Nephi 31:19-20, Nephi teaches that we must 'endure to the end' and 'press forward with a steadfastness in Christ'; Jeremiah's obedience in the moment of rescue exemplifies this steadfastness.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 19:38-41 teaches that if we 'repent and keep [the Lord's] commandments, and search these commandments, ye shall find that they are all true,' and that 'He that hath light, and receiveth not light, is condemned by the light.' Jeremiah receives light (Ebed-Melech's instruction) and acts upon it immediately, thus positioning himself for rescue. Additionally, D&C 29:34 teaches that the Lord 'maketh all things manifest unto [His] servants'; Ebed-Melech's practical wisdom in instructing Jeremiah shows the principle that God's servants are given knowledge needed to accomplish righteous purposes.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The position of Jeremiah with rags and ropes, being lifted from darkness to light, from pit to daylight, mirrors the temple's movement from outer courts toward the center of light and presence. The rags become sacred garments for this transition. The moment of trust and obedience in response to a voice from above prefigures the covenant principles by which we advance through temple ordinances—listening, trusting, obeying the voice of one called to guide us.

commentary.christological_typology: Jeremiah, bound in grave-clothes (rags) and ropes, lifted from the pit by the voice and hands of another, is a powerful type of Christ's resurrection. Just as Jeremiah cannot resurrect himself but depends entirely on Ebed-Melech's strength, Christ's resurrection is accomplished by the power of the Father (John 10:17-18), not by His own power alone. The instruction to 'put the rags under your arms' prefigures the grave-clothes that Jesus leaves behind in the tomb (John 20:6-7)—items that facilitated entombment but are left behind at resurrection. Ebed-Melech's voice calling down to Jeremiah from above is a type of the Father's voice calling forth the dead (John 5:25, 'The dead shall hear the voice of the Son of God'). The foreigner who rescues the prophet, despised by his own nation, prefigures how Christ, rejected by His own people, becomes the agent of universal salvation. Most profoundly, the narrative teaches that resurrection is not a solitary act but a communal one: Jeremiah needs thirty men, ropes, rags, and Ebed-Melech's knowledge and compassion. Similarly, Christ's resurrection inaugurates a covenant community and a resurrection of all who believe—his rising from the dead prefigures the resurrection of all His people.
commentary.application: Verse 12 offers practical and spiritual applications for modern believers: (1) When receiving help or instruction from someone rescuing us from difficulty, listen carefully and obey completely. Jeremiah's trust in Ebed-Melech's specific instruction—rather than trying to extract himself or ignoring the details—results in his successful rescue. In family counseling, medical treatment, spiritual guidance, or professional coaching, precise obedience to clear instruction is often the pathway to healing. (2) Recognize that receiving help requires vulnerability and trust. Jeremiah must place himself in a position where he is entirely dependent on another human being. There is a lesson here about accepting help graciously and without pride—which is often the hardest work. (3) Understand that a rescue is successful when both the rescuer and the rescued cooperate. Jeremiah's 'doing so' is essential; he is not a passive object being extracted but an active participant in his own deliverance. In our spiritual life, God works through our agency and cooperation; we are not passively saved but actively participate in our own salvation through faith and obedience. (4) Honor those who extend mercy, especially those who do so at personal risk or cost. Ebed-Melech has acted despite danger; Jeremiah's immediate obedience honors that sacrifice. In our relationships, we should show respect and gratitude to those who help us, especially when they do so despite social pressure or institutional opposition.

text_kjv: So they drew up Jeremiah with cords, and took him up out of the dungeon: and Jeremiah remained in the court of the prison.

commentary.narrative: After Ebed-melech's dangerous intercession with the king, the rescue is executed with understated efficiency. The verb choices in the Hebrew—vayyimshekhu ('they pulled') and vayyaalu ('they brought up')—create a sense of purposeful extraction without dramatization. This mirrors the stark realism of the prophet's actual predicament: he is not freed from custody but merely relocated to less lethal confinement. The court of the guard (chatsar ha-mattarah) represents the same relatively favorable condition Jeremiah occupied earlier (37:21), where he had access to daily bread and could receive visitors.
commentary.narrative_continued: The cistern from which Jeremiah is pulled was a place of slow death—mud, exposure, and starvation. His removal from it is not liberation but rather a reprieve, a return to a more survivable form of imprisonment. This distinction matters: Zedekiah does not have the courage to release the prophet entirely, only to spare him from execution. The language of extraction—pulling him up with ropes—emphasizes both the physical effort required and the prophet's utter dependence on others for survival. Jeremiah cannot climb out; he must be lifted. This physical reality becomes a metaphor for his entire predicament: unable to save himself, reliant on divine providence and human mercy.
commentary.narrative_continued_2: The brevity of this verse's description of the actual rescue contrasts sharply with the detailed setup (the debate among the officials, Ebed-melech's careful preparation, the collection of rags and worn clothes). The narrative structure communicates something theologically significant: the moment of rescue is not the point of the story. The point is the conflict, the intercession, the king's capitulation, and the return to uncertain captivity. Jeremiah is 'remained' (vayyeshev—literally 'sat' or 'dwelt') in the court, a word suggesting stability after turbulence, though stability of a severely constrained kind.

word_study.meaning: Third masculine plural qal imperfect of meshakh—'to draw, pull, drag.' The verb suggests forceful, sustained action. In contexts of rescue or extraction, it emphasizes the effort required to move something or someone against resistance or gravity.
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering's choice of 'pulled' captures the physical strain. This is not a gentle lifting but a deliberate extraction. The verb recalls earlier uses in Jeremiah where meshakh describes the consequences of rebellion (22:3, 29:22)—here it is repurposed for rescue, suggesting divine reversal of calamity.

word_study.term_english: took him up / lifted him out
word_study.meaning: Third masculine plural qal imperfect of alah—'to go up, ascend, bring up.' Alah often carries connotations of elevation, ascent toward the sacred, or movement out of a lower condition. In this rescue context, it is literally movement upward from the cistern.
word_study.significance: The double verb (pulled and brought up) emphasizes completion: the extraction is not partial. The verb alah connects to themes of ascent throughout Jeremiah—the ascent of the Chaldeans, the ascent of the Lord's word. Here it marks Jeremiah's ascent from death to a conditional survival.

word_study.term_english: court of the prison / court of the guard
word_study.meaning: Chatsar = 'court, courtyard, enclosure.' Mattarah = 'guard, watch, custody.' The phrase denotes the open courtyard area of a military prison or guardhouse, an intermediate space between total confinement and freedom.
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering's 'court of the guard' clarifies the institutional setting. This is not a dungeon but a guarded yard—visible light, air, potentially contact with other prisoners or sympathetic guards like Ebed-melech. The improvement from the cistern is literal and psychological, yet the word 'court' echoes repeatedly in Jeremiah's confinement narrative, reinforcing that he remains a prisoner regardless of location.

cross_references.connection: Jeremiah is previously assigned to the court of the guard, where he receives daily bread. This verse establishes it as the relatively favorable confinement to which he is returned after his rescue from the cistern.

The dungeon (cistern) into which Jeremiah was cast is described as containing no water but mud. His removal from it fulfills the conditional rescue threatened in the earlier confrontation with the officials.

The 'court' (chatsar) language in temple and palace architecture. Jeremiah's confinement to a 'court' reflects the restricted but semi-public spaces of official buildings, neither fully private nor openly accessible.
Though Jeremiah's earthly protectors are weak, the psalmist's declaration that the LORD will take him up resonates with themes of divine rescue and sustenance during persecution.

commentary.historical_context: Cistern imprisonment was a method of slow execution in the ancient Near East—distinct from dungeon confinement in that it relied on exposure, starvation, and the weight of one's own body sinking into mud. Archaeological evidence from ancient Judah shows cisterns repurposed as prisons, their shaft-like construction making escape impossible without external aid. The 'court of the guard' (chatsar ha-mattarah) was likely a military compound attached to the royal palace or garrison, where prisoners of political or religious significance were held under observation rather than locked away. The Babylonian siege of Jerusalem (586 BCE) created a security state where the king's grip on power was tenuous; Jeremiah's imprisonment in successive locations reflects the political volatility of these final months.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The principle of rescue through the faithfulness of others parallels Alma 26:27, where Alma describes how God preserved the sons of Mosiah through trials. Like Ebed-melech's courageous intercession, the Book of Mormon repeatedly illustrates that divine rescue often works through human instruments willing to act on behalf of the persecuted.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 121:7-8 addresses the suffering of the Lord's servants in prison and bonds: 'And none of these iniquities shall be upon thy head, if thou art found spotless, pure, and white.' Jeremiah's rescue from one prison to another, though not complete deliverance, operates within the principle that the righteous are sustained even when not fully delivered from trial.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The court of the guard, like the temple court (mentioned prominently in verse 14), represents a semi-sacred space—a place where order and institutional authority govern movement. Jeremiah remains confined within structured space, unable to access full freedom, a condition that mirrors aspects of mortal existence itself where souls are confined in bodies and bound by covenants.

commentary.christological_typology: Jeremiah's extraction from the cistern prefigures Christ's resurrection—a lifting up from depths, an ascent from conditions of death into restored relationship and renewed mission. The dependence on others for rescue and the transition from death-like confinement to functional (if restricted) life point to Christ's resurrection as the ultimate rescue and restoration. Like Jeremiah remaining in the court of the guard, the risen Christ appears within constraints (post-resurrection appearances) while possessing freedom.
commentary.application: For modern covenant members, this verse teaches the reality that deliverance from trial is often partial and gradual rather than complete or instantaneous. Ebed-melech's rescue of Jeremiah illustrates a key principle: divine deliverance frequently works through the courageous faithfulness of others. We are called to be instruments of rescue for those in spiritual and practical need, even when full liberation is not immediately possible. Second, the court of the guard reminds us that survival itself—continuation of life, opportunity to speak truth, maintenance of witness—can be a form of victory when complete freedom is denied. Third, the emphasis on Jeremiah being pulled up, unable to save himself, confronts us with our own spiritual helplessness and the necessity of relying on powers beyond ourselves.

text_kjv: Then Zedekiah the king sent, and took Jeremiah the prophet unto him into the third entry that is in the house of the LORD: and the king said unto Jeremiah, I will ask thee a thing; hide nothing from me.

commentary.narrative: Zedekiah's rescue of Jeremiah from the cistern (via Ebed-melech's intervention) is immediately followed by a clandestine summons. The king sends for the prophet and brings him not to the palace but to the third entrance of the temple—a detail that appears nowhere else in scripture and thus has puzzled interpreters. This choice of venue is deliberate and revealing: Zedekiah seeks sacred ground, perhaps hoping that the temple setting will lend authority to his inquiry or invoke divine favor for his desperate consultation. The selection of a restricted architectural entry (mavo ha-shelishi, 'third entrance') indicates a desire for privacy and security, away from the court officials who have repeatedly acted against Jeremiah.
commentary.narrative_continued: The king's demand—'I will ask thee a thing; hide nothing from me'—echoes his earlier private consultation with Jeremiah in 37:17. But the escalation is evident: he now uses the emphatic verb kachad ('to hide, conceal') with a negative imperative, demanding complete transparency. The phrase al tekhached mimmenni davar ('do not conceal anything from me') is absolute and somewhat threatening in tone. Zedekiah recognizes that Jeremiah has consistently told him unwelcome truths, yet he desperately wants to hear the prophet's word—but only if it is truthful. The king stands at a threshold of decision regarding the Babylonian siege, and his oscillation between listening to Jeremiah and heeding his court officials has left him spiritually exhausted.
commentary.narrative_continued_2: What makes this scene theologically acute is that Zedekiah is meeting the prophet in the Lord's house while simultaneously resisting the Lord's word. The irony is performative: by choosing the temple, Zedekiah implicitly invokes the God whose counsel he will ultimately reject. The prophet Jeremiah is now in the position of being asked for truth while facing the reality that truth-telling has already nearly cost him his life. The third entry itself remains architecturally mysterious—we do not know its function or its relationship to the main temple spaces, only that it was known well enough to Zedekiah to serve as a meeting place.

word_study.term_original: וַיִּשְׁלַח הַמֶּלֶךְ צִדְקִיָּהוּ וַיִּקַּח אֶת־יִרְמְיָהוּ (wayyishlach ha-melekh Zidqiyahu wayyiqqach et-Yirmeyahu)
